extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a phase 2a pediatric trial for MIS-C (a severe PASC/Long COVID phenotype in children), not adult Long COVID per se. Most quantitative outcome data presented in figures only (no table with means/SDs for continuous outcomes). Per-arm means and SDs for PedsQL GI scores and spike antigen concentrations are not reported as numbers in text — data only in figures. CRP at baseline: larazotide mean 144 (SD 96) mg/liter; placebo mean 178 (SD 68) mg/liter — verbatim from Table 1. Win ratio reported as 2.38 (95% CI 1.04-5.43, p=0.04). Spearman correlations reported: IFNgamma vs spike antigen r=0.37, p=0.004; IL-6 vs spike antigen r=0.67, p<0.001; GI symptoms vs spike antigen r=-0.5, p=0.003. Fisher's exact p-values for GI recovery at day 7 and day 14 stated as p<0.001. Irritability continuous comparison by t-test p=0.01 also reported. Outcomes 7, 8, 9 (cytokines, antibodies) have no per-arm quantitative data in text — data only in figures. The effect_measure for binary Fisher's exact comparisons is listed as odds_ratio as a placeholder since no OR was explicitly calculated; the paper reports only p-values from Fisher's exact test without effect sizes. n_analyzed for spike antigen outcomes refers to the subset with spike antigen detected at enrollment (5 larazotide, 3-4 placebo).

summary: This phase 2a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested larazotide — an oral drug that blocks zonulin receptors to strengthen the gut barrier — as an add-on therapy in 12 children (median age 5.7 years) hospitalized with multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C), a severe post-COVID condition. Children receiving larazotide (n=6) showed faster clearance of circulating SARS-CoV-2 spike protein antigen compared to placebo (n=6), with all 5 antigen-positive larazotide patients clearing antigen by day 21 versus only 2 of 4 antigen-positive placebo patients, and a significantly greater proportion achieving clearance at days 7, 14, and 21 (p=0.002, p<0.001, p<0.0001 respectively). Larazotide-treated children also recovered gastrointestinal symptoms faster (significantly more recovery at days 7 and 14, p<0.001) and returned to usual activities more quickly through 6-month follow-up (p=0.03). The trial enrolled only 12 of a planned 20 participants due to declining MIS-C cases, making the small sample size the primary caveat; no drug-related adverse events were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Win ratio analysis across all primary outcomes (spike antigen clearance, return to usual health/activities, PedsQL score) yielded a win ratio of 2.38 (p=0.04, 95% CI 1.04–5.43) for larazotide vs placebo; spike antigen clearance significantly greater at day 21 (p<0.0001), but N=12 total.

summary: The REGAIN trial tested an eight-week online group rehabilitation programme — combining weekly supervised home-based exercise and psychological support sessions — against usual care (a single advice session) in 585 adults who had been hospitalised with COVID-19 and reported lasting symptoms at least three months after discharge. The primary outcome, health-related quality of life measured by the PROMIS preference score, improved significantly in the intervention group at both three months (adjusted mean difference 0.03, 95% CI 0.01–0.05, p=0.02) and 12 months (0.03, 95% CI 0.01–0.06, p=0.02), driven mainly by improvements in fatigue, depression, and pain. summary: The Listen trial tested a personalised self-management support intervention — up to six one-to-one sessions with trained healthcare practitioners plus a co-designed handbook — in 554 adults with long COVID who had not been hospitalised during their acute COVID-19 illness, recruited across 24 sites in England and Wales. The primary outcome, capacity for routine daily activities (Ox-PAQ routine activities scale), showed a small non-significant improvement in the intervention group compared to usual NHS care (adjusted mean difference −2.68 points, 95% CI −5.38 to 0.02, p=0.052), falling well below the pre-specified minimum important difference of 7.51 points. Secondary outcomes showed statistically significant improvements in fatigue (fatigue impact score −7.93, p<0.001), emotional wellbeing (Ox-PAQ emotional wellbeing −5.29, p=0.001), mental health (SF-12 mental component +2.36, p=0.004), and self-efficacy (+2.63, p<0.001), though physical health and social engagement were unchanged; no intervention-related serious adverse events were reported.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested a 16-week home-based exercise training (HBET) programme — three sessions per week of aerobic and strength exercise, semi-supervised via video calls — in 50 adults who had survived severe or critical COVID-19 and been discharged from ICU roughly five months earlier. The primary outcome, the physical component summary of the SF-36 quality-of-life questionnaire, was significantly higher in the exercise group than the control group after 16 weeks (mean difference 16.8 points, 95% CI 5.8–27.9, effect size 0.74). The exercise group also improved lower-limb functional capacity (30-second sit-to-stand: +2.38 repetitions) and had significantly lower rates of persistent muscle weakness (5% vs 35%) and myalgia (19% vs 55%); no adverse events related to the intervention were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome SF-36 physical component summary: EMD 16.8 points (95% CI 5.8 to 27.9, p<0.001, ES 0.74) in favour of HBET vs control.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II trial tested 10 sessions of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) — 100% oxygen at 2.4 atmospheres for 90 minutes — versus sham treatment in 80 previously healthy adults aged 18–60 with long COVID at a single Swedish university hospital. The primary outcomes were changes in RAND-36 physical functioning (PF) and role limitations due to physical health (RP) at 13 weeks; neither differed significantly between groups (PF: least square mean difference 0.63, 95% CI −7.04 to 8.29, p=0.87; RP: 2.35, 95% CI −5.95 to 10.66, p=0.57), with both groups improving similarly. An exploratory finding at 52 weeks showed a statistically significant advantage for HBOT in the proportion of patients achieving a clinically meaningful improvement in physical functioning (65.8% vs 40.6%, p=0.033), and the safety profile was broadly comparable between arms, though 49% of HBOT participants had adverse events probably related to treatment versus 24% on placebo.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcomes not statistically significant: PF LSD 0.63 (95% CI −7.04 to 8.29, p=0.87); RP LSD 2.35 (95% CI −5.95 to 10.66, p=0.57).

summary: The PuRe-COVID trial tested a 12-week stepwise pulmonary rehabilitation programme delivered one-on-one by primary care physiotherapists in 76 Belgian adults with long COVID experiencing fatigue and/or respiratory symptoms. The programme included endurance training, strength training, breathing exercises, and inspiratory muscle training across five progressive phases. Patients in the rehabilitation group walked 39 metres further on the 6-minute walk test at 12 weeks compared to controls (95% CI 18–59 m, p<0.001), and also showed greater reductions in fatigue (CIS-fatigue -6 points, p=0.011) and dyspnoea. The trial was stopped before reaching its target of 134 participants (only 76 enrolled), so findings should be interpreted as preliminary; four patients experienced post-exertional malaise during the programme but none withdrew because of it.

summary: The RECOVE trial tested an 8-week supervised concurrent training program (combined resistance and endurance exercise), inspiratory muscle training, or both, versus WHO self-management recommendations in 80 non-hospitalised adults with long COVID lasting over 12 weeks. The primary outcome was estimated VO2max: no statistically significant differences between groups were found, though the concurrent training groups achieved individual within-group improvements of approximately 7.5–7.8% (effect sizes 0.28–0.36). Concurrent training with or without inspiratory muscle training significantly outperformed the other groups on lower-body strength (14.5–32.6% improvement, ES 0.27–1.13), fatigue, and depression scores, and no adverse events occurred during any training session.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2max showed no significant between-group differences (P > 0.05); within-group improvements in CT and CTRM were 7.5% and 7.8% respectively (ES 0.28 and 0.36) but did not reach statistical significance versus comparators.

summary: This randomized sham-controlled trial tested transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) — 30 minutes daily for 20 days at 10 Hz — versus inactive sham stimulation in 42 adults aged 18–45 with post-COVID fatigue lasting at least 12 weeks. Both groups showed statistically significant reductions in fatigue severity (Fatigue Severity Scale), but the sham group improved more than the active taVNS group after treatment (mean FSS 4.79 vs 5.05, p=0.034 between groups favoring sham), with only small effect sizes (Cohen's d ≈ −0.19). taVNS did produce autonomic changes consistent with increased parasympathetic activity (decreased SNS index, decreased LF/HF ratio), but the study was likely underpowered and one co-author is a co-founder of the company that manufactured the stimulation device.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary fatigue outcome (FSS) after treatment: sham taVNS mean 4.79 vs taVNS mean 5.05; between-group difference p=0.034 favoring sham, Cohen's d = −0.190 (small effect against active treatment).

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested two yogic breathing techniques — Bhramari Pranayama (humming breath) and Sheetali Pranayama (cooling breath) — practiced for 30 minutes daily over 6 months in 90 post-COVID patients aged 19–40. Both techniques significantly improved lung function: forced vital capacity (FVC) increased by approximately 0.5 L in the Bhramari group and 0.4 L in the Sheetali group compared to controls, with FEV1 improving by 0.3 L in both groups. Heart rate variability also improved, with RMSSD rising by 5.5 ms in the Bhramari group and 4.8 ms in the Sheetali group, indicating enhanced parasympathetic nervous system activity. The study was single-centre with a small sample per arm (28–30 participants), limiting generalisability.

trial_rating.result_basis: FVC improved by mean difference 0.5 L (Bhramari, P<.04) and 0.4 L (Sheetali, P<.04) vs control; RMSSD improved by 5.5 ms (Bhramari, P<.01) and 4.8 ms (Sheetali, P<.02) vs control.

summary: This Tunisian single-centre study tested a 6-week supervised respiratory muscle training programme (twice weekly, including chest physiotherapy, diaphragmatic training, breathing and cough exercises) in 30 patients with persistent symptoms one month after hospitalisation for moderate-to-severe COVID-19 pneumonia, compared to 12 matched controls who received no intervention. summary: This study tested 6 weeks of inspiratory muscle training (IMT) using a pressure-threshold device versus sham training in 18 long COVID patients (9 per arm) who had persistent exertional breathlessness and confirmed diaphragm muscle weakness approximately 31 months after hospitalization for COVID-19. The primary outcome — inspiratory muscle endurance (time to task failure) — improved significantly in the IMT group compared to sham (median 365s at baseline vs 983s post-training, p=0.05), and exertional dyspnea scores (Borg scale) also improved (7 to 6, p=0.03), with benefits persisting 6 weeks after training ended. The trial was very small (9 per arm), largely open-label, and powered for within-group rather than between-group differences, limiting the strength of conclusions.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested the ReCOVery APP — a multidisciplinary telerehabilitation mobile application covering diet, sleep, physical exercise, breathing, cognitive training, and community participation — in 100 adults with long COVID (average 16 months post-infection, average 16 persistent symptoms) in Spain. Participants in the intervention group received usual primary care plus APP access and three motivational sessions over 6 months; controls received usual care only. The APP did not significantly improve the primary outcome of quality of life (SF-36 physical health T2-T0: +5.33 intervention vs +7.50 control, p=0.541; SF-36 mental health T2-T0: +14.48 vs +11.87, p=0.559). A key limitation was very poor adherence: only 13% of intervention participants used the app at a level defined as significant, and 62% stopped using it after the first 3 months.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome SF-36 physical health change (T2-T0): intervention +5.33 vs control +7.50, p=0.541, CI -9.16 to 4.84; SF-36 mental health change: +14.48 vs +11.87, p=0.559, CI -6.25 to 11.48 — neither significant.

summary: RegeneCyte (human umbilical cord blood containing stem cells, monocytes, and lymphocytes) was tested in a phase IIa randomized, single-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 30 long COVID patients aged 18-65 with persistent fatigue for 6-18 months. Participants received three intravenous doses every three weeks; preliminary results from the first 15 subjects show that at 12 weeks, 90% of treated patients were classified as non-fatigued on the Chalder Fatigue Scale versus 0% in the placebo group, with 80% of treated patients reaching normal physical fatigue levels versus 0% on placebo. The primary outcome of this paper is subjective state fatigue (VAS slopes); the trial's primary outcome (trait fatigue measured by questionnaires) was reported in a companion paper (Mischke & Zaehle, Brain Stimulation, 2025). The gamified Go/No-Go task was not pre-registered. P50 analysis had reduced n (verum n=19, sham n=16 at pre/post; verum n=18, sham n=15 at follow-up) due to 5 exclusions. The occipital alpha interaction (stimulation x assessment) was significant at F(2,74.45)=4.18, p=0.020, partial eta2=0.10; the sham group showed stronger alpha increase at post vs verum (mean difference=0.06, p=0.011, d=0.33) and reduction from post to follow-up in sham (mean difference=0.05, p=0.010, d=0.35). D-prime in Go/No-Go showed significant stimulation condition main effect (F(1,49)=6.22, p=0.016, partial eta2=0.11) and session x condition interaction (F(3,110.20)=5.57, p=0.001). summary: This double-blind randomized controlled trial tested four consecutive daily sessions of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) applied to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in 40 adults with long COVID-related cognitive fatigue. The primary outcome (subjective trait fatigue) showed no significant benefit from active versus sham stimulation; among the secondary outcomes reported here, tDCS also had no significant effect on subjective state fatigue ratings or behavioral performance on a cognitive task. The only notable finding was a statistically significant interaction in occipital alpha brainwave activity, where the sham group showed a greater fatigue-related increase in alpha power at post-assessment compared to the active stimulation group (mean difference = 0.06, p = 0.011, d = 0.33), suggesting a possible but limited neurophysiological stabilizing effect that did not translate into measurable clinical benefit.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary and secondary subjective/behavioral outcomes were all non-significant; e.g., VAS exhaustion slopes: stimulation condition F(1,38.44)=1.12, p=0.296; the only significant finding was a secondary EEG interaction (occipital alpha, p=0.020) with no corresponding behavioral or subjective improvement.

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested 8 weeks of home-based inspiratory muscle training (IMT) in 281 adults with long COVID (average 9 months post-infection, 88% female) whose primary symptom was breathlessness. The primary outcome — overall health-related quality of life measured by K-BILD total score — did not differ significantly between the IMT and control groups in the intention-to-treat analysis (IMT: 58.2±12.3 vs control: 59.5±12.4). However, IMT produced clinically meaningful improvements in breathlessness-specific outcomes: the Transition Dyspnoea Index improved by 2.0 points in the IMT group versus 0.9 in controls (p=0.005), and the K-BILD breathlessness and chest symptoms domains both improved beyond their minimal clinically important thresholds, alongside gains in respiratory muscle strength and estimated aerobic fitness.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome K-BILD total score showed no significant between-group difference in the intention-to-treat population (IMT: 58.2±12.3 vs control: 59.5±12.4, p<0.05 threshold not met for between-group comparison); significant results were limited to secondary outcomes and the per-protocol subgroup.

summary: This interim safety report from the HOT-LoCO trial tested hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO2) versus sham treatment in 20 previously healthy adults with long COVID (post-COVID condition) at Karolinska University Hospital, Sweden. The interim analysis does not report primary efficacy outcomes — those are physical functioning and role physical scores on RAND-36 at 13 weeks — but documents baseline characteristics and safety data only. The enrolled cohort had severely impaired health-related quality of life (RAND-36 physical functioning score 31.75 vs. population norm of 83.5, p<0.001) and reduced exercise capacity (6-minute walk test 442m vs. 662m norm, p<0.001). Thirty-one adverse events occurred across 60% of subjects, with no serious adverse events; the most common were cough and chest pain/discomfort, and all were transient, leading the independent safety board to conclude HBO2 has a favorable safety profile.

trial_rating.result_basis: No primary efficacy outcome data reported in this interim analysis; baseline RAND-36 physical functioning was 31.75 vs. norm 83.5 (p<0.001), confirming severe impairment at entry, but no between-group treatment effect is yet available.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding home-based breathing and chest mobility exercises (3 times per week for 12 weeks) to a standard cardiac rehabilitation program improved cardiorespiratory fitness in 46 long COVID patients with cardiovascular comorbidities such as coronary artery disease and hypertension. Patients who received the additional exercises walked 52 meters further on the 6-minute walk test (467 m vs 415 m, p=0.032), and showed significantly higher peak expiratory flow rate (503 vs 411 L/min, p=0.031) and peak cough flow (465 vs 366 L/min, p=0.016) compared to those on cardiac rehabilitation alone. No significant differences were found in quality of life or inflammation markers (CRP, D-dimer), and no adverse cardiovascular events occurred during the trial.

summary: The REGAIN trial tested an eight-week online supervised group rehabilitation programme combining physical exercise sessions and psychological support against best-practice usual care (a single online consultation) in 585 adults with post-COVID-19 condition who had previously been hospitalised. The primary economic outcome was cost-effectiveness over 12 months: the REGAIN intervention cost £305 more per patient (95% CI: -£123 to £732) and generated 0.026 additional QALYs (95% CI: -0.005 to 0.052), yielding an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £11,941 per QALY, well below the UK NHS £30,000 willingness-to-pay threshold. The 84% probability of cost-effectiveness at that threshold supports offering the programme to hospitalised post-COVID patients, though results are based on modest and statistically non-significant differences in both cost and quality of life, and the findings may not generalise to non-hospitalised patients or minority ethnic groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: Incremental QALYs of 0.026 (95% CI: -0.005 to 0.052) are non-significant; incremental cost £305 (95% CI: -£123 to £732) also non-significant; ICER £11,941/QALY with 84% probability of cost-effectiveness at £30,000 threshold.

summary: This 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested vortioxetine (5–20 mg/day) versus placebo in 147 Canadian adults with WHO-defined long COVID, focusing on whether baseline metabolic dysfunction, elevated BMI, and inflammation modified cognitive outcomes. The primary outcome was change in Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) score; vortioxetine produced a statistically significant between-group improvement at 8 weeks (mean difference 0.621 points, p=0.047), with the benefit concentrated in participants who had high baseline CRP, elevated TG-HDL ratio, and higher BMI. This is a post-hoc analysis of a previously published trial, not a pre-specified primary analysis, so the findings are hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 12-week home-based pulmonary rehabilitation program — comprising daily walking, diaphragmatic strengthening, and resistance training — against usual medical care alone in 60 adults aged 40–70 with post-COVID-19 syndrome presenting with fatigue, dyspnea, and exercise intolerance. The primary outcome, six-minute walk test distance, improved substantially more in the rehabilitation group (439.7 m) than the control group (347 m) after 12 weeks, a difference of roughly 93 m. The rehabilitation group also showed meaningfully lower fatigue scores (Chalder: 11.1 vs. 13.4), higher physical fitness index (52.3 vs. 36.7), better quality of life on the SF-36 (66.4 vs. 47.6), and greater dyspnea reduction, all at p<0.001, with no notable safety concerns reported.

domains.support: Lottery method with 1:1 allocation; allocation concealment via SNOSE (Sequentially-Numbered, Opaque, Sealed Envelopes); no significant baseline differences detected between groups.
Open-label design; participants and treating clinicians were aware of assignment. Patients were asked not to vary usual care, but compliance could not be fully verified in the control group.
4/51 (7.8%) withdrew from intervention arm; 4/47 (8.5%) lost in control arm. Dropout rates are low and balanced. Analysis appears per-protocol rather than ITT.
All outcomes are self-reported patient-reported outcomes; outcome analyst remained blinded, but open-label design may introduce response bias. All instruments are validated.
Trial was pre-registered (NCT05765591). Multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR) was applied. Outcomes appear consistent with registration.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports between-group effects as Beta-coefficients from a Univariate General Linear Model adjusted for age and BMI; these are interpreted as adjusted mean differences (intervention minus control) for absolute change scores. Note that positive Beta-coefficient for PSQI and HADS-Anxiety indicates improvement in the BT group (i.e., the control group worsened or improved less, and the BT group had greater improvement in change scores — the directionality is: positive beta = BT group improved more, for scales where lower=better; negative beta = BT group improved more for scales where higher=better). Per-arm follow-up means and SDs for timepoints 2 and 3 are not provided in tables — only absolute change from baseline means are shown in figures (as mean with SE bars) without numeric values in the text or supplemental tables referenced. Therefore, endpoint values at timepoints 2 and 3 per arm could not be extracted. The paper states data are expressed as mean (SE) in figures but exact values are not provided. The RR data for improvement categorization (e.g., SF-36 pain RR=2.8 [1.69;4.64], energy/fatigue RR=2.0 [1.31;3.05]) are reported as supplemental figure data and not extracted as separate outcomes. Table 1 missing the BT group column header for sample sizes (table appears to show only Control N=47 in header but BT group data is present). ICU admission rates are provided (BT: 3.9%, Control: 2.1%) but not used to calculate percent previously hospitalized as ICU is a subset. Baseline PSQI SD for control arm listed with comma decimal '11.13 (4,17)' — extracted as 4.17.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 sessions of balneotherapy (thermal mineral water immersion plus aquatic exercises) over one month against a no-treatment control in 98 adults with long COVID, most of whom were middle-aged women with symptoms lasting over one year. The primary outcome was change in questionnaire scores across multiple validated scales; the largest improvements in the balneotherapy group were in musculoskeletal pain (SF-36 pain subscale beta-coefficient -21.6, 95% CI -30.48 to -12.78, p<0.0001) and fatigue (SF-36 energy/fatigue beta-coefficient -17.5, 95% CI -24.23 to -10.66, p<0.0001), with additional significant short-term gains in sleep quality, anxiety, and several quality-of-life domains. Gains in sleep, anxiety, and emotional well-being were not sustained at the one-month follow-up, and 17 of 51 participants in the balneotherapy group reported mild transient worsening of symptoms, primarily fatigue, especially in early sessions.

trial_rating.result_basis: SF-36 pain subscale beta-coefficient -21.6 (95% CI -30.48 to -12.78, p<0.0001) and energy/fatigue beta-coefficient -17.5 (95% CI -24.23 to -10.66, p<0.0001) vs. control at end of intervention.

domains.support: Explicitly non-randomized, open-label, dose-escalating design. Participants enrolled sequentially into higher dose groups; no randomization or allocation concealment.
Open-label with no blinding; patients knew their dose and treatment. No placebo arm; historical control used instead.
Long COVID 1000 mg BID arm had 9/21 (43%) dropouts. Dropout data carried forward for analysis. ME/CFS arms had lower but unreported dropout rates.
All outcomes are self-reported; study is unblinded; assessors are the participants themselves who know they are receiving treatment. High risk of performance/detection bias.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a non-randomized, open-label dose-escalation study with historical control (not an RCT). The 'control' is a historical placebo showing 5.9% improvement on Chalder Likert from Cho et al. 2005 meta-analysis — no concurrent placebo arm exists. 2. All outcome data are reported as percentage change from baseline on a normalized 0-100% scale; absolute scores (raw means and SDs at each timepoint) are NOT reported in the paper. Therefore sd, se, ci_95_low, ci_95_high for arm_results are null throughout. 3. The paper reports FSS and PROMIS-7a results only for Long COVID arms (arms 4 and 5); ME/CFS arm FSS and PROMIS results are not reported in accessible tabular or numeric form. 4. Adverse event data for ME/CFS arms 1 and 2 reference '1000 mg BID group' with n=24 in the text but the arm enrolled N=29; the text says '2/24 in the 1000 mg BID group' which may be an error or refer to a subset — extracted verbatim. 5. The Long COVID 500 mg BID arm (arm 4) Chalder Bimodal 2-week value shown in Table 3 as '46.8%***' appears under the '6-Weeks' row for bimodal — Table 3 Long COVID section header reads '2-Weeks' and '6-Weeks' for Chalder Fatigue at 6 Weeks columns; the table is somewhat garbled/merged. Values extracted as best interpretation from text and table. 6. p-values reported only as thresholds (* p<0.05, ** p<0.005, *** p<0.0005 or similar); no exact p-values provided. 7. Baseline Chalder scores described as ranging 76-92% of maximum but no per-arm breakdown given. 8. ME/CFS arm age (median 47) and sex (73.7% female) reported for the group overall, not per arm. Long COVID demographics not reported. 9. The 'Insomnia' AE is reported as '1/26 in the 500 mg BID group' in text but arm 1 enrolled N=23 — possible text error; extracted with n=1 for arm 1.

summary: This non-randomized, open-label dose-escalation trial tested anhydrous enol-oxaloacetate (AEO), a nutritional supplement, in 76 ME/CFS patients (average illness duration 8.9 years, 73.7% women) and 43 long COVID patients with fatigue lasting at least 6 months. The primary outcome was change in Chalder Fatigue Scale score at 6 weeks compared to a historical placebo benchmark of 5.9% improvement; ME/CFS patients showed 22.5–27.9% reductions in fatigue (Likert scoring, p<0.005) and up to 33.3% achieved clinical normalization on bimodal scoring, while long COVID patients at 500 mg twice daily showed up to 46.8% achieving clinical normalization. Key caveats are substantial: the study was unblinded with no concurrent placebo group, was funded by the supplement manufacturer (Terra Biological LLC), one author is a company officer, and dropout rates were high in the long COVID arm, all of which severely limit interpretation of the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Chalder Fatigue Scale (Likert) improved 22.5–27.9% from baseline in ME/CFS groups vs historical placebo of 5.9% (p<0.005); 33.3% of ME/CFS patients and 46.8% of long COVID patients reached bimodal score ≤4.

summary: Treamid (a bisamide derivative of dicarboxylic acid, BDDA), an oral anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic drug, was tested in 59 adults who had recovered from COVID-19 pneumonia and had persistent lung damage, reduced lung function (FVC and/or DLCO below 80% predicted), and moderate-to-severe breathlessness. After 4 weeks of daily 50 mg oral Treamid versus placebo, 41% of the Treamid group achieved the primary endpoint of clinically significant improvement in FVC and/or DLCO, compared to 17% in the placebo group (p=0.036); Treamid also reduced breathlessness after exercise (Borg scale: -0.9 vs -0.4, p=0.018). The trial was small (roughly 30 patients per arm), industry-funded by the drug's developer, and the female-subgroup benefit was an exploratory post-hoc analysis requiring confirmation in larger trials.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary endpoint responder rate 41% (12/29) Treamid vs 17% (5/30) placebo, p=0.036.

summary: This study tested three intravenous infusions of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs, 4×10⁷ cells/dose) versus placebo in 100 severe COVID-19 patients from Wuhan, with 78 patients assessed at a 3-year follow-up. The primary lung imaging outcome was not statistically significant: 47% of MSC-treated patients showed normal CT scans versus 34% of placebo patients (OR=1.68, 95% CI: 0.65–4.34, p=0.28). The one statistically significant finding was a higher general health score on the SF-36 quality-of-life survey in the MSC group (median 67 vs 50, difference 12.86, 95% CI: 1.44–24.28), with no significant differences in exercise capacity, pulmonary function, or long COVID symptom rates between groups; no increase in tumor incidence or other safety signals was observed over three years.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary CT normalization outcome was non-significant: OR=1.68, 95% CI 0.65–4.34, p=0.28; the only significant finding was a secondary quality-of-life measure (GH score difference 12.86, 95% CI 1.44–24.28, p=0.028).

domains.support: Computer-generated random number list via SPSS with variable block sizes (2, 4, 6) to avoid selection bias. No significant baseline differences between groups reported.
Open-label for participants; control group received no specific instructions and was asked to continue usual lifestyle. Participants could not be blinded to group assignment.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Patients with FAS < 35 showed significant improvement in VO2peak (p < 0.05 within subgroup) regardless of study group, while those with FAS >= 35 showed no change in exercise capacity. 34 of 62 patients (55%) had extreme fatigue at baseline.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. Baseline VO2peak in Table 1 shows IG mean as 21.5 SD 6.1, but text states 21.6 SD 6.3 at start of results section — the text values (21.6/6.3) were used as they correspond to the analyzed per-protocol sample (n=30) rather than the full enrolled sample. 2. Anxiety severity baseline in Table 1 appears anomalous: IG 4.9 SD 0.9, CG 4.7 SD 0.8, while overall depression severity is listed as 7.1 SD 4.4 and overall anxiety as 7.1 SD 4.8 — this may indicate a table formatting/entry error where IG and CG anxiety rows were swapped or mislabeled; values extracted as printed. 3. Peak power output SD for IG change from baseline (17.8W) is derived from abstract statement '6.1 ± 17.8 W'. 4. No post-treatment follow-up period; assessments ended at 3 months. 5. Outcomes omitted due to space: FEV1 predicted (%) and VC predicted (%) changes (Table 2 data: IG change 1.1 SD 6.3, CG change -0.6 SD 6.9, between-group 1.69 CI -2.00 to 5.39; VC% IG 0.7 SD 6.5, CG 0.8 SD 6.4, between-group -0.08 CI -3.69 to 3.52). Steps per day and exercise-related physical activity sub-outcomes not separately extracted.

summary: A 3-month online-supported, app-guided physical activity program (150 min/week of moderate exercise, individually tailored) was tested against a waiting-list control in 62 long COVID patients with significant fatigue (FAS score ≥22) recruited at Hannover Medical School. The primary outcome, peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), did not improve significantly in either group: the intervention group gained 0.9 ml/min/kg versus 0.3 ml/min/kg in controls, with no significant between-group difference (p=0.098 within intervention group; between-group mean difference -0.6 ml/min/kg, 95% CI -1.8 to 0.8). Fatigue scores improved in both groups equally, likely reflecting natural recovery over time rather than a treatment effect; a post-hoc subgroup analysis found that only patients with moderate fatigue (FAS <35) showed any improvement in exercise capacity, regardless of group assignment.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2peak between-group mean difference was -0.6 ml/min/kg (95% CI -1.8 to 0.8), p=0.098 within the intervention group; no significant between-group difference detected; post-hoc power analysis showed only 12% statistical power, with 810 patients required to detect a significant effect.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a conference abstract (European Psychiatry 2024). Severe data limitations: per-arm sample sizes not reported (only total N=96); baseline HAM-D mean 12.85±5.97 appears to be an overall figure, not per-arm. Post-treatment per-arm means and SDs not reported for either outcome — only p-values given. The 30% greater improvement in fatigue is reported as a relative comparison without absolute values. Fatigue severity distribution at baseline (moderate 66.7%, severe 33.3%) is reported for the overall sample, not per arm. Depression severity distribution at baseline (mild 57.3%, moderate 32.3%, severe 6.4%) is also overall. Per-arm n for HAM-D baseline is ambiguous — assigned the overall mean to both arms as a placeholder but this may not reflect true per-arm values.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested oral L-arginine supplementation (1.66 g twice daily) added to standard SSRI antidepressant therapy versus SSRI alone in 96 elderly outpatients (aged over 65) with long COVID-related fatigue and depression persisting at least 3 months after acute infection. After 8 weeks, patients receiving L-arginine showed 30% greater improvement in fatigue severity compared to the SSRI-only group, and also had a significantly greater reduction in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. No notable safety concerns were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Fatigue symptom severity improved 30% more in the L-arginine group vs SSRI-only (p=0.008); HAM-D score reduction was also significantly greater in the L-arginine group (p=0.002).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Table 1 baseline data is reported for N=134 (67 per arm), but Table 2 uses N=62 per arm (per-protocol completers). The baseline values in Table 2 match Table 1 exactly, suggesting Table 2 reports all randomized participants' baselines alongside completers' follow-up (or slight rounding). The between-group effect for SF-36 Mental Health change score (T1-T0 difference: 1.98 - (-1.26) = 3.24) was calculated from Table 2 data; the paper states p=0.046 for this comparison. The paper reports 'p<0.05' in the abstract for the 1.98-point mean increase but does not provide an explicit between-group effect size or CI. Severity of persistent symptoms measured by 1-10 VAS was noted as collected but VAS severity scores are not separately tabulated in outcome tables (only symptom count is reported quantitatively). The paper reports a linear regression model (Table 3) with SF-36 Mental Health T1-T0 as dependent variable; regression coefficients extracted but not duplicated as separate outcome objects. Health Literacy scoring note: higher scores indicate poorer literacy per paper, so higher_is_better=false.

summary: A randomized controlled trial tested an 8-session online multimodal rehabilitation program — covering physical, cognitive, and respiratory exercises plus nutrition, sleep hygiene, and emotional management via weekly group videoconferences and a Moodle platform — in 134 Spanish adults with long COVID (mean age 49, 84% female) recruited from patient associations, added on top of usual primary care. The primary outcome was health-related quality of life measured by the SF-36; the intervention group showed a statistically significant improvement in mental health-related quality of life (mean increase of 1.98 points, p=0.046) compared to a decline of 1.26 points in the control group, though no significant difference was found for physical health-related quality of life or any secondary outcome. The model explaining mental health improvement accounted for only 12% of variance, and baseline imbalances in symptom count and physical functioning between groups are a noted limitation.

trial_rating.result_basis: SF-36 Mental Health T1-T0: intervention group +1.98 points vs control group -1.26 points, p=0.046; R2 adjusted=0.126.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The paper reports the group*time interaction p-values from linear mixed models adjusted for gender, which are the between-group effect p-values. Between-group effect sizes (mean differences) were calculated from the change-from-baseline values reported in the tables. 2. Adverse event data are in Supplemental Table S1 which was not provided in the paper text; counts not extractable. 3. Outcomes omitted due to size constraints: AT VO2 %pred (P=0.109, ns), VE L/min (P=0.091, ns), delta VO2/delta WR (P=0.159, ns), FVC% predicted, FEV1% predicted, FEV1/FVC% predicted - all pulmonary function %pred values extracted via Table 3 endpoints but change-from-baseline CIs available in table. All CPET and PFT endpoint values are included. 4. The median time from COVID-19 diagnosis to enrollment was 14 weeks (reported as overall, not per arm). 5. The 'between_group_effects' p_value for insomnia was reported as '>0.99' - recorded as 0.990 with p_value_exact=false. 6. For outcome_id 6 (O2 pulse %pred), the between-group effect MD was calculated as arm1 endpoint minus arm2 endpoint at 4 weeks, but note significant baseline imbalance; the interaction p-value from the model (0.042) is the key statistic.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 4-week supervised aerobic exercise program (12 sessions on a cycling ergometer, using either moderate- or high-intensity interval training) in 24 long COVID patients aged 18–75 with persistent symptoms. The primary finding was that 67.8% of patients in the exercise group showed reduced or resolved symptoms after 4 weeks, compared to 16.7% in the control group (p=0.013). Peak oxygen uptake (peak VO2) improved by 4.64 mL/kg/min in the exercise group versus a decline of 1.06 mL/kg/min in the control group (p=0.001), while no significant improvements were found in mental health, quality of life, or pulmonary function measures.

trial_rating.result_basis: Peak VO2 improved by 4.64 mL/kg/min in the exercise group vs. -1.06 mL/kg/min in the control group (p group*time=0.001); symptom improvement in 67.8% vs. 16.7% of controls (p=0.013).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Major limitation: nearly all outcome data (Mental Fatigue Scale individual scores, GAD7, PHQ9, PHQ4, PSS10, PCL6, CGI-I, CGI-S, GAF, CDRS, MOCA, fatigue severity scale, modified fatigue impact scale, pain scale, smell assessment) appear only in figures (Figures 5 and 6) with no numeric values in text or tables. Per-arm means and SDs are not reported for any clinical scale. The symptom percent data (outcome_id=1) are group-level proportions read from text descriptions of Figure 5, not tabulated. The two AE cases of skin irritation are reported at the overall trial level without arm breakdown. Perceptual threshold and treatment intensity values (Sham PT: 0.3 ± 0.17 mA, Active PT: 0.317 ± 0.08 mA; Sham treatment: 0.5 ± 0.21 mA, Active treatment: 0.6 ± 0.14 mA) are extracted and noted but not entered as outcomes. The study is a pilot feasibility trial not powered for efficacy; no formal statistical comparisons between arms were performed on clinical outcomes. Crossover note: sham arm crossed to active taVNS in weeks 3-4 — this is a partial crossover, so arm definitions apply to the blinded phase only.

summary: This pilot randomised controlled trial tested at-home, self-administered transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) — a non-invasive device that delivers electrical stimulation to the ear to activate the vagus nerve — in 12 adults with confirmed long COVID symptoms including fatigue, brain fog, anxiety, depression, and others. The primary outcomes were feasibility and safety, not efficacy; the trial was explicitly underpowered to detect clinical effects. Descriptively, participants receiving active taVNS for two weeks saw their reported long COVID symptom burden fall from 46% to 31% of nine tracked symptoms, versus no change in the sham group (68% to 68%), and those completing four weeks of active treatment showed the largest reductions in mental fatigue scores, but no inferential statistics were reported for symptom outcomes. The intervention was safe, with no cardiac adverse events and only two mild cases of skin irritation across all sessions.

trial_rating.result_basis: No p-values or confidence intervals were reported for any symptom outcome; the only quantitative comparison is descriptive: active group symptoms fell from 46% to 31% over two weeks versus sham remaining at 68%, with the study explicitly stated to be underpowered to determine efficacy.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a conference abstract (European Psychiatry 2025), not a full paper. Critical information is missing: per-arm sample sizes (only total N=240 reported), baseline values for all outcomes, randomization procedure, allocation concealment, and blinding. The t-statistics are reported (t=11.437, t=18.355, t=10.836) but not extracted as a separate field. p-values are reported as p<0.001 throughout. summary: A remote medical-psychological rehabilitation program was tested in 240 Ukrainian adults with post-COVID anxiety and depressive disorders, also affected by wartime trauma. By day 63, the intervention group showed dramatically lower depression scores (PHQ-9: 6.9 vs 15.6 in controls), anxiety scores (GAD-7: 4.0 vs 13.0), and PTSD symptoms (PCL-5: 13.3 vs 29.2), all statistically significant. No safety concerns were reported, but the absence of randomization details, blinding, or pre-registration limits confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: PHQ-9 depression 6.94 (intervention) vs 15.57 (control), p<0.001; GAD-7 anxiety 3.99 vs 12.97, p<0.001; PCL-5 PTSD 13.30 vs 29.18, p<0.001 — all primary outcomes show large between-group differences.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a 6-month follow-up study of the HENIVOT RCT, not a long COVID intervention trial per se. The population is ICU survivors of acute COVID-19 hypoxemic respiratory failure assessed for long-term outcomes. The study design arm sizes differ between primary paper (N=54 helmet, N=55 HFNC randomized) and follow-up completion (N=35 helmet, N=36 HFNC). Note: Table 2 headers show N=31 helmet and N=33 HFNC for symptoms, N=30 each for pulmonary function, and N=35/N=36 for quality of life sections — these varying Ns are preserved in arm_results. The 30-s chair stand test p-value (0.65) is reported but no between-group effect size or CI is provided. The EQ-VAS high-flow group IQR in Table 2 has a formatting issue (value '[60-80]' appears on next line); extracted as median=70, IQR 60-80 based on text and table. Outcomes from Table 3 (intubated vs non-intubated subgroup) are captured in subgroup_analyses rather than as separate outcome entries to avoid duplication. Additional outcomes not extracted as separate objects due to space: maximal mid-expiratory flow 25-75 (MEF25-75), alveolar ventilation volume, residual volume/TLC ratio, FEV1<80% binary, FEV1/FVC<80% binary, TLC<80% binary, residual volume<80% binary, 6MWT interruption, 6MWT unable to walk predicted distance, various minor symptoms (dry cough, sore throat, rhinitis, smell disorder, taste disorder, dizziness, myalgia, chest pain, sicca syndrome, inappetence, diarrhoea, decreased visual acuity). Laboratory test results (hemoglobin, platelets, WBC, bilirubin, transaminases, creatinine, BUN, eGFR) reported in supplemental tables not available in main text.

summary: This pre-specified follow-up analysis of the HENIVOT randomized trial assessed 6-month outcomes in 71 ICU survivors with moderate-to-severe COVID-19 hypoxemic respiratory failure who had been treated with helmet noninvasive ventilation (NIV) or high-flow nasal oxygen. The primary outcome — the proportion of patients reporting any symptom at 6 months — did not differ between groups (90% helmet vs. 85% high-flow, p=0.71), and no significant differences were found in pulmonary function, physical performance, or quality of life between the two treatments. The only significant between-group difference was lower arthralgia in the helmet group (16% vs. 55%, p=0.002); separately, patients who required invasive mechanical ventilation during the acute illness had significantly worse pulmonary function and quality of life at 6 months regardless of initial treatment assignment.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (proportion with any symptom at 6 months) showed no significant difference: 90% helmet vs. 85% high-flow, p=0.71, OR=1.67 (95% CI 0.36–7.65).

summary: This randomised controlled trial tested two 8-week exercise-based rehabilitation programmes — face-to-face and remote — against usual care in 181 adults with post-COVID syndrome who had previously been hospitalised with COVID-19. Both interventions significantly improved exercise capacity measured by the Incremental Shuttle Walking Test: face-to-face rehabilitation produced a mean gain of 52 metres over usual care (95% CI 19–85 m, p=0.002) and remote rehabilitation produced a gain of 34 metres (95% CI 1–66 m, p=0.047), both exceeding the established 35-metre minimal clinically important difference. Neither intervention improved self-reported quality of life or symptom scores compared to usual care, and an exploratory immune substudy (n=31) found that face-to-face rehabilitation increased CD8+ T-cell and NK cell counts relative to usual care, with no safety signals attributable to the interventions.

trial_rating.result_basis: Face-to-face rehabilitation improved ISWT by mean 52 m (95% CI 19–85 m, p=0.002) and remote by 34 m (95% CI 1–66 m, p=0.047) versus usual care, both exceeding the 35 m MCID.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) applied for 25 minutes after aerobic exercise in 44 young adults (aged 18-45) with post-COVID syndrome lasting more than 12 weeks. The primary finding was that taVNS enhanced cardiac vagal control during post-exercise recovery: the RMSSD index (a measure of heart rate variability reflecting vagal activity) increased significantly in the taVNS group after stimulation (p=0.028) but not in the placebo group, and the parasympathetic nervous system index showed a greater rate of increase in the taVNS group (p=0.009). However, taVNS produced no significant advantage over placebo for blood lactate clearance or blood pressure reduction, meaning its practical impact on exercise recovery was limited to autonomic signaling measures rather than metabolic or cardiovascular outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: RMSSD increased significantly in the taVNS group post-stimulation (p=0.028) vs non-significant increase in placebo; no significant between-group differences in blood lactate (p=0.006 within-group but similar across both groups) or blood pressure (p=0.01 both groups equally).

summary: This double-blind RCT tested daily 1-hour sessions of lower-extremity electrical stimulation (E-Stim) applied to the gastrocnemius muscles for 4 weeks in 18 previously hospitalised long COVID patients with persistent leg muscle weakness and deconditioning. After 4 weeks, only the active E-Stim group showed improved muscle perfusion recovery after stimulation (oxyhemoglobin rose from t60 to t70, p=0.040) and increased gastrocnemius muscle endurance over the 1-hour session (p=0.031), while the sham group showed no improvement in either measure. The intervention was well-tolerated with no adverse events, though the trial was small, the two groups were not well-matched at baseline (the active group had more severe prior illness), and the sample size fell short of the pre-specified target of 32.

trial_rating.result_basis: Active group oxyhemoglobin increased post-stimulation at 4 weeks (p=0.040, d=0.334) vs sham which continued to decline (p<0.001, d=0.632); group×time interaction p=0.022. Muscle endurance increased in active group (p=0.031, d=0.397) with significant group×time interaction (p=0.048).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 weeks of Baduanjin exercise training (BET) — a traditional Chinese mind-body practice involving gentle postures, breathing, and meditation — in 40 adults with idiopathic chronic fatigue who had also recovered from COVID-19. The primary outcome, forced vital capacity (FVC), improved significantly in the BET group (from 2.07 L to 2.18 L) compared to no change in controls (2.03 L to 2.02 L), with a between-group difference significant at p=0.001. All secondary outcomes also improved significantly in the BET group, including 6-minute walk distance (298 m to 358 m), fatigue scores, sleep quality, depression, and quality of life, with no changes in the control group; however, the trial is limited by a very small sample (20 per arm), no long-term follow-up, and no objective adherence monitoring.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome FVC improved from 2.07 to 2.18 L in BET group vs 2.03 to 2.02 L in controls, p=0.001 between groups; within-BET-group p<0.001.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports 'delta score 27.50' for the treatment group and 'delta score 9.50' for the control group in the abstract, but Table 2 shows delta scores of 10.33 and 2.11 respectively. The abstract delta scores appear to be cumulative rank sums (Wilcoxon test statistic) rather than mean differences; Table 2 values were used as primary data. The 95% CI reported in Table 2 for the control group (17.54-20.96) and treatment group (11.04-15.02) appear to be for the post-intervention means rather than for the delta scores. The OR=0.00, p=0.99 reported in the abstract refers to the logistic regression of the intervention itself (Table 3 shows OR=0.81, p=0.26 for WHO Stress Management), creating inconsistency. ISI score baseline comparison p=0.00 is stated in the paper but this seems counterintuitive given that both groups had insomnia at baseline; this may reflect a non-parametric test value rounded to zero. Age was the only demographic characteristic that differed significantly between groups (p=0.03) but exact means/SDs by group were not reported in tables.

summary: This quasi-experimental study tested the WHO Stress Management (WSM) module — a five-session online program combining mindfulness and relaxation — in 36 Indonesian adults with post-COVID insomnia recruited from a Telegram self-isolation group. The WSM group showed a mean Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) score drop from 19.94 to 9.61 (delta 10.33), compared to a drop from 18.56 to 16.44 (delta 2.11) in the sleep hygiene psychoeducation control group (p=0.00 on Wilcoxon and Mann-Whitney tests). However, logistic regression found no significant causative effect of WSM on clinical insomnia improvement (OR 0.81, p=0.26), and the authors note that the online delivery format likely limited participant engagement and masked confounders such as anxiety and depression.

trial_rating.result_basis: WSM group ISI score decreased by 10.33 points (19.94 to 9.61) vs 2.11 points in controls (18.56 to 16.44), p=0.00; but logistic regression OR 0.81, p=0.26 for clinical significance.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL DATA QUALITY ISSUES: (1) All quantitative data appear only in bar chart figures (Figs 1-5); no tables provided. Percentages are reported verbatim in the results text, but exact n per subgroup are not stated — event counts were back-calculated from stated percentages assuming equal subgroup sizes within each disorder type across the two arms. However, the per-subgroup ns are uncertain: summing inferred subgroup ns (15+23+25+17+25=105) exceeds stated arm 1 total of 80, so the subgroup assignments are not additive across the whole arm (i.e., participants may have had only one disorder type per arm, and the per-subgroup n may represent only that subgroup, not the full arm). The inferred n per subgroup (e.g., 15 per arm for polymenorrhea based on 13.3% = ~2/15) is speculative. (2) No baseline demographic data (age, BMI, time since infection) reported per arm. (3) Allocation method not described — this is NOT a confirmed RCT; described as a controlled study without randomization details. (4) Follow-up duration stated as 3-6 months post-treatment but exact treatment duration not specified. (5) The Ukrainian-language abstract reverses group numbering (group 1 = standard, group 2 = modified) relative to the English text (group 1 = modified, group 2 = standard) — extraction follows English text convention. (6) Adverse event percentages given as ranges (e.g., 15-20%, 60-70%) without exact denominators.

summary: This Ukrainian trial tested a modified multi-component regimen—combining natural estrogen-based oral contraceptives, melatonin, vitamin D3, magnesium-B6, L-arginine, quercetin, folic acid, and vitamin B12—against standard Ukrainian Ministry of Health protocols in 158 women of reproductive age (18–45) who developed menstrual disorders within six months of COVID-19 recovery. Across all five disorder types, the modified regimen produced dramatically lower relapse rates (8.7–23.5% vs. 56–80%) and higher rates of complete menstrual normalization (72–84% vs. 33–52%), with all differences statistically significant at P<0.05. Adverse effects such as edema, breast tenderness, and hypertension were also substantially less frequent in the modified-therapy group (15–20% vs. 60–70%), attributed to the use of natural rather than synthetic estrogens.

trial_rating.result_basis: Complete menstrual normalization achieved in 72–84% (modified) vs. 33–52% (standard), and relapse rates 8.7–23.5% vs. 56–80%, all P<0.05; however, no randomization, blinding, or pre-registration reported, and assignment to groups appears non-randomized.

The study is reported in Russian with English abstract/translation. Arm-level sample sizes for subgroups (Group I, II, III within each treatment arm) were taken from Table 3. The p-value of 0.001 for nasal sIgA between-group comparison in Group I is stated as p=0.007 within-group for treatment arm; the intergroup difference is marked as p<0.001 (#). Between-group effect sizes for nasal sIgA outcomes were calculated as mean difference (arm1 minus arm2 at 30 days). Symptom prevalence data from Tables 4 and 5 (acute and post-COVID clinical manifestations) are descriptive/retrospective and not outcomes of the intervention; they are not extracted as outcome objects but all numerical data is present in the paper tables. summary: This open-label controlled study tested intranasal interferon alpha-2b (IFN α-2b) gel, applied twice daily for 30 days, in 65 adults aged 18–60 who had recovered from COVID-19 within the past 1–9 months, compared to 65 untreated post-COVID controls. The primary outcome was secretory IgA (sIgA) levels in saliva and nasal swabs; among patients treated within 1–3 months of infection, salivary sIgA rose more than 3-fold (from 1.84±0.28 to 5.78±1.96 mg/ml, p=0.001) and nasal sIgA rose 1.5-fold (from 28.61±3.0 to 39.83±3.85 mg/ml, p=0.007), while untreated patients showed persistently low sIgA for up to 9 months. No respiratory infections were recorded in the treated group during the study period, versus a 27.6% incidence in the untreated group (p<0.001), and no adverse events were reported in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Salivary sIgA increased from 1.84±0.28 to 5.78±1.96 mg/ml (p=0.001) and nasal sIgA from 28.61±3.0 to 39.83±3.85 mg/ml (p=0.007) in the IFN α-2b group at 1–3 months post-COVID.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 10 days of daily 90-minute inhaled 'active hydrogen' (H(H2O)m) inhalation therapy added to standard rehabilitation (physiotherapy, magnesium, B vitamins, L-carnitine) versus standard rehabilitation alone in 60 healthcare workers with post-COVID-19 chronic fatigue syndrome. The primary finding was a large improvement in exercise capacity: the 6-minute walk distance increased from 429m to 569m (+140m) in the hydrogen group versus no significant change in controls, with the hydrogen group walking ~30% further than controls at day 10 (p<0.0001). Additional significant improvements in the hydrogen group included reduced arterial stiffness index (8.8 to 6.8 m/s, p<0.0001), reduced pulmonary shunt fraction (8.98% to 5.34%, p<0.01), reduced venous lactate (2.5 to 1.5 mmol/L, p<0.001), and improved venous oxygen tension (26.9 to 34.8 mmHg, p<0.0001); no adverse events were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance increased from 429±45m to 569±60m in the hydrogen group versus no significant change in controls; hydrogen group was ~30% higher than controls at day 10 (p<0.0001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Crossover design: all 20 participants completed both arms. Per-arm n=20 for all outcomes (each participant contributed data to both conditions). Baseline values for each arm reflect participants at entry into that condition (post-washout values used as pre for second condition). The paper reports intervention x time p-values from two-way ANOVA in Table 2 — these are used as between-group p-values. Calculated between-group mean differences are endpoint post-treatment differences (arm1 post minus arm2 post), which reflects the crossover contrast available from Table 2. The paper's primary between-group p-values (from delta of change comparisons via paired t-test) are: 6MWT p=0.02, TUG p=0.002, Barthel p=0.02; these are reported as between_group_effects p_values. For other outcomes, the intervention x time interaction p-value from two-way ANOVA is used as the between-group p-value. Training cardiopulmonary monitoring data (SpO2, HR, systolic/diastolic BP) appear only as figures with summary statistics in text — these are not extracted as formal outcomes. The 95% CI values in Table 2 are for Hedge's g effect sizes, not for mean differences; they are not entered into the between_group_effects CI fields. Note: the paper states TUG delta-of-change p=0.002 in the results text (Fig 3E) despite the two-way ANOVA intervention x time p=0.01 — the paired t-test p=0.002 is used as the primary between-group comparison. Sequence effects were significant for MRC, PCFS, MoCA, and Barthel Index, indicating potential carryover.

summary: This randomized crossover trial tested 8 weeks of eccentric cycling (ECC) against standard rehabilitation (elastic band strength exercises) in 20 adults who had been hospitalized in an ICU for COVID-19 and were recruited 6 months after discharge. The primary functional outcomes favored eccentric cycling: 6-minute walk distance improved by 140 meters with ECC versus 97 meters with standard rehabilitation (p=0.02 for between-group difference), and Timed Up and Go performance improved 16.5% with ECC versus 8.4% with standard rehabilitation (p=0.002). Both interventions were safe with no adverse events reported, but the two-week washout period between crossover arms was short and some carryover effects were detected, which limits confidence in the between-group comparisons.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved 139.5m (315 to 455m) with ECC vs 96.7m (296 to 393m) with STD REHAB, between-group delta p=0.02; TUG improved 16.5% vs 8.4%, p=0.002.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 12-week multicomponent physiotherapy program (combining strength, resistance, balance, and gait training; twice weekly, 60 minutes per session) in 59 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome in Brazil. The primary outcomes were functional mobility and quality of life, measured by the 6-minute walk test (6MWT), Berg balance scale, and SF-36 questionnaire. The intervention group improved on all three measures — walking distance increased by 54 meters, Berg score by 3.1 points, and SF-36 score by 6.3 points — but none of these improvements reached statistical significance. High dropout meant only 12 of 31 intervention participants completed all 24 sessions, substantially limiting the study's power.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT improved by 54.1 m in the intervention group vs. -7.3 m in controls, intergroup p=0.13; Berg scale p=0.87; SF-36 p=0.81. No statistically significant primary outcome.

summary: This randomized controlled pilot study tested online occupational therapy (OT) delivered either as live interactive sessions or prerecorded videos over 12 weeks in 158 adults with post-COVID syndrome (mean age 38 years, 86% female) who reported significant fatigue and cognitive impairment. The primary outcome was feasibility and acceptance: 83% of participants in the interactive OT group rated their experience as positive or very positive, compared to 48% in the video group (p=0.001). For secondary efficacy outcomes, participants receiving interactive OT showed significantly greater improvement in health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-3L mean difference +0.11 vs. control, 95% CI 0.05–0.17, p=0.003) and cognitive function (Neuro-QoL mean difference +3.95 vs. control, 95% CI 2.04–5.86, p<0.001) at 12 weeks; the study was unblinded and underpowered for confirmatory efficacy conclusions, and dropout was high (32.5% in the interactive group by week 12).

trial_rating.result_basis: Interactive OT vs. control: EQ-5D-3L mean difference +0.11 (95% CI 0.05–0.17, p=0.003) and Neuro-QoL mean difference +3.95 (95% CI 2.04–5.86, p<0.001) at 12 weeks; pilot study with no pre-specified primary efficacy endpoint power calculation.

summary: A 6-week comprehensive rehabilitation program — combining aerobic walking, strength, balance, flexibility, and breathing exercises with patient education — was tested in a randomized controlled trial of 38 long COVID patients aged 25–60 in a low-resource outpatient setting in India. The primary outcomes were functional capacity (six-minute walk test), fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale), and quality of life (EQ-5D-5L); the intervention group improved six-minute walk distance by 66 metres (well above the 30.5 m minimal clinically important difference), reduced FSS scores by 15 points, and improved EQ-5D VAS scores by 13.5 points, all with large effect sizes (Cohen's d ranging from 0.73 to 1.37). There were no dropouts and no adverse events reported, though the study was single-site with an unblinded outcome assessor.

trial_rating.result_basis: Six-minute walk distance increased by 66.27 ± 15.17 m in the intervention group vs. control (p < 0.0001, Cohen's d = 1.37); FSS decreased by 15.05 ± 5.88 points (p < 0.0001); EQ-5D VAS improved by 13.52 ± 5.46 points (p < 0.0001).

The paper reports almost all quantitative outcomes as percent change from baseline only, without providing absolute pre/post values or SDs — this severely limits effect size extraction. Absolute values are provided only for 6MWT baseline (median with IQR per arm) and overall FEV1 baseline (median IQR pooled). 2. Psychological and cognitive outcome data (Table 1) are reported only as Wilcoxon Z statistics and p-values across all rehabilitation groups combined, with no per-arm means/SDs. 3. Allostatic load is reported as categorical distribution (% in each severity category) before and after, not as continuous scores per arm. 4. The note in the abstract vs methods section reverses the group numbering (abstract English version lists groups differently from methods). We followed the methods section: arm1=whirlpool/hydromassage, arm2=Biolong baths, arm3=NaCl mineral baths, arm4=control. 5. Between-group effects are not directly reported; the paper reports only within-arm pre/post changes with p-values from Wilcoxon tests. No between-group inferential statistics are provided. 6. Several figures referenced (Figs 1, 2, 3) contain allostatic load distribution data that supplements text; extracted from text descriptions. 7. Omitted outcomes due to lack of any quantitative data: superoxide dismutase, sinus tachycardia/bradycardia rates (reported as percent of group but not per-arm post values with statistics), all complaint frequency outcomes (narrative percent only). 8. The Schulte Tables Efficiency of Work subscale did not reach significance (Z=-1.9, p=0.064) and is noted but all data remain null.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested three types of balneotherapy (whirlpool baths, 'Biolong' medicated baths, and sodium chloride mineral baths), each combined with exercise therapy, in 160 adults with post-COVID syndrome (median age 50) at an outpatient rehabilitation centre in Moscow. All three active treatment groups showed significant reductions in symptoms such as fatigue, headache, and dyspnoea compared to an untreated control group, with the whirlpool bath group showing a 12.1% increase in forced vital capacity (p<0.01) and 9.6% increase in FEV1 (p<0.05), and the Biolong bath group showing a 26.2% reduction in cortisol (p<0.01) and an 8.3% improvement in 6-minute walk distance (p<0.05). All rehabilitation groups also showed significant improvements in depression, anxiety, and cognitive measures, while the control group showed no meaningful change. The control group was not actively treated rather than receiving a placebo, which limits causal interpretation of the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Whirlpool bath group: FVC increased 12.1% (p<0.01), FEV1 increased 9.6% (p<0.05); Biolong group: 6-minute walk improved 8.3% (p<0.05), cortisol reduced 26.2% (p<0.01); control group showed no significant change on any measure.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested EEG alpha-rhythm neurofeedback (biofeedback) training versus sham training (identical exercises without feedback) in 20 adults with post-COVID syndrome experiencing anxiety, depression, fatigue, and cognitive complaints. Both groups showed significant reductions in trait anxiety, psychological stress, depression, and fatigue after 12–15 sessions. The neurofeedback group showed additional benefits over sham on general fatigue (U=19.5, p=0.019), immediate word recall (U=25.5, p=0.036), and verbal working memory (U=23.5, p=0.034), though the trial was very small (10 per arm) and lacked pre-registered power calculations, limiting confidence in these findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group comparison on primary fatigue outcome: general fatigue subscale U=19.5, p=0.019; immediate word recall U=25.5, p=0.036; verbal working memory d' U=23.5, p=0.034; however N=10 per arm with no pre-specified primary outcome or power calculation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is in Russian with English translation provided. Tables 1 and 2 present data as M±SD (mean±SD) with numerator=before, denominator=after treatment. Tables 3 and 4 present data as median [Q1; Q3]. The paper states treatment was 15 days (3 weeks). Follow-up was 6 months post-rehabilitation completion. The study study period was 4 months total. Within-group p-values are reported (Wilcoxon test), but between-group p-values are not explicitly stated for most outcomes - the p<0.049 threshold for spirometry and p<0.05 for HRV are noted in the abstract/text as within-group results for arm 1. No between-group statistical comparison results (p-values or effect sizes) are reported. All between_group_effects p_values are set to 0.05 as threshold only where paper indicates significant within-group change in arm 1 but not arm 2. summary: This open randomised trial tested interval hypo-hyperoxic training (IHHT) — alternating inhalation of low-oxygen (12–15% O2) and high-oxygen gas mixtures using the OXYTERRA device across 15 daily sessions — added to standard rehabilitation versus standard rehabilitation alone in 50 patients (mean age 61.7 years) with post-COVID syndrome persisting more than 3 months. The IHHT group showed statistically significant improvements in lung function (vital capacity, FVC, FEV1, and peak expiratory flow all p<0.05), blood oxygen content (SaO2 rose from 94.3% to 97.2%, p<0.01), heart rate (reduced from 82.8 to 75.7 bpm, p<0.01), and autonomic regulation (total heart rate variability power doubled from 623 to 1265, p<0.05), while the comparison group showed no significant changes in most measures. No adverse events were reported during the intervention or 6-month follow-up, and benefits were reported to persist for 3–6 months post-rehabilitation.

trial_rating.result_basis: FEV1 improved from median 72.2% to 79.1% predicted (p<0.05) in the IHHT group vs no significant change in controls (72.4% to 72.9%); SaO2 improved from 94.3% to 97.2% (p<0.01); heart rate fell from 82.8 to 75.7 bpm (p<0.01); total HRV power rose from 623 to 1265 (p<0.05).

summary: This open-label randomized trial tested sequential transcranial electrical stimulation — combining brain micropolarization (targeting the neocortex) followed immediately by diencephalic brain stimulation (targeting limbic structures) — in 142 adults aged 45–69 with chronic cerebrovascular disease (dyscirculatory encephalopathy) who were 3–4 months post-COVID-19. Patients receiving the sequential combination (n=48) showed statistically significant improvement across all measured symptoms compared to baseline, with symptom severity scores on a visual analogue scale improving 1.2–1.6 fold (p<0.05–0.001), and neuropsychological test scores improving 1.1–2.0 fold; both single-modality comparison groups showed narrower improvements affecting only specific symptom clusters. There was no control arm receiving sham stimulation or medication alone, which limits causal interpretation, and three participants withdrew due to uncomfortable pressure sensations around the eyes during diencephalic stimulation.

summary: This Russian randomized controlled trial tested whether adding VedaBiotic, a fifth-generation multisymbiotic (probiotic/prebiotic combination), to a standard physical rehabilitation program improved outcomes in 128 long COVID patients (mean age 57, all with prior bilateral viral pneumonia) at a inpatient rehabilitation centre. The primary finding was that the group receiving VedaBiotic (n=32) showed significantly greater reductions in symptoms and inflammatory markers compared to the rehabilitation-only group (n=64): fatigue resolved in 50% vs 81% still affected, cough resolved completely (0% vs 22% still affected, p=0.001), and D-dimer normalized only in the VedaBiotic group (dropping from 302 to 136 ng/mL, p=0.012, vs non-significant reduction in controls). No adverse events were reported, but the trial has notable limitations including unequal group sizes and open-label design with no placebo control.

trial_rating.result_basis: D-dimer normalized only in VedaBiotic group: 302 [279;440] to 136 [0;177] ng/mL, p=0.012; cough resolved in 100% of VedaBiotic group vs 78% control, p=0.001; fatigue persisted in 50% vs 81%, p=0.009.

summary: The DISSOLVE trial (NCT04645368) tested bovhyaluronidase azoximer (Longidase), an enzyme-immunomodulator conjugate that breaks down hyaluronic acid, in 160 adult post-COVID patients with residual lung abnormalities, comparing 15 intramuscular injections over 75 days (n=81) against observation-only controls (n=79) across 13 Russian centres. The primary outcome—reduction in residual lung abnormalities on CT scan—was not significantly different between groups at 180 days (-13.5% vs -13.8%, p=0.327), though treated patients showed significantly greater improvements in forced vital capacity (9.0% vs 5.0% at day 75, p=0.046), oxygen saturation (1.07% vs 0.57% at day 75, p<0.001), 6-minute walk distance (27.8% vs 17.1% at day 75, p=0.049), and dyspnea scores (-0.84 vs -0.58 mMRC points at day 75, p=0.002). The trial was open-label with no blinding or placebo control, and was published with acknowledged support from the drug manufacturer (NPO Petrovax Pharm), limiting confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (CT residual lung abnormalities) showed no significant between-group difference at day 180: -13.47% vs -13.75%, p=0.327.

summary: This trial tested two Ayurvedic herbal formulations — Femicycle (containing Symplocos racemosa, Asparagus racemosus, Saraca indica, Glycyrrhiza glabra, and Curcuma longa) and Femimens (containing Vitex agnus castus, Withania somnifera, Zingiber officinale, and Trigonella foenum-graecum) — in 53 women aged 18–25 with menstrual disorders that developed within 3 months of moderate or severe COVID-19, compared against 51 women who received only standard rehabilitation (diet, vitamins, psychotherapy). After 6 months, women in the herbal treatment group had significantly fewer menstrual problems: infrequent menstruation affected 1.89% versus 31.37% in the comparison group (OR 0.042 [0.005–0.332]), dysmenorrhea persisted in 11.32% versus 35.29% (OR 0.234 [0.084–0.653]), and PMS in 7.55% versus 29.41% (OR 0.196 [0.060–0.640]). No side effects were reported in the herbal treatment group, though the study lacks blinding, the products appear to be commercially linked to the authors, and the formulations are classified as dietary supplements rather than medicines.

summary: This open-label randomised trial tested L-carnitine (50–75 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks, added to standard rehabilitation therapy) versus standard therapy alone in 90 children, adolescents, and young adults aged 10–25 with long COVID cardiovascular and autonomic symptoms. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This study is NOT an RCT; it is an open-label quasi-experimental comparative study with no described randomization. design_type set to quasi-experimental. 2. Baseline imbalances exist: fatigue severity (experimental 2.65 vs control 2.31, p=0.0001) and sleep disorder severity (1.70 vs 1.00, p=0.04) differ significantly at baseline, complicating interpretation. 3. Table 3 p-values are reported as combined pairs (e.g., '0.0001/0.02') where the first value appears to refer to Day 1 between-group comparison and the second to Day 5; this notation is ambiguous and has been interpreted accordingly. 4. For FAS/chronic fatigue outcome (Table 4), only binary classification (above/below threshold of 22) is reported, not continuous FAS scores; no p-value is reported for the between-group comparison at Day 10 (text states 'no statistically significant differences'). 5. By day 10, the treated group showed statistically significant reductions in the frequency and severity of joint and muscle pain (12.7% vs 45.7% still affected), headache (18.2% vs 51.4%), dizziness, impaired concentration, and smell loss, with fatigue severity significantly lower as early as day 5 (mean score 1.71 vs 2.23, p=0.02); no adverse events were reported. The study has substantial methodological limitations: it was open-label with no blinding, had no placebo control, groups were not fully matched at baseline (fatigue scores differed significantly on day 1), and the 10-day follow-up with no post-treatment observation period means durability of effects is unknown.

trial_rating.result_basis: Joint and muscle pain prevalence 12.7% (treated) vs 45.7% (control) at day 10 (p not explicitly stated but marked significant); fatigue severity 1.71 vs 2.23 at day 5 (p=0.02); headache prevalence 18.2% vs 51.4% at day 10 (p<0.05).

The Schober test is measured in two parts: 'initial' measurement (always 15.00 ± 0.00 cm for both groups/timepoints, as this is the fixed starting mark) and 'final' measurement (the actual flexion endpoint). summary: This pilot study tested enhanced external counterpulsation (EECP) — a non-invasive device that applies synchronized compression to the legs to improve circulation — in 30 patients with persistent lung damage and ventilatory impairment an average of 15 months after COVID-19 pneumonia. Patients in the EECP group (n=15) received 20 one-hour sessions over four weeks; controls (n=15) received standard care only. EECP produced significant improvements in total lung capacity (65% to 76%, p<0.001), vital capacity (57% to 73%, p=0.006), FEV1 (65% to 82%, p=0.041), and 6-minute walk distance (313 to 352 metres, p=0.007), while none of these measures improved in the control group; however, lung diffusing capacity (DLCO) did not improve in either group, indicating that underlying structural damage was not reversed. summary: This exploratory crossover trial (n=21 adults with long-COVID and self-reported cognitive complaints) tested whether 3 hours/day of portable supplemental oxygen via a concentrator (POC) for 2 weeks improved cognitive performance compared to standard of care. The primary outcome was the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) total score, which showed no overall difference between POC and control (adjusted mean difference -0.09, 95% CI -1.031 to 0.850); a post-hoc Period 1 analysis suggested a possible advantage for POC (difference 1.705, 95% CI 0.140 to 3.271), driven partly by attention and visuospatial subscores. Only 43% of participants met the pre-defined compliance threshold, and the study was explicitly descriptive with no formal hypothesis testing, making all findings preliminary.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary MoCA outcome: adjusted mean difference -0.090 (95% CI -1.031, 0.850), a null result; post-hoc Period 1 difference was 1.705 (95% CI 0.140, 3.271) but was unplanned and based on n=21 with 43% compliance.

summary: This small Ukrainian RCT tested the addition of Tivorel (levocarnitine 20mg + arginine hydrochloride 42mg, IV then oral) plus quercetin 240mg/day for one month to standard care in 40 hospitalized adults with type 2 diabetes and post-COVID syndrome. Compared to standard care alone, the combination treatment reduced fasting glucose 1.8-fold, lowered HbA1c by 28.2%, cut total cholesterol by 18.2%, raised HDL by 38.6%, and reduced CRP by 50.5% and D-dimer by 25.4%, with all primary group comparisons reaching statistical significance. The study has no blinding, no placebo control, very small arms (n=20 per group), and no pre-registration, making results hypothesis-generating only.
