Patients were blinded to drug vs placebo, but physicians conducting testing were not described as blinded. Study is described as 'blind' without specifying who was blinded.

No information on dropouts, withdrawals, or CONSORT flow diagram. Sample sizes vary across meridians in the results tables, suggesting not all patients had all meridians tested, but reasons are not explained.

Outcome is electrodermal impedance measured by an unvalidated device (EAV). The physiological basis is stated to be unknown. No validated clinical outcome measures (e.g. patient-reported symptom scales) are used. Physician blinding to group assignment is unclear.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This study measures electrodermal impedance via EAV (electroacupuncture according to Voll), a device/method with no established clinical validity. The outcomes are not recognized clinical endpoints for long COVID. 2. The intervention is a single-session diagnostic procedure (medicament testing), not a therapeutic intervention in the conventional sense. The 'treatment' and 'follow-up' occur within the same diagnostic session (pre-test vs post-test during the same visit). Duration fields are null as this is a within-session measurement. 3. Table 3 (positive responders) and Table 4 (negative responders) each show per-arm n, pre-test AMV mean±SD, and post-test AMV mean±SD for different meridian subsets. The n values per meridian vary because not all patients had all meridians affected. 4. Table 3 mentions 12 meridians but the text also references 'Ma' (Stomach) as one that showed restoration; however no Ma row appears in the table as extracted — likely a discrepancy in the paper. 5. Figure 2 and Figure 3 contain pre-test EAV readings plotted with means and standard errors, but numerical values are only available in Table 3 and Table 4. 6. P-values are reported as thresholds (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001) between groups and vs pre-test, not exact values. Between-group p-values were extracted as the threshold stated in table notes (*** = p<0.001 coded as 0.001, ** = p<0.01 coded as 0.01). 7. The duplicate entry for arm_id=2 in baseline_demographics.per_arm is an artifact — only one control arm exists. 8. Negative responder outcomes (Table 4): the He, Du, Pa/Mi(D), Hau, Ni, Bl meridians showed p<0.01 between groups; Al showed p<0.001 between groups; Ne showed p<0.01 between groups. These are all showing worsening (more negative drop) in the intervention arm compared to placebo for the negative-responder subgroup. 9. The study does not report conventional long COVID clinical outcomes (fatigue scores, QoL, functional status). This paper is of very limited relevance to a conventional long COVID meta-analysis.

summary: This study tested electroacupuncture according to Voll (EAV) diagnosis combined with medicament testing (MT) — placing an RNA polymerase nosode, ribavirin tablets, and dexamethasone pills into a device honeycomb while measuring skin electrical impedance at acupuncture points — in 99 long COVID patients aged 16–50 in Uzbekistan. In the 50-patient treatment group, MT with these three substances produced statistically significant normalization of electrodermal activity readings at 12 meridian points compared to pre-test values and to the placebo control group (p<0.001 for key meridians including nervous degeneration and circulation). A critical caveat is that EAV and medicament testing have no established physiological basis and are not validated diagnostic or therapeutic tools; the outcome measure is device readings of skin electrical impedance, not any clinical symptom or functional endpoint, making the clinical relevance of these findings uninterpretable.

trial_rating.result_basis: Post-MT AMV on nervous degeneration meridian: main group 5.65 ± 1.14 vs pre-test -3.87 ± 1.66 (p<0.001 vs control), but this measures device impedance readings, not a validated clinical outcome; no clinical symptom data were analyzed as a primary endpoint.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper was submitted as a CONSORT-EHEALTH checklist form, not as the full manuscript. As a result, almost all quantitative data (per-arm means, SDs, sample sizes per arm, exact timepoint definitions in weeks) are missing — only inferential statistics (beta coefficients, t-values, p-values from HLMs) are quoted verbatim from the manuscript. Per-arm n_randomized breakdown is not reported in this form. Timepoints T1-T5 are referenced but their timing in weeks is not specified. The intervention duration of 6 weeks is stated. Between-group comparisons for Hypothesis 1 combined IG+ACG vs CompG; for Hypothesis 2 compared IG vs ACG with no significant group differences found. For work ability, beta=0.78 (t271=2.73, p=0.01) for IG+ACG vs CompG; for social participation beta=0.27 (t277=2.89, p=0.004) for IG+ACG vs CompG. For symptom severity vs CompG: T1-T2 interaction beta=0.14 (t549=4.31, p<0.001); T2-T4 interaction beta=0.14 (t549=4.57, p<0.001). For IG vs ACG (Hypothesis 2): no significant group differences in any outcome. Hypothesis 3 regression: symptom reduction predicted social participation (beta=-0.34, t111=-2.11, p=0.04, R2=0.24) but not work ability (beta=-0.18, t111=-1.92, p=0.06, R2=0.32). Data for figures referenced but not extractable from this form. Total N=1020 patients recruited. | Pass3 agent: PDF is CONSORT checklist only (not main paper). HLM betas reported, no CIs.

summary: This German RCT (the ASAP project) tested a 6-week digital rehabilitation program combined with personal coaching ('personal pilots') for 1,020 adults with long COVID (post-acute COVID-19 syndrome, PACS) in Bavaria. Patients were randomised to either a tailored intervention group (IG, receiving clinic-based diagnostic assessment plus personalised digital exercises averaging 50 minutes/day) or an active control group (ACG, receiving symptom-targeted digital exercises plus personal pilot support but no formal assessment), with a non-randomised usual-care comparison group (CompG) included via propensity score matching. Both the IG and ACG showed significantly greater symptom reduction and higher work ability and social participation compared to the untreated CompG, but there was no significant difference in any outcome between the IG and ACG, meaning the additional diagnostic assessment and tailoring did not produce greater benefit than the simpler intervention. No harms were reported in any group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Symptom severity reduction was significantly greater in IG+ACG vs CompG (group×time interaction β=0.14, t549=4.57, p<0.001); work ability was higher in treatment groups vs CompG (β=0.78, t271=2.73, p=0.01); but IG vs ACG showed no significant difference on any primary outcome.

The table header in Table 1 erroneously labels both groups as 'Group 1'; from context Group 1=omeprazole monotherapy (arm_id=2 in this extraction, as arm_id=1 is the primary intervention) and Group 2=omeprazole+Kolofort (arm_id=1). Note: arm_id assignment follows schema convention (arm_id=1=primary intervention=Kolofort+omeprazole; arm_id=2=control=omeprazole alone). 3. The p-values reported in Table 1 (p=0.001 for both VAS outcomes at baseline) are suspicious — these appear to indicate within-group pre-post significance markers rather than between-group baseline differences, as the baseline values are not significantly different. The paper states no significant difference at baseline. 4. The conflict of interest disclosure notes industry support from Materia Medica, the manufacturer of Kolofort. 5. The between-group p-value for the primary outcome (epigastric pain VAS at day 28) is stated as p<0.01. 6. SF-36 between-group significance markers (**) in Table 2 apply to GH, RP, BP, RE, and MH subscales; PF, VT, and SE did not reach between-group significance. The calculated between-group differences for non-significant subscales are included for completeness.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding Kolofort (a drug containing processed antibodies to S100 protein, TNF-alpha, and histamine) to standard omeprazole therapy (80 mg/day) improved functional dyspepsia symptoms in 42 post-COVID-19 outpatients aged 26–47. By day 28, the combination group had significantly lower epigastric pain scores on a 10-point VAS compared to omeprazole alone (p<0.01), and showed faster resolution of other dyspeptic symptoms (heaviness, early satiety, nausea) by day 5 (p<0.02); however, full symptom resolution at day 28 reached ~90% in both groups with no statistically significant difference between them (p=0.06). The combination group also showed greater quality-of-life improvements on SF-36 pain, general health, role-emotional, and mental health subscales. The study was funded by the drug manufacturer (Materia Medica), which is a significant conflict of interest.

trial_rating.result_basis: Epigastric pain VAS significantly lower in combination group at day 28 (p<0.01), but complete dyspepsia resolution was ~90% in both groups with no significant difference (p=0.06); baseline VAS scores also differed significantly between groups (p=0.001), raising concerns about randomization balance.

summary: This 6-week randomized controlled trial tested whether adding manual diaphragm release (18 physiotherapist-delivered sessions) to inspiratory muscle training via a POWERbreath device was more effective than inspiratory muscle training alone in 52 men with post-COVID-19 syndrome who had hypertension and mild-to-moderate lung fibrosis. The primary outcome, maximum inspiratory pressure (a measure of breathing muscle strength), increased by 48.2% in the combined treatment group (from 82.0 to 121.5 cmH2O) compared with a non-significant 4.4% increase in the training-only group. Secondary outcomes also favored the combined group: systolic blood pressure fell by 16.7% vs 2.5%, dyspnea scores improved by 48.9% vs 12.8%, fatigue scores fell by 51.6% vs 17.7%, and 6-minute walk distance increased by 13.5% vs 3.9%; the study was limited to men only and did not include objective measures of diaphragm function such as ultrasound.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome PImax increased 48.17% in the combined group (82.0 to 121.5 cmH2O) vs non-significant 4.35% in the control group; between-group interaction p<0.001, partial eta-squared=0.330.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether incentive spirometry (IS) or diaphragmatic breathing (DB) exercises added to standard care could improve breathlessness in 60 long COVID patients with confirmed diaphragmatic dysfunction following mild-to-moderate acute COVID-19. After 8 weeks, 75% of the IS group and 55% of the DB group showed improvement on the mMRC dyspnoea scale, compared with only 15% in the standard care group; both active interventions also significantly improved 6-minute walk distance and oxygen saturation, while standard care alone produced no significant change in any outcome. IS outperformed DB on several measures including 6-minute walk distance (397 m vs 358 m at follow-up). The trial was open-label and small (20 patients per arm), limiting confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: mMRC dyspnoea scale improved from 1.9 to 0.7 in the IS group and 1.6 to 0.9 in the DB group (both p<0.001), versus no significant change in standard care; 75% vs 55% vs 15% responder rates across groups.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 weeks of supervised endurance training versus concurrent (combined resistance and endurance) training versus no exercise in 42 non-hospitalized adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome (symptoms persisting over 12 weeks, no post-exertional malaise). Both exercise groups showed significant improvements in peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) compared to controls: endurance training gained +3.9 ml/min/kg and concurrent training gained +3.2 ml/min/kg, with a significant time-by-group interaction (partial eta² = 0.267). Fatigue severity scores fell significantly in both exercise groups (Hedges' g = 0.63 and 0.82) but not in controls, though health-related quality of life improved across all three groups including the non-exercising control; two participants withdrew due to symptom worsening, and the overall dropout rate was 36%, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: VO2peak time*group interaction p=0.002, partial eta²=0.267; endurance group +3.9 ml/min/kg (g=1.75), concurrent group +3.2 ml/min/kg (g=1.02), control group non-significant trend +0.9 ml/min/kg (p=0.054).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding systemic ozone therapy (10 intravenous infusions of ozonized saline over 30 days) to standard drug therapy improved outcomes in 140 adults aged 18–45 with post-COVID asthenic syndrome—a condition marked by chronic fatigue, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, and anxiety. Patients who received ozone therapy alongside the succinic acid-based drug showed substantially greater reductions in inflammatory markers (TNF-α down 39%, IL-1β down 33%, IL-6 down 36% versus the drug-only group) and larger improvements across all symptom scales: fatigue scores fell 36.7% more, insomnia scores 50.5% more, and anxiety scores 45.8% more than in the comparison group, with 94.2% of ozone-treated patients rated as disease-free at 30 days versus 62.9% in the control group. No adverse events were reported in either group, though the study was conducted at a single centre in Crimea without blinding, which limits how broadly the findings can be applied.

trial_rating.result_basis: 94.2% of ozone therapy patients rated CGI-S 'no disease' vs 62.9% controls (p=0.001); insomnia score (ISI) 50.5% lower in ozone group (p<0.001); fatigue score (MFI-20) 36.7% lower (p=0.001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Paper is bilingual (Russian/English). The 'change in main group' values for the primary and secondary endpoints (Table 5) represent mean change within the intervention arm (arm_id=1). The paper reports the difference of mean changes as the between-group effect (e.g., 17.91 W for work capacity). The change values for the control group (arm_id=2) are negative, indicating slight worsening. The baseline p-value for post-occlusive microcirculation was 0.062 (not significant at 0.05), but groups had numerically different means (T=110.60 vs R=157.66), with arm_id=1 (intervention) starting lower. The paper describes change in post-occlusive microcirculation as +80.42% in the abstract but Table 5 shows absolute change of 80.42 BPU units in intervention group; the percentage likely refers to percent change from baseline [(191.02-110.60)/110.60 = 72.7%] or is computed differently. Oxygen kinetics units not explicitly stated (likely ml/min/kg or L/min). Age reported as median with IQR only; no mean age reported in Table 1. The note in the text states 'average age 58 years in main group and 47 years in control group' which likely refers to median given Table 1 shows medians of 62 and 50 - these are approximate descriptions. Arm_id=1 is the intervention (T=therapy/dynamic inversion table); arm_id=2 is the control (R=rehabilitation/standard care). The between-group effect for the difference in changes (Table 5) was used for between_group_effects where verbatim values were available.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a dynamic inversion table — a motorized platform that repeatedly tilts patients at low frequencies to alter gravitational pressure on blood vessels — against standard rehabilitation in 70 adults with long COVID (persistent symptoms for over 12 weeks post-infection). The treatment group (n=35) completed 10 daily 30-minute sessions on the device; the control group (n=35) followed standard rehabilitation guidelines. The primary outcome, exercise work capacity during cardiorespiratory stress testing, increased by 13.31 W in the treatment group versus a decline of 4.60 W in controls (p<0.001). Post-occlusive microvascular blood flow, a marker of endothelial function, rose by 80.42% in the treatment group while declining slightly in controls; no adverse events were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome: work capacity +13.31 W (treatment) vs -4.60 W (control), difference 17.91 W, 95% CI [12.03; 23.8], p<0.001. Groups differed significantly at baseline on several secondary measures, with the treatment group starting worse.

summary: This 12-week quasi-experimental study tested a combined Progressive Muscle Relaxation Technique (PMRT) and Spinal Muscle Training (SMT) protocol, delivered via telerehabilitation, against standard neurosurgical care (SNC) in 60 male manual labourers aged 40-50 in Karnataka, India with long COVID-associated paraspinal back pain. The primary outcomes were serum IL-17 (an inflammation marker) and functional independence (Katz ADL score): the PMRT+SMT group reduced IL-17 from 31.13 to 18.96 pg/mL versus 31.05 to 28.89 pg/mL in the SNC group (p<0.001, Cohen's d=3.84), and improved ADL scores from 2.93 to 5.03 versus 2.50 to 3.53 in controls (p<0.001, Cohen's d=2.33). Key caveats are the non-randomised design with allocation by clinic scheduling slot, an all-male sample, small N of 30 per arm, and no long-term follow-up, all of which limit confidence in the findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: IL-17 reduced by 12.17 pg/mL in the experimental group vs 2.16 pg/mL in controls (between-group p<0.001, Cohen's d=3.84); ADL improved by 2.10 points vs 1.03 points (between-group p<0.001, Cohen's d=2.33).

summary: Brainmax (a succinic acid complex with trimethylhydrazinium, a neuroprotective antioxidant) was tested against placebo in 160 adults with post-COVID fatigue syndrome, enrolled 3–12 months after confirmed COVID-19 infection. Over 41 days of sequential parenteral then oral therapy, Brainmax produced a median 19.5-point reduction in fatigue on the MFI-20 scale compared to 3 points in the placebo group (p<0.001), along with significant improvements in sleep quality, fatigue, dizziness, and anxiety scores. Adverse events were mild and transient, with no serious adverse events recorded in either group; however, the drug is approved and marketed only in Russia, and the study was funded by the manufacturer.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome: MFI-20 median change -19.5 [-27; -11] points in Brainmax group vs -3 [-7; 1] points in placebo group, p<0.001.

summary: This open-label controlled trial tested combined inhalations of nitric oxide (60 ppm) and molecular hydrogen (<4%) for 90 minutes daily over 10 days in 34 adults with long COVID respiratory symptoms, enrolled on average 22 months after confirmed COVID-19 infection. Compared to an untreated control group (n=17 per arm), the treatment group showed significant reductions in dyspnea, cough, fatigue, and palpitations (p<0.005), a 46.7-metre improvement in 6-minute walk distance (p=0.01), better quality of life on SF-36 (p=0.006), and reduced oxidative damage markers (FORT score fell from 595 to 391.5 units, p=0.001). The study is open-label with only 17 patients per arm and no blinding or sham control, which substantially limits the reliability of these findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk distance increased by 46.7±43.5 m in the treatment group vs no change in controls (p=0.01); FORT oxidative damage score dropped from 595.0 to 391.5 units (p=0.001 within group; between-group p<0.001).

summary: This Russian multicenter double-blind placebo-controlled RCT tested BRAINMAX (a succinic acid/trimethylhydrazinium complex, given sequentially as IV then oral formulation over 41 days) in 160 adults with post-COVID syndrome assessed 3–12 months after infection. summary: This double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial tested EchA Marine, a dietary supplement derived from sea urchin eggs and rich in Echinochrome A, in 46 long COVID patients (18–60 years) across three Argentine hospitals over 90 days. The primary outcome was health-related quality of life measured by the EQ-5D-3L questionnaire: after three months, the treatment group showed statistically significant improvements in mobility (p=0.013) and pain/discomfort (p=0.005), as well as in overall health perception by VAS (p=0.022) and time trade-off scores (p=0.003), while the placebo group showed no improvement in these dimensions. Secondary inflammatory biomarkers also shifted favourably, with IL-2 falling (84 vs 90 pg/ml, p=0.038) and anti-inflammatory IL-10 rising (15.5 vs 12.4 pg/ml, p=0.038) in the treatment group; however, the trial is small (24 treated, 22 placebo), and two of the study authors are founders or employees of the company that supplied the supplement.

trial_rating.result_basis: Pain/discomfort dimension: F=8.863, p=0.005; mobility: F=6.738, p=0.013; overall multivariate treatment effect at endpoint: Pillai's Trace=0.323, p=0.048.

summary: A 63-day remote medical and psychological rehabilitation program—incorporating cognitive-behavioural therapy, mindfulness, art therapy, and body-oriented practices—was tested in 240 Ukrainian adults with anxiety and depressive post-COVID syndrome during the ongoing war. At 3-month follow-up, 92.6% of the treatment group (n=122) had minimal anxiety on the GAD-7 versus 51.7% with severe anxiety in the comparison group, and 84.3% of the treatment group had minimal depression on the PHQ-9 versus 37.3% with severe depression in controls (all p<0.001). No participants in the treatment group had clinically significant PTSD symptoms at follow-up, while the comparison group's PTSD case count grew from 44 to 47; 73.8% of the treatment group reached the highest quality-of-life tier versus 6.8% in controls. The study is unblinded and conducted in a wartime context that may limit generalisability, and the comparison group received no structured alternative intervention.

trial_rating.result_basis: GAD-7 mean score at Day 153: treatment group 1.11 ± 1.63 vs comparison group 13.14 ± 4.60, t=27.197, p<0.001; PHQ-9 mean score: 2.31 ± 3.14 vs 16.18 ± 7.90, t=17.98, p<0.001.

summary: This randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested whether hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) — at four different combinations of oxygen concentration and chamber pressure — improved symptoms and cognitive function in 101 long COVID patients with an average illness duration of about 21 months. After 10 treatment sessions, there were no statistically significant differences between any of the four groups on any primary outcome, including quality of life scores, a 6-minute walking test, or five neurocognitive tests. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding systemic ozone therapy (10 daily intravenous infusions of ozonated saline) to standard pharmacological treatment (Brainmax, a meldonium/antioxidant combination) improved symptoms in 140 adults aged 18–45 with post-COVID asthenic syndrome. The primary finding was that patients receiving adjunctive ozone therapy showed substantially greater improvements across all outcomes: fatigue scores (MFI-20) fell 74.7% vs 60.3% in controls, insomnia scores (ISI) fell 81.3% vs 42.9%, anxiety scores (HAM-A) fell 72.8% vs 48.3%, and cognitive scores (MoCA) improved 17.1% vs 4.9%, with 94.2% of ozone-treated patients rated symptom-free vs 62.9% in the control group. A notable caveat is that both groups received an active drug rather than placebo, making it impossible to isolate ozone therapy's effect from pharmacotherapy alone, and the study was conducted at a single site in Crimea with no reported pre-registration.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. Baseline spirometry data is reported for the combined cohort (n=106), not separately per arm. The same baseline value has been assigned to both arms as the most accurate representation. 2. The paper uses 'M ± m' notation where m=SE (standard error of mean), not SD - all variability values placed in 'se' field accordingly. 3. The Stange test baseline uses '+' notation (32.9 + 2.2) rather than '±', treated as SE. 4. CGI denominators: Group I shows n=55 in CGI results (26.7% of 15 = 56.1, 35.7% of 20 = 56.0, suggesting 55 or 56); the text says 90.9% recognized treatment as effective (50/55=90.9%), implying n=55 for CGI analysis in Group I, suggesting 1 patient not evaluated. 5. No primary outcome is explicitly designated. 6. HADS scores reported as frequency of atypical depressive symptoms (categorical counts), not continuous scale scores - no mean HADS subscale scores reported. 7. The comparison group received vitamin B12 (not a true inert placebo tablet) but IV placebo. 8. Baseline values for Table 2 are combined (n=106) with no per-arm breakdown - this limits between-group change-from-baseline calculations. 9. The paper reports fold-reduction ratios (e.g., 'reduced 6-fold' for chest pain) as the primary between-group comparison metric, not standard effect sizes. | Pass3 agent confirmed: M±SEM only (no SDs, no CIs). Baseline combined for both groups.

summary: This Russian randomised controlled trial tested cytoflavin (a combination of inosine, nicotinamide, riboflavin, and succinic acid) added to standard outpatient rehabilitation in 106 adults (average age 52) with post-COVID syndrome, comparing it against placebo plus vitamin B12 over 30 days. Patients receiving cytoflavin showed substantially greater reductions in anxiety and clinical depression on the HADS scale — anxiety ratings fell nearly 9-fold versus 2.5-fold in the control group, and clinical depression ratings fell 12.5-fold versus 5.5-fold (p<0.01) — alongside greater improvements in respiratory function, chest pain, headache, and tachycardia. The control group received an active comparator (vitamin B12) rather than a fully inert placebo, and both groups also received psychotherapy, physiotherapy, and vacuum spinal therapy, making it difficult to isolate cytoflavin's specific contribution.

trial_rating.result_basis: Anxiety frequency fell from 48.2% to 5.4% in the cytoflavin group versus 56.0% to 22.0% in controls; clinical depression from 25.0% to 2.0% versus 22.0% to 4.0% (p<0.01 for between-group differences on HADS).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Paper is in Ukrainian with an English abstract. The note symbol § in the original is used as ± per the submission note. The paper states values as (M ± m) where m is the standard error of the mean (SEM), not SD — however, following standard convention in Ukrainian medical literature and the paper's notation, these are reported as SD in this extraction but may actually be SEM; meta-analysts should verify. Randomization is described in the title and methods as dividing patients into two groups but no explicit randomization procedure is described — the study may be quasi-experimental rather than a true RCT. The intervention arm combines erdosteine AND breathing exercises, making it impossible to attribute effects to either component alone. The overall ACQ baseline score reported in the text (3.6 ± 0.1) differs slightly from per-arm values in Table 1 (arm1: 3.8 ± 0.2; arm2: 3.4 ± 0.1), suggesting the overall figure may be a rounded average. Clinical effectiveness of 99.3% stated in conclusions but calculation methodology not explained. Between-group p-values are not reported for most outcomes; within-group p<0.05 is reported for statistically significant changes. The paper does not report any adverse events.

summary: This controlled trial tested whether adding erdosteine (300 mg twice daily, an antioxidant mucolytic) plus structured breathing exercises to standard inhaled corticosteroid/formoterol therapy improved outcomes in 30 adults with bronchial asthma and post-COVID syndrome over 2 months. In the 15-patient treatment group, asthma control scores improved from 11.1 to 16.6 on the ACT (a clinically meaningful change of 5.5 points, exceeding the 3-point threshold) and from 3.8 to 2.4 on the ACQ-7, compared to smaller, non-clinically-meaningful improvements in the 15-patient control group receiving standard therapy alone. Lung function measures (FVC, FEV1, airway flow rates) and 6-minute walk distance (471 to 515 metres, exceeding the 25-metre minimal important difference) improved significantly only in the treatment group, though the study is limited by its very small sample size and lack of blinding or randomisation details.

trial_rating.result_basis: ACT score improved by 5.5 points (11.1 to 16.6) in the treatment group vs 2.9 points in controls; ACQ-7 improved by 1.4 points vs 0.4 points; 6MWT distance increased by 43 metres vs 14 metres, p<0.05 for treatment group outcomes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Baseline DASS-21 total score differs between arms (MBCT: 39.00±6.01 vs Control: 47.27±11.79), suggesting imperfect matching despite the authors' claim of group matching on psychological distress. The Bonferroni post-hoc table (Table 5) reports pre-test to post-test mean differences with SE (Resilience: 35.25±2.14; Psychological distress: 40.77±1.57) but these appear to be pooled/overall contrasts rather than per-arm values and are not easily attributable to a single arm, so they are not included as arm_results. The paper describes 8 sessions but does not specify session frequency (assumed weekly based on 8-week MBCT protocol). The F-statistics and eta-squared from the mixed ANOVA (Table 4) are reported in the between_group_effects p_values; no CI or effect size with CI was provided for between-group comparisons.

summary: This quasi-experimental study tested 8 weekly sessions of online individual mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) in 30 adults aged 25-55 who had been discharged from hospital after COVID-19 in Tehran, Iran, and who had moderate symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress (DASS-21 score ≥39) at enrolment. MBCT produced large improvements in both primary outcomes: resilience scores rose from 26.5 to 72.7 (vs. 25.7 to 30.1 in controls), and psychological distress scores fell from 39.0 to 5.7 (vs. 47.3 to 46.5 in controls), with both between-group differences highly significant (p=0.0001) and effect sizes above η²=0.87. These gains were maintained at a 2-month follow-up. Key caveats are the very small sample (15 per arm), lack of randomisation (matching-based allocation), self-report outcomes only, and no active control condition, all of which substantially limit causal inference.

trial_rating.result_basis: Resilience post-test: MBCT group 72.67±6.33 vs. control 30.13±9.06 (F=45.21, p=0.0001, η²=0.89); psychological distress post-test: MBCT 5.73±2.96 vs. control 46.47±5.75 (F=154.54, p=0.0001, η²=0.94).

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested 8 weeks of creatine monohydrate (8 g/day), creatine plus glucose (8 g + 3 g/day), or glucose-only placebo in 15 adults with long COVID (5 per arm). Both creatine groups raised brain creatine levels significantly at multiple locations versus placebo, with the creatine-glucose combination showing significant within-group reductions in five symptoms — body aches, breathing difficulties, concentration difficulties, headache, and general malaise — with large effect sizes for body aches (d=1.33), headache (d=1.12), and concentration difficulties (d=0.80). trial_rating.result_basis: Two-way ANOVA interaction effects for all symptom outcomes were non-significant (p>0.05); within-group reductions in the creatine-glucose arm reached significance (e.g. headache p≤0.05, d=1.12) but no between-group superiority over placebo was established, with only n=5 per arm.

summary: A Russian randomized controlled trial tested Baktiminal, a metabiotic supplement containing metabolites of Bacillus subtilis and fructooligosaccharides (one capsule twice daily for 28 days), against no additional treatment in 40 outpatients with post-COVID gastrointestinal symptoms and fatigue. The treated group showed a statistically significant 44% reduction in total gastrointestinal symptom scores (from 45.2 to 25.5 points on the GSRS scale, p<0.0001), with significant improvements in diarrhea, dyspepsia, and abdominal pain, while the control group improved by only 8%. Fatigue scores also improved significantly in the treated group (51.5 to 43.3 points, p<0.05), and gut microbiome analysis in a subset of 10 treated patients showed restoration of Lactobacillus spp. and Akkermansia muciniphila, which was completely absent at baseline in all post-COVID patients tested. No adverse events were reported, though the small sample size, single-centre design, lack of blinding, and use of an unregistered dietary supplement substantially limit the reliability of these findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Total GSRS score decreased from 45.2 to 25.5 points (44% reduction) in the treated group vs 42.2 to 38.9 (8% reduction) in controls, between-group difference p<0.0001.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical limitation: per-arm means and SDs are NOT reported for the primary outcomes (flanker score, BDNF) at either timepoint — data appear only in figures. The baseline fluid composite mean (94.95) and crystallized composite mean (111.3) and discrepancy mean (16.35) are reported as overall sample averages, not per arm. The overall sample resting HR mean (79.62 bpm) is also only reported for the full sample at baseline vs. normative comparison, not per arm. F-statistics and adjusted p-values are reported for group-by-session interaction effects for flanker (F(1,1)=11.69, p_adj=0.014, pe2=0.41), BDNF (F(1,1)=9.76, p_adj=0.0314, pe2=0.22), and long-term HR (F(1,1)=46.92, p_adj=0.027, pe2=0.365), and short-term HR change (t=-2.61, df=14.811, p_adj=0.04), but no per-arm means or SDs accompany these statistics. Partial eta squared is reported as effect size for ANOVA outcomes. The linear regression between BDNF change and flanker change: F=37.79, R2_adj=0.825, p_adj=0.003. Per-arm n is inferred as 10 each (20 completers, 1:1 randomization, 2 lost to follow-up from 22). Randomization arm sizes for those lost to follow-up not specified. Outcomes not quantitatively extractable due to data only in figures: Dimension Change Card Sorting, List Sorting Working Memory, Oral Reading Recognition, Picture Vocabulary, Pattern Comparison, Picture Sequence Memory, GDNF, IL6, IL10, TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, heart rate variability. The supplemental Table 1 with original p-values, adjusted p-values, effect sizes, and 95% CIs is referenced but not included in the paper text.

summary: This open-label pilot study tested 40 Hz vibratory and auditory treatment (VAT) — simultaneous vibrotactile and sound stimulation delivered via a portable device — in 20 adults with long COVID-associated cognitive impairment. Over 4 weeks of daily home use (20 sessions), the treatment group showed a statistically significant improvement in the Flanker test of selective attention and response inhibition compared to controls (group-by-session interaction F(1,1)=11.69, p=0.014, partial eta squared=0.41), and plasma BDNF levels increased significantly in the treatment group, with BDNF change strongly correlated with Flanker score change (R²=0.825). The study is unblinded with no sham control, a conflict of interest (one author receives royalties from the device manufacturer), and only 10 participants per arm, so results must be interpreted with caution.

trial_rating.result_basis: Flanker test group-by-session interaction F(1,1)=11.69, p_adjusted=0.014, partial eta squared=0.41; 80% of treatment group improved vs 20% of controls.

summary: This multicenter prospective quasi-experimental study (TUN-EndCOV) tested sulodexide (250 LSU twice daily for 21 days) against no treatment in 290 long COVID patients from Tunisia who had confirmed endothelial dysfunction at baseline. Sulodexide produced significantly higher rates of chest pain resolution (83.7% vs. 43.6%, p<0.001) and palpitations resolution (85.2% vs. 52.9%, p=0.009), along with greater improvement in endothelial function (median delta-EQI 0.66 vs. 0.18, p<0.001). The main caveat is that this was a non-randomized, non-blinded quasi-experimental design with no placebo control, which substantially limits causal inference despite the large observed effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: Chest pain recovery 83.7% vs. 43.6% (p<0.001); palpitations recovery 85.2% vs. 52.9% (p=0.009); median delta-EQI 0.66 vs. 0.18 (p<0.001).

summary: This trial tested 16–18 days of mountain spa rehabilitation, with or without ubiquinol (coenzyme Q10, 2×100 mg/day), in 36 long COVID patients who had been hospitalised with severe COVID-19 and still had persistent symptoms 3–7 months later. The primary biological finding was that platelet mitochondrial Complex I-linked oxidative phosphorylation capacity was markedly reduced in patients at baseline (approximately 30–46% below healthy controls) and recovered significantly only in the group receiving ubiquinol: CI-linked OXPHOS increased by 25% after rehabilitation plus supplementation (p=0.043) and by 50% after an additional 12–14 days of home supplementation, compared to a non-significant 12% increase with rehabilitation alone. Clinically, 62.8% of symptoms resolved in the ubiquinol group versus 51.8% in the rehabilitation-only group, and lung function improved in both groups; the study was small (14 and 22 patients per arm) and unblinded, with ubiquinol donated by the manufacturer.

trial_rating.result_basis: CI-linked OXPHOS capacity increased 25% in MRQ2 vs MRQ1 (p=0.043) and 50% in MRQ3 vs MRQ1 (p=0.072); rehabilitation-only group showed only 12% increase (ns).

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial tested weekly intravenous recombinant C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH, Ruconest) against placebo in 36 adults with post-COVID neurological and fatigue symptoms lasting more than 4 weeks. Depression scores (BDI-II) improved by 32% (8.7 points) during 8 weeks of C1-INH treatment, and fatigue scores showed a trend toward improvement, but most changes were not statistically significant and the study was explicitly exploratory with no pre-specified primary outcome or power calculation. Long COVID patients also showed markedly reduced immune signaling compared to healthy controls, but no serious safety signals were identified with C1-INH.

trial_rating.result_basis: BDI-II improved by 8.7 points (32%) with C1-INH (p=0.0010), but fatigue (FSS +0.6 points, p=0.5337) and pain (McGill -0.4 points, p=0.6270) did not reach significance; no pre-specified primary outcome was designated.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, controlled trial tested oral oxaloacetate (OAA) at 2,000 mg/day for 42 days against a rice flour placebo in 69 adults with long COVID who had moderate-to-severe fatigue and post-exertional malaise. The primary outcome—fatigue reduction on the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire—was not met, with a negligible between-group effect size (Cohen's d = -0.093, p = 0.71). Secondary measures showed OAA-treated participants had greater early improvement in fatigue and total symptom burden on the DSQ-SF at day 21, and significantly better performance on objective cognitive tests (total cognitive efficiency +10.7% vs. -0.04%, p = 0.007 at day 42). The trial was funded by Terra Biological LLC, whose officer co-authored the paper and holds a commercial interest in OAA—a conflict of interest that warrants scrutiny of the positive secondary findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome CFQ total score change: OAA -7.36 ± 1.40 vs. control -6.63 ± 1.38, t = -0.38, p = 0.71, Cohen's d = -0.093.

summary: A supervised 8-week mixed exercise program combining cardiovascular and resistance training was tested in 15 adults with post-COVID condition (PCC), compared to 10 PCC patients receiving usual care, at Université de Sherbrooke. The primary physical capacity outcomes showed significant improvements in the exercise group: sit-to-stand test improved 31% vs 11% in controls (p=0.043) and bicep curl improved 15% vs 4% (p=0.040), with daily physical activity levels also increasing significantly (p=0.007). Importantly, the program did not worsen fatigue or trigger post-exertional malaise, and plasma proteomics showed a downward trend in inflammatory markers S100A8 and CST3 following exercise; however, the study was non-randomized with a small sample size and excluded PCC patients who had previously experienced post-exertional malaise, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Sit-to-stand improved 31% vs 11% (p=0.043); bicep curl improved 15% vs 4% (p=0.040); physical activity scale interaction effect p=0.007.

summary: A randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind crossover study tested a single oral dose of ketone ester (395 mg/kg) against placebo in 12 adults previously hospitalized for COVID-19 (average 18 months post-hospitalization), measuring cardiac function by echocardiography. The primary outcome, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), did not improve with ketone esters (mean difference -0.7%, 95% CI -4.0 to 2.6%, p=0.66). A secondary measure of heart muscle contractility, global longitudinal strain (GLS), did improve significantly by 1.9 percentage points (95% CI 0.1 to 3.6%, p=0.04), indicating a modest acute benefit in myocardial function. The study was very small (n=12) and the positive GLS result should be interpreted cautiously given the null primary outcome and limited statistical power.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome LVEF showed no significant difference between ketone ester and placebo: mean difference -0.7% (95% CI -4.0 to 2.6%), p=0.66.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-group crossover study (n=20) where all participants completed all four exercise conditions (VR, no-VR, SSE-VR, 6MWT) — there are no separate randomized arms. Arm IDs are used here to represent the four conditions rather than parallel groups. The primary key comparison reported is VR vs. no-VR for dyspnea (p=0.004, t(19)=-3.269, verbatim). Overall ANOVA F-statistics are reported for each outcome across all four conditions. The 6MWT MAP value of '1,001.6 ± 8.4 mmHg' in the original text appears to be a typographical error; the value is likely 100.16 ± 8.4 mmHg and has been extracted as such. Several figures referenced in the paper contain data that are also reported in the text (HR, SpO2, dyspnea, leg fatigue). Baseline values before each condition are noted as recorded but not reported numerically in the paper text. Exercise characteristics per condition (distance, speed, duration) are extracted from Table 2. Correlations reported: handgrip vs leg fatigue at VR end (r=-0.621, p=0.003); handgrip vs leg fatigue at SSE-VR end (r=-0.450, p=0.047); handgrip vs dyspnea at SSE-VR end (r=-0.484, p=0.030); WAI vs dyspnea at baseline (r=-0.450, p=0.046); WAI vs dyspnea at VR end (r=-0.508, p=0.022); body fat vs dyspnea at SSE-VR (r=0.461, p=0.041); body fat vs 6MWT (r=-0.498, p=0.025); muscle mass vs dyspnea at SSE-VR (r=-0.466, p=0.038). These correlation outcomes were not extracted as separate outcome objects but are noted here.

summary: This study tested stationary cycling with a virtual reality (VR) headset versus cycling without VR in 20 long COVID patients (mean age 54, 80% male) with mild cognitive impairment, recruited 2 months after hospital discharge. The primary finding was that VR exercise produced significantly lower dyspnea scores than non-VR exercise (Borg CR-10: 0.5 vs. 1.1, p=0.004), with patients also spontaneously choosing to exercise more than twice as long when given free choice in the VR condition (21.8 vs. 10 minutes fixed). The study was unblinded, had no control arm, enrolled only 20 patients all infected with the Delta variant, and used a single-session crossover design rather than a rehabilitation programme.

trial_rating.result_basis: VR dyspnea score 0.5 ± 0.6 vs. no-VR 1.1 ± 0.9, p=0.004 (paired t-test, n=20).

summary: This RCT tested a 3-week, five-days-per-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program in 32 adults (average age 58) with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19, comparing a virtual reality-enhanced version (VR headset during cycle ergometer training and VR-guided relaxation) against traditional rehabilitation. Both groups significantly improved their 6-minute walk test distance — the primary outcome — with the VR group gaining an average of 57 meters and the control group 39 meters, both exceeding the minimal clinically important difference, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Both groups also showed significant reductions in perceived stress and post-exercise dyspnea, with no meaningful difference between VR and traditional formats; lung function was essentially normal at baseline and did not change significantly in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6MWT distance improved significantly within both groups (p<0.001 each), VR +57m vs control +39m, but between-group comparison was non-significant (p=0.264, Cohen's d=-0.411).

domains.support: Block randomization (block size=6) was used; groups were well-balanced at baseline on all key characteristics. Allocation was performed by a designated person (MK) after baseline testing.

Participants could not be blinded to their group allocation due to the nature of the intervention. The assessor (ML) was blinded to group allocation, but performance bias from participant knowledge of group assignment cannot be ruled out.

Dropouts occurred (n=4 IG, n=4 CG from FU1 analyses with n=34 total), with analyses conducted on completers rather than ITT. Authors state dropouts did not differ on key characteristics but analyses are per-protocol.

Validated neuropsychological instruments were used. The cognitive assessor (ML) was blinded to group allocation. Patient-reported questionnaires were self-administered, with inherent susceptibility to expectation bias.
The study was registered retrospectively (not prospectively). Multiple outcomes were tested without full pre-specification of primary vs. secondary outcomes, increasing risk of selective reporting.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: For individuals with shorter disease duration (-1 SD), no significant association between symptom count and short-delayed recall. For average disease duration, significant negative correlation (b=-0.26, p=0.012). For longer disease duration (+1 SD), stronger negative effect (b=-0.56, p<0.001). Same pattern for long-delayed recall (interaction p=0.003).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: KEY DESIGN NOTE: This is a waitlist-crossover RCT. The 2x2 ANCOVA results (Table 2) are the primary between-group comparisons (IG vs CG, BL to FU1, n=34 completers). The Table 3 data are from an exploratory analysis combining both groups after crossover (n=31 total trained), not a randomized comparison — these pre/post means and SDs are provided for completeness but reflect all completers pooled, not a randomized arm comparison. Per-arm SDs are NOT reported for the primary 2x2 ANCOVA results; only adjusted means (M_adj) and SEs are available. SDs for the combined pre-post analysis (Table 3) are provided for the pooled combined group only. Baseline SDs for individual arms from Table 1 are available for demographic variables (age, BMI, weight, height) but not for cognitive/psychological outcomes. The 2x3 ANCOVA interaction effects are reported in Supplementary Table 2 (not provided in full text); the 2x2 ANCOVA interaction p-values and partial eta-squared from Table 2 are extracted as between-group effect sizes. Cohen's d values from Table 3 are for the combined pre-post comparison and are extracted as 'smd' in the exploratory combined-group outcomes (outcomes 5-21 arm_results reflect the combined group). The n=31 for Table 3 is noted as 'df+1=31' from the t-test degrees of freedom. Fatigue analysis had n=28 (df=27+1). Word fluency SDs in Table 3 appear unusually small for formal-lexical (SD=1.22 and 1.43) — these are verbatim from paper. Outcomes 5-21 arm_results only have data for arm_id=1 (combined group) as the per-arm split was not reported for Table 3. The 6-month follow-up (FU2) data for within-group stability were described narratively but no per-arm means/SDs were provided for FU2 in the text.

summary: A three-month tablet-based training program combining cognitive exercises, relaxation techniques, and physiotherapy was tested in 40 adults (mean age 50, 80% female) with post-COVID-19 condition in Austria, randomized to intervention (n=20) or waitlist control (n=20). The primary finding was that the intervention group showed significant reductions in subjective cognitive complaints (p<0.001) and depressive symptoms on the ADS-L scale (p<0.001) compared to the control group, and their MoCA Memory Index Score remained stable while the control group's declined significantly (p=0.008 for decline in controls). Effects were not sustained after training ended, no improvements were seen in attention, executive function, fatigue, anxiety, or quality of life in the main group comparison, and the study was not prospectively registered.

trial_rating.result_basis: Subjective cognitive complaints improved significantly in the intervention group (p<0.001) while unchanged in controls (p=0.387); depression (ADS-L) improved in intervention group (p<0.001) while unchanged in controls (p=0.328); group×time interaction for subjective cognitive complaints: F(1,29)=5.83, p=0.022, ηp²=0.167.

summary: This pilot study tested a one-month telerehabilitation program — 12 supervised video-based exercise sessions plus three therapeutic education workshops — in 15 adults with ongoing symptomatic COVID-19 (persistent fatigue lasting under 3 months) who had been hospitalised but not intubated. A comparison group of 6 patients received standard physiotherapy. Fatigue measured by the Chalder Fatigue Score improved significantly across both groups (from 25.2 to 21.1 in the telerehabilitation group and 27.6 to 26.2 in the standard care group, p=0.010 time effect), alongside meaningful gains in aerobic capacity including an ~18% rise in VO2max (p=0.005) and a 15% improvement in 6-minute walk distance (p=0.019), with no adverse events reported. The study is a very small, non-randomised pilot with no untreated control arm, making it impossible to separate intervention effects from natural recovery.

trial_rating.result_basis: CFS-11 improved from 25.2 to 21.1 (tele-R) and 27.6 to 26.2 (trad-R), significant time effect p=0.010, but no group difference and no control arm without rehabilitation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The paper reports mixed ANOVA group*time interaction F-statistics and partial eta-squared values but does NOT report mean differences with CIs for between-group comparisons; between-group effect_values were calculated as (arm1 post-mean minus arm2 post-mean). The interaction F-statistics and partial eta-squared are: MoCA F(1,24)=5.500, p=0.03, partial_eta2=0.186; Stroop-C F(1,24)=7.895, p=0.01, partial_eta2=0.248; RAVLT Sum F(1,22)=11.491, p=0.003, partial_eta2=0.343; RAVLT IR F(1,22)=4.744, p=0.04, partial_eta2=0.177; RAVLT DR F(1,22)=11.074, p=0.003, partial_eta2=0.335; TMT-A F(1,24)=3.926, p=0.059, partial_eta2=0.141; PHQ-9 F(1,23)=5.975, p=0.03, partial_eta2=0.206; Stroop W-C (executive) F(1,24)=4.243, p=0.05, partial_eta2=0.150. 2. Table 1 lists n=13 per group for demographics but text states experimental n=15 assigned, 14 completing, and Table 2 header shows n=13; the discrepancy for control group (16 assigned, 13 analyzed) is not fully explained. 3. The Stroop Words vs Colors between-group effect p-value (p=0.05) assigned to the Stroop Colors-Words interaction applies to the combined Stroop W-C subtest (executive function), not individually to Stroop-W. 4. Many outcome figures referenced in text but specific figure data not extractable from removed images. 5. Follow-up within-group mean differences reported in text for EG: MoCA MD=-2.38 SE=0.76 p=0.005; Stroop-C MD=-2.46 SE=0.96 p=0.018; TMT-A MD=-1.69 SE=0.576 p=0.007; RAVLT Sum MD=-11.07 SE=3.701 p=0.007; RAVLT IR MD=-6.38 SE=3.03 p=0.047; RAVLT DR MD=-7.308 SE=2.54 p=0.009; PHQ-9 MD=-6.00 SE=1.66 p=0.002 (these are pre-post within-EG differences, not between-group). 6. The paper labels MFE-Q as a primary measure but does not report a significant interaction for it. 7. Table 2 note: values are raw scores for MoCA, T scores for most attention/memory tests, and scaled scores for Stroop, TMT, DSC, ANIMALS. The between-group mean differences calculated here are therefore on heterogeneous scales and should be interpreted with caution.

summary: This quasi-experimental pilot study tested an 8-week multimodal immersive virtual reality (IVR) intervention — combining cognitive training, physical exercise, and mindfulness — delivered twice weekly in group sessions of 5 participants, in 13 adults with post-COVID-19 condition (long COVID) who had cognitive complaints and elevated depression or anxiety scores, compared to 13 controls receiving usual care. The IVR group showed significant improvements in global cognition (MoCA mean change: 26.15 to 28.54), processing speed (Stroop Colors), verbal episodic memory (RAVLT Sum mean change: 37.31 to 48.38), and depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 mean change: 14.38 to 8.38), with large effect sizes (partial η² ranging from 0.177 to 0.343), while the control group showed no significant changes on any measure. The study is substantially limited by its non-randomised quasi-experimental design, small sample size, unblinded assessors, baseline group differences in memory scores, and absence of an active control, meaning causal attribution is uncertain.

trial_rating.result_basis: PHQ-9 depressive symptoms improved by mean 6.0 points in the IVR group vs no significant change in controls (F(1,23)=5.975, p=0.03, partial η²=0.206); RAVLT Sum group×time interaction F(1,22)=11.491, p=0.003, partial η²=0.343.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. CRITICAL LIMITATION: Post-treatment (T1, T2, T3) per-arm means and SDs are NOT reported in any table. Table 2 only provides baseline (T0) values. The mixed-effects regression model coefficients (intercept, Age, BMI, Day, Time, Group, Time:Group) reported in Tables 3-6 are model coefficients, NOT per-arm means/SDs at each timepoint. The actual timepoint-specific outcome values appear only in Figures 2 and 3 (data only in figures for T1, T2, T3). Therefore, per-arm arm_results for T1, T2, T3 cannot be extracted and are omitted. Between-group effects are reported only as regression model Time:Group interaction coefficients (b values) with p<0.05 thresholds, not as mean differences with CIs, severely limiting quantitative extraction. The coefficient b=-0.119 for ST EC T0-T1 and b=-1.826 for SD OAP EC T1-T2 are Time:Group interaction terms from mixed effects models (Group A relative to Group B), not standard mean differences. Note also that the paper uses 'SD' ambiguously — both as 'Standard Deviation' (for oscillation measures) and as 'Mean Spatial Distance' parameter; extraction uses context to distinguish these. Table 1 reports age/BMI as median (IQR) format based on Wilcoxon test usage, but values are labeled as mean+SD in the results text; treated as mean+SD per text. Group B n=23 at T0 per Figure 1 caption but n=22 per text; used n=22 for analyzed sample in mixed models per text.

summary: This randomized trial compared a 5-week spa-resort rehabilitation program (including thermal water exercise, land-based balance training, and cognitive therapy) against a supervised home-based program in 60 long COVID patients with fatigue, respiratory, cognitive, or psychological symptoms. The primary balance outcomes—antero-posterior sway amplitude (SD OAP) and mean stay time (ST)—were measured via force platform before treatment, immediately after, and at 3 and 6 months. The home-based program produced faster improvements immediately post-treatment (significant reduction in SD OAP and increase in ST with eyes closed), while the spa-resort program showed continued improvement in SD OAP from post-treatment to 3-month follow-up, suggesting more gradual but sustained gains. The trial was small (21–23 analyzed per group) and the two groups differed significantly in age at baseline (spa group mean 50 vs. home group mean 57 years), limiting direct comparison.

trial_rating.result_basis: Home-based group showed significant reduction in SD OAP (Time effect p<0.05) and increase in ST (Time effect p<0.05) at T0-T1 in EC condition; spa group showed significant decrease in SD OAP from T1 to T2 (time:Group interaction b=1.826, p<0.05); no other parameters reached significance.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial tested a marine oil supplement enriched in specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs) at doses of 500 mg, 1500 mg, or 3000 mg daily for 12 weeks in 53 adults with post-COVID syndrome. The primary outcome was change in serum levels of three pro-resolving lipid mediators (14-HDHA, 17-HDHA, 18-HEPE) and the ratio of pro-inflammatory to pro-resolving markers: all three mediators increased significantly across all dose groups (p=0.002, p=0.0007, and p=0.00001 respectively), and the inflammatory-to-resolving ratio improved significantly (p=0.025), with no dose-response difference between groups. Fatigue and dyspnea showed a non-significant trend toward improvement across all treated groups, with a 9% mean reduction in fatigue scores between weeks 4 and 12 in the 500 mg group; the placebo arm had only 5 participants, severely limiting interpretation of clinical outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: Pro-resolving mediator ratio decreased significantly (p=0.025) across all treatment groups, but fatigue improvement was non-significant (9% mean reduction in FSS for 500 mg group, no p-value reported for between-group comparison) and dyspnea showed no significant differences (Chi-square p=0.509).

This is an equivalence/non-inferiority design in practice though not labeled as such. 2. The decrement (delta) values in Table 1 for the OL group SUDs is listed as 6.80 in the table but one text passage says 6.08 — the table value 6.80 is used as primary since it is consistent with 8.55-1.75=6.80. 3. Within-arm Cohen's d and ANOVA F/p-values for pre vs post (within each group) are reported in Table 1 (e.g., SUDs IP: F=1557.13, p<10^-4; Cohen's d=1.85; SUDs OL: F=1568.14, p<10^-4, Cohen's d=2.17) but these are within-arm effects, not between-group. Between-group ANOVA rows in Table 1 give the F and p for IP vs OL comparisons. 4. No CIs reported for any effect. 5. No trial registration mentioned. 6. Session duration was 45 minutes each, 3 sessions planned within approximately 3 weeks. 7. The paper also reports Cohen's d for between-group differences (SD column of 'Difference' rows in Table 1), which are very small (0.02-0.07), indicating negligible between-group effects.

summary: This study tested remote EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) therapy, delivered via an AI-assisted platform with eye-tracking, versus standard in-person EMDR therapy in 160 adults aged 25–49 with long COVID-related PTSD symptoms. Both formats produced large reductions in all three outcome measures: SUDs scores dropped by ~6.6 points (in-person) and ~6.8 points (online) from a baseline of ~8.4–8.6; PCL-5 scores fell by ~20 and ~22 points respectively; and IES-R scores fell by ~28 points in both groups. No statistically significant differences were found between the two delivery formats on any measure, supporting equivalence of remote and in-person delivery. The main caveat is that this is a non-inferiority comparison between two active treatments with no placebo or waitlist control, so the absolute efficacy of EMDR itself cannot be independently confirmed from this trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary comparison between online and in-person groups showed no significant difference: SUDs decrement ANOVA F=1.51, p=0.22; PCL-5 decrement F=0.89, p=0.34; IES-R decrement F=0.09, p=0.76. This is a null equivalence result with no control arm.

summary: This Turkish RCT tested motion-controlled video game-based virtual reality (VR) exercise (Microsoft Xbox One Kinect) against conventional exercise (aerobic cycling, strength, stretching) in 74 adults with post-COVID-19 condition, over 8 weeks of supervised sessions three times per week. The primary outcome was pain intensity (VAS 0-10): the VR group reduced pain by 2.22 points versus 0.85 points in the conventional group, a statistically significant and large between-group difference (mean difference -1.37, 95% CI -1.73 to -1.00, p<0.001, partial η²=0.487). Arm 1 (intervention) and Arm 2 (waitlist control) represent the same 22 participants at different time periods; only 16 completed the post-intervention phase. summary: This pilot study tested four weekly online forest bathing sessions (guided virtual mindfulness-based nature engagement) in 22 adults with long COVID. The primary outcomes were anxiety, rumination, social connection, and self-reported long COVID symptom severity; compared to a four-week waitlist control period, participants showed a 49% reduction in anxiety (Cohen's d = 1.61), 48% reduction in rumination, 78% increase in social connection, and 22% reduction in long COVID symptom scores, all statistically significant. Key caveats are the very small all-female sample (N=16 completers), absence of a concurrent control group, no blinding, and the fact that three authors delivered the intervention themselves.

trial_rating.result_basis: Anxiety decreased 49% (mean 3.37 to 1.73, t=8.03, p<0.001, d=1.61); long COVID symptoms decreased 22% (mean 3.99 to 3.11, t=3.65, p<0.01, d=0.73); N=16 completers from 22 enrolled, no concurrent control group.

summary: This pilot RCT tested whether adding EMG-driven robotic upper-limb training (Luna EMG robot, 45 min twice daily) to standard inpatient neurological rehabilitation improved outcomes in 30 adults with post-COVID post-viral fatigue syndrome, all of whom had been transferred from ICUs after severe COVID-19. The primary outcome was muscle fatigue measured by EMG; the robot group showed a non-significant trend toward improvement (median change 0, range -14.9 to 34.7) while the control group showed a non-significant trend toward worsening (median change 2.8, range -55.4 to 11.3), with no significant between-group difference (p=0.909). Both groups improved significantly on functional independence (FIM, Barthel Index), handgrip strength, and self-reported fatigue (FAS), but none of these secondary outcomes differed significantly between groups. The intervention was safe with no adverse events or dropouts, but the study was too small (n=15 per arm) to draw conclusions about efficacy.

summary: This randomized trial compared a 12-week hybrid exercise program (twice-weekly supervised in-person sessions plus once-weekly tele-exercise) against fully unsupervised tele-exercise (three times weekly) in 49 previously hospitalized long COVID patients with a mean age of approximately 59 years. Both programs improved physical fitness, body composition, and lung function, with six-minute walk distance increasing by roughly 81 meters in the hybrid group and 55 meters in the tele-exercise group. The two formats produced different cognitive benefits: the hybrid group improved in visuospatial ability (score 3.2 to 3.5, p=0.008) while the tele-exercise group improved in memory (score 3.3 to 3.8, p=0.003) and had higher attention scores post-intervention; adherence was high in both groups (85-87%) with no adverse events.

summary: This randomized single-blind placebo-controlled trial tested 14 days of home-based molecular hydrogen (H2) gas inhalation (300 mL/min via nasal cannula, twice daily for 60 minutes) in 50 adults with acute post-COVID-19 syndrome, recruited 21-35 days after a positive PCR test. H2 inhalation improved 6-minute walk test distance by 64 m compared to 9 m in the placebo group (p<0.001), exceeding the 30 m minimal clinically important difference for chronic respiratory disease, and also increased forced vital capacity by 0.19 L versus -0.01 L in placebo (p=0.004) and forced expiratory volume in one second by 0.11 L versus -0.08 L in placebo (p=0.025). summary: This pilot study tested a 12-session Nordic walking program in 16 long COVID patients and 13 COVID-19 controls (without persistent symptoms), measuring blood lactate levels after each session to assess aerobic exercise capacity across different genetic profiles. Long COVID patients consistently produced higher lactate concentrations than controls during exercise, with statistically significant group differences observed in carriers of specific variants of the ACTN3 (CT and TT genotypes, sessions 1–7) and AMPD1 (CC and CT genotypes) genes, indicating impaired aerobic metabolism that improved over the course of the program. The study is a small, non-randomized pilot with 29 total participants, no randomization, no pre-intervention cardiopulmonary testing, and no control for diet or baseline fitness, substantially limiting the generalizability of its findings.

The inter-group p-value for SDNN (p=0.021) is reported in the text as a group difference but the time-by-group interaction F-value (0.579; p=0.567) is non-significant — the p=0.021 appears to refer to the between-groups main effect from ANOVA. summary: This pilot RCT tested superficial neuromodulation (NESA XSIGNAL device, 15 sessions over two months) versus a sham placebo device in 16 women with post-COVID-19 condition and dysautonomia. The primary outcome was heart rate variability (HRV): SDNN increased in the treatment group (49.06 to 69.68 ms) but decreased in controls (84.65 to 42.26 ms), with a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.021), though no significant time-by-group interaction was found. Fatigue, sleep quality, and pain threshold improved in both groups equally, with no significant differences between real and sham treatment, and the authors concluded a placebo effect cannot be ruled out. The study was severely underpowered, enrolling only 16 of a planned 60 participants.

trial_rating.result_basis: SDNN between-group difference p=0.021, but no significant time-by-group interaction; all other primary outcomes (MFIS p=0.978, PSQI p=0.352, PPT C5-C6 p=0.844) showed no significant group differences, with both real and sham groups improving equally.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 12 weeks of face-to-face versus asynchronous online Mat Pilates (three sessions per week) in 49 adults aged around 52 years with long COVID, all presenting with fatigue as a defining symptom. Only the face-to-face group showed significant improvements in the primary fatigue outcome: total Fatigue Assessment Scale scores dropped from 33.5 to 26.7 (p<0.01), alongside gains in upper limb endurance (16 to 23 repetitions), trunk flexion isometric strength (6.6 to 12.7 kg), and 6-minute walk distance (463 to 514 m). Online Pilates produced no significant changes on any outcome, and neither format affected body composition or cardiometabolic blood markers. Notably, the inactive control group showed significant increases in systolic (114 to 122 mmHg) and diastolic (75 to 81 mmHg) blood pressure over the 12 weeks, suggesting ongoing cardiovascular deterioration without exercise.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL LIMITATION: All primary and secondary outcome quantitative data (means and SDs for IFNγ, TNFα, MDA, protein carbonyls, SOD) appear only in figures (Figures 1-5) with no numerical values in text or tables. Only p-values, F-statistics, and partial eta-squared values for between-group effects were reported in text. Per-arm means and SDs cannot be extracted. RPE and VAS data reported as mode (range) only in Table 1, not mean±SD. The 4 AEs reported were described as occurring across both HIIT groups combined (n=4, 5.97%), not separated by arm. Within-group p-values extracted: HIIT IFNγ p=0.047, TNFα p<0.001; Combined IFNγ p=0.033, TNFα p<0.001; Control IFNγ p=0.860, TNFα p=0.496; HIIT MDA p=0.037, protein carbonyls p=0.047; Combined MDA p=0.014, protein carbonyls p=0.018; all groups SOD p<0.001. Between-group interaction F-statistics: IFNγ F(2,36)=0.179, η2=0.010, p=0.837; TNFα F(2,8)=2.189, η2=0.354, p=0.175; MDA F(2,56)=0.345, η2=0.012, p=0.710; protein carbonyls F(2,38)=0.032, η2=0.002, p=0.968; SOD F(2,62)=0.610, η2=0.019, p=0.546. Note: the paper states n=104 total analyzed but CONSORT details suggest initial randomization was ~112 across 3 groups; exact per-arm n at randomization not stated, only at analysis.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 8 weeks of cycling-based high-intensity interval training (HIIT), with or without daily Triphala herbal supplementation (1000 mg/day), in 104 young adults (mean age 22 years) with long COVID symptoms including fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Both the HIIT-only and HIIT-plus-Triphala groups showed significant within-group reductions in the pro-inflammatory cytokines IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha, and in oxidative stress markers MDA and protein carbonyls, compared to no change in the placebo control group; however, the between-group interaction effect was not statistically significant for any primary outcome (IFN-gamma: p=0.837; TNF-alpha: p=0.175), meaning the trial did not formally demonstrate superiority of HIIT over control. Triphala added no statistically significant benefit beyond HIIT alone and was safe with no liver or kidney toxicity detected.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcomes IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha showed within-group reductions in HIIT groups but no significant group-by-time interaction: IFN-gamma F(2,36)=0.179, p=0.837; TNF-alpha F(2,8)=2.189, p=0.175.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested eight weeks of twice-weekly supervised water-based (AQUA) or land-based (LAND) exercise training versus no exercise in 74 children aged 10-12 years with post-COVID-19 condition. Both exercise programs significantly increased absolute VO2max compared to baseline (AQUA p=0.001, LAND p=0.004), and post-intervention VO2max was significantly higher in the AQUA group versus the control group (p=0.023); relative VO2max increased significantly only in the AQUA group (p=0.017). Neither exercise program reduced fatigue scores, and no adverse events were recorded in either training group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Relative VO2max group-by-time interaction F=4.32, p=0.017; post-intervention difference between LAND and CONTROL was 4.3 ml/kg/min (95% CI 0.01 to 8.6), with no significant between-group differences for AQUA vs LAND or AQUA vs CONTROL at post-intervention.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. Most ICF outcome data are presented only in bar charts/figures (Figures 2-4) without numeric tables for individual category scores per arm at each timepoint. Only Table 3 provides medians (combined across groups, or for groups separately per regression model) for selected categories. Waiting-list arm median values for most ICF b- and d-categories are not extractable from text or tables. 2. The between-group F and p-values in Table 3 are from a general linear model adjusted for age (between-subjects factor); these are not simple pairwise comparisons. 3. The CCQ score format is ambiguous: the paper describes 10 items each 0-6, with total divided by number of questions; however, values reported (e.g., mean 20.0) suggest the total sum was used, not the averaged score. Extracted as reported. 4. Within-group p-values for mMRC and CCQ (Wilcoxon test and Friedman test) are extracted from Table 4 as within-group statistics, not between-group comparisons. 5. Symptom duration: telerehabilitation group 51 weeks (SD 27) = ~11.75 months (SD 6.25); waitlist 58 weeks (SD 31) = ~13.5 months (SD 7.25) — converted to months for baseline demographics. 6. Hospitalization: 7/67 (10%) in telerehabilitation arm and 6/42 (14%) in waitlist arm hospitalized during acute infection — percent_previously_hospitalized set to 10% for arm 1 (telerehabilitation). 7. Omitted ICF categories not in Table 3 but shown in figures: sexual functions, gastrointestinal functions, body temperature, smell/olfactory, long-term memory, sleep, cardiovascular, taste, tactile, joint mobility, widespread pain, making the bed, walking, family relationships — no per-arm numeric data extractable from text.

summary: This Swedish randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week multidisciplinary group telerehabilitation program (combining breathing exercises, mindfulness, ACT-based therapy, physical training, and psychoeducation delivered via Microsoft Teams) in 109 adults with long COVID who had persistent symptoms for at least 12 weeks after SARS-CoV-2 infection. The primary outcome was functioning and activity measured across 38 ICF categories; the telerehabilitation group showed improvements in more ICF categories than the waiting-list controls, particularly in activities and participation domains such as recreation, household tasks, stair climbing, and lifting, though statistically significant between-group differences were rare — breathing function actually improved more in the waiting-list group at 8 weeks (p=0.034). At 6 months, many participants in both groups still reported severe fatigue and cognitive impairment, highlighting the chronic nature of the condition.

trial_rating.result_basis: Between-group differences were rarely statistically significant on the primary ICF outcomes; within-group improvements were seen across multiple ICF categories in the telerehabilitation group (e.g. pain at multiple sites: Wilcoxon p=0.003; climbing stairs: p=0.02), but the between-subjects group factor was non-significant across nearly all regression model outcomes (all group F p-values >0.05).

The paper also reports a comparison arm of CAD patients (n=96) but this is a non-randomized observational comparison cohort, not a randomized arm; CAD data not included in primary extraction. 5. Workload at VT1 percent-predicted change: IT 6.8±12.9%, CT 6.8±11.5%; O2 pulse at VT1 percent-predicted change: IT 3.2±8.9%, CT 7.2±17.7%; these percent-predicted change values are also reported in the paper alongside absolute values. 6. summary: This randomized controlled trial tested moderate-intensity aerobic interval training (IT) versus continuous training (CT) on cycle ergometers in 110 long COVID patients (mean age 49, average 260 days post-infection) undergoing 4-6 weeks of inpatient medical rehabilitation in Germany. The primary outcome, peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), improved by a mean of 2.7% across all PCS patients, but the difference between IT and CT was not statistically significant (IT: +0.8% vs CT: +4.1%, p=0.157), meaning neither modality was superior to the other. Both groups showed significant improvements in fatigue, anxiety, depression, and quality of life, and the overall gains in exercise capacity were comparable to those seen in coronary artery disease patients undergoing guideline-based cardiac rehabilitation; no post-exertional malaise or training-specific fatigue was detected in either group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome VO2peak improvement did not differ between IT and CT (IT +0.8% vs CT +4.1%, p=0.157); the trial was designed to detect equivalence, not superiority, and the non-significant between-group result is the primary finding.

Table 3 reports both mean and median for QOL outcomes. The n_randomized_total of 49 is inferred: 28 intervention (26 completed + 2 withdrew) + 20 control (originally 23 but 3 did not attend post-test — however text says 'control group: n=20' at final and mentions 3 did not attend post-test, so original control randomized was 23, but the text is ambiguous).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested an 8-week resistance training program (twice weekly, 60 minutes per session at 70% of 1-repetition maximum) in 46 adults aged 65 and older who had recovered from COVID-19 and reported ongoing post-COVID symptoms such as dizziness, fatigue, and balance problems. The primary finding was a significant improvement in overall postural stability (overall stability index with eyes open) in the training group compared to controls (Z = -3.12, p = 0.0017, effect size R = 0.533), along with reduced fall risk on an unstable surface (fall-risk index 6-2, Z = -2.06, p = 0.04, R = 0.354). The training group also showed greater improvements in psychological wellbeing and social relationship domains of quality of life, and higher health satisfaction scores, compared to controls. The trial was small (26 intervention, 20 control) and conducted at a single site using gym-based resistance machines, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Overall stability index (eyes open) improved significantly in the intervention group vs control: Z = -3.12, p = 0.0017, R = 0.533 (large effect by rank-biserial correlation).

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a 6-week outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program — combining aerobic cycle training, resistance exercise, respiratory training, and stretching — in 59 post-COVID-19 patients with persistent symptoms, comparing an active inspiratory muscle training (IMT) group (n=39) against a placebo IMT group (n=22). The primary outcome, maximum inspiratory pressure (PImax), improved significantly in both groups (p<0.001), with a median increase of 52% in the IMT group and 47.5% in the placebo group, but there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups (p=0.28), meaning the additional resistive breathing device did not provide extra benefit over the general exercise program. The IMT group did show greater improvement in spirometric parameters — FEV1 rose 8.02%, FVC by 13.24%, and PEF by 9.67% — but the unequal group sizes (39 vs 22) and the preliminary nature of this dataset limit the strength of these conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome PImax improved in both groups (p<0.001 within-group) but the between-group comparison was non-significant (p=0.28, r=0.141), meaning the key experimental question — whether IMT adds benefit — was not confirmed.

summary: A 12-week Nordic Walking program (one 45-minute session per week) was tested in 16 long COVID patients and 13 healthy controls in Spain. Long COVID patients showed consistently higher blood lactate concentrations after exercise than controls throughout the program (group effect F=5.604, p=0.024), indicating impaired aerobic metabolism. Long COVID patients also improved on quality-of-life measures after the program: total SF-36 score rose from 37.2 to 48.4 (p=0.004) and EQ-5D from 41.3 to 58.8 (p=0.005), and fatigue scores (MFIS total) fell from 59.6 to 48.6 (p=0.009). Key caveats include the non-randomized design, small sample, predominantly female long COVID group (94%), and that the lactate meter frequently exceeded its upper range in long COVID patients, meaning true values may have been even higher.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome (lactate group difference) was statistically significant (F=5.604, p=0.024) but showed no time or interaction effect; SF-36 total improved by 11.2 points in long COVID group vs. 1.4 in controls (interaction p=0.002), a modest change against a low baseline.
