extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a quasi-experimental two-arm study without randomization; both arms receive active intervention differing only in number of sessions (16 vs 24). There is no control/comparator arm receiving no treatment or usual care. Mid-term timepoint differs between arms: Group 1 mid-term is at week 4 (after 8th session), Group 2 mid-term is at week 6 (after 12th session), so mid-term weeks_from_randomization is approximate. End-of-intervention is week 8 for Group 1 and week 12 for Group 2; a single timepoint_id=3 was used for both but the absolute calendar time differs. The main statistical results are within-group time effects (mixed ANOVA), not between-group comparisons: SDSD F(2,32)=3.674, p=0.037, partial eta2=0.187; SDNN F(2,32)=4.237, p=0.023, partial eta2=0.209; RMSSD F(2,32)=4.303, p=0.022, partial eta2=0.212; pNN50 F(2,32)=3.019, p=0.063, partial eta2=0.159 (marginal). Pairwise mean differences (pooled across groups, baseline to mid-term): SDSD MD=0.059ms p=0.033; SDNN MD=0.066ms p=0.037; RMSSD MD=0.079ms p=0.044. No between-group interaction effects were significant for any measure. Frequency-domain measures showed no significant time or interaction effects. Between_group_effects entries for time-domain outcomes reflect group-x-time interaction p>0.05 (not significant). The study notes that mid-term for Group 1 is the 8th session and for Group 2 is the 12th session — these are not exactly equivalent time points.

summary: A multimodal immersive virtual reality (IVR) intervention combining cognitive training, physical exercise, and mindfulness was tested in 18 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCC) in Spain, comparing 16-session (reduced) versus 24-session (extended) formats over 8–12 weeks, with heart rate variability (HRV) as the primary outcome. Contrary to expectations, time-domain HRV parameters (RMSSD, SDNN, SDSD) significantly decreased from baseline to mid-intervention in both groups, with partial recovery by the end, and no significant improvements were observed in either time-domain or frequency-domain measures at final assessment. There were no significant differences between the two session-length groups, and no control arm was included, making it impossible to isolate intervention effects from natural disease course.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary HRV outcomes showed no significant group-by-time interactions (p > 0.05 for all); RMSSD decreased significantly from baseline to mid-term (MD = 0.079 ms, p = 0.044) with no significant improvement at endpoint relative to baseline.

The MRC Dyspnea -4 week pre-baseline vs baseline comparison: delta=0.22, p=0.239; -2 week pre-baseline vs baseline: delta=0.08, p=0.679. Note: the Breathing VAS week 10 change from baseline is positive (0.99, p=0.02 indicating loss of effect/worsening), then recovers at week 12 (-0.82, p=0.04). summary: This waitlist-controlled RCT tested a 3-week web-based yogic breathing and meditation program (Isha Kriya, Nadi Shuddhi, and Simha Kriya) in 188 adults with long COVID recruited from U.S. long COVID clinics. The primary outcome was compliance (feasibility), which was met: 74% of the 68 completers met the adherence threshold. Secondary outcomes showed significant improvements in mood disturbance (MD = -10, p = .02), dyspnea perception (MD = -5.5, p = .007), dyspnea sensory dimension (MD = -5.1, p = .003), and somatic symptom burden (MD = -2.0, p = .02), all with small-to-medium effect sizes; perceived stress and quality of life did not improve. High attrition (120 of 188 lost to follow-up) and an unblinded, predominantly White female sample limit generalizability, and the paper is an unpublished preprint.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome was compliance (feasibility), not a clinical efficacy endpoint; PSS, the key secondary outcome, showed no significant change (MD = -0.53, p = .63). Significant secondary findings were exploratory.

summary: This randomized double-blind trial tested 8 weeks of inspiratory muscle training (IMT) at 50% maximal inspiratory pressure versus sham (no-load device) in 19 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome persisting an average of 35 months after infection. The primary outcome, maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP), improved significantly more in the IMT group (125.50 vs. 93.67 cm H2O; mean difference 31.83 cm H2O; p=0.036; Cohen's d=0.50), with additional significant improvements in sleep quality (PSQI: 4.40 vs. 9.00, p=0.011) and quality of life (SF-36 group-by-time interaction p=0.030). The trial was very small (N=10 vs. N=9) and several secondary outcomes including lung function and 6-minute walk distance did not reach statistical significance, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome MIP improved by 31.83 cm H2O (95% CI 2.43 to 61.32; p=0.036; Cohen's d=0.50) in favor of IMT.

summary: A 2-week balneotherapy program (mineral baths, sapropel wraps, pool exercise, halotherapy) was tested in 173 Lithuanian adults with self-reported COVID-19 history and persistent musculoskeletal symptoms, randomized to ambulatory BT, ambulatory BT plus nature therapy, inpatient BT, or an untreated control group. All three BT groups showed significant within-group reductions in MSK pain intensity (61-73% immediately post-treatment in ambulatory groups), neck muscle tension (28-38% decrease sustained to 6 months), fatigue (20-23% post-treatment, p<0.001), and sleep disturbance (38-39% post-treatment reduction), while the control group showed no meaningful change. Between-group differences were statistically significant mainly at the immediate post-treatment timepoint (e.g., pain intensity: control vs ABT MD=1.97, p<0.001; neck tension η²=0.195 at T1), with differences largely disappearing by 3-6 months. This is a secondary analysis of a stress-recovery trial with COVID-19 status determined by self-report only, small subgroup sizes (n=38-51 per arm), and outcomes measured partly with non-validated Likert scales, limiting the strength of conclusions.

trial_rating.result_basis: Pain intensity reduced 61-73% post-treatment in BT groups vs increase in controls (between-group η²=0.152, p<0.001 at T1); neck muscle tension between-group effect η²=0.195 at T1; however, most differences disappeared by 3-6 months and this is a secondary subgroup analysis with n=38-51 per arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. CRITICAL DATA LIMITATION: Table 2 reports pooled totals across BOTH arms combined (not per-arm), making it impossible to extract per-arm means or SDs. The table columns are labeled 'Total Pre-test' and 'Total Post-test' representing combined group means (n=35). No per-arm disaggregated data are reported anywhere in the paper. The effect sizes reported (Cohen's d 0.63-1.93) are described as 'within-group comparisons for both the experimental and control groups' but are pooled/aggregated. Table 3 reports p-values for between-subjects effects and within-subjects contrasts but without means, SDs, or effect sizes per arm. Combined total pre/post means from Table 2: Chalder Fatigue Scale pre=24.46, post=16.34, Cohen's d=1.46; Two-minute walk test pre=62.50, post=81.14, Cohen's d=1.06; CRP pre=7.85, post=3.74, Cohen's d=1.80; Handgrip pre=25.34, post=28.89, Cohen's d=1.46; WBC pre=14491.43, post=8222.86, Cohen's d=1.93; Depression pre=67.60, post=50.80, Cohen's d=1.12; FEV1/FVC pre=288.69, post=147.86, Cohen's d=0.69 (note: FEV1/FVC values of 288 and 147 appear implausibly large for a ratio, possibly reported as a percentage or in unusual units); Quality of life pre=45.57, post=62.69, Cohen's d=1.60. The FEV1/FVC ratio values (288.69 to 147.86) are anomalous — normal FEV1/FVC is ~0.7-0.8 or 70-80%; these values may represent a different metric or reporting error. Per-arm n_analyzed is unclear: 47 randomized, 35 analyzed total, but per-arm split of the 35 analyzed is not stated. Trial registration not reported.

summary: An 8-week selected exercise rehabilitation (SER) program combining breathing, stretching, strength, and aerobic exercises was tested against standard care in 35 COVID-19 survivors with pulmonary damage and persistent fatigue, recruited from Al-Zahra Hospital in Isfahan, Iran. The SER group showed significantly greater improvements than controls across all measured outcomes at 8 weeks, including fatigue (Chalder scale: 24.5 to 16.3), CRP (7.8 to 3.7 mg/L), WBC (14,491 to 8,223 cells/µL), handgrip strength (25.3 to 28.9 kg), two-minute walk test (62.5 to 81.1 m), and quality of life scores, with large effect sizes (Cohen's d 0.63–1.93). The study had notable limitations including a small final sample (n=35 across both arms), no long-term follow-up beyond 8 weeks, and no control for natural recovery given that pre-tests were conducted near hospital discharge when inflammatory markers were still acutely elevated.

trial_rating.result_basis: Chalder Fatigue Scale improved from 24.5 to 16.3 (Cohen's d=1.46), CRP from 7.8 to 3.7 (d=1.80), WBC from 14,491 to 8,223 (d=1.93); between-group p<0.001 for all outcomes.

summary: This small Russian RCT (n=28) tested aquatic walking exercises in a pool containing diluted sodium chloride-bromine brine versus plain freshwater pool exercises in long COVID patients at a Moscow rehabilitation centre, all of whom also received a standard rehabilitation programme including physiotherapy and massage. The primary finding was that the brine group showed a 40% increase in 6-minute walk test distance (p=0.01), a twofold increase in oxidative metabolism index (p<0.01), and compared to controls, a threefold greater oxidative metabolism index (p<0.001), doubled microcirculation index (p<0.05), and 20% greater reduction in BMI (p<0.05). No serious adverse events occurred in either group. The trial is very small, open-label, and uses non-standard physiological measures as endpoints, limiting the interpretability of results.

trial_rating.result_basis: 6-minute walk test improved 40% in brine group (T=10.0, p=0.01); oxidative metabolism index threefold higher vs control (U=32.0, p<0.001); microcirculation index doubled vs control (U=120.0, p<0.05).

Intra-group ANOVA F-statistics (e.g., 95.49, 16.10 for PCFS; 16.77, 4.50 for 6MWT) are reported in Tables 2 and 3 rather than p-values for within-group comparisons — these F-values were not extracted into between_group_effects as they are intra-group statistics. 7. summary: This placebo-controlled RCT tested Chatushashti Prahari Pippali (CPP) — a processed long pepper (Piper longum) preparation — at 500 mg twice daily for 8 weeks, added to WHO rehabilitation guidelines, versus rehabilitation plus placebo in 112 Indian adults with post-COVID syndrome. The CPP plus rehabilitation group showed statistically significant improvements over placebo plus rehabilitation across all primary symptom outcomes (cough, dyspnea, fatigue, headache) and the 6-minute walk test, with intergroup percentage differences ranging from 76% (fatigue) to 96% (cough); 49 of 54 CPP-treated patients achieved complete symptomatic relief versus 1 of 56 controls. The trial was open-label (not blinded) and conducted at a single Ayurvedic institution in India, limiting generalisability; no adverse events were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Post-COVID Functional Scale improved from 2.44 to 0.08 in CPP group vs 2.36 to 2.01 in placebo group (intergroup p<0.001); 6MWT improved from 237m to 264m vs 208m to 230m (intergroup p<0.001); 49/54 CPP patients achieved complete relief vs 1/56 controls.

summary: A supervised 8-week multicomponent exercise program (aerobic training plus respiratory exercises, 3 sessions/week at 50–80% maximum heart rate) was tested against WHO physical activity recommendations alone in 48 Honduran adults with long COVID symptoms persisting beyond 4 weeks. The exercise group showed large improvements in functional capacity (sit-to-stand: 14.96 to 25 repetitions vs. 16.4 to 18 in controls; 6-minute walk: 620 to 800 m vs. 600 to 700 m), anxiety (STAI: 30 to 70 points), sleep quality (Pittsburgh: 8 to 20), and cognitive function (MMSE: 18 to 29). The study did not report formal between-group statistical test results (p-values or confidence intervals) for any outcome, and ethics committee approval was not obtained prior to the study.

summary: The PAX LC trial tested a 15-day course of nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (Paxlovid) versus placebo–ritonavir in 100 adults with long COVID across the USA, using a fully decentralised design. The primary outcome—change in PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score from baseline to day 28—showed no significant difference between groups (adjusted mean difference –0.55, 95% CI –2.32 to 1.21, p=0.54), well below the 5-point threshold considered clinically meaningful. No deaths or serious adverse events occurred, though dysgeusia was markedly more common with nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (48% vs 6%), partially compromising blinding.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome PROMIS-29 PHSS adjusted mean difference –0.55 (95% CI –2.32 to 1.21), p=0.54; no significant improvement at day 28.

The figure (Fig. 1) showing categorical recovery period distributions for each symptom across the 4 recovery categories is also only in graphical form with no extractable numeric values. Only prevalence counts at enrollment and qualitative descriptions of recovery ordering are available from the text. The paper is observational, single-arm, no control group. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study has a complex design: the primary comparison is early (within 3 days) vs. late (after 3 days) antibiotic initiation (arm_id 1 vs 2, n=179 vs n=32), but the paper also extensively reports on vaccinated (n=59) vs unvaccinated (n=152) subgroups as quasi-arms (captured as arm_id 3 and 4 in outcomes 4-6). The paper is primarily about acute COVID-19 recovery, not long COVID per se — LC incidence is a secondary endpoint (21/211 = 10% overall). SpO2 data reported as means without SD for the early/late antibiotic comparison but with SD for vaccinated/unvaccinated comparison. The adjusted regression coefficient (b) for SpO2 by antibiotic timing from Table 5 (b=2.63, 95% CI 1.71-3.56) is extracted as an adjusted mean difference. Long COVID duration reported as median 1 month (IQR 1-2 months) for both vaccinated and unvaccinated (log-rank p=0.935) but not broken down by antibiotic timing. The theoretical framework (SARS-CoV-2 bacteriophage behavior) is unconventional and the study has significant risk of bias due to non-randomized design, physician-directed treatment allocation, and heterogeneous antibiotic regimens.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This study uses four groups for outcomes: (1) interferon-treated (arm_id=1, n=142) vs (2) interferon-naive (arm_id=2, n=108) for thyroid/antibody outcomes stratified by treatment; (3) long COVID at 3 months (arm_id=3, n=46) vs (4) no symptoms at 3 months (arm_id=4, n=190) for comparing thyroid function in relation to long COVID; and (5) all 129 patients with complete serial antibody data (arm_id=5) for overall antibody trajectory. The study does not report per-arm long COVID rates stratified by interferon treatment. Long COVID overall prevalence: 19.5% (46/236) at 3 months, 10.4% (17/163) at 6 months — these are whole-cohort rates, not stratified by interferon exposure. The Ct value OR in Table 3 logistic regression (0.25, 95% CI 0.08-0.79) likely refers to a per-unit or categorical comparison — interpret with caution as the exact parameterization was not fully specified. Some antibody positivity evolution data appear only in Figure 2 without precise per-timepoint percentages in text.

Per-arm Ns in sensitivity cohort reported as 8,550 (half of 17,100 total). The paper states 31,264 patients total after matching (Fig 3) and 17,100 for sensitivity (Abstract). The matched cohort sizes are 15,632 per arm for primary and 8,550 per arm for sensitivity. Additional subgroup data for general symptoms, respiratory/cardiovascular symptoms, digestive symptoms, and other symptoms are in supplementary Figure S3 and not fully extractable from main text. subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Both subgroups showed significant improvement within each group. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. CRITICAL DATA LIMITATION: All primary quantitative outcome data (means, medians, SDs, RTEs for FACIT-Fatigue, EQ-5D index, EQ-5D VAS, and modified Chalder scores at T0/T1/T2) are presented ONLY in figures (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3) with no numeric tables. Only responder rate counts and percentages are extractable from text. The paper uses Relative Treatment Effect (RTE, a rank-based non-parametric probability measure) rather than mean differences, making traditional effect size extraction impossible. Days since disease onset reported as median 37 [IQR 30-46] days. Days of fever: median 3 [IQR 1-5]. The study is industry-funded with two authors being manufacturer employees — high conflict of interest. Pre-registration status not mentioned.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a prospective observational cohort study comparing cognitive outcomes across three treatment exposure groups (no immunomodulatory treatment, dexamethasone only, dexamethasone+tocilizumab) defined by era of ICU admission rather than randomization. Groups are not comparable due to temporal confounding: the no-treatment group was admitted earliest (March-April 2020), had higher CRP/PCT, longer ICU stays, and was tested at a different time point from ICU discharge. The primary finding is that TMT-B/A (executive functioning) was significantly worse in the dexamethasone+tocilizumab group vs. no treatment (T-score 40.3±13.5 vs 49.1±9.3, p=0.007). No AEs reported (observational study). MoCA raw scores also reported (overall median 26 [IQR 24-27]) but not stratified by arm in the abstract — arm data from Table 2. Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) median 3 [IQR 2-4] across all groups (p=0.82) also extracted in Table 2 but not included as separate outcome. HADS total score (median 8 [IQR 4-15]) also in Table 2 but subscores extracted separately. Some outcome data appear in Fig. 3 as SD units relative to normative population without exact numeric values — noted but not extractable.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a retrospective observational cohort study, not a traditional clinical trial. There is no pre-post design; the outcome is PASC development after COVID-19, assessed retrospectively from EHR. SSRI exposure was pre-existing (prior to COVID-19 infection), making this a prevention rather than treatment study. The outcome (PASC) is binary and the main effect measures are IPW-adjusted relative risks from Poisson regression. Per-arm event counts (175/1521, 215/1803, 2352/14584) are derived from text ('12%', '12%', '16%') — exact counts verbatim from paper. Age data reported only as categorical distribution (18-49, 50-59, 60-69, ≥70) without medians per arm, so age_mean/median left null. The paper reports 3 arms, requiring comparison of arm1 vs arm3 and arm2 vs arm3 as primary analyses, and arm1 vs arm2 as secondary. Table 1 has some apparent labeling confusion (rows and values appear misaligned in source text) but quantitative data extracted from both the table and results text are consistent.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an observational retrospective cohort study examining post-acute COVID-19 sequelae (incident diabetes), NOT an intervention trial. Arm 1 = COVID-19 survivors (exposed); Arm 2 = contemporary controls (unexposed, same period); Arm 3 = historical controls (pre-pandemic). The study reports burden rates per 1000 people at 12 months (not raw counts or percentages), and HRs from Cox survival models with IPTW. Per-arm event rates in figures are presented as burden per 1000 people at 12 months with 95% CIs — exact mean rates extracted from figure text: COVID-19 diabetes 48.38 (47.04–49.76), contemporary control 34.93 (34.74–35.11), antihyperglycaemic use: COVID-19 27.04 (26.05–28.07), contemporary control 14.69 (14.57–14.81), composite: COVID-19 58.10 (56.66–59.58), contemporary control 40.07 (39.87–40.27). Subgroup HR values for care settings are visible in Figure 2 but exact HR numeric values are not stated in text (only shown on log scale in figure); exact excess burdens by care setting ARE stated: non-hospitalised diabetes 42.70 (41.39–44.05) vs control 34.42 (34.24–34.61), excess 8.28 (implied); hospitalised diabetes 112.63 (104.61–121.22) vs control 34.42; ICU diabetes 182.92 (163.92–203.84) vs control 34.42. Also: non-hospitalised antihyperglycaemic 48.63 (47.27–50.01), hospitalised 123.93 (108.32–141.61), ICU 65.10 (58.82–72.02); composite non-hosp 20.10 (19.25–20.98), hosp 91.35 (83.80–99.54), ICU 123.48 (107.31–141.89) — these appear to be excess burdens per 1000. The study population is predominantly White male US veterans, limiting generalizability. Follow-up median 352 days (IQR 244–406) ≈ 50 weeks. Person-years: COVID-19 163,881; contemporary control 3,763,155; historical control 3,916,979.

This is a large observational cohort study examining post-acute COVID-19 sequelae (dyslipidaemia), not a treatment intervention trial. The paper reports higher-threshold lipid level outcomes (TC>210/220/230, TG>160/170/180, LDL>140/150/160, HDL<35/30/25 mg/dL) and BMI increase outcomes (>3%, >5%, >10%) but provides no specific HRs/CIs in text — these are referenced as appendix p 13 only. The study is not eligible as a treatment trial for the long COVID intervention meta-analysis — it is an observational study characterizing dyslipidaemia as a post-acute sequela of COVID-19.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Interaction term between female sex and hypertension was significant (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.22-0.70, p=0.001) with males as reference, indicating that hypertension's protective effect against long COVID was stronger in females.
Interaction term between female sex and CCB use was significant (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.03-0.85, p=0.031) with males as reference, confirming CCB protective effect was specific to females.

The primary finding is protective association of CCB with 6 long COVID symptoms in females. Table 1 note: 590 missing values for CCB field suggests most of the 981 analyzed patients had missing CCB data; the 33 female CCB users reflect only those with complete medication records. Outcome 1 (overall long COVID OR=0.51) refers to hypertension vs. no hypertension in females, not CCB comparison — this has been separated into outcomes 1 and 9 for clarity. IQR for parvovirus-B19 IgM in vaccinated group appears inverted in source (median 0, IQR 0.05-0.41) which may indicate the median is between the IQR bounds — extracted verbatim. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is primarily a cross-sectional biomarker study with observational comparison of vaccination groups, not a treatment trial with randomized allocation. Quantitative cytokine values (means, SDs, SEs) for IL-1β, IL-18, TNF, IL-6 per vaccination group are presented only in figures (Fig. 3a, Fig. 4a) without tabulated numeric values — set as not_reported. Arm definitions are complex: the 'treatment' groups are post-infection vaccination (1x or 2x) vs unvaccinated PCC controls. The study also includes resolved PCC and no PCC groups as comparators but the main intervention comparison is within the ongoing PCC group. The n=13 for GI symptom subgroup refers to ongoing PCC patients with GI symptoms regardless of vaccination status. The ranges reported for IL-1β and IL-18 in the GI subgroup analysis appear to represent full observed ranges, not IQR, so they are stored in iqr_low/iqr_high fields as approximations. The symptom frequency data (Fig. 5) with percentages per vaccination group is presented only in a figure without tabulated values. No formal statistical test results (p-values) for the primary IL-1β/IL-18 comparisons between vaccination groups are reported as exact values in text — results described as significant only in figure panels using ANOVA with Tukey's post-hoc. Multiple testing across 25 cytokines without correction is a notable limitation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm prospective observational cohort study — all 327 patients received SPA rehabilitation without a control group. Primary reported outcomes are post-SPA improvement scores on a 0-3 FSS scale, subgrouped by obesity, chronic respiratory disease, and DLCO status. Multivariate logistic regression results for predictors of fatigue/dyspnea and rehabilitation outcomes were reported as 'data not shown' with only select OR values disclosed in text. Barthel Index improvement values reported only for dyspnea-improved vs. not-improved subgroups (13.2±9.9 vs. 5.9±6.7, p=0.02) — not for overall cohort pre/post. Table 2 (dyspneic vs. non-dyspneic) and Table 3 (normal vs. reduced DLCO) and Table 4 (fatigue vs. no fatigue) contain extensive comparative data reported as subgroup cross-sectional comparisons at baseline, not pre-post treatment comparisons. DLCO data available only in ~one-third of patients (n=96). The mMRC overall mean 1.5±1.1 is reported in text but not in tables. Some column headers in Table 5 use 'Sì' (Italian for 'Yes') for chronic respiratory conditions presence. No long-term follow-up data available. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is primarily a metagenomics/microbiome study of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) in COVID-19 patients, not a clinical outcomes trial of long COVID symptoms. The probiotic intervention (SIM01) is tested for its effect on gut resistome, not on long COVID symptom resolution. All quantitative outcomes are metagenomic measures (ARG counts, abundances); no per-arm means or SDs are reported in text — all data appear only in figures (box plots, scatter plots). PACS is reported as a binary outcome (prevalence %). The study includes: (1) longitudinal cohort of 90 COVID-19 patients (66 antibiotic-naive, 24 antibiotic-experienced) + 66 matched non-COVID-19 controls; (2) open-label pilot of SIM01 during acute infection (n=22 SIM01 + n=10 controls); (3) open-label pilot of SIM01 after viral clearance (n=20). Detailed demographics are in supplementary tables (not in main text). P-values reported mostly as ranges (p<0.001, p<0.01) or exact values (e.g., p=2.85e-05). Control group for acute probiotic study (n=10) was from independent infectious disease team. Antibiotic-experienced group used: amoxicillin clavulanate (n=12) or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline (n=12).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL DATA INTEGRITY CONCERN: The methods section contains text that explicitly instructs table generation from sample sizes ('based on this please create new tables and data'), strongly suggesting that Tables 6, 7, 8, and 9 contain AI-generated or fabricated data rather than empirically collected results. The methods text also contains a description of what tables would contain rather than actual results (e.g., 'Table 7 summarizes the changes...', 'Table 9 synthesizes the data...'). All extracted numeric outcome values (GHQ-12 scores, Borg Scale scores, SF-36 percentage improvements, fatigue distributions) should be treated as potentially fabricated. No SDs are reported for any outcome. The reference list (refs 1-7, 8-32) appears to cite self-medication literature unrelated to long COVID or TCM, further raising authenticity concerns. The follow-up timepoint duration is unclear — '14-day follow-up' is mentioned but treatment was 3 months; the relationship between these timepoints is inconsistent. The abstract states GHQ-12 decreased from 14.5 to 9 at follow-up (combined groups), consistent with Table 6 combined column. The abstract also states average Borg reduction of 3.5 points, but per-arm data shows FZYF reduction of 3 and FZAS reduction of 4. The note in Table 7 states assessments used GHQ-12 but the abstract/methods describes PHQ-9 for depression and mMRC for dyspnea inconsistently. Given the fabricated data concern, this paper should be flagged for exclusion from meta-analysis pending verification.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a health economics/health services research study evaluating 11 distinct healthcare pathway types, not a conventional single-intervention trial. Arms in this extraction correspond to pathway categories, not randomized treatment groups. The 'low-selected' pathway (arm 1) is the reference/lowest-service comparator. Outcome 7 (EQ-5D by recovery/NDC status) uses a different arm coding: arm 1=fully recovered no NDC (n=339), arm 2=fully recovered with NDC (n=139), arm 3=not recovered no NDC (n=592), arm 4=not recovered with NDC (n=475) — these 4 arms are health state subgroups, not pathway arms. The adjusted EQ-5D values for these subgroups are: 0.89 (SE 0.007), 0.84 (SE 0.011), 0.76 (SE 0.011), 0.66 (SE 0.016) respectively; these could not be mapped cleanly to the 11-pathway arm structure and are reported as unadjusted values from Table 3. Full regression coefficient tables (Tables S2-S5) are in supplementary materials not provided. Incremental QALY and cost data by pathway appear only in figures (Figures 2 and 3 forest plots) with only the absolute values in Table 4; incremental effects not numerically extractable from the text except for the overall ICER. The study is predominantly observational/health services research and the 'intervention' is the healthcare system pathway type experienced, not a directly administered treatment.

This is an observational study of ovarian hormone effects on long COVID/ME/CFS symptoms via digital app data — NOT an interventional treatment trial. The 'intervention' is self-selected contraception use (combined hormonal vs none vs progestin-only), not a randomized treatment. Per-arm absolute means and SDs for symptom scores are not reported in text or tables — only IRRs and ORs from mixed-effects models are available. Combined hormonal contraception n=70 is calculated from 66 (combined pill) + 4 (patch). Progestin-only n=92 is calculated from 52 (IUS) + 22 (progestogen-only pill) + 18 (implant). The summary abstract reports OR=0.827 for symptom score with combined contraception but Table 2 reports IRR=0.827 (negative binomial model) — the OR in the abstract is technically an IRR. Individual symptom regression results (32/36 symptoms) are in appendix and not extractable from main text. Crash frequency data by phase visible only in Figure 2H; exact percentages not in text.

The PHR-specific results (outcomes 17) are described qualitatively as significant but without extractable per-arm numeric values — data only in figures. summary: This single-arm before-after study enrolled 297 long COVID patients at a specialist NHS clinic, of whom 102 completed follow-up assessments after receiving tailored multimodal interventions (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychological support, dietary changes). Among the 102 completers, 91 (89%) reported improved fatigue with an average FSS decrease of 16.86 points, while 11 showed no improvement or worsening. summary: This retrospective cross-sectional study examined bronchodilator responsiveness in 134 post-COVID patients presenting with exertional dyspnea to an inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation clinic in Germany. Following inhalation of 200 mcg Salbutamol, the post-COVID cohort (n=94 for primary analysis) showed a mean FEV1 increase of 181.5 mL (SD 186.6), significantly greater than a historical Swedish reference population (118 mL, p<0.0001) and an internal healthy control group (n=19; mean delta-FEV1 107.9 mL). Approximately 29% showed >200 mL FEV1 response and 12% met full significant bronchodilator criteria, with no significant difference by sex, age, BMI, or prior hospitalization, suggesting post-viral airway hyperresponsiveness may occur in a substantial minority of long COVID patients regardless of acute disease severity.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is primarily an observational/diagnostic study rather than a treatment trial; the 'intervention' is a single diagnostic bronchodilator challenge (Salbutamol 200 mcg), not a therapeutic course. No pre-COVID spirometry data available as baseline comparator. Most spirometry values (pre- and post-BD absolute FEV1, FVC absolute values) are reported only in figures without extractable numeric means/SDs. The TLC and RV change values represent difference from predicted (age/sex-matched normal) rather than pre-post treatment change. The control group comparison uses both an internal healthy volunteer group (n=19) and a historical Swedish population study (n=1050, ΔFEV1=118 mL, SD=152 mL). The between-group effect for outcome_id=1 was calculated as 181.5-107.9=73.6 mL (post-COVID minus internal control group); p-value from one-sample t-test vs 118 mL (historical Swedish reference) was p<0.0001. The figure caption for delta-FEV1 by sex shows 'ΔFEV1=179.0 mL' for males in one place and the text states 173.0 mL elsewhere — both extracted. SD for RV change stated as 0.9248 in figure (likely in liters: SD=924.8 mL); SD for TLC change stated as 1.266 (likely in liters: 1266 mL). FEV1 SEM stated as 0.01924 (likely ratio, not mL — not transcribed to SE field). subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Both subgroups showed significant improvement in UPSIT-TC scores after 2-4 months of treatment (p=0.001 for smell+taste group; p=0.008 for smell-only group), but the majority remained hyposmic (77.8% and 71.4% respectively).

summary: This retrospective single-arm before-after study evaluated oral prednisolone (10mg twice daily) plus zinc gluconate (10mg three times daily) for 2-4 months in 71 long COVID patients with persistent olfactory and/or gustatory dysfunction (≥1 month) following Omicron-variant infection in Taiwan. Among those returning for objective re-testing, UPSIT-TC scores improved significantly in both the smell+taste group (mean 23.50 to 25.28, p=0.001) and smell-only group (mean 22.19 to 23.81, p=0.008), though the majority remained objectively hyposmic (77.8% and 71.4%). At phone follow-up (mean ~10 months), 91.2% of the smell+taste group and 77.8% of the smell-only group reported subjective improvement in olfaction, though the study lacked a control group and had ~50% dropout for objective testing, preventing causal attribution of recovery to treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: No control group — improvements cannot be distinguished from natural recovery. Approximately 50% of enrolled patients did not return for the second objective testing visit (18/34 returned in smell+taste group, 21/36 in smell-only group), creating serious selection/attrition bias. The UPSIT-TC score range for smell-only group at second visit (mean 23.81, SD 8.10) reuses the same SD value as baseline — this may be a paper reporting issue. Follow-up duration is approximate: treatment was 2-4 months and phone follow-up mean was ~10.35-10.42 months from first visit; total duration calculated as ~45 weeks. Baseline UPSIT-TC scores for the smell+taste group (n=34, mean 23.50, SD 7.02) and WETT scores (n=34, mean 25.82, SD 6.96) are for the full enrolled group, while second-visit scores (n=18) are for those who returned. The paper authors note no sample size calculation was performed.

summary: This uncontrolled pilot study tested the feasibility of patient-reported outcome measures (PSS-10, GAD-2, SSS, MYMOP) among 14 Long COVID patients who completed an 8-week virtual Integrative Medical Group Visit (IMGV) program called Nourish to Flourish at a university post-COVID clinic. Statistically significant pre-post improvements were observed in perceived stress (PSS-10 decreased 3.43 points, p=0.007) and the MYMOP primary symptom score (decreased 1.25 points, p=0.004), while GAD-2 showed a non-significant trend (decreased 1.43 points, p=0.091); Fibromyalgia SSS subscales showed no change. summary: This prospective multicenter cohort study (PoCoRe, N=1,028) assessed outcomes of multimodal inpatient post-COVID rehabilitation across 6 German centers, comparing depressed (PHQ-2 positive, n=734) versus nondepressed (n=294) patients. summary: This prospective cohort study of 730 severe COVID-19 survivors evaluated a multidisciplinary post-COVID programme (pulmonary rehabilitation, nutrition, psychology, and specialist medical care) against usual follow-up without programme attendance over 18 months. Baseline prevalence for myalgia was stated as 38% in Discussion but not in a table. The between_group effects for the Poisson regression are labeled as risk_ratio (prevalence ratio) rather than adjusted_odds_ratio for Models 1 and 2 — these are all prevalence ratios from modified Poisson regression; the field 'adjusted_odds_ratio' was used as the closest schema match but these are actually adjusted prevalence ratios. summary: This single-center retrospective cohort study with prospective follow-up surveyed 200 post-COVID patients attending a German university hospital post-COVID center between December 2022 and July 2023, describing utilization frequencies and patient-reported effectiveness of over 15 symptomatic treatment modalities. At follow-up (mean 6.3 months post-baseline, n=165), beta-blockers had the highest proportion of users reporting strong-to-very-strong symptom improvement (31.6%), followed by plasmapheresis (33.3% of 15 users), antibiotics (29.6%), and glucocorticoids (24.4%), while psychotherapeutic interventions yielded lower rates (3.6-11.0%). The study had no control group, no randomization, and no validated outcome instruments, precluding causal inference about any treatment's effectiveness.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a descriptive observational study with no comparison group and no validated continuous outcome measures — all effectiveness data are proportions of therapy users reporting 'strong' or 'very strong' improvement on a non-validated 4-point ordinal scale. The denominators for follow-up effectiveness outcomes (Table 5) do not always match baseline utilization rates (some patients may have started or discontinued therapies between baseline and follow-up); the paper notes follow-up n=165. Follow-up duration calculated as approximately 6.3 months (SD=2.2) after baseline presentation = ~27 weeks. Figure 2 shows distribution of all improvement levels per therapy but only Table 5 numerical data were extractable. The paper states 15% of follow-up users reported plasmapheresis (n=15 of 165), while baseline records showed only 3.5% (n=7) underwent plasma exchange — discrepancy likely because some patients received plasmapheresis after baseline presentation. No p-values reported for any outcome. No adverse event data reported.

summary: This single-arm, open-label pilot observational study evaluated MYP plus — an herbal formulation of Astragali Radix, Salviae Radix, and Aquilariae Lignum — in 50 South Korean long COVID patients with severe fatigue and/or brain fog over 4 weeks. All primary and secondary clinical outcomes significantly improved (p<0.01), including a 46% reduction in mKCFQ11 fatigue score, 52% reduction in brain fog VAS, and 59% improvement in SF-12 quality of life. However, the absence of a placebo control group means these improvements cannot be causally attributed to the intervention and may reflect natural recovery or placebo effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Abstract reports TGF-beta post value as 242.0±701.0 pg/mL; Table 2 reports 243.9±708.1 pg/mL — Table 2 values used as primary. The study uses ITT labeling but effectively all enrolled completed (n=50 enrolled = n=50 completed), making ITT and per-protocol identical. Change scores in Table 2 are reported as absolute reductions without sign; direction inferred from pre/post values (decrease for symptoms, increase for SF-12). SF-12 subscale data (physical 43.0±19.8→72.6±21.2; mental 42.3±16.8→71.0±20.8) extracted from Table 2 and match figure description. No figure-only data identified. Post-COVID duration reported as 20.3±14.6 weeks (mean ~5.1 months); converted to months for demographics field.

summary: This single-arm retrospective before-after study evaluated pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) in 55 PASC patients (mean age 57.9 years, 63% previously hospitalized for COVID-19) at a US tertiary center. All 8 pre-specified functional and psychological outcomes improved significantly after PR: 6-minute walk distance increased by ~405 m, chair rise repetitions by 4.3, gait speed by 0.27 m/s, TUG time decreased by 3.3 seconds, mMRC by 1.2 points, SOBQ by 28.8 points, HADS by 3.6 points, and CAT by 9.6 points (all p<0.0001); only PHQ-9 did not improve significantly (p=0.74). Regression analyses identified hypertension, diabetes, ILD, prior outpatient COVID management, and specific inpatient drug therapies as factors associated with attenuated PR response, though the absence of a control group limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Preprint (not peer-reviewed). Single-arm pre-post design with no control group; all between-group comparisons are subgroup regression analyses within the treated cohort, not RCT arms. The paper_id used is the preprint DOI. Rehabilitation program duration not reported in paper. The T-value reported for PHQ-9 was 'S-value of 4' (Wilcoxon signed-rank test), not a parametric T; p=0.7402. Balance test is mentioned in methods but no pre/post values reported for it. N analyzed per outcome not individually specified; assumed n=55 for all based on overall cohort size. Change means calculated as post minus pre.

summary: This single-center prospective cohort study examined 6-month pulmonary outcomes in 286 ICU survivors of critical COVID-19 requiring ventilatory support, comparing those who received corticosteroids per RECOVERY trial criteria (n=181) to those who did not (n=68, all from the first pandemic wave). Corticosteroid-treated patients had significantly lower DLCO % predicted at 6 months (mean 77% vs. 88%; adjusted MSD -8.3, 95% CI -14.2 to -2.4, p<0.05), though this fell just below the pre-specified 10% clinically significant threshold. No significant differences were found in any of the eight RAND-36 health-related quality of life domains between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study examines corticosteroid treatment as an exposure rather than a prospectively randomized intervention; the comparison group (no corticosteroids) consists entirely of first-wave survivors, introducing substantial confounding by era and disease severity. Per-arm means for DLCO and RAND-36 are reported as mean with 95% CI rather than mean ± SD, so sd fields are null and ci_95_low/ci_95_high are used instead. The RAND-36 analysis had n=41 (no corticosteroids) and n=128 (corticosteroids) — slightly fewer than DLCO analysis. BMI medians with IQR are reported in Table 1 but no SD is given; BMI was not extracted as an outcome. The study period spanned March 2020–August 2021 with follow-up approximately 5–6 months post-ICU discharge. 37/286 enrolled participants had no data for either exposure group (neither corticosteroids nor no-corticosteroids per inclusion criteria — these are the excluded 'rescue treatment' cases per the flowchart; 68+181=249 of 286 total). p-values are stated only as <0.05 threshold, not exact values.

summary: This ambispective longitudinal cohort study in China enrolled 104 outpatients with post-COVID-19 chronic cough (>8 weeks) during the Omicron wave, comparing inhaled budesonide/formoterol (ICS, n=51) to conventional symptomatic treatment alone (NICS, n=53) over 60 days. Both groups showed significant improvements in cough (CET) and dyspnea (mMRC) scores, with no statistically significant between-group differences at either 30 or 60 days. However, ICS treatment was associated with significantly greater improvements in spirometric parameters (FEV1%, FEV1/FVC, MMEF%, MVV%) and FeNO50 at 60 days, indicating that ICS improves lung function but not symptom burden compared to usual care in this population.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Between-group effect values (actual differences) for CET, mMRC, and pulmonary function outcomes are not reported — only p-values for group comparisons are given. Lung function secondary outcome n varies (35 ICS / 32 NICS for spirometry; 34 ICS / 31 NICS for FeNO/CaNO; 30/30 for BPT) because only patients attending face-to-face day 60 visits were tested. The p=0.000 for MMEF% between-group change is reported as '0.000' in the paper (likely p<0.0005). BPT change column reports n converting from positive to negative (12/29=41.4% ICS; 6/26=23.1% NICS). Some pulmonary function data may also appear in figures (Fig 3) but Table 3 contains the key quantitative values. Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 (asthma subgroup) were not provided in the main text.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: High EPS was associated with significantly higher recovery (60% vs 4.3% moderate vs 5.5% low), improvement (33.3% vs 17.4% vs 5.5%), greater FSS reduction, higher health status scores, and faster improvement (all p<0.0001); moderate and low EPS did not differ significantly from each other.

summary: This retrospective single-center cohort study assessed the effectiveness of pacing strategies in 86 patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome (WHO definition, >12 weeks symptoms) at Angers University Hospital, France, followed for a median of 10 months. All patients were advised to implement energy-envelope pacing; adherence was measured by the Engagement in Pacing Subscale (EPS). Recovery (return to work with full remission) occurred in 33.7% and improvement in 23.3% of patients; on multivariable logistic regression, EPS score was the only independent predictor of recovery (adjusted OR 40.43, 95% CI 6.22–262.6, p<0.001), and patients with high EPS adherence had substantially higher recovery (60%) and improvement (33.3%) rates than those with moderate (4.3%/17.4%) or low (5.5%/5.5%) adherence.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm retrospective cohort — no randomized comparator group. Post-hoc subgroups (Recovered/Improved/Not-recovered-improved and EPS tertiles) were compared, but pacing adherence was self-selected. FSS and health status data presented as medians with IQR (not means/SDs), so SD fields are null. EPS scores also presented as medians per group (R: 4.4 [4.0-4.8]; I: 4.1 [4.0-4.4]; no-R/I: 3.0 [2.8-3.2]). Health status score for Improved group at last assessment: median 4 [3,4]; no-R/I group: median 3 [2,3] — these are not extracted as separate outcome objects to avoid excessive duplication but noted here. Outcomes 3-9 represent per-subgroup within-group FSS data rather than separate intervention arms. Kaplan-Meier curves shown in figures but no HR values reported in text. Follow-up duration calculated from median 10 months (43 weeks) for the overall cohort.

summary: This prospective observational cohort study of 145 long COVID patients (36% female, 64% male) undergoing ~4-week inpatient multimodal exercise-based rehabilitation in Germany found significant pre-post improvements in cardiopulmonary exercise capacity (VO2peak +1.1±2.9 ml/min/kg, p<0.001; peak workload +14.2±18.9W, p<0.001) and pulmonary function, with no control group. Women presented with higher relative baseline exercise capacity but greater fatigue and lower wellbeing; they showed significantly greater improvement in submaximal workload at VT1 (time×group interaction p=0.026) and FEV1/VC (p=0.027) compared to men, suggesting potential sex-specific benefits of intensified respiratory muscle training in long COVID rehabilitation.

summary: This prospective longitudinal observational study followed 114 post-COVID patients (predominantly healthcare workers with occupationally acquired SARS-CoV-2) through multidisciplinary inpatient rehabilitation and for 12 months afterward, assessing work ability and return to work (RTW). At 12 months post-rehabilitation, only 48.6% had returned to work and median WAI total score (21.0) indicated poor work ability, which had significantly worsened from baseline (median 24.5; p<0.001, r=0.484). Fatigue severity (FIS total) was the strongest predictor of both RTW (OR per unit=0.969, p<0.001) and perceived work ability, with physical capacity (6MWD) and subjective health perception (SPSH) also independently predicting WAI total, suggesting that targeted fatigue management and physical rehabilitation are critical unmet needs in post-COVID occupational reintegration.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm observational study with no control group; all within_group_change data reflect T1-to-T4 change without a comparator. Predictor variables (FIS, 6MWD, SPSH, HADS-D, DSST1, DSST2, PIA, MVPA) are reported as regression coefficients only at T4 — individual means/SDs at T4 are stated to be in Supplementary Material Table A5, which was not available in the provided text. WAI dimensions 2, 5, 7 showed no significant change (p=0.110, 0.315, 1.000 respectively) and are not separately extracted as outcome objects to limit size; their T1/T4 medians and IQRs are in Table 2. Logistic regression for RTW: FIS total B=-0.031, SE=0.009, OR=0.969 (95%CI 0.953-0.986), p<0.001, Nagelkerke R2=0.247. Multiple linear regression for WAI total: FIS beta=-0.399, 6MWD beta=0.196, SPSH beta=0.237, adjusted R2=0.473. Mediation analyses reported with path coefficients (beta) and bootstrap CIs. RTW denominator: text states 54 (47%) returned to work and 57 (50%) did not, totaling 111 with 6 in reintegration — percentages in Table 1 use n=114 as denominator including those in reintegration.

summary: This retrospective proof-of-concept study examined the effects of oral lactoferrin, a Multi-Element Product (MEP; containing magnesium, quercetin, curcumin, resveratrol, vitamin E, zinc, folic acid, selenium, and cholecalciferol), or their combination in 294 children diagnosed with long COVID at 3 months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection, followed in a single tertiary clinic in Rome. Using logistic regression (reference: lactoferrin alone, OR 7.6, 95% CI 5.1–11.4), MEP alone (OR 5.7, 95% CI 3.8–8.5) and MEP+lactoferrin (OR 5.06, 95% CI 3.3–7.6) were associated with lower odds of persistent long COVID at 6 months — suggesting a potential benefit compared to lactoferrin monotherapy — though no significant associations were found when treatment was initiated at 6 months or later. The study is severely limited by the absence of an untreated control group, non-randomized allocation, and inability to separate treatment effects from spontaneous recovery.

summary: This multicenter single-arm observational study in Hong Kong evaluated individualized Chinese Medicine (herbal prescriptions based on CM syndrome differentiation) for 3-6 months in 150 post-COVID-19 patients discharged from public hospitals, with a 3-month no-treatment follow-up. Over the treatment period, statistically significant improvements were observed in 6-minute walk test distance (linear mixed model: each visit increment ~10-27m increase from baseline, p<0.001), Lung Function Questionnaire scores (p<0.001), and proportion at risk of COPD (19.3% to 11.97% at end of treatment, p<0.001). The percentage with a balanced (Gentleness) Body Constitution increased from 8.45% at baseline to 15.6% after 6 months of treatment, and the proportion with CM-defined post-COVID syndromes decreased from 71.3% to 47.5%; however, without a control group, these changes cannot be attributed solely to the CM intervention.

summary: This prospective observational cohort study assessed sex differences in response to six weeks of outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation (OPR) among 263 post-Covid syndrome patients (54.4% female) in Vienna, Austria. All participants improved significantly across all outcomes (6MWD, PCFS, MIP, FEV1, DLCO, dyspnea; all p<0.0001), but women — despite less severe acute Covid-19 — retained greater symptom burden at discharge, with only 19.4% of women vs. 38.5% of men achieving full functional remission (PCFS=0). Women showed significantly worse inspiratory muscle strength, FEV1, dyspnea scores, and functional status than men both before and after rehabilitation, indicating that current OPR protocols do not fully bridge the sex gap in post-Covid recovery.

summary: This single-center prospective observational study in Czech Republic enrolled 2,729 COVID-19 survivors and compared outcomes between 232 patients treated with oral glucocorticoids (CS; mean initial prednisolone dose 27.6mg for mean 13.3 weeks) and 1,895 managed by watchful waiting (WW), based on physician-decided allocation. At follow-up (mean 21 weeks), subjective improvement scores (SIS 6.6 vs 6.7, p=0.361) and radiological improvement scores (RIS 5.7 vs 5.6, p=0.707) did not differ significantly between groups, but the CS group showed significantly greater improvement in static lung volumes (VC change +358.9ml vs +100.4ml, p<0.0001) and DLCOc (+9.19 %predicted) compared to WW, with the caveat that the CS group had markedly worse baseline pulmonary function, creating severe confounding by indication.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is a preprint (Research Square). The DOI in the paper header (10.21203/rs.3.rs-3407766/v1) is the preprint DOI, not the final published DOI. Table 13 was truncated in the provided text — only the first row (absolute VC change) was visible; the full table with TLC, RV, DLCOc, KCOc changes and their SDs per arm was not extractable from the truncated text. The VC change SD column appears to list both mean and SD in what seems like swapped columns (mean=358.88, SD=493.72 for CS group) — these values were extracted as stated. The 13.01 %predicted VC improvement in CS group is mentioned in the abstract and discussion but the corresponding value for WW group is not explicitly stated in comparable %predicted units. The note in the text that 'patients in WW group presented with significantly higher rates of improvement of static lung volumes compared to patients in WW group' appears to be a typographical error in the paper (likely meant 'CS group vs WW group'). Logistic regression adjusted analysis was performed for SIS=0 and RIS=0 as binary outcomes; no adjusted analyses for continuous PFT outcomes were reported. Adverse events from glucocorticoid therapy are discussed qualitatively in the introduction but not systematically reported for study participants.

summary: This prospective observational cohort study of 242 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 in New York City used unsupervised hierarchical cluster analysis to identify three PASC symptom phenotypes and three corresponding therapy groups among the 122 patients (50%) who developed long COVID symptoms. Patients who received psychiatric interventions (talk therapy, antidepressants, anti-anxiety medications; n=12) reported 100% symptom improvement, those receiving physical/occupational therapy (n=38) reported 97% improvement, and those receiving few interventions (n=72) reported 83% improvement (P=0.042); after adjustment for COVID-19 severity and age, receiving psychiatric or physical therapy (Groups B/C vs A) was associated with significantly greater likelihood of improvement (aOR 14.5, 95% CI 1.5-142.9, P=0.022). summary: This single-arm observational study of 46 critically ill COVID-19 patients with post-COVID-19 cholangiopathy characterized the endoscopic features of this condition across 141 ERCP procedures. Key features included centripetal intrahepatic bile duct destruction with vanishing bile ducts, biliary casts in 85% of patients, and peribiliary liver abscesses in 33%, consistent with secondary sclerosing cholangitis in critically ill patients (SSC-CIP). Prognosis was poor with a 1-year LT-free survival of only 44%; ERCP with cast removal improved cholestasis parameters in ~58% of recorded values, and peak bilirubin at ICU days 25-36 was an independent predictor of worse survival (HR 1.08 per unit increase, p<0.001).

summary: This single-center Russian retrospective observational study compared 1-year cardiovascular outcomes in 339 COVID-19 survivors (Alpha variant) assigned to telemedicine rehabilitation (n=118), inpatient day-hospital rehabilitation (n=46), or no rehabilitation (n=175) after hospital discharge. Using propensity score matching to adjust for respiratory distress syndrome and COPD, the study found that telemedicine rehabilitation was associated with significantly fewer cardiovascular deaths compared to no rehabilitation (0% vs 2.5%, p=0.086), and inpatient rehabilitation was associated with significantly fewer cardiovascular hospitalizations (6.5% vs 19.6%, p=0.064); combined rehabilitation groups also showed fewer cardiovascular hospitalizations than no rehabilitation (6.7% vs 12.8%, p=0.063). These findings are limited by non-randomized design, small samples, relaxed significance threshold (p<0.1), and inability to fully adjust for unmeasured confounders such as baseline health motivation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is primarily in Russian with an English abstract; full text extracted from bilingual version. PSM analysis produced different matched sample sizes for different comparisons: arm1 PSM vs arm2 (n=46/46), arm2 vs arm3-PSM1 (n=46/46), arm1 vs arm3-PSM2 (n=118/118), arm1+arm2 vs arm3-PSM3 (n=164/164). Per-arm event counts for the I+II combined group are: cardiovascular death 1(0.6%) vs 4(2.4%), MI 2(1.2%) vs 3(1.8%), stroke 2(1.2%) vs 2(1.2%), AF 1(0.6%) vs 1(0.6%), PE 0 vs 0, hospitalization 29(17.7%) vs 26(15.9%), CV hospitalization 11(6.7%) vs 21(12.8%). Table 5 contains the PSM-matched comparison results; the n_analyzed values for arm_results reflect PSM-matched sizes where applicable. No per-arm means or SDs reported (all outcomes are binary event counts). Significance threshold was p<0.1 throughout due to small sample sizes.

summary: This single-arm retrospective proof-of-concept study evaluated a 3-month personalized pulmonary rehabilitation program in 17 non-hospitalized long COVID patients in Belgium. The program included cycling, treadmill walking, arm exercises, strength training, and inspiratory muscle training 2-3 times per week. All patient-reported outcomes (QoL, anxiety, depression, dyspnea, functional status) improved significantly (p<0.05), and objective exercise capacity measures also improved significantly: 6MWT increased from 497 to 577 m (p<0.001), VO2max from 21 to 24 mL/kg/min (p=0.007), and peak load from 116 to 141 W (p<0.001); quantified CT demonstrated significant increases in airway volume and decreases in small vessel blood volume (BV5%), while standard pulmonary function tests showed no significant changes.

summary: This retrospective study reviewed medical records of 426 adults (ages 20–40, 60% women) who had mild SARS-CoV-2 infection between 2020–2023 and developed tongue lesions, reporting on 13 distinct lesion types including enlarged fungiform papillae (most common, 94%), depapillation, strawberry tongue, and geographic tongue. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study is descriptive with no formal statistical testing of treatment vs. no-treatment differences; median durations are reported as the main quantitative outcome. The per-arm Ns across all 13 lesion subtypes sum to far more than 426 because each patient had 3–5 concurrent lesions counted separately per pathology. Total follow-up was up to 36 months (1,080 days = ~154 weeks, rounded to 156 weeks). The figure (Fig. 1) shows a distribution bar chart but numeric data are also given in text/Table 2. The '50% reduction' summary statistic is stated without supporting calculation or CI. Two patients were found to have tongue cancer on follow-up (not a treatment outcome). No between-group statistical effect sizes were calculable given only median and min/max (no SDs). summary: This prospective observational cohort study compared CPET-derived cardiorespiratory fitness in 57 post-COVID-19 endurance athletes with exercise intolerance to 34 COVID-unaffected matched endurance athlete controls in South Africa, with both groups reassessed after 8 weeks of self-directed endurance training. At baseline, the post-COVID-19 group showed significantly lower ventilatory threshold (p=0.004), lower maximal workload (p=0.05), and higher respiratory exchange ratio (p=0.05), with increased odds of skeletal muscle oxygen extraction limitation (OR=5.21, p=0.03) and exercise-induced hypoxia (OR=7.02, p=0.05). After 8 weeks of endurance training, the post-COVID-19 group demonstrated significant within-group improvements in VO2peak (p=0.005), maximal workload (p<0.001), MIP (p=0.04), and O2-pulse (p=0.03), and showed significantly greater MIP improvement than controls (p=0.03), indicating progressive recovery of respiratory muscle strength but persistent exercise capacity deficits.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 (within-group pre-post comparisons for COVID-19 and N-COVID-19 groups separately) were referenced in text but not included in the provided paper extract; within-group p-values for VO2peak (p=0.005, d=0.41), maximal workload (p<0.001, d=0.5), MIP (p=0.04, d=0.38), and O2-pulse (p=0.03, d=0.31) in the COVID-19 group were extracted from the results text. VT change values in Table 3 appear to be in percentage units (not ml/min) given the very small numbers (median -0.01, IQR -0.04 to 0.03), which is inconsistent with baseline values of ~65-73 ml/min — likely a reporting issue in the table (possibly expressed as l/min or percentage). VO2 at VT in Table 2 is labeled as ml·min-1 but follow-up change in Table 3 shows values of -0.01 to 0.06, suggesting possible unit inconsistency. The between-group CI for baseline RER (CI=0-0.05) appears to indicate direction favoring COVID-19 group having higher RER. The between-group CI for maximal workload at baseline (CI=0-1.10 from text, CI=0-1 in table) is internally consistent. Supplementary Figure 1 showing aerobic capacity heterogeneity not available in text.

summary: This single-arm before-after study of 61 children aged 4–17 years with post-COVID-19 syndrome (U09.9) enrolled for sanatorium rehabilitation 3–14 months after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection examined gut microbiota and clinical recovery. All children showed markedly reduced obligate gut bacteria (bifidobacteria, lactobacilli, E. coli) at admission, with 33 children additionally receiving an oral bifidobacteria-containing probiotic for 6–11 days alongside general sanatorium health activities. By discharge, gut microbiota parameters improved substantially in both groups and symptoms (fatigue, weakness, abdominal complaints) resolved, with the probiotic subgroup achieving clinical well-being and exercise tolerance recovery faster (approximately 3.7 and 2.7 days, respectively) than the rehabilitation-only group (up to 5.05 and 5.6 days). No formal statistical testing between arms was performed and no control group was included.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Paper is in Russian with English abstract and bilingual tables. Discharge microbiota percentages from Figure 2a/2b are for the overall group (n=61) not separated by arm — it is unclear which values apply to which arm. summary: This single-center retrospective study from China compared 72 long COVID patients with cardiac injury who received potassium and magnesium supplementation plus lifestyle advice against 72 controls receiving lifestyle advice only, assessed over 14 days. The supplementation group showed significantly higher post-treatment serum potassium (4.86 vs. 3.73 mmol/L) and magnesium (0.92 vs. 0.83 mmol/L), improved HRV parameters (SDNN, rMSSD, LF/HF ratio), fewer premature contractions, and markedly lower Minnesota Heart Failure questionnaire scores (24 vs. 72) and NRS symptom scores (2.65 vs. 7.82), all statistically significant in multivariable regression adjusted for age, sex, creatinine, total cholesterol, and LDL. However, the non-randomized, physician-decided allocation and short 14-day observation window limit causal interpretation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The adjusted beta coefficients in Table 3 for premature contractions (-5.61) and Minnesota questionnaire (-6.7) are expressed per 100 contractions and per 10 points respectively (per table footnote context), while the raw between-group differences at endpoint (arm1 vs arm2) are much larger (152 vs 861 for premature contractions; 24 vs 72 for Minnesota). The adjusted β values appear to be scaled regression coefficients, not simple mean differences; verbatim adjusted effects extracted as reported. NRS 95% CI in abstract is listed as -6.5 to -7.9 (inverted bounds), likely a typographic error in the paper; extracted verbatim with note. Baseline HRV data for the control group is not provided numerically in the main tables (Table S1 referenced for full HRV data — supplementary table not included in paper text). Initial SDNN for supplementation group (113±39) and post-treatment (154±21) reported only for arm 1; control group initial HRV values not available in extracted text. LF (ms²) data for final timepoint from Table S1: arm1=not stated separately in text for LF baseline; arm2 values for initial HRV not provided numerically.

summary: This retrospective cohort study compared 155 non-critically ill COVID-19 inpatients who received in-hospital physical/occupational therapy rehabilitation with 162 who did not, at Stony Brook University Hospital (March–August 2020). The rehabilitation group was significantly older (median 76 vs 52 years), had more comorbidities, worse pre-admission functional status, longer hospital stays (median 9 vs 5 days), and was discharged with more assistive equipment and supplemental oxygen. Functional scores (Modified Mental Status 2.72/3, ICU Mobility 6.87/10, Modified Barthel Index 45.58/75) were significantly below normal at discharge (all p<0.0001) and were strongly associated with pre-admission dependency status, with older age and several comorbidities (CKD, psychiatric disorders, anemia, neurological disorders) independently predicting worse scores.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is primarily about in-hospital rehabilitation of acute (non-long COVID) COVID-19 patients, not post-acute/long COVID treatment. It was published as a preprint (Research Square). Functional scores were only measured in the rehab group (n=155) at discharge; no functional score data were collected for the non-rehab group, limiting between-group comparisons on functional outcomes. The study is observational with severe confounding by indication. The Discussion mentions average scores of 2.65 (Mental Status), 6.59 (ICU Mobility), and 40.07 (Barthel Index) for 'overall' cohort, but the table reports rehab-group-specific values of 2.72, 6.87, and 45.58 — these appear to represent different groupings or typographical inconsistencies; verbatim table values used for extraction. Some outcome data (discharge equipment percentages, follow-up referral types) appear primarily in figures and were not fully extractable as precise numeric tables. summary: This prospective cohort study assessed whether corticosteroid use during acute COVID-19 hospitalization (n=104 corticosteroid, n=202 no corticosteroid; predominantly dexamethasone 6mg/day for median 10 days) prevented persistent symptoms at 4 months post-admission in 306 discharged patients in France. In multivariable-adjusted logistic regression, corticosteroid use was not associated with having at least one persistent symptom (adjusted OR=1.00, 95% CI: 0.58-1.71, p=0.99) or with the number of persistent symptoms (adjusted IRR=1.04, p=0.74), with no significant association found for dyspnea or asthenia specifically. The null finding was robust across subgroups (ICU, ventilated patients) but the study is limited by confounding by indication as corticosteroid recipients had substantially more severe acute illness.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm event counts for individual persistent symptoms (asthenia, dyspnea, etc.) at follow-up are not reported in text or tables — only overall rates (e.g., 38.9% dyspnea, 37.6% asthenia in the full cohort of 193/306) are given without arm-level breakdown. The forest plot (Figure 2) contains additional adjusted OR estimates for individual symptoms and subgroups but exact values for most are not reported in text; only asthenia (OR=1.33) and dyspnea (OR=0.82) are stated. summary: This single-arm, prospective longitudinal study evaluated a 6-week Adapted Physical Activity (APA) protocol — two 30-minute individualized cardiorespiratory sessions per week — in 50 non-hospitalized long COVID patients (mean age 52 years, 44% female) in Tunisia, assessed at baseline, immediately post-intervention, and at 5-7 months follow-up. Significant improvements were observed in SF-12 physical (median 35.5 to 48.0) and mental (36.0 to 49.0) component scores, HADS anxiety (median 10 to 6) and depression (median 9 to 5) scores, and dyspnea prevalence (86% to 52%), all p<0.001 with large effect sizes (η²p 0.55–0.73). Benefits were partially sustained at medium-term follow-up (5-7 months) but were more pronounced for physical outcomes and anxiety than for depression; the absence of a control group precludes causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm study only; no control group — all between_group_effects arrays are empty. Table 4 reports mean±SD for SF-12 and HADS subscores alongside median (IQR) values reported in text — both sets captured per arm. E3 timepoint is 5-7 months post-intervention; 32 weeks used as midpoint estimate for weeks_from_enrollment. Functional capacity (6MWT) and spirometry (FVC, FEV1) are mentioned as measured outcomes in the Methods section but no quantitative results for these measures are reported in the Results section or tables — these outcomes were omitted due to lack of numeric data. Adverse events not reported. The paper reports Friedman test chi-squared statistics and partial eta squared effect sizes for overall time effects, and Wilcoxon effect sizes (r) for pairwise comparisons; these are captured in notes but not mappable to the structured schema.

summary: This prospective single-arm observational study evaluated a multidisciplinary Long COVID Recovery Clinic in Australia (March 2022-June 2023) that incorporated personalised exercise prescription including cardiovascular training, inspiratory muscle training, and peripheral strength training. Of 119 enrolled adults with Long COVID (symptoms >12 weeks), 72 (61%) completed the programme with a median attendance duration of 112 days. Completers showed statistically significant improvements in 6-minute walk test distance (+63 m, p<0.001), maximum inspiratory pressure (+11.7 cmH2O, p=0.002), Timed-Up-and-Go (-1.0 sec, p<0.001), 10-metre walk test speeds, and Modified COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale scores for other symptoms and overall health, with no adverse events attributable to exercise.

summary: This single-arm observational study (NOSTALGIA program) examined Alflutop (bioactive concentrate from small sea fish, an injectable chondroitin sulfate-containing preparation) administered intramuscularly every other day for 10 injections in 50 Russian post-COVID patients with persistent lower back pain and/or osteoarthritis. Over 8 weeks of follow-up, VAS pain scores declined significantly from 5.6 ± 1.5 at baseline to 1.0 ± 1.0 at 2 months (p < 0.05), and 80% of patients were pain-free by the final visit; HADS anxiety scores also decreased significantly (9.0 ± 1.9 to 3.0 ± 1.7, p < 0.05), while depression scores remained low and unchanged throughout. The absence of a control group means these improvements cannot be attributed specifically to Alflutop versus natural recovery.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Single-arm study with no control group; all within-group changes are the only available effect data. The abstract reports baseline VAS as 6.6 ± 1.5 while the results section states 5.6 ± 1.5 — the table confirms 5.6 ± 1.5 as the Visit 1 value used throughout analysis; the 6.6 figure in the abstract/methods appears to be the enrollment criterion range midpoint or a discrepancy. The Global Rating of Change Scale results are reported as proportions and descriptive categories (e.g., 50% moderate improvement = 3 points, 25% significant improvement = 5 points at Visit 2) rather than as a single mean ± SD; mean scores could not be reliably computed from these distributions without arm-level SD. Depression scores (HADS) showed no significant change and remained at 3 ± 1.0 across all 4 visits (p < 0.05 notation in table for Visit 2 appears inconsistent with no change — likely a table formatting artifact). 5 patients received adjunctive NSAIDs in the first 14 days.

summary: This single-center retrospective study from Poland examined salivary gland pathologies in 138 patients (aged 20–40) with confirmed mild COVID-19, identified from 1,256 dental clinic records from 2020–2023. The most common pathologies were xerostomia (43.5%), ectasia (29.7%), sialadenitis (10%), Sjögren's syndrome (6.5%), recurrent sialadenitis (6.5%), and neoplastic metaplasia (3.6%). Treated patients showed markedly shorter mean duration of xerostomia (10.5 vs. 547 days), ectasia (9.5 vs. 543.5 days), and sialadenitis (17.5 vs. 185 days) compared to untreated patients, with statistical significance (α≤0.05) for xerostomia, ectasia, and sialadenitis, though no formal between-group inferential statistics or adjustment for confounding were reported.

summary: This non-randomized quasi-experimental study examined the effect of SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin 10mg added to metformin) versus continued metformin/sulfonylurea therapy on cardiovascular biomarkers (ST2 peptide and homocysteine) in 43 type 2 diabetes patients followed for 9 months after COVID-19 recovery, compared to 32 non-diabetic COVID-19 controls. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical limitations: (1) The coagulogram table reports pre/post values for 'patients after COVID-19' without splitting by arm — it is unclear whether the table reflects both groups combined, arm 1 only, or arm 2 only; values extracted as arm_id=1 (combined) are approximate. (2) HFUDG outcomes are qualitative only (spectral pattern descriptions, Doppler images in figures) — no numeric amplitude values are reported in text or tables; result_source set to not_reported. (3) Group assignment was by physician decision/prior treatment received, not randomization. (4) The study period was September 2020–April 2021, preceding widespread vaccination. (5) Peripheral edema reduction and paresthesia resolution noted qualitatively after sulodexide but not quantified. (6) 14 men and 35 women reported overall only; per-arm sex breakdown not provided.

summary: This single-arm before-after study evaluated a 3-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) programme (5 sessions/week, 3 hours/session including respiratory muscle training with IMT/PEP/Respifit S devices, endurance exercise, and breathing education) in 80 post-COVID patients (mean age 51 years, 54% female) in Croatia. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm pre-post study with no control group; all comparisons are within-group (pre vs. post). Heart rate context: baseline value appears to be resting heart rate before 6MWT and the post-PR value is peak heart rate after 6MWT (not directly comparable as a pre-post rehabilitation metric in the traditional sense — the increase reflects exercise capacity). summary: This multicenter prospective observational study compared 12-month outcomes between 253 long COVID patients undergoing standard inpatient rehabilitation (IR; predominantly mild initial COVID-19, mostly female) and 91 patients undergoing follow-up rehabilitation after hospitalization (FUR; predominantly severe COVID-19, mostly male) across four German pulmonary rehabilitation facilities. Both groups showed statistically significant improvements in fatigue, quality of life, participation restrictions, and work ability during the 27-day rehabilitation program (medium to large effect sizes), with effects largely maintained at 12 months. Return to work rates were high in both groups (~87-89%) at 12 months, but FUR patients returned to work a median of 4.5 weeks later than IR patients (median 5.5 vs. 1 week, p<0.01), and FUR patients showed a concerning increase in neurocognitive symptoms during follow-up, suggesting that post-hospitalization long COVID patients require ongoing monitoring beyond rehabilitation discharge.

summary: This non-randomized prospective cohort study compared surgical correction of isolated horizontal venous reflux (EVLO, subfascial ligation, or foam sclerotherapy of perforant veins) versus conservative treatment (compression, wound dressings, phlebotonic drugs) in 59 post-COVID-19 patients with new-onset complicated chronic venous insufficiency (CEAP C3/C4/C6). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL DATA QUALITY ISSUE: Table I reports group-summed item scores across all 20 participants (e.g., Energy total=155 at baseline = sum of all 20 respondents' scores on 5 items), NOT per-person means or SDs. Individual-level means and SDs are not reported anywhere in the paper, making it impossible to compute standard effect sizes or conduct meta-analysis. AE percentages are reported for the supplement arm only (e.g., stomachache 25%), which translates to approximately 5 of 20 participants, but exact Ns are not stated. Percentage changes (+123%, -51%, -48%, +40% for supplement users; +10%, -21%, -22%, +6% for non-users) are reported in Table I but are derived from group-summed scores, not per-person means. summary: This uncontrolled retrospective multicenter Russian real-world study assessed the immunomodulator azoximer bromide (Polyoxidonium) in 16,365 adults and children (≥6 months) with acute infectious-inflammatory upper respiratory diseases, including a small number with COVID-19 and post-COVID syndrome. After a 10-day treatment course (mostly intranasal/sublingual, often combined with antibiotics or symptomatic drugs), 40% of patients achieved complete symptom relief and 99.77% showed positive dynamics on a 5-point physician scale; for the post-COVID subgroup, 29% had complete relief and 71% had marked improvement. No comparison group was included, no statistical testing was performed, and improvement cannot be attributed to the study drug rather than natural disease course.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT primarily a long COVID study — it is a large uncontrolled real-world registry study of azoximer bromide for acute upper respiratory infections. Post-COVID syndrome was a minor subgroup (exact N not reported). The study has no control group, no baseline symptom scores, no validated outcome instruments, and physician-assessed outcomes without blinding. Symptom resolution data are reported as proportions resolved by day 3 or day 5, not as continuous scores with means/SDs — no per-arm means or SDs available. Figure 1 (symptom resolution curves) and Figure 2 (5-point scale by disease type) contain additional data not fully captured in text; exact N for post-COVID and COVID-19 subgroups not reported. Median patient age is 28 years overall; sex breakdown given separately for children (48% female / 52% male) and adults (58% female / 42% male) but not for the post-COVID subgroup. The 10-day treatment duration was reported for 85% of cases (range 5–20 days).
