summary: This preclinical study investigated the role of Notch2-expressing activated regulatory T cells (aTregs) in allergic rhinitis, using human blood samples from 46 AR patients and 41 controls alongside mouse models. The study found that Notch2+ aTregs are depleted in AR patients and that their loss drives inflammatory pyroptosis (a form of cell death) in remaining aTregs via a Notch2/RREB1/Foxo1 signaling axis; adoptive transfer of Notch2-overexpressing aTregs into AR mice significantly reduced nasal symptom scores, serum IgE, tissue eosinophilia, and Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) compared to untreated AR mice. This is a mechanistic laboratory study with no human intervention; findings are preclinical and require translation to clinical trials before any conclusions about human treatment can be drawn.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper does not meet eligibility criteria for a Long COVID clinical trial meta-analysis. It is a mechanistic/translational study of allergic rhinitis immunopathology involving Notch2 signaling in regulatory T cells. The study involves: (1) observational cross-sectional human blood sampling (41 healthy controls, 46 AR patients); (2) mouse conditional knockout experiments; (3) in vitro MoT cell line experiments; and (4) a mouse adoptive transfer experiment. There is no clinical trial, no randomization of human patients to treatment arms, and no Long COVID condition studied. All JSON fields requiring trial design, arm-level outcomes, and quantitative clinical endpoint data are null/empty as a result. The human cohort data (VAS scores, IgE, Treg frequencies) appears only described narratively or referenced to figures without extractable per-arm means/SDs applicable to a trial context.

trial_rating.result_basis: Adoptive transfer of Notch2+ aTregs significantly reduced nasal symptom scores, OVA-IgE, eosinophil counts, PAS+ cells, and Th2 cytokines vs untreated AR mice (p<0.05 for all); empty vector controls showed no significant improvement, but no quantitative effect sizes (means/SDs) are provided in the abstract or results text.

summary: This laboratory and observational study investigated how platelet-derived extracellular vesicles (pEVs) carrying a small RNA molecule called tRF-His-GTG-1 drive excessive neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation in 10 Long COVID patients and 60 acute COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls. Long COVID patients showed significantly elevated lipid droplet accumulation in neutrophils (mean fluorescence intensity 74.35 ± 12.61) compared to recovered patients (38.77 ± 5.50, p<0.005), alongside elevated pEV levels and pEV-carried tRF-His-GTG-1, which impairs a cellular lipid-clearance process (lipophagy) via TLR8-mTOR signaling and suppression of RAB7A. In ex vivo experiments on neutrophils from 27 COVID-19 patients, a tRF-His-GTG-1 inhibitor significantly reduced lipid droplet levels, NET release, and inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β and IL-8), suggesting this RNA molecule as a potential therapeutic target, though no clinical intervention trial was conducted and findings require validation in larger cohorts.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a randomized controlled trial and should not be included in a meta-analysis of Long COVID clinical trials. It is a cross-sectional mechanistic/translational study. The 'arms' in this extraction represent cross-sectional comparison groups: arm_id=1 is Long COVID (n=10), arm_id=2 is Recovered COVID-19 (n=10), arm_id=3 is Healthy Controls (n=20). There is also acute COVID-19 data (severe n=6, moderate n=10, mild n=24) not represented as arms here. The ex vivo tRF-His-GTG-1 inhibitor treatment on n=27 COVID-19 patient neutrophils is a laboratory experiment, not a clinical intervention. Most quantitative outcome data for Long COVID vs comparators is presented in figures without extractable per-arm means/SDs in text, except where explicitly stated. LD accumulation MFI, EV concentrations, and pEV percentages had verbatim values. RAB7A, tRF-His-GTG-1, and NET release data for Long COVID group lacked extractable means/SDs from text. Also noted: after anti-COVID-19 treatment in acute patients, LD MFI changed from 141.81±12.40 to 63.29±8.38, and NET DNA from 198.40±28.41 to 67.87±15.66 (p<0.005), but this is a pre-post comparison in acute COVID-19, not a Long COVID trial. The correlation between LD levels and NET DNA in COVID-19 patients: r=0.68, p<0.005. The correlation between pEV tRF-His-GTG-1 and LD accumulation: r=0.77, p<0.005. Correlation between neutrophil tRF-His-GTG-1 and RAB7A: r=-0.84.

trial_rating.result_basis: Long COVID neutrophil lipid droplet accumulation (MFI 74.35 ± 12.61) was significantly higher than recovered patients (38.77 ± 5.50, p<0.005); tRF-His-GTG-1 levels in pEVs correlated with lipid droplet accumulation (r=0.77, p<0.005); ex vivo inhibitor reduced NET DNA release and cytokines in patient neutrophils (p<0.005).

summary: This observational neuroimaging study compared 86 Long COVID patients, 67 recovered COVID patients, and 26 COVID-negative healthy controls using MRI to measure choroid plexus (ChP) volume and cerebral blood flow (CBF). Long COVID patients had significantly enlarged ChP volume (median 2026 mm³) compared to both recovered COVID patients (median 1844 mm³, p=0.02) and healthy controls (mean 1469 mm³, p<0.001), and reduced ChP blood flow (31 vs 42 mL/100g/min in healthy controls, p=0.001). This is a cross-sectional study with no intervention and imbalanced age groups, so causal conclusions cannot be drawn.

summary: This observational imaging study used 7-Tesla MRI to compare hippocampal subfield volumes in four groups: Alzheimer's disease patients (n=32), people who had mild COVID-19 (n=13), people who had severe COVID-19 requiring ICU admission (n=9), and healthy controls (n=29). summary: This observational study measured plasma levels of six inflammatory and neurochemical proteins (GFAP, TREM2, CX3CL1, BDNF, GDNF, NGF) in 25 Long COVID patients and 25 healthy controls (median age ~35-39, 92% women) approximately 8 months after infection, alongside a comprehensive neuropsychological battery. Long COVID patients showed significantly worse performance on Trail Making Test, Hopkins Verbal Learning Test, and Stroop tests, and had lower plasma levels of TREM2, CX3CL1, GDNF, and NGF compared to controls. Linear regression found that higher GFAP levels were associated with worse Trail Making Test performance (TMT-A: β=−2345, p=0.03; TMT-B: β=−2232, p=0.01), while higher TREM2 and CX3CL1 levels were associated with better verbal fluency and immediate recall scores. This is a cross-sectional observational study with no intervention; it cannot establish causation, and the small, predominantly female sample limits generalisability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a clinical trial — it is a cross-sectional observational case-control study comparing long COVID patients to healthy controls. There is no intervention, no randomization, and no treatment allocation. It should not be included in a meta-analysis of Long COVID clinical trials. Per-arm means and SDs for all neuropsychological and biomarker outcomes are NOT reported in the text — figures are described qualitatively ('more severe impairment', 'decreased levels') with actual numeric distributions visible only in figures (box plots), so result_source is 'not_reported' for all arm_results. The between_group_effects for outcomes 11–19 are linear regression betas (B) with 95% CIs from Table 1, which represent within-long-COVID associations between plasma proteins and cognitive z-scores, NOT between-group comparisons of long COVID vs controls. These have been coded as between_group_effects for data capture purposes but should be interpreted as within-arm regression coefficients only. The p-value noted as <0.0001 in Figure 1 caption for TREM2 comparison is inferred from figure label; exact group-level means/SDs not extractable. Non-significant regression associations (all p>0.05 rows in Table 1) were not extracted as separate outcomes to limit response size. Omitted non-significant associations: GFAP vs Digits D/R/Verbal Fluency/HVLT-I/Stroop; TREM2 vs Digits D/R/HVLT-I/TMT-A/TMT-B/Stroop; CX3CL1 vs Digits D/R/TMT-A/TMT-B/Stroop; BDNF vs all tests; GDNF vs Digits D/R/Verbal Fluency/HVLT-I/Stroop; NGF vs Digits D/R/Verbal Fluency/HVLT-I/Stroop.

trial_rating.result_basis: TMT-A worse performance associated with higher GFAP (β=−2345, 95% CI −4486 to −203.9, p=0.03) and higher NGF (β=−108.4, p=0.04); observational associations only, no intervention effect size available.

summary: This pilot observational study examined cognitive outcomes roughly 2.9 years after COVID-19 infection in 20 racially diverse older adults (mean age 63.4 years, 65% non-White) hospitalized in 2020. The primary finding was that longer hospitalization duration was significantly associated with worse performance across multiple cognitive domains including global cognition, verbal memory, auditory working memory, attention/processing speed, and verbal fluency. Participants who experienced long-term loss of smell or taste (>4 weeks) also scored significantly lower on memory tests. The study is severely limited by its very small sample (N=20), cross-sectional design, and lack of a pre-COVID cognitive baseline.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a clinical trial — it is a cross-sectional observational pilot study with no randomization, no intervention arms, and no control group. The JSON schema has been completed as accurately as possible, but most RCT-specific fields (arms, randomization, allocation concealment, per-arm results with means/SDs) are inapplicable and set to null or empty. No per-arm quantitative means or SDs are reported for any outcome — only p-values from univariate analyses comparing symptom subgroups. The paper reports only two comparisons: (1) long-term loss of smell/taste vs. not, and (2) longer vs. shorter hospitalization duration. The p-value for simple attention/processing speed is reported as p<0.001 (threshold, not exact). Sample size is 20 total with no subgroup ns reported. This paper should likely be excluded from an RCT meta-analysis.

trial_rating.result_basis: Longer hospitalization associated with poorer global cognition (p=0.001), processing speed (p<0.001), verbal memory (p=0.014); long-term smell/taste loss associated with lower CERAD total score (p=0.016).

summary: The APPLE-Tree trial tested a 12-month multidomain lifestyle intervention — delivered via group video sessions and individual goal-setting calls by non-clinical facilitators — in 747 older adults in England with subjective cognitive decline or mild cognitive impairment. The primary outcome was cognitive performance (Neuropsychological Test Battery composite score) at 24 months; the intervention group showed a slightly larger improvement than controls, but the difference did not reach statistical significance (adjusted mean difference 0.06, 95% CI −0.00 to 0.13, p=0.055). No notable safety concerns were reported, and adherence was high (82% attended at least 5 of 10 sessions).

Per-arm Ns for the primary analysis are not disaggregated (only total analyzed N=635/746 is given). Baseline demographics are not reported in this abstract. This paper does NOT concern Long COVID — it is a dementia prevention RCT in adults with SCD/MCI; it should be flagged as out of scope for a Long COVID meta-analysis.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary NTB composite score adjusted mean difference at 24 months: 0.06 (95% CI −0.00 to 0.13), p=0.055 — does not meet the conventional threshold for statistical significance.

summary: This laboratory and invertebrate-model study tested the essential oil of Eugenia brejoensis (EOEb), a Brazilian plant, against multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolated from COVID-19 patients—not Long COVID patients. The oil inhibited bacterial growth at concentrations of 0.512–4.096 mg/mL, inhibited biofilm formation, and showed synergistic effects with ciprofloxacin against P. aeruginosa (FICI values 0.52–0.75) and with gentamicin against one A. baumannii isolate (FICI = 0.52). In a mealworm (Tenebrio molitor) infection model, EOEb at 1.024 mg/mL improved survival from 0% to 30% against A. baumannii and to 60% against P. aeruginosa; this is a preclinical study with no human subjects and no relevance to Long COVID as a condition.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. INELIGIBLE PAPER: This is a preclinical antimicrobial/pharmacology study, not a Long COVID clinical trial. The JSON fields for study design, participants, sample sizes, demographics, outcomes, and adverse events are all null/empty because none of these constructs apply. The paper reports quantitative data for: MIC50 and MBC values for EOEb against 5 A. baumannii strains (Table 3: MIC50 1.024-2.048 mg/mL, MBC 1.024-4.096 mg/mL) and 5 P. aeruginosa strains (Table 4: MIC50 0.512-4.096 mg/mL, MBC 1.024->4.096 mg/mL); FICI values for gentamicin+EOEb (A. baumannii: 0.52-2) and ciprofloxacin+EOEb (P. aeruginosa: 0.52-1); antibiofilm inhibition percentages; and T. molitor survival rates (70% and 90% survival at 4.096 and 2.048 mg/mL EOEb respectively; 30% and 60% survival in larvae infected with A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa respectively after EOEb treatment). None of this data is extractable into the Long COVID clinical trial schema.

summary: This study tested the Verifiability Approach (VA), a verbal credibility assessment tool, on 410 Italian adults to determine whether it could distinguish people genuinely reporting COVID-19 symptoms from those instructed to fabricate them. Participants who had actually had COVID-19 and were told about the VA provided far more verifiable details (mean 10.96) than informed malingerers (mean 2.32), a large and statistically significant difference (F=280.61, p<0.001, partial η²=0.41). The study is not a clinical trial of a Long COVID treatment and has no patient population in the medical sense; it is a psychological methods experiment conducted online with healthy volunteers, with no actual verification of reported details and no clinical outcomes measured.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. ELIGIBILITY FLAG: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial and should be excluded from a meta-analysis of Long COVID interventions. It is a psychology experiment on malingering detection using the Verifiability Approach. There is no clinical intervention, no Long COVID patient cohort, and no health outcome measurements. The 'long COVID' component is a secondary descriptive element (symptom checklist endorsement) that yielded null results. Participants in the 'honest' groups had prior COVID-19 infection but are not Long COVID patients receiving treatment. All extracted data are from the deception-detection experiment. Per-arm means for perceived success for arms 2 and 4 (not-informed groups) were not individually reported; only the main effect means (informed: M=3.55, SD=1.92; not-informed: M=3.06, SD=1.42; honest: M=3.85, SD=1.92; malingerers: M=2.77, SD=1.24) and the arm 1 vs arm 3 cell means were reported. The interaction F-values reported in Tables 3 and 4 include: verifiable details F(1,406)=142.34, p<0.001, partial eta2=0.26; ratio F(1,406)=77.264, p<0.001, partial eta2=0.16; perceived success F(1,406)=21.40, p<0.001, partial eta2=0.05. ANOVA main effects: information on verifiable details F(1,406)=138.23, p<0.001, partial eta2=0.25; condition on verifiable details F(1,406)=422.56, p<0.001, partial eta2=0.51; information on ratio F(1,406)=8.101, p=0.005, partial eta2=0.02; condition on ratio F(1,406)=66.702, p<0.001, partial eta2=0.14. Simple effect of informed vs not-informed among honest: F(1,406)=538.21, p<0.001, eta2=0.57. Simple effect of informed vs not-informed among malingerers: F(1,406)=0.02, p=0.90, eta2=0.001. Simple effect of honest vs malingerers when informed: F(1,406)=280.61, p<0.001, eta2=0.41. Simple effect of honest vs malingerers when not-informed: F(1,406)=36.49, p<0.001, eta2=0.08.

summary: This preclinical mouse study tested two cytomegalovirus (CMV)-based vaccine vectors expressing the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (MCMV-S and RAE-1γ MCMV-S), delivered via intranasal, intramuscular, or intraperitoneal routes, comparing immune responses against licensed COVID-19 vaccines (Spikevax, BNT162b2, Ad26.COV2.S). The primary finding was that intranasal immunization with RAE-1γ MCMV-S generated substantially higher numbers of spike-specific tissue-resident memory CD8+ T cells (TRM) in the lungs than any licensed vaccine tested, with none of the licensed vaccines inducing notable TRM numbers; however, licensed vaccines produced superior antibody responses. The study has no human participants and no SARS-CoV-2 challenge experiments, limiting direct conclusions about vaccine efficacy.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial. It is a preclinical mouse study evaluating MCMV-based vaccine vectors against SARS-CoV-2 in healthy C57BL/6J mice. There are no human participants, no Long COVID population, no randomization, and no clinical outcomes. All quantitative outcome data (IgG ELISA OD values, T cell frequencies, viral titers) appear exclusively in figures with no numeric values provided in the main text or tables. Per-arm means, SDs, medians, and IQRs cannot be extracted. Between-group effect sizes, CIs, and exact p-values are not reported in text (only significance symbols * p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001 in figures). The n per group is stated as n=4-5 for the licensed vaccine comparison experiments and n=5 for MCMV vector experiments. This paper should be excluded from a Long COVID clinical trial meta-analysis.

trial_rating.result_basis: RAE-1γ MCMV-S intranasal prime-boost generated the highest frequency and number of CD8+CD69+CD103+ TRM cells in lungs (p<0.05 vs licensed vaccines by Kruskal-Wallis/Dunn's test); licensed vaccines induced no notable TRM numbers, while MCMV vectors reached 40-50% of lung CD8+ T cell population.

summary: This study validated the modified COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale (C19-YRSm), a patient-reported outcome measure, in 1,278 Long COVID patients attending 10 UK specialist clinics, using Rasch measurement theory. The Symptom Severity (10 items) and Functional Disability (5 items) subscales both demonstrated good internal reliability (Cronbach's α 0.82 and 0.81 respectively) and unidimensionality, supporting their use as valid measurement tools. Minor issues were identified with the 'Cough' and 'Smell/Taste' items, but post-hoc analyses showed that removing or rescoring these items had negligible impact on patient score ordering (Spearman correlation ≥0.98 with original), so the authors recommend retaining the full scale for continuity. The study also provides interval-level score transformations enabling parametric statistical analysis in future research.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a clinical trial. It is a cross-sectional psychometric validation study of the C19-YRSm patient-reported outcome measure using Rasch analysis. There are no intervention arms, no randomization, no control group, and no treatment outcomes. The study reports only psychometric properties (fit statistics, reliability indices, DIF results, item locations) for an observational sample of Long COVID patients. summary: This observational study used whole-brain MR spectroscopic imaging (wbMRSI) to examine brain metabolite levels in 30 Long COVID patients (median 14 months post-infection, mostly mild-to-moderate COVID-19) compared to 30 age-, sex-, and BMI-matched healthy controls. The primary finding was significantly reduced myo-inositol (mI) levels — a marker of glial cell activity — bilaterally in the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes and in the cerebellum of Long COVID patients, with the effect more pronounced in the right hemisphere. This pattern of decreased mI, rather than the increases typically seen in neuroinflammation, may reflect exhaustion or functional downregulation of astrocytes following prolonged immune activation. No significant differences were found in neuronal integrity (NAA) or membrane/energy metabolism markers (choline, creatine), and mI levels did not correlate significantly with specific cognitive test scores, limiting clinical interpretation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is NOT a clinical trial or RCT — it is a cross-sectional observational neuroimaging case-control study. The JSON schema has been completed as best as possible but many fields (randomization, allocation concealment, follow-up duration, adverse events, RoB2) are not applicable. The 'arms' represent PCS patients vs. healthy controls as observational comparison groups. For the 30 healthy control participants, MRSI data were collected before the pandemic using the same scanner/protocol. Median timespan from positive PCR to MRS was 14.2 months. summary: This paper is not a clinical trial of an intervention in Long COVID patients. It presents RobustPALMRT, a new statistical framework for robust hypothesis testing in linear regression, and applies it to re-analyze immune cell proportion data from the Mount Sinai-Yale Long COVID study (99 Long COVID patients, 77 healthy controls). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL FLAG: This paper is NOT a clinical trial. It is a statistical methodology paper (introducing RobustPALMRT) that uses the MY-LC observational immune profiling dataset as a case study. summary: This observational study examined whether unprompted olfactory identification (asking patients to name a smell without multiple-choice options) and prompted olfactory identification (with multiple-choice options) are associated with different cognitive domains in 91 Long COVID patients with persistent smell dysfunction. Using hierarchical linear mixed-effects models, unprompted identification scores were significantly associated with five cognitive domains: working memory (digit-span forward, χ²=12.30, p<0.001), global cognition (MoCA, χ²=10.20, p=0.001), verbal fluency (χ²=8.79, p=0.003), episodic memory (logical memory, χ²=7.84, p=0.005), and executive function (digit-span backward, χ²=4.27, p=0.04). Prompted identification was associated with only two domains—executive function and global cognition—suggesting that unprompted smell identification may serve as a richer screening tool for cognitive decline in Long COVID patients. This was a non-interventional, cross-sectional/longitudinal observational study with no control group, limiting causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a clinical trial or RCT. It is an observational cohort study examining associations between olfactory and neurocognitive performance in post-COVID-19 patients. There is no randomization, no intervention, no control arm, and no treatment being tested. The study design fields have been completed as best as possible given the non-trial design. All outcome data are medians with IQRs (not means/SDs) from a single cohort. The 'between_group_effects' arrays are all empty because there are no comparison arms — the key results are chi-squared values from hierarchical mixed-effects model steps (Table 2), which represent contribution of neurocognitive variables to model fit rather than treatment effects. N=91 unique participants contributed N=146 total observations due to repeat visits. Time since infection reported as median 493 days (IQR 298-714 days), not months. The paper does not report a sample size as 'n_randomized'; 91 is the number of enrolled unique participants and 146 is the analytic dataset size with repeated measures.

trial_rating.result_basis: Unprompted identification significantly predicted by digit-span forward (χ²=12.30, p<0.001) and MoCA (χ²=10.20, p=0.001), while prompted identification was associated with only 2 of 7 cognitive domains; no effect sizes (r², Cohen's d) reported for clinical magnitude.

summary: This cross-sectional observational study examined 61 hospitalized COVID-19 patients in Germany (33 critical/severe, 28 moderate) to assess reactivation of latent herpesviruses — Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and HHV-6A/B — and associated T-cell immune changes. EBV reactivation was detected in 68–73% of patients regardless of COVID-19 severity, far exceeding rates for CMV (7–12%) or HHV-6B (11–15%), which were not significantly elevated. In EBV-positive patients, CD8+ T cells showed signs of exhaustion and terminal differentiation: reduced CD28 and CD11a expression and increased CD57, suggesting impaired capacity to control EBV infection. This is an observational study with no follow-up data on Long COVID outcomes; it cannot establish whether EBV reactivation causes post-acute sequelae, only that the immune changes observed are consistent with mechanisms proposed in Long COVID pathophysiology.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a clinical trial of Long COVID — it is a cross-sectional observational study of acute COVID-19 patients examining herpesvirus reactivation and T cell phenotypes. It does not meet criteria for a Long COVID RCT or interventional trial. There are no treatment arms, no randomization, no intervention, and no Long COVID outcomes measured. The study_design arms array is empty because there is no intervention. The 'arm_id 1' in baseline_demographics refers to Critical/Severe COVID-19 patients and 'arm_id 2' to Moderate COVID-19 patients (the two comparison groups used in the paper). Arm_id 3 used in outcomes refers to EBV+ patients (compared against EBV- patients). Nearly all quantitative outcome data appears only in figures (box plots) with no numeric values reported in tables or text — only p-values are reported for most immunological outcomes. summary: This randomised pilot trial tested a single half-day online group intervention combining narrative therapy ('journey of life') and breathing retraining, co-designed with young people, for 32 adolescents aged 12–18 with Long COVID attending tertiary NHS clinics in London. The primary outcome was the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) Impact Score; both intervention and control groups improved slightly over six months (mean reduction of 1.17 vs 0.92 respectively), but there was no statistically significant difference between groups on any measure. All secondary outcomes—wellness score, quality of life, fatigue, Nijmegen breathing questionnaire, and exercise capacity—improved over time in both groups with no between-group differences. A notable finding was that 84% of participants had breathing pattern disorders at baseline despite normal spirometry, highlighting this as an underrecognised feature of Long COVID in adolescents.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Participants imaged within 16 months had higher DVRs in most regions; difference was significant for NAWM (1.05 vs 1.02, p=0.042) and trending for whole brain (1.08 vs 1.06, p=0.059), suggesting neuroinflammation may be higher earlier in disease course.

summary: This observational neuroimaging study used PET brain scanning with the radioligand [11C]PK11195 to measure glial cell activation (a marker of neuroinflammation) in 14 Long COVID patients with neurological and psychiatric symptoms, compared to 11 healthy controls and 13 multiple sclerosis patients. The primary finding was that Long COVID patients showed no significant elevation in TSPO binding (a measure of brain inflammation) in any brain region compared to healthy controls, and blood biomarkers of brain damage (GFAP and NfL) were also normal; Long COVID patients consistently had lower TSPO binding than MS patients across most regions. As an exploratory finding, within the Long COVID group, higher anxiety and depression scores correlated strongly with greater TSPO binding in limbic regions (hippocampus and amygdala, ρ up to 0.88), suggesting these signals may reflect altered glial metabolism in mood-related brain areas rather than active inflammation. The study's small sample size and use of a first-generation radioligand with lower sensitivity are important limitations.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT a randomized controlled trial — it is a cross-sectional observational neuroimaging study with no intervention or randomization. The RoB2 and standard RCT fields (randomization method, blinding, allocation concealment, arm types, follow-up) are not applicable. Arms are defined as observational cohorts (LC patients, healthy controls, MS patients). RAND SF-36 subsection scores (energy/fatigue, pain, emotional wellbeing, social functioning) were reported in supplementary Tables S2-S4 but not fully available in main text — correlations with DVRs noted but subsection-level scores not included here. Cortex gray matter DVR, cingulate cortex DVR, corpus callosum DVR, and brain stem DVR also reported in Table 3 but omitted from outcomes to manage output size; all showed no significant differences between LC and HC. Full MRI parenchymal fraction data for all 11 regions available in Table 4. NfL and GFAP sample sizes were smaller (n=13 LC, n=10 HC, n=12 MS) as noted in figure legend. Some PET DVR values reported as median (IQR) for non-normally distributed variables (NAWM, pallidum, corpus callosum).

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary comparison of TSPO DVR between LC and HC showed no significant differences in any brain region; e.g. thalamus DVR LC 1.18 vs HC 1.20, corrected p=0.404; whole brain DVR LC 1.08 vs HC 1.08, p=0.587.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: This paper is an exploratory proteomic sub-study (n=10, imbalanced allocation Arm1 n=4 / Arm2 n=6) of a parent RCT; randomization details are not described here, sample-level QC created analyte-level missingness and variable effective N, and all analyses are explicitly acknowledged as underpowered and hypothesis-generating with no correction for multiple testing applied to differential protein expression.

summary: This study tested weekly intravenous C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH, RUCONEST) against placebo in 10 adults with persistent neurological symptoms following SARS-CoV-2 infection, using a randomized double-blind crossover design. The paper reports exploratory plasma proteomic findings from this subset, not primary clinical efficacy outcomes: C1-INH treatment was associated with downregulation of complement and bradykinin-pathway proteins (C9, KLKB1, KNG1, SERPINE1) and upregulation of neuroimmune markers (NRP2, CD83, CXCL13) during active treatment, with most changes reverting after cessation. The study is explicitly hypothesis-generating with only 10 participants, no formal statistical power for clinical endpoints, and clinical outcome measures (cognitive, fatigue, pain scales) were not the focus of this proteomics sub-report.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a proteomic mechanistic sub-study of parent RCT NCT04705831 (Melamed et al. Front Neurol 2025); it does NOT report per-arm means, SDs, or between-group effect sizes for the clinical outcome measures (MoCA, FSS, RBANS, MIDAS, GSRS, HIT-6, BDI-II, present pain intensity) — those quantitative data are exclusively in the parent trial publication. All quantitative outcome data in this paper are proteomic: log2 fold-changes and Spearman rho correlation coefficients between protein changes and clinical change scores. The 'effect_value' fields in outcomes 10-17 contain Spearman rho values (not SMDs); the 'smd' effect_measure type was used as the closest available field since rho is a correlation coefficient rather than a between-group effect size in the conventional sense. Protein-level log2FC data appear predominantly in figures and supplementary Excel files (not reproduced as numeric tables in the text), preventing full numeric extraction. Arm 1 n=4 and Arm 2 n=6 reflect an imbalanced crossover allocation noted by the authors as a feasibility constraint. Time since COVID infection reported only as median in weeks stratified by sex (males: 11.5 weeks both arms; females: 11.5 weeks both arms), not converted to months because of insufficient arm-specific detail. No adverse events are reported in this sub-study paper; referral to parent trial for those data.

trial_rating.result_basis: No primary clinical outcome p-value is reported in this proteomics sub-study; the eight FDR-significant protein-clinical correlations (e.g. ITLN1 vs pain intensity rho=0.913, FDR=0.011) are exploratory associations in N=10, with the authors explicitly stating all findings are hypothesis-generating.

summary: This mechanistic study from Erasmus MC examined whether immune cells (PBMCs) from Long COVID patients show an exaggerated type I interferon (IFN-I) response when exposed to synthetic viral mimics that activate the RIG-I and cGAS immune sensing pathways. Across two cohorts totalling 57 Long COVID patients and 35 recovered controls, Long COVID PBMCs produced significantly higher IFN-I bioactivity after stimulation: for example, Microx-LC patients showed elevated responses to both the RIG-I agonist 3p-RNA and the cGAS agonist G3-YSD compared to healthy controls, and unsupervised clustering placed 90% of high-responders in the Long COVID group. A moderate correlation was found between RIG-I-stimulated IFN-I output and fatigue severity in the Microx cohort (r=0.45, p=0.001), pointing to IFN-I pathway hyperresponsiveness as a potential contributor to Long COVID fatigue. This is a laboratory mechanistic study rather than a clinical trial, so no intervention was tested and no safety data apply; the findings support further investigation of IFN-I pathway inhibitors as a therapeutic strategy.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL NOTE: This paper is NOT a clinical trial. It is an observational cross-sectional case-control mechanistic study measuring in vitro IFN-I bioactivity in PBMCs. There is no randomization, no blinding, no therapeutic intervention, and no treatment follow-up. All quantitative IFN-I bioactivity data (primary outcomes) appear ONLY in figures (Fig. 1A, 1B, 1C) with no numeric values in tables or text — only significance thresholds reported (p<0.01, p<0.001, p<0.0001). The between_group_effects p-values for biomarker outcomes are threshold-only (not exact), inferred from figure legend annotations. Between-group effect values and CIs for IFN-I outcomes are not calculable as no means/SDs are provided. Correlation statistics (Spearman r and p-values) for IFN-I vs FAS are verbatim from text. RoB2 assessment is inapplicable (not a trial) but has been completed as 'high' to flag ineligibility for RCT meta-analysis. Immf-HC BMI data not reported in table. CFQ data for Immf-HC not reported. Some n values in table use footnote 'n' column suggesting partial data for some variables (e.g., BMI n=22 for Immf-LC). The FAS correlation comparison arm IDs in outcome 8 use 'rate_ratio' as a proxy — these are actually Spearman r values, not true effect measures; extraction reflects stated correlation coefficients.

trial_rating.result_basis: RIG-I-stimulated IFN-I bioactivity significantly higher in Microx-LC vs Microx-HC (p<0.01); 90% of high-responders in unsupervised clustering were Long COVID patients (37/41); fatigue correlation r=0.45, p=0.001 in Microx-LC cohort.

summary: This Norwegian observational cohort study tested two add-on questionnaire items ('bolt-ons') — one assessing breathing problems and one assessing cognitive functioning — alongside the standard EQ-5D-5L quality-of-life instrument in 220 non-hospitalised adults approximately 30 months after PCR-confirmed COVID-19 infection in 2020. The breathing bolt-on showed good construct validity, correlating strongly with established dyspnoea measures (Spearman rho 0.54–0.74 with mMRC and Dyspnea-12 scales) and modestly increased the explained variance in overall health scores (R² rose from 0.542 to 0.565 when added to the five standard EQ-5D dimensions). The cognition bolt-on also showed strong correlations with self-reported cognitive symptom scales (rho 0.68–0.75 with DePaul and Chalder Fatigue items) but did not add explanatory power beyond the standard EQ-5D items (R² unchanged at 0.543). Both bolt-ons reduced ceiling effects, with the proportion of participants reporting perfect health on all items falling from 21% (five EQ-5D items alone) to 11% when both bolt-ons were added.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a clinical trial — it is a single-arm observational cohort study evaluating psychometric properties of EQ-5D-5L bolt-on items in Long COVID patients. There is no randomization, no control arm, and no intervention being tested. The JSON fields for study_design arms, randomization, blinding, allocation concealment, per-arm sample sizes, baseline demographics per arm, between-group effects, and adverse events are not applicable and have been set to null or single-arm values accordingly. The primary analytical results are Spearman correlation coefficients (not means/SDs for treatment effects) and regression R-squared values. All correlation tables (Tables 5 and 6) with Spearman rho values have been noted but not extracted as formal outcome arm_results since there are no comparison arms. Item-level distribution data (Table 2) gives counts per response category for bolt-on and other instruments but not means/SDs. The FVC z-score mean was -0.170 (SD 0.929), FEV1 z-score -0.475 (SD 0.969), FEV1/FVC z-score -0.589 (SD 0.795), TLCO z-score 0.023 (SD 1.321) — these z-score versions of the lung function data were also in Table 4 but only raw values extracted as primary outcomes. mMRC distribution: 66% class 0, 26% class 1, 7% class 2, 1% class 3, 0% class 4 (n=218-220). Ceiling effects: 21.4% at ceiling for 5 EQ-5D items, 15.9% with breathing bolt-on added, 14.1% with cognition bolt-on added, 10.9% with both bolt-ons. No p-values were reported for the regression model comparisons.

trial_rating.result_basis: This is a measurement validation study, not an intervention trial; no clinical intervention was tested. The cognition bolt-on added no explanatory variance (R² 0.543 vs 0.542 for standard EQ-5D), and the breathing bolt-on added only a marginal increment (R² 0.565 vs 0.542).

summary: This study tested whether adding 'bolt-on' questions about cognition (CO) and social participation (SP) to the standard EQ-5D-5L quality-of-life questionnaire improves its ability to capture health problems in 3,335 German healthcare workers who developed post-COVID syndrome after occupational SARS-CoV-2 infection. The primary finding was that adding the cognition bolt-on meaningfully improved the instrument's performance: it reduced ceiling effects (from 18.8% to 14.8% reporting perfect health), improved discrimination between clinically distinct groups in 10 of 13 comparisons, and increased explanatory power for post-COVID symptom severity by 5 percentage points (ΔR²=0.05). The social participation bolt-on showed more limited benefit, improving group discrimination in only 6 of 13 comparisons and adding negligible explanatory power (ΔR²≤0.01), likely due to conceptual overlap with the existing 'usual activities' domain.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a clinical trial and does not meet eligibility criteria for a Long COVID clinical trial meta-analysis. It is a cross-sectional psychometric validation study of EQ-5D-5L bolt-on dimensions in a healthcare worker cohort — there is no randomization, no intervention, no control arm, and no treatment being tested. All 'outcomes' extracted here represent psychometric validation metrics (known-groups validity via relative efficiency, and explanatory power via adjusted R²), not clinical trial endpoints. The paper_id doi appears to be a pre-publication doi and may not be final. EQ VAS mean and SD for the total sample were not reported in the extracted text (only n=2934 and ceiling proportion 18.8%). The 'arm_results' objects in outcomes 1-6 represent subgroups (e.g., PHQ-4 severity levels, work absence categories) rather than trial arms — this structure is used because no better mapping exists. Table 2 contains the full EQ-5D-5L item response distributions. Spearman correlation coefficients for all EQ-5D-5L dimensions and bolt-ons vs external instruments are fully reported in Table 4. Additional explanatory power data for disease subgroups are in Tables 7 and 8. The 12-month follow-up mentioned in the Discussion refers to planned longitudinal data collection, not reported in this paper.

trial_rating.result_basis: Adding the cognition bolt-on improved adjusted R² for PCS symptom severity from 0.495 to 0.558 (ΔR²=0.05); relative efficiency for physician-diagnosed post-COVID groups improved to 1.22 (95% CI 1.16–1.28). Social participation bolt-on showed negligible explanatory gain (ΔR²≤0.01).

title: Psychometric validation of a cognition and social participation bolt-on for the EQ-5D-5L in SARS-CoV-2 infected German healthcare workers

summary: This is an in vitro laboratory study (not a clinical trial) testing whether low-frequency ultrasound with microbubbles, combined with fibrinolytic enzymes (rtPA, nattokinase, or lumbrokinase), can break down amyloid-like fibrin microclots of the type hypothesised to contribute to Long COVID pathology. Using a lab-on-chip model with porcine plasma-derived microclots, the study found that 150 kHz ultrasound with microbubbles reduced mean microclot diameter from ~17.5 µm to ~8 µm and cut the count of large clots (>30 µm) by over 80%, driven by mechanical forces rather than enzymatic activity. None of the three enzymes significantly reduced clot size on their own or added measurable benefit at 150–300 kHz ultrasound; only at 500 kHz did rtPA and lumbrokinase show a statistically significant reduction in large-clot count compared to control. This is preclinical bench research with no human participants, so findings cannot be directly applied to patient care.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is a preclinical in vitro experiment using a porcine plasma lab-on-a-chip model — it does NOT involve human Long COVID patients and is NOT a clinical trial. It should be excluded from a clinical meta-analysis. All quantitative values (mean diameters, large-clot counts) are approximate ('~') values read from text descriptions of figures, as no data tables are provided; SD values are shown in figures but not reported numerically in text, so all SDs are null. The arm_results values are approximate inferences from text (e.g., '~8 µm', '~17.5 µm', '~50 microclots') and should be treated with caution. n_analyzed=3 is inferred from 'three independent experimental repetitions' stated in Methods. Exact p-values are not reported in text; significance is described categorically. Many pairwise comparisons between enzyme arms at each frequency are not detailed numerically in text. Arms 3, 4, 7, 10, 11, 13, 15 have approximate mean diameters only (~10-11 µm range) with no exact values. Large-clot counts per arm are only partially available from text (~275 control; ~50 at 150 kHz no enzyme; ~300 rtPA only; ~100 rtPA+150 kHz; ~100 nattokinase+150 kHz). RoB2 tool is not applicable to in vitro studies.

trial_rating.result_basis: No clinical trial was conducted; this is an in vitro study. Enzymes alone showed no significant reduction in clot diameter (all static conditions ~17–18 µm vs control ~17.5 µm). At 150 kHz and 300 kHz, enzymatic addition produced no statistically significant improvement over ultrasound alone. Only at 500 kHz did rtPA and lumbrokinase reach significance for large-clot reduction (p-values not numerically reported in text).

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Cardiac autoantibody-positive Long COVID patients had significantly higher prevalence of headache (47% vs 26%, p=0.031) and hypertension (38% vs 20%, p=0.042), and higher CRP (median 1.9 vs 1.2 mg/L, p=0.028) and BMI (27.6 vs 25.6 kg/m2, p=0.025).
No significant differences in clinical parameters were found between vascular autoantibody-positive and -negative Long COVID patients.

Pulmonary autoantibody-positive patients had significantly higher proportion of females (89% vs 59%, p=0.006), lower creatinine (63 vs 69 μmol/L, p=0.030), and lower troponin T (3.6 vs 4.0 ng/L, p=0.033); sex confounding likely explains the laboratory differences.

Patients positive for any tissue autoantibody had significantly higher rates of anosmia/ageusia (75.5% vs 37.5%, p=0.043) and higher CRP (2.05 vs 1.15 mg/L) compared to those negative across all tissues.

HEp-2-positive Long COVID patients were older (53 vs 46 years, p=0.015), more often female (77% vs 57%, p=0.036), and had higher CRP (1.95 vs 1.2 mg/L, p=0.038); no significant differences in specific symptoms were found.

summary: This observational study from Hungary tested whether tissue-specific Western blot assays targeting cardiac, vascular, and pulmonary antigens could detect autoantibodies in 114 long COVID patients compared to 36 pre-pandemic healthy controls. Autoantibodies were detected in 83% of long COVID patients versus 53% of controls (p<0.05), with vascular autoreactivity being the only tissue-specific finding to reach significance (34% vs. 8%, p<0.05); cardiac (54% vs. 33%, p=0.16) and pulmonary (34% vs. 30%, p=0.51) differences were non-significant. The dominant signal was IgM-class antibodies, which persisted on longitudinal follow-up at 141 days, while standard ANA HEp-2 testing showed no discriminatory value between patients and controls. Key limitations include lack of a COVID-recovered comparator group (only pre-pandemic controls), single-centre non-blinded design, semi-quantitative Western blot methodology, and inability to establish whether detected autoantibodies are pathogenic or epiphenomenal.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a clinical trial — it is an observational cross-sectional/longitudinal cohort study with no intervention, no randomization, and no treatment arms. The RCT extraction schema is largely inapplicable. Arms 1 and 2 represent Long COVID patients (n=114) and pre-pandemic historical controls (n=36) respectively. Within the Long COVID cohort, subgroup comparisons were made by autoantibody status (arms 3/4 = cardiac aab positive/negative; arms 5/6 = overall aab positive/negative). Many between-group effect measures were not calculated (ORs were only shown in forest plot figures without verbatim numeric values in text). Exact event counts for IgM 60% and IgG 50% prevalence were calculated from stated percentages and n=114 (68 and 57 events respectively). Longitudinal follow-up data (n=30 for cardiac, n=12 for vascular, n=23 for lung at ~141 days) are described qualitatively only — no numeric outcome data were extractable. ANA HEp-2 exact prevalence percentages not stated numerically in text for the main comparison figure. Risk of bias assessment applied as 'high' across all domains because this is not an RCT. Outcomes 8-13 represent within-Long COVID subgroup comparisons, not Long COVID vs. controls. BMI data in Table 1 is reported as median (IQR) not mean/SD.

trial_rating.result_basis: Overall autoantibody prevalence 83% vs 53% in controls (p<0.05); vascular autoreactivity 34% vs 8% (p<0.05); cardiac 54% vs 33% (p=0.16, non-significant); pulmonary 34% vs 30% (p=0.51, non-significant).

summary: This cross-sectional study examined how APOE gene variants (including SNPs rs7412 and rs429358) relate to neurological and cognitive symptoms in 141 Long COVID patients attending a specialist outpatient clinic in Brazil, all of whom had neurological involvement at least 12 weeks after COVID-19 diagnosis. The key findings were that the APOE ε2ε3 genotype was associated with fewer depressive symptoms (OR 0.14), while the ε3ε3 genotype was associated with increased depression risk (OR 2.36); the ε3ε3 genotype was also linked to reduced anosmia risk, whereas ε3ε4 carriers had higher anosmia risk. The ε4 allele showed no significant association with Long COVID symptoms overall. Major limitations include a small, predominantly female sample (77% women), very low frequencies of certain genotypes limiting statistical power, and the cross-sectional design precluding causal inference.

summary: This pooled safety analysis examined depemokimab 100 mg — a twice-yearly subcutaneous anti-IL-5 biologic — in 1,290 patients with type 2 eosinophilic asthma or chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps across four Phase III trials (SWIFT-1/-2 and ANCHOR-1/-2). The primary focus was tolerability: 73% of depemokimab patients and 78% of placebo patients experienced at least one adverse event, with the most common events being respiratory infections, COVID-19, and nasopharyngitis — similar between groups. Serious adverse events were notably less frequent with depemokimab than placebo (5% vs 10%; RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34–0.75), with no fatal or treatment-related serious adverse events reported; this is a pooled safety analysis rather than an efficacy trial, and the lower SAE rate in the treatment arm is likely driven by depemokimab's known efficacy in reducing asthma exacerbations.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a Long COVID trial. It is a pooled safety analysis of four Phase III trials of depemokimab (an anti-IL-5 biologic) in type 2 asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). COVID-19 appears only as an incidental adverse event (respiratory infection during the pandemic period), not as a study condition or primary outcome. There are no Long COVID participants, no Long COVID outcomes, and no Long COVID-relevant efficacy data. The paper should be excluded from a Long COVID meta-analysis. Incidence rate data (per 1000 patient-years) also available from Table 2 but not extracted as outcome-level data since the study is not relevant to Long COVID. The between-group RR for most common AEs was reported in Figure 2 but specific numeric values for each AE were not provided in text or tables and therefore not extracted.

trial_rating.result_basis: This is a safety pooled analysis with no primary efficacy outcome; the main finding is that on-treatment AEs occurred in 73% (depemokimab) vs 78% (placebo) of patients, with SAE RR 0.50 (95% CI 0.34, 0.75) — a safety descriptor, not an efficacy endpoint.

summary: This laboratory study (not a clinical trial) tested tacrolimus-loaded small extracellular vesicles (Tac-sEVs) derived from human dermal fibroblasts as a potential topical delivery system for cytokine-driven skin inflammation relevant to long COVID, using in vitro cell culture and ex vivo porcine skin models — no human patients were enrolled. The primary finding was that Tac-sEVs achieved significantly deeper penetration into the dermal layer (~4.5 mg) compared to free tacrolimus (~3.6 mg) and commercial tacrolimus ointment (~3.4 mg, p<0.0001), while also suppressing SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein-induced IL-4 production in fibroblast cells. Cell viability remained high (>90% by Alamar Blue; 133% survival by CCK-8), suggesting acceptable biocompatibility in vitro. This is preclinical bench research only; no human efficacy or safety data exist, and the long COVID relevance is speculative extrapolation from cytokine suppression experiments in cell culture.

summary: This 52-week open-label extension study tested atogepant 60 mg once daily as a preventive migraine treatment in 186 Japanese adults, split between chronic migraine (CM) patients who completed a prior 12-week placebo-controlled trial and a de novo episodic migraine (EM) cohort. The primary outcome was safety and tolerability; atogepant was well tolerated with no new safety signals, and 84–90% of participants completed the full year. As an exploratory (non-inferential) efficacy finding, CM patients reduced monthly migraine days by 6.4 days from a baseline of 18.2, and EM patients by 3.4 days from a baseline of 7.5, with reductions sustained through weeks 49–52; many AEs were attributable to COVID-19 vaccination rather than the drug.

summary: This randomized sham-controlled pilot trial tested transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) — a non-invasive ear-based electrical nerve stimulation device — in 45 adults with persistent fatigue following COVID-19 infection, comparing above-threshold stimulation, sub-threshold stimulation, and sham (inactive electrode) over 4 weeks. Fatigue scores on the MFI-20 improved across all three groups, but no statistically significant differences were found between the active stimulation arms and sham, meaning taVNS did not outperform placebo on the primary outcome. The device was well tolerated with only mild side effects (skin irritation and vertigo each in 7.7% of participants), though the 8.9% dropout rate was higher than prior taVNS studies.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical limitation: All quantitative outcome data (per-arm means, SDs, medians for MFI-20 subscales, BDI-2, PCSS, and all SF-36 domains) are presented exclusively in figures (Fig. 1A-R) and in a Supplementary Table 1 that was not provided in the paper text. No numeric values (means, SDs, CIs, or p-values for between-group comparisons) are reported in the main text or any extractable table. Only selected within-group intragroup p-values are mentioned narratively (e.g., General Fatigue Verum1 baseline-to-visit1 p=0.009; Physical Fatigue Verum1 p=0.037; Mental Fatigue Sham p=0.03; Reduced Activity Sham p=0.025; Reduced Motivation Verum1 p=0.035; BDI Verum1 p=0.015; SF-36 Physical Functioning Sham p=0.013; SF-36 Bodily Pain Verum2 p=0.043; SF-36 Vitality Sham p=0.018; SF-36 Social Functioning Verum2 p=0.009; SF-36 Health Transition Sham p=0.026). No between-group p-values or effect sizes are reported numerically. The 236 min/day mean stimulation duration is an overall mean across all groups; per-arm breakdown not reported. Adverse events are reported as overall counts (not broken down by arm). The primary endpoint (MFI-20) was powered for the 20-item total score but the paper only discusses subscales; the power calculation referenced MFI-20 total but no total score data are extractable. Study design was modified mid-trial to add a crossover extension phase for Sham and Verum1 participants; outcomes at visit 2 (week 8) reflect crossover to Verum2 for those subgroups, not continued original allocation. Dropout allocation: 2 Sham, 1 Verum1, 1 Verum2 dropped out shortly after visit 0; additionally 2 Verum1 and 2 Sham declined crossover after visit 1 (these are separate from the primary 4-week completers).

trial_rating.result_basis: No significant between-group differences detected on MFI-20 at any timepoint; paper reports 'no significant differences (Pdiff) could be observed between the visits or within the groups' with no p-value for the primary between-group comparison exceeding the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of p=0.017.

summary: This observational study examined whether body mass index (BMI) modulates brain structure and immune markers in 61 Long COVID patients recruited from a German university hospital between 2021 and 2022. Using MRI-based voxel-based morphometry, higher BMI was significantly associated with reduced gray matter volume in the right thalamus (p=0.039, family-wise error corrected). BMI also correlated with elevated IL-6 (p=0.021) and reduced IL-7 (p=0.021) in blood, while thalamic gray matter volume showed a borderline association with IL-8 (p=0.050, not significant after multiple comparison correction). The study is cross-sectional with a small cohort and no control group, so causal direction cannot be determined; the thalamic finding may partly reflect pre-existing obesity-related brain differences rather than a Long COVID-specific effect.

summary: This is a preclinical animal study, not a clinical trial, examining neuroinflammation in female transgenic mice (hACE2, C57BL/6) infected with the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant (BA.1.17) and assessed 28 days post-infection. Compared to 11 uninfected controls, the 7 surviving infected mice showed significantly elevated brain levels of the inflammatory cytokine IL-18 (p=0.014) and increased astrocyte activation marker GFAP (p=0.047), while markers of microglial activation (Iba1, CD11d) and the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB signalling pathway were unchanged. The study provides mechanistic evidence that post-COVID neuroinflammation in females may involve astrocytic activation and IL-18-mediated pathways rather than a broad inflammatory response, but results are limited by very small sample sizes, high infection mortality (5/12 animals died), and the absence of histological or region-specific brain analysis.

summary: This observational MRI study compared brain tissue microstructure and neurochemical levels in 19 people with long COVID, 12 people who had recovered from COVID-19 without ongoing symptoms, and 16 healthy controls who had never been infected. Using multiple MRI techniques, the study found altered myelin signal intensity (T1w/T2w ratio) across all three group comparisons, with long COVID patients showing increased signal in the precentral and middle temporal gyrus compared to never-infected controls, and recovered individuals showing higher signal than long COVID patients in brainstem, cerebellum, and white matter tracts. Diffusion imaging also revealed tissue microstructural differences between groups, and neurochemical analysis found long COVID patients had higher N-acetylaspartate and lower glutamine in the posterior cingulate cortex compared to recovered individuals. The study is cross-sectional with a small sample (47 total), uses uncorrected voxel-wise thresholds that risk Type I error, and includes a notable age imbalance between groups (long COVID mean age 48 vs. recovered controls 35), limiting causal inference.

Duration of illness reported as 0.78±0.69 years for long COVID (approximately 9.36±8.28 months). summary: This laboratory study isolated IgG antibodies from 39 post-infectious ME/CFS patients (including 15 with post-COVID ME/CFS), 20 multiple sclerosis patients, and 41 healthy controls, then exposed human endothelial cells (HUVECs) to these antibodies to test effects on mitochondrial structure and cell metabolism. IgG from ME/CFS patients caused significant mitochondrial fragmentation in endothelial cells compared to healthy controls (p=0.0004), with the effect more pronounced in samples from female patients; the fragmented-mitochondria subgroup also showed increased spare respiratory capacity on metabolic testing. Proteomics analysis of immune complexes revealed that post-COVID ME/CFS samples were enriched for proteins linked to blood clotting and platelet activation, while post-infectious ME/CFS samples showed alterations in extracellular matrix organisation, suggesting the two conditions have partially distinct immune signatures. This is a mechanistic laboratory study, not a clinical trial — no intervention was tested in patients, and findings require validation in vivo before clinical implications can be drawn.

summary: This Mendelian randomization (MR) study used genetic variants as instrumental variables to test whether COVID-19 causally increases the risk of hypopituitarism (underactive pituitary gland) in people of European ancestry. Using GWAS data (8,316 COVID-19 cases and 910 hypopituitarism cases), the primary inverse-variance weighted analysis found that genetic liability to COVID-19 was associated with a 28% higher odds of hypopituitarism (OR = 1.283, 95% CI 1.017–1.617, p = 0.035). The weighted median method corroborated this finding (OR = 1.327, p = 0.037), though MR-Egger and weighted mode results were non-significant; colocalization analysis showed no shared causal genetic variant between the two conditions (PP.H4 = 9.55%), limiting mechanistic inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a clinical trial and is NOT eligible for inclusion in a Long COVID clinical trial meta-analysis. It is a two-sample Mendelian randomization study using GWAS summary statistics to infer causality between COVID-19 and hypopituitarism. There are no intervention arms, no randomized participants, no clinical outcomes measured in patients, and no per-arm means/SDs. The RoB2 tool is not applicable to this study design. The GWAS exposure dataset (EBI ebi-a-GCST011082) uses hospitalized COVID-19 vs. population as exposure definition, not Long COVID. All extracted outcome data represent MR effect estimates (log-ORs with SEs), not clinical trial outcomes. The colocalization analysis found PP.H4.abf = 9.55%, suggesting no shared causal genetic variant between COVID-19 and hypopituitarism despite the MR causal signal.

trial_rating.result_basis: IVW OR = 1.283 (95% CI 1.017–1.617, p = 0.035) based on only 5 SNPs; two of four MR methods non-significant; colocalization PP.H4 = 9.55%.

summary: This is a preclinical mouse study, not a clinical trial in human patients. Researchers injected the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein S1 subunit directly into the brains of mice to model neuroinflammation relevant to Long COVID, then tested whether chlorpromazine (an antipsychotic drug) could block the resulting brain inflammation and behavioral changes. S1 protein injection activated microglia (brain immune cells) specifically in the lateral septum, increased inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β and TNFα), and caused anxiety- and depression-like behaviors in the mice. Pre-treatment with chlorpromazine significantly reduced microglial activation and anxiety-like behavior, though its effect on depression-like behavior (sucrose preference) was only marginal; the study has no direct human relevance as it uses an artificial brain injection model rather than actual SARS-CoV-2 infection.

It does not involve human participants with Long COVID and should not be included in a meta-analysis of Long COVID clinical trials. All quantitative outcome data (means, SDs, SEs) are presented only in figures (bar graphs with error bars), not in tables or text — therefore all mean/SD fields are null with result_source='not_reported'. Sample sizes are available from figure legends for individual cell/slice counts (electrophysiology/IHC) and per-group mouse numbers (behavioral experiments: EPM PBS n=10, S1 n=10, CPZ n=6, CPZ+S1 n=5; OFT PBS n=10, S1 n=10, CPZ n=8, CPZ+S1 n=7; SPT PBS n=7, S1 n=8, CPZ n=8, CPZ+S1 n=7). Statistical significance is reported as p<0.05 (*) or p<0.01 (**) or p<0.001 (***) thresholds only — no exact p-values available. A separate PAP-1 (selective Kv1.3 inhibitor) experiment cohort (OFT: PBS n=8, S1 n=7, PAP-1 n=6, PAP-1+S1 n=6; EPM: n=7 each group; SPT: PBS n=7, S1 n=7, PAP-1 n=6, PAP-1+S1 n=6) was conducted but not represented as separate arms above. The 4-arm structure encoded above reflects the primary CPZ experiment only.

trial_rating.result_basis: Chlorpromazine significantly reduced S1-induced Kv1.3 channel current density and Iba1 soma size in lateral septum microglia (p<0.05 to p<0.001), and reduced elevated plus maze anxiety measures (p<0.05); however sucrose preference (depression proxy) did not reach statistical significance between S1 and S1+CPZ groups.

summary: This observational study used RNA sequencing to profile endothelial colony-forming cells (ECFCs) isolated from 12 post-COVID-19 patients (sampled at 3 and 6 months after infection with the original Wuhan variant) and 5 healthy controls. Compared to healthy controls, post-COVID ECFCs showed widespread gene expression changes at both timepoints, including downregulation of vascular protective genes (NOS3, KLF2, ANGPT1, TGFB1) and upregulation of inflammatory and pro-apoptotic markers (CASP1, CXCL5, TLR2, TIMP3), pointing to sustained endothelial dysfunction through 6 months post-infection. Only 3 genes differed between the 3- and 6-month post-COVID samples, indicating the transcriptomic disruption was stable rather than resolving. Notably, no gene expression differences were detected between patients with and without Long COVID symptoms, and the study is limited by a very small sample size (n=6 per timepoint).

summary: This small exploratory randomized trial tested whether adding osteopathic care (up to 7 sessions of manual techniques including high-velocity, myofascial, and cranial methods) to standard physical therapy improved fatigue and functional status compared to physical therapy alone in 28 Brazilian adults with long COVID and prominent fatigue symptoms. At 2 months, the combined group showed substantially lower fatigue scores on the Fatigue Severity Scale (mean difference −10.41 points, 95% CI −14.47 to −6.35) and better functional status on the Post-COVID Functional Scale (mean difference −0.70, 95% CI −1.11 to −0.29). The trial enrolled only 28 of a planned 104 participants, making it severely underpowered; no inferential p-values were reported, results are explicitly exploratory, and two authors are trained osteopaths with potential conflicts of interest.

summary: This is a preclinical animal study, not a human clinical trial. Researchers infected Golden Syrian hamsters with SARS-CoV-2 (Delta variant) to characterize how the autonomic nervous system changes over 8 weeks post-infection. Heart rate variability (HRV) analysis revealed a triphasic pattern: elevated parasympathetic activity in the acute phase (days 1-4), autonomic exhaustion in the sub-acute phase (days 7-14), and a sustained return of parasympathetic hyperactivity in the post-acute phase (days 28-56). Early treatment with either mitoTEMPO (a mitochondrial antioxidant) or ruxolitinib (a JAK1/2 inhibitor, 1 mg/kg/day for 14 days starting 4 days before infection) prevented the post-acute HRV elevation without affecting the acute or sub-acute phases, suggesting innate immune activation and mitochondrial oxidative stress during early infection drive long-term autonomic remodeling relevant to Long COVID dysautonomia.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a preclinical animal study (hamster model), NOT a human clinical trial — the RoB2 tool is not strictly applicable. Most quantitative outcome data (SDRR, rMSSD, pRR100, SD1, SD2, HF power, LF power at multiple timepoints) are presented only in figures (Fig. 2-8) without tabulated numeric values; extracted text-reported values only. Per-arm means and SEs were extracted where explicitly stated in the Results text. Values reported as mean ± SEM throughout. The paper reports percent changes from baseline rather than absolute values for many HRV comparisons (e.g., 'SDRR...increased by 51%'). Absolute values for SDRR, rMSSD, pRR100, SD1, SD2, HF at most timepoints are only in figures and therefore not extractable as verbatim numbers. Arms 3 and 4 (mTEMPO and Ruxo treatment) were only used in Fig. 8 analysis (n=4 each); most longitudinal data (Fig. 1-7) covers only arms 1 and 2. Outcome IDs 2-7 outcomes data mostly from figures only; text-stated values extracted. The n=3 for RSA analysis (Fig. 7C-D) is a subset of the main n=6 SARS-CoV-2 and n=5 Mock groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: Time-domain HRV indices (SDRR, rMSSD, pRR100) were significantly elevated at 28 DPI in SARS-CoV-2 group vs baseline but restored to baseline levels with mTEMPO or ruxolitinib treatment (p<0.05 to p<0.001); RSA amplitude was 91.3±5.8 bpm at 28 DPI vs 63.3±4.3 bpm at baseline (p<0.0001).

summary: This retrospective multi-center study from three hospitals in Zhejiang, China developed and validated a machine learning model to predict which Long COVID patients (n=330) would respond to a 14-day course of low-dose oral methylprednisolone (8 mg daily). The primary outcome was a clinically meaningful improvement in quality of life, defined as a greater than 10-point increase in SF-36 total score; 266 of 330 patients (81%) met this threshold. A logistic regression model using seven clinical features—fatigue, SF-36 score, lung function (FEV1/FVC), sleep quality (PSQI), IL-6, CRP, and neutrophil percentage—achieved AUC values of 0.87–0.87 across external validation cohorts, and the study found that patients with higher inflammation markers (CRP, IL-6) and lower baseline quality of life were most likely to respond. This is a prediction tool study with no control arm, so the overall effectiveness of methylprednisolone itself versus no treatment cannot be determined from this data.

summary: This study developed and validated 'metabo-time,' a blood-based metabolic score derived from serum NMR spectroscopy measurements of 143 metabolites and lipoproteins, designed to objectively quantify where a COVID-19 patient sits on the spectrum from acute infection to recovery. Tested in hospitalized COVID-19 patients from New York (N=42) and Spain (N=74), with 246 healthy controls, metabo-time distinguished acute infection from controls with near-perfect accuracy (AUC=0.997) and correlated strongly with days since hospitalization (Kendall's tau=0.52, p=8.57e-31); it also predicted systemic oxidative stress recovery better than elapsed time alone (R²=0.487 vs 0.212). This is a biomarker development and validation study, not an interventional trial — no treatment was tested and no therapeutic effect on Long COVID symptoms was measured; the tool's clinical utility for stratifying or treating Long COVID patients remains to be demonstrated in prospective studies.

summary: ETD001, a novel inhaled blocker of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), was tested for safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics in 98 healthy adult volunteers in a Phase 1 first-in-human trial. Participants received single inhaled doses from 0.06 to 10.8 mg or repeat twice-daily doses up to 4.65 mg for 14 days; no serious adverse events occurred and adverse events were balanced across active and placebo groups, with only one mild event (chest discomfort) possibly attributable to the drug. No cases of hyperkalaemia — a known risk class effect for ENaC blockers that derailed earlier candidates — were confirmed, and the drug showed a slow absorption profile consistent with prolonged lung retention supporting twice-daily dosing. ETD001 has since entered Phase 2 testing in cystic fibrosis patients not receiving CFTR modulator therapy.

summary: This observational study developed a shortened 12-item version (PCCSQ-12) of the 40-item Post-COVID-19 Condition Stigma Questionnaire, tested in 99 Long COVID patients recruited from a clinic in Alberta, Canada. The PCCSQ-12 preserved the original six-factor structure of Long COVID stigma and demonstrated strong internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.89) and split-half reliability (0.86). The instrument correlated significantly with health outcomes including quality of life (r = 0.73), symptom burden (r = 0.63), and functional status (r = 0.59), supporting its validity. This is a psychometric validation study, not a clinical intervention trial — no treatment was tested and no clinical effect size applies.

summary: This laboratory study examined whether 'pseudoserum' (clotting-factor-depleted plasma fractions) from 13 Long COVID patients and 10 type 2 diabetes patients could alter the structure and breakdown of fibrin clots formed from healthy, purified fibrinogen. When disease-derived pseudoserum was incubated with purified fibrinogen and then clotted with thrombin, the resulting fibrin networks showed dense, disorganised architecture with anomalous aggregates, closely mirroring the abnormal clot structures seen in patients' own plasma. Fibrinolysis was significantly and substantially impaired in both disease groups compared to controls, with Long COVID pseudoserum producing a mean optical density range of 0.025 vs 0.062 for controls (p<0.0001). This is a small mechanistic laboratory study with no therapeutic intervention; it demonstrates that non-clotting molecules circulating in Long COVID plasma can drive abnormal fibrin formation and resistance to clot breakdown, but does not test any treatment.

summary: This is a preclinical animal study, not a human clinical trial. Researchers infected Syrian golden hamsters with three SARS-CoV-2 variants — wild-type (B.1), Alpha (B.1.1.7), and Beta (B.1.351) — and assessed multi-organ pathology at 14 and 28 days post-infection to model Long COVID. All three variants caused persistent inflammation and fibrosis in the lungs, heart, and kidneys at 28 days, indicating incomplete organ recovery one month after infection; wild-type and Alpha variants produced significantly greater lung, cardiac, and renal fibrosis than Beta (p<0.0001), while Alpha drove the greatest splenic germinal-centre expansion. The study establishes a variant-dependent post-acute organ injury model in hamsters but has no direct applicability to human treatment — it is a pathophysiology and model-validation study with no therapeutic intervention tested.

summary: This is a laboratory biochemistry study, not a clinical trial involving patients. Researchers at Linköping University tested whether amyloid fibrils formed from seven synthetic peptides derived from the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein could disrupt the fibrin clotting and dissolving (fibrinolysis) process in vitro, as a proposed mechanism for the fibrin microclots observed in Long COVID patients. Two of the seven Spike peptides had notable effects: the Spike601 peptide (residues 601–620) bound and sequestered fibrinogen, delaying clot formation but not impairing breakdown; the Spike685 peptide (residues 685–701, just after the furin cleavage site) caused fibrin clots to form denser networks and resist plasmin-mediated dissolution in a concentration-dependent manner. The study proposes a molecular mechanism for microclot persistence in Long COVID but has no patient population, no clinical outcomes, and no translational validation—findings remain purely mechanistic and in vitro.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is not a clinical trial and is ineligible for meta-analysis extraction. summary: This is a preclinical mechanistic study — not a clinical trial in Long COVID patients — that examined how kynurenic acid (KYNA), an inflammatory metabolite elevated in Long COVID, impairs working memory circuits in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) of macaques and explores whether blocking its production can reverse these deficits. The study found that KYNA directly suppresses the sustained neuronal firing needed for working memory by blocking NMDA and nicotinic α7 receptors, with aged macaques (which have naturally higher KYNA levels) showing the greatest cognitive impairment and the greatest benefit from KAT-II inhibitors. Systemic administration of the KAT-II inhibitor PF-04859989 improved working memory performance in aged macaques (significant correlation with age, r=0.598, p=0.039; largest effect in animals >21 years, p<0.004), and N-acetylcysteine (NAC, already approved for human use) also improved working memory at 1 mg/kg (p=0.02 vs vehicle). These findings are relevant to Long COVID because plasma kynurenine levels are elevated in PASC patients and correlate with cognitive deficits, but all intervention data here come from non-human primates, not human patients.

summary: This laboratory study investigated CDK8, a kinase enzyme, as a regulator of stem-like cell properties in pituitary adenomas (benign brain tumours). Using patient-derived tumour cells, established cell lines, and mouse xenograft models, researchers found that CDK8 stabilises the stem cell protein SOX2 by phosphorylating it at serine-251, which blocks a degradation pathway mediated by the E3 ubiquitin ligase HERC5. Pharmacological inhibition of CDK8 with compounds MSC2530818 and BI-1347 significantly reduced tumour sphere formation, SOX2 protein levels, and cell proliferation in vitro, and CDK8 inhibitor BI-1347 suppressed tumour growth in mice (reduced tumour volume, p<0.01; reduced tumour weight, p<0.001). This is a preclinical mechanistic study with no human clinical trial component; findings require validation in human clinical trials before therapeutic conclusions can be drawn.

summary: This proteomics study examined how a Pfizer/BNT162b2 COVID-19 booster dose affects plasma protein profiles in 9 healthy adults when blood was stimulated in vitro with SARS-CoV-2 spike protein to mimic reinfection. Compared to pre-booster samples, post-booster spike-stimulated blood showed substantially higher levels of complement proteins (C5, C7, C9, C1Q) and coagulation factors (fibrinogen chains FGB, FGG, FGA elevated 32- to 701-fold), as well as immunoglobulins IgM and IgG1, indicating a stronger immune and inflammatory response after the booster. Notably, the same pathways associated with COVID-19 severity and mortality — complement activation, platelet degranulation, and blood coagulation — were upregulated, raising questions about mechanisms underlying rare post-vaccination adverse reactions, though this is an in vitro model in healthy individuals and cannot establish clinical risk.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial and does not meet inclusion criteria for a Long COVID meta-analysis. There are no Long COVID patients, no randomization, no clinical outcomes (fatigue, cognition, dyspnea, etc.), and no treatment intervention for Long COVID. The study design has 4 'groups' that are not trial arms in the conventional sense — the same 9 subjects provide both pre- and postbooster samples, each split into stimulated and unstimulated conditions in vitro. Per-arm means and SDs for protein abundance are not reported numerically in the text or tables — only LFQ ratios (fold-change) between group comparisons are provided in Table 1. Quantitative Western blot validation data (chemiluminescence intensities) for FGB and SERPINA1 are described as 'mean ± SEM (n=7)' and noted as p<0.01 but exact values are only in Figure 4c, which is not readable from the text. Age range 33-43 years, BMI mean 28.88 ± 3.07 SD reported for all subjects combined, not per arm. 5 male, 4 female (44.4% female). The full DEP list with LFQ ratios for Group D vs B is provided in Table 1 (54 proteins total across two table segments); only a selection extracted here. Omitted from outcomes: the remaining ~45 proteins in Table 1 with LFQ ratios between 2.29 and 9.57 (insulin-like growth factor II, haptoglobin, fibrinogen alpha chain, ORM2, PCYOX1, PON3, MASP1, ORM1, PVR, SPP2, ACTC1, HBB, GSTP1, TF, LCAT, TFRC, HBA1, STOM, F5, C9, IGHG1, GPLD1, EFEMP1, PROS1, HPR, APOC1, SERPING1, VTN, HRG, APOE, LPA, C1QC, SERPINA10, VASN, LUM, SERPINF2, ATRN, SELENOP, MST1, CPB2, SERPIND1, TGFBI, C7, LGALS3BP, ITIH3, IGFALS).
