summary: This study applied Latent Transition Analysis (LTA), a statistical modelling framework, to 5,094 COVID-19 patients from the multinational ORCHESTRA cohort to identify distinct Long COVID phenotypes and track how patients move between them over 24 months of follow-up. The model identified seven disease states: two acute-phase states and five post-COVID states (Healthy, Respiratory PCC, Fatigue PCC, Sensorial PCC, and Severe Symptom), with most patients recovering over time—the proportion in the Healthy state rose from 32.6% at 6 months to 39.2% at 24 months. Female sex, older age (41–60 and >60), and chronic respiratory disease were associated with worse trajectories, with women over 60 having only a 26.6% probability of reaching the Healthy state by 24 months versus 72.2% for young men infected during the fourth wave, and an average predicted recovery time of 89 months compared to 21 months. This is a methodological study rather than an intervention trial; it provides no treatment effect data but offers a validated analytical tool for future Long COVID research.

summary: This observational study examined endovascular pathology in 61 children and young adults (median age 15, up to 25 years) with long COVID compared to 23 healthy pediatric controls, measuring fibrin amyloid microclots, endothelial cytokines, cell-free DNA (a marker of neutrophil extracellular trap formation), and conducting lab experiments to test whether spike protein-activated neutrophils damage endothelial cells. Microclot burden was significantly elevated in long COVID patients (p=0.0003), spontaneous neutrophil extracellular trap formation was markedly increased (p<0.0001), and cell-free DNA was higher in long COVID than controls (p=0.003); in lab experiments, neutrophils activated by spike protein immune complexes caused measurable endothelial cell injury and barrier disruption. The authors caution that anticoagulation therapy should not be used without supporting evidence from randomized controlled trials, and note that symptom severity did not reliably correlate with biomarker levels, highlighting the need for objective diagnostic tools.

summary: This observational study (not an intervention trial) examined brain MRI and blood protein markers in 269 adults approximately one year after mild COVID-19, comparing those with Long COVID cognitive impairment (Cog-PASC, n=44 across cohorts) to those with other Long COVID symptoms (Other-PASC) and those without significant Long COVID (NS-PASC). People with cognitive impairment showed distinct brain changes not seen in other Long COVID groups, including cortical thinning in the cingulate and insular cortices, increased iron deposition in the hippocampus, enlarged choroid plexus volume, and elevated blood markers of brain cell damage (GFAP and neurofilament light chain). These findings were replicated in an independent validation cohort and persisted after matching for age, sex, and education, pointing to a neurodegenerative process specific to cognitively impaired Long COVID patients that differs from both normal COVID recovery and non-cognitive Long COVID. The study is cross-sectional, conducted at a single Korean tertiary centre, and involves small numbers in the Cog-PASC group, so causal conclusions cannot be drawn.

summary: This preclinical and observational study investigated whether the probiotic Bifidobacterium adolescentis could reduce post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis, using a cohort of 33 COVID-19 survivors and a bleomycin-induced fibrosis mouse model. In the clinical data, patients with residual lung fibrosis at 6 months post-discharge were significantly older (mean age 57 vs 42 years) and had a markedly lower Bifidobacterium/Blautia to Streptococcus ratio (B/S index 4.0 vs 38.3, p=0.001). In aging mice, oral B. adolescentis supplementation reduced collagen deposition, inflammatory markers (TGF-β, IL-17, α-SMA, Collagen I/III), and lung injury scores to levels comparable to young fibrosis mice, acting through the gut-lung axis via PGE2/PPAR/Th17 signaling pathways. This is entirely preclinical and observational — no human intervention was tested, the clinical sample was only 33 patients from a single centre, and the mouse model does not accurately replicate post-COVID lung remodelling.

summary: This is a mechanistic observational study, not a clinical trial testing an intervention. Researchers used single-cell multiomics on blood and lung fluid samples from over 200 Long COVID patients across five cohorts to characterize immune dysregulation. They identified a distinct CD14+ monocyte transcriptional state (LC-Mo), enriched in patients who had mild-to-moderate acute COVID-19, that correlated with fatigue severity and was associated with profibrotic gene expression in lung macrophages from patients with severe respiratory symptoms. Plasma levels of TNF, CCL2, and CXCL11 remained persistently elevated up to 9 months post-infection, and monocytes from patients with high LC-Mo expression showed impaired interferon responses when stimulated ex vivo.

summary: This observational study from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center compared immune, transcriptomic, and proteomic profiles of 46 Long COVID patients against 44 recovered controls across two cohorts (2020–2021 and 2023–2024). Long COVID patients showed persistent upregulation of JAK-STAT, IL-6, complement, and T cell exhaustion pathways for more than 180 days after infection, with plasma IL-6 receptor levels significantly elevated in Long COVID versus recovered controls at all timepoints measured (p=0.004 at day 90–180, p=0.00002 beyond 180 days). Machine learning models trained on these pathway signatures distinguished Long COVID from recovered controls with AUC values of 0.82–0.85, pointing to JAK-STAT and IL-6 signaling as potential therapeutic targets; the authors have since initiated a clinical trial of the JAK1 inhibitor abrocitinib (NCT06597396).

summary: This exploratory observational study used hyperpolarized xenon-129 (129Xe) MRI to examine links between lung gas exchange and cognitive function in 12 Long COVID patients (average 32 months post-infection) who had persistent respiratory and cognitive symptoms. Standard pulmonary function tests and 129Xe MRI showed no significant differences between Long COVID participants and healthy controls, yet lower 129Xe gas exchange (RBC:gas ratio) correlated strongly with worse sleep disturbance (ρ=−0.91, p<0.001) and poorer lung gas exchange correlated with higher cerebral perfusion on brain MRI (ρ=−0.70, p=0.04); better gas exchange (RBC:membrane ratio) also correlated with better executive function scores (ρ=0.67, p=0.03). Participants subjectively reported significantly reduced cognitive function in everyday life, but objective cognitive test scores were broadly within normal limits — a notable discordance. The study is limited to 12 participants with no brain MRI control group, making causal conclusions impossible.

summary: This observational study from Ulm University examined cognitive profiles in 54 Long COVID patients (Post-COVID-19 syndrome, PCS) compared to 42 healthy controls, 25 COVID-19 convalescents, and 12 post-viral patients of other causes, using a comprehensive neuropsychological battery covering memory, attention, and executive function. Cluster analysis identified two distinct PCS subgroups: a small severe cognitive impairment group (PCS-SCI, 7.5% of PCS patients, n=10) with pronounced deficits in attention, memory, and executive function, and a larger mixed group (92.5%) whose objective cognitive performance was indistinguishable from controls and convalescents despite subjective complaints. Critically, cognitive impairments in PCS were not explained by depression, anxiety, or fatigue severity in statistical models, though the severe subgroup had higher rates of lifetime psychiatric history (60% vs 22%) and universal severe fatigue. The study is observational with no intervention, and its small severe-subgroup size (n=10) limits conclusions about this clinically important minority.

summary: This observational cohort study examined whether blood biomarkers measured before and after initiating veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (V-V ECMO) could predict survival in 16–22 patients with severe COVID-19-related ARDS at a single US centre. The primary question was whether interleukin-10 (IL-10), previously proposed as a mortality predictor in non-COVID ARDS patients on ECMO, would perform similarly here; it did not — pre-ECMO IL-10 levels were nearly identical between survivors and non-survivors (31.1 vs 33.5 pg/mL, p>0.99, AUC 0.51). Several other biomarkers showed exploratory associations with mortality, including lower pre-ECMO Angiopoietin-1 and higher mitochondrial DNA and IP-10, but the very small sample size precludes multivariate analysis or firm conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial. It is a prospective observational biomarker study of acute COVID-19 ARDS patients treated with VV-ECMO, with outcomes defined as survival vs non-survival to hospital discharge. There is no randomization, no intervention arm vs control arm in the usual RCT sense — 'arms' here represent survivor/non-survivor outcome groups. Post-ECMO biomarker data (n=22) for most biomarkers are reported only in figures (Fig. 1) and not in table form; per-arm means and SDs for post-ECMO samples are therefore not_reported in this extraction except for IL-10 which is reported textually. ROC curve data are reported in Supplemental Tables S1/S2 which are not available in the provided text. summary: This observational study used EEG, diffusion MRI, and computational cognitive modeling to characterize brain changes in 70 adults who had recovered from COVID-19 (mild to moderate acute illness) compared to 26 adults who had recovered from other respiratory infections. Post-COVID participants showed reduced low-frequency (theta/alpha) oscillatory activity during working memory, cognitive control, and decision-making tasks, alongside reduced white matter integrity in specific tracts including the cingulum bundle and thalamo-occipital fasciculi. Cluster analysis identified two distinct neurophysiological subgroups within the post-COVID group: one characterized primarily by working memory and decision-making deficits (linked to cingulum and thalamo-occipital integrity), and another by impaired proactive cognitive control (linked to thalamo-parietal tract integrity). This is a mechanistic observational study with no intervention; it does not test a treatment and findings are limited by cross-sectional design and moderate sample size.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a clinical trial and should NOT be included in a meta-analysis of Long COVID clinical trials. It is a cross-sectional observational cohort study with no intervention, no randomization, and no treatment arms. The 'arms' in this extraction represent diagnostic groups (COVID vs non-COVID), not treatment allocations. Per-arm means and SDs for most outcomes are not reported numerically in text — most EEG/DTI effect sizes are reported as Bayesian posterior medians with HDIs from regression models rather than group-level descriptive statistics. No baseline demographic table with per-group age/sex breakdown was provided in extractable form. The overall age mean (40.1) and median (39) are for the full sample. EEG cluster-level effect sizes (Cohen's d) are approximations reported per the authors' novel method, not standard between-group Cohen's d. Many outcome values appear only in figures (time-frequency plots, topographic maps) with no accompanying numeric tables. The between_group_effects for EEG outcomes use the authors' reported 'mean adjusted Cohen's d' as the effect_value in the smd field, which is a non-standard cluster-level approximation.

summary: This observational study tested whether eye-tracking metrics (fixation stability, saccades, smooth pursuit, and pupil light responses) could serve as objective biomarkers of cognitive impairment in 103 adults with Long COVID. Eye movement parameters showed statistically significant but modest correlations with standard neuropsychological test scores, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.21 to 0.37, strongest for saccadic measures and executive function tasks. Machine learning clustering of eye-tracking data identified three oculomotor subgroups that differed significantly on cognitive scores (e.g., Stroop color-word: group means 29.9 vs 37.2 vs 43.4, p=0.004; semantic fluency p=0.020), suggesting eye tracking may complement but not replace formal neuropsychological assessment. The study is cross-sectional with no control group, saccade data were available for only ~50 participants, and the clustering solution showed only modest cohesion (silhouette=0.32), so findings are preliminary.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a clinical trial — it is a cross-sectional observational study with no intervention, no randomization, and no control group. It does not meet criteria for inclusion in a meta-analysis of Long COVID clinical trials. No arms exist in the traditional sense; the study uses data-driven k-means clustering to create post-hoc subgroups (Cluster 0, 1, 2) with n=17, 64, and 22 respectively. These clusters are represented as arm_ids 10, 11, 12 in outcomes 10-12. The between-group comparisons reported are post-hoc Bonferroni-corrected pairwise differences from Kruskal-Wallis/ANOVA. Per-cluster data for Digit Span Backward, TMT-A, TMT-B, SCWT Color, SCWT Word, and Phonological Fluency are also available in Table 4 but not extracted as separate outcome objects to limit output size — these are available verbatim in Table 4. Correlation coefficients between eye-tracking metrics and neuropsychological tests are reported in Table 3 (partial Spearman correlations adjusted for age and education) but are not extracted as between-group effects as they are correlational, not interventional. Time since infection mean was 620.88 days (SD 377.19 days), converted to months as 20.36 months (SD 12.57 months).

trial_rating.result_basis: Correlations between eye-tracking metrics and cognitive tests ranged |ρ|=0.21–0.37; between-cluster differences significant for Stroop color-word (p=0.004) and semantic fluency (p=0.020), but saccade subgroup N=51–53 and clustering silhouette=0.32 indicate modest and uncertain effects.

summary: This observational neuroimaging study used 7 Tesla fMRI to examine brain connectivity in 19 Long COVID patients and 16 healthy controls while they performed the Stroop colour-word cognitive task. Long COVID patients were significantly slower on the Stroop task in both scanning sessions (Run 1: p=0.001–0.017 across stimulus types; Run 2: p=0.052 for incongruent), and showed widespread deficits in inter-network connectivity across the Salience, Language, Central Executive, Sensorimotor, and Visual brain networks compared to controls, with deficits worsening in the second scan session after cognitive exertion. With longer illness duration, connectivity to key networks (Salience, Default Mode) weakened further, though compensatory increases appeared in visual processing regions such as the lingual gyri. This is a small exploratory cross-sectional study with no intervention; results are correlational and causation cannot be inferred.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT an RCT — it is a cross-sectional case-control observational neuroimaging study. There is no intervention, no randomization, and no treatment arms. The 'arms' represent the Long COVID patient group vs healthy controls. Response time data (means) are fully reported in Table 2 but SDs are not provided for any condition, limiting effect size calculations. fMRI connectivity outcomes (Tables 3, 4, 5) report only cluster sizes and p-FWE values — no per-group mean connectivity values or SDs are given. All fMRI outcome effect values are therefore null. The study reports illness duration as median 0.50 years (range 0.16-3 years), not months. The abstract states 'p=0.001, 0.003' for overall LCov vs HC RT differences across Runs 1 and 2; Table 2 provides condition-specific p-values which were extracted. Between-run p-values for LCov (InCon p=0.015, Congr p=0.049) indicate significant practice/conflict adaptation effects only in Long COVID. The design_type field is set to quasi-experimental as the closest approximation; the study is observational. RoB2 is not formally applicable but was assessed to flag study design limitations.

trial_rating.result_basis: Long COVID patients had slower Stroop response times than healthy controls in Run 1 (incongruent: 2.053s vs 1.574s, p=0.003; congruent: 1.794s vs 1.314s, p=0.001); multiple fMRI connectivity clusters showed p-FWE<0.05 differences, but this is a non-interventional observational study with n=19 LCov and n=16 HC.

summary: This study tested whether a single session of the six-minute step test (6MST), a submaximal stepping exercise, could acutely improve blood vessel function in 26 adults with long COVID compared to 21 healthy controls. The primary outcome was brachial artery flow-mediated dilation (FMD%), a measure of endothelial function: long COVID participants showed a significant increase in FMD% immediately after the 6MST (4.53% before vs. 6.83% after, p=0.0005, Cohen's d=1.038), though their post-exercise values remained well below those of healthy controls (6.83% vs. 10.07%, p=0.002). The long COVID group also had reduced exercise capacity, lower peak oxygen uptake, higher diastolic blood pressure, and greater leg fatigue during the test; notably, cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 peak) did not independently predict the vascular improvement after adjustment for confounders.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a non-randomized cross-sectional observational study, not an RCT — the 'arms' represent comparison groups (long COVID vs healthy controls), not randomized treatment allocations. Per-arm means and SDs for VO2 peak (mL/kg/min) are referenced in the univariate regression table (Table 3) and in-text but exact group-level means and SDs are not explicitly tabulated — only the regression coefficient and R² are reported. Cardiorespiratory variables (VO2, VCO2, VE, RER over time during 6MST) are presented only in figures (Fig. 4) with no tabular data available. SBP data across time points are fully tabulated but no significant between-group differences were found; these are not extracted as separate outcomes to manage output size. The paper does not report formal adverse events. The study self-describes as cross-sectional observational. Risk of bias applied using RoB2 adapted for the non-randomized design context. The FMD% pre-control value is stated as '9.88 ± 2.67' in one paragraph and the between-group post-6MST comparison references '10.07 ± 2.66' — both verbatim values are extracted at their respective timepoints.

trial_rating.result_basis: FMD% increased from 4.53% to 6.83% post-6MST in long COVID group (p=0.0005, Cohen's d=1.038); no control intervention arm, cross-sectional design only.

summary: This observational proteomics study analyzed blood plasma from 53 Long COVID patients, 62 recovered individuals without Long COVID, and 35 healthy uninfected controls, all sampled 3 months after mild, non-hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 infection. The primary finding is that both recovered and Long COVID groups showed plasma protein profiles clearly distinct from uninfected controls, with surprisingly little difference between the two infected groups; Long COVID patients specifically showed elevated oxidative stress markers (higher VNN1 and PON3, lower PRDX6 and glutathione) and increased DNA damage (8-OHdG) compared to fully recovered individuals. Six proteins—PCSK9, CST3, C1Q, CPB2, KNG1, and GAPDH—were elevated in Long COVID and linked to inflammation, coagulation, and metabolic disruption, though ELISA validation was inconsistent for several of these. The study is exploratory with a small cohort drawn from the early pandemic period, and its cross-sectional design cannot establish whether these biomarker differences cause Long COVID symptoms or simply co-occur with them.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a clinical trial — it is a cross-sectional observational proteomics study with no randomization and no intervention. RoB2 tool is not applicable. All quantitative outcome data (means, SDs) are presented only in figures (bar graphs with error bars) and not as numeric values in the text or tables; result_source is set to 'not_reported' throughout. The paper reports statistical significance thresholds (p≤0.05) but not exact p-values for most comparisons. ELISA validation used a subset: 40 PCC, 20 convalescent, 20 uninfected. Omitted biomarker outcomes due to data being figures-only: PCSK9 ELISA, C1QA ELISA, CST3 ELISA, DPP4 ELISA, Cu/Zn SOD ELISA, GAPDH DIA-MS peptide intensity, CPB2 DIA-MS peptide intensity, KNG1 DIA-MS peptide intensity, CST3 DIA-MS peptide intensity, PCSK9 DIA-MS peptide intensity. Age means/SDs not reported — only age ranges provided.

trial_rating.result_basis: 8-OHdG was significantly elevated in Long COVID vs convalescent (p≤0.05); only 2 proteins differed between PCC and convalescent groups by proteomics; PCA showed partial but overlapping group separation, indicating modest discriminatory signal.

summary: This observational lipidomics study from the University of Tokyo measured sphingolipids and glycerophospholipids in serum samples from 199 COVID-19 patients (13 of whom developed Long COVID/PASC), collected at up to 8 time points during acute illness, compared with 109 healthy controls. The primary finding was negative: no individual sphingolipid or glycerophospholipid species showed a statistically significant difference between patients who developed PASC and those who did not, after correction for multiple comparisons. An exploratory time-course analysis identified a potential signal for phosphatidylglycerol (PG), which showed a distinctive transient spike around days 10-12 in the PASC group (peak ~66,729 vs ~22,035 in non-PASC), but this is hypothesis-generating only given the very small PASC sample size of 13 patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is an observational biomarker/lipidomics cohort study with NO intervention and NO randomization. It does not meet eligibility criteria for a clinical trial meta-analysis of Long COVID treatments and should be excluded. Detailed per-arm means/SDs for most lipid species are stated to be in Supplemental Tables 1-7 which are not provided in the text; only selected estimated marginal means from the LMM for PG at selected timepoints are reported in the main text. F-statistics and denominator degrees of freedom are provided for LMM group×time effects: PG overall F(6, 669.779)=5.373, p<0.001; PG(32:0) F(6, 674.788)=6.94, p<0.001; PG(34:4) F(6, 656.337)=5.03, p<0.001. Most quantitative lipid data (means, SDs per arm per timepoint) are only available in supplemental tables not provided in the paper text. Demographic characteristics (age, sex, BMI) are stated to be in Supplemental Table 1, not provided in the main text. All p-values reported as <0.001 or thresholds. LMM fixed-effect estimate for Days 10-12 vs reference: beta=49,699.773, SE=9,092.193, t=5.466, p<0.001.

summary: This pilot randomised controlled trial tested a 12-week remotely delivered physical activity (PA) coaching programme — combining wearable activity tracking, weekly one-to-one physiotherapist sessions, personalised feedback, and collaborative goal-setting — against usual care in 50 adults with Long COVID (mean age 46, 76% female, averaging 42 months post-infection). The primary outcome was feasibility: recruitment (89%), retention (92%), and adherence (83%) all met pre-specified thresholds, with no adverse events. At three months, the coaching group walked approximately 4,600 more steps per day and covered 119 metres further on the six-minute walk test compared to usual care, with improvements in fatigue (FACIT-FS +11 points), dyspnoea (mMRC −1 grade), and quality of life (EQ-5D-5L +21 points); these gains were maintained or grew at six months. Anxiety and depression scores did not improve, and baseline imbalances in dyspnoea severity and time since infection between groups are a notable limitation of this small pilot.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested speleotherapy (underground climate therapy — spending 2 hours per session, six sessions over three weeks, in certified therapeutic caves) as an add-on to standard treatment in 42 adults with Long COVID across nine centers in Germany, Austria, and Italy. The primary outcome for the Long COVID subgroup was improvement in lung function (FEV₁, FVC, PEF) and respiratory muscle strength, neither of which improved significantly in the speleotherapy group; FEV₁ actually improved more in the control group. However, patients receiving speleotherapy reported significant improvements in dysfunctional breathing (Nijmegen Questionnaire, p=0.014), dyspnea (p=0.026 post-treatment, p=0.001 at 3-month follow-up), problems with stair climbing and muscle exertion (p=0.042), and anxiety and sleep disturbances (p=0.021). The trial was underpowered for the Long COVID subgroup (n=42, power 0.7), was retrospectively registered, and the lead investigator is president of the German Speleotherapy Association and received payment for organizing the study.

summary: This observational study used machine learning to predict which adults hospitalized with acute COVID-19 (385 patients from 20 US hospitals, May 2020–March 2021) would develop long COVID within 12 months. Five ML models trained on admission-time clinical data, antibody titers, and viral load achieved modest predictive accuracy on held-out test data (AUROC 0.64–0.66, AUPRC 0.51–0.54). The strongest predictors of long COVID were low anti-spike IgG antibody levels and high viral load at admission, followed by chronic respiratory, cardiac, or neurologic disease, and female sex. The models were developed in a pre-vaccine, hospitalized-only cohort and may not generalise to milder illness or current patient populations with hybrid immunity.

trial_rating.result_basis: Test-set AUROC ranged from 0.637 to 0.658 across five models, and AUPRC from 0.51 to 0.54, indicating modest discrimination above chance (AUROC 0.5) but well below strong predictive performance.

summary: This study does not test a clinical intervention; it develops a theoretical causal modelling framework for Long COVID using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and Bayesian networks. The framework maps hypothesised biological pathways from acute COVID-19 to persistent organ dysfunction and symptoms across four time periods, tested through four illustrative scenarios rather than patient data. Key illustrative findings show that patients reporting symptoms at both the acute phase and 3+ months later (consistent with Long COVID definitions) have a 36-40% modelled probability of persistent organ dysfunction, compared to 1-7% for those with mild or severe acute disease alone. The framework has not yet been validated against real clinical trial or observational data, limiting its current utility to hypothesis generation and study design guidance.

There are no study arms, no enrolled participants, no randomization, no interventions, and no measured clinical outcomes. All numerical values in the paper are illustrative conditional probabilities within the Bayesian network model (e.g., P(mild disease)=0.1), not trial outcome data. All quantitative fields have been set to null accordingly.

summary: This Belgian feasibility RCT tested whether adding personalised nutritional counselling (via weekly dietitian teleconsultations) to pacing-based physiotherapy improved physical performance in 65 adults with Long COVID (mean symptom duration ~78 weeks), compared to standard physiotherapy alone over 12 weeks with 6-week follow-up. The primary exploratory outcome was the 1-minute sit-to-stand test (1-MSTS): the combined therapy group gained roughly 1 more repetition than controls at 12 weeks (mean difference 0.97 repetitions, 95% CI −1.75 to 3.70), a non-significant and clinically uncertain difference, though the gap widened to 2.14 repetitions (95% CI −1.26 to 5.54) at 18-week follow-up. The trial was primarily designed to assess feasibility rather than efficacy, and was not powered to detect significant effects; dropout reached 27.7% by follow-up, partly due to high study burden from frequent hospital visits.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Participants with lower baseline capacity (<75% predicted) achieved substantially greater 6MWD improvements (r=0.257, small-to-moderate effect size); higher-performing participants showed smaller gains.
Younger participants (<65 years) achieved significantly greater 6MWD gains (Z=2.117, r=0.244); weak negative correlation between age and 6MWD change (r=-0.262, p<0.05).

No significant sex differences in magnitude of 6MWD change (p>0.05). However, men achieved significantly greater respiratory muscle strength (PImax: r=-0.578, p<0.001; PEmax: r=-0.538, p<0.001) and chest expansion at 10th rib (r=-0.241, p=0.037). Women were more likely to report headaches, chest pain, and muscle/joint pain at 6 months.

summary: A six-week outpatient multi-component rehabilitation programme — combining aerobic cycling, respiratory muscle training with an inspiratory muscle trainer (at 45–80% of PImax), strength training, stretching, and speech/voice exercises — was tested in 75 Long COVID patients (median age 65, all with dyspnoea and functional impairment) in a randomised controlled trial with six-month follow-up. The primary outcomes of six-minute walk distance (6MWD), maximal inspiratory pressure (PImax), and maximal expiratory pressure (PEmax) all showed large, statistically significant improvements immediately post-intervention that were sustained at six months: median 6MWD rose from 300 m to 368 m (+50 m from baseline to follow-up, p<0.001, r=0.615), PImax rose from 49 to 77 cmH₂O (+25 cmH₂O, p<0.001), and PEmax from 63 to 95 cmH₂O (+23 cmH₂O, p<0.001). A notable caveat is that after the six-week programme ended, cough and headache prevalence increased slightly at the six-month follow-up, and marginal declines in PImax and PEmax occurred between the end of treatment and follow-up, though both remained far above baseline.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Multivariable MR showed VTE predisposition remained significantly associated with long COVID after adjusting for all three acute COVID-19 severity phenotypes, suggesting effects are not fully mediated by acute disease severity.
Replication with stricter controls (proven SARS-CoV-2 infection without long COVID) showed consistent positive association between genetically predicted VTE risk and long COVID.
Replication using externally derived genetic instruments from the Million Veteran Program yielded consistent significant positive associations with long COVID.
Replication in PHOSP-COVID (n=1,097; 697 cases, 400 controls) of hospitalized COVID-19 patients showed significant positive association consistent with primary analysis.

summary: This Mendelian randomization (MR) study used genetic data to test whether a biological predisposition to venous thromboembolism (VTE) causally increases the risk of developing Long COVID, in people with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. Using 35 genetic variants linked to VTE from FinnGen (412,181 participants) and testing them against Long COVID outcomes in the Long COVID Host Genetics Initiative (3,018 cases, 994,582 controls), the study found that genetically predicted VTE risk was associated with a 21% higher odds of Long COVID (OR 1.21, 95% CI 1.08–1.35, p=0.0012), an effect that held up across multiple sensitivity analyses and independent replication cohorts and was independent of acute COVID-19 severity. Gene-focused analyses identified PAR-1 (the thrombin receptor encoded by F2R) as a candidate molecular mediator, with higher genetically predicted PAR-1 levels associated with 1.80-fold odds of Long COVID (95% CI 1.07–3.04). This is not an interventional trial but a genetic epidemiology study; it provides evidence for a causal role of thromboembolic pathways in Long COVID pathogenesis and identifies PAR-1 as a potential therapeutic target, but does not test any treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is a Mendelian randomization (genetic epidemiology) study, NOT a clinical trial or RCT. Full quantitative data for these are in supplementary tables not provided.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary MR estimate: OR 1.21 (95% CI 1.08–1.35, p=1.2×10⁻³) per log-odds increase in genetically predicted VTE risk for Long COVID; statistically significant but modest in absolute magnitude.

summary: Researchers at Ohio State University developed a paper-based immunoassay using mass spectrometry to detect SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N) protein in plasma, testing it as a potential diagnostic tool for Long COVID. The assay was applied to plasma samples from 10 Long COVID patients (confirmed prior SARS-CoV-2 infection with persistent symptoms for at least 12 weeks) and 10 healthy controls with no infection history. Long COVID patients showed MS signal intensities up to two orders of magnitude higher than controls (p < 0.01), with no overlap between groups, supporting the hypothesis that residual viral antigen persists in Long COVID. This is a proof-of-concept diagnostic technology study with a very small sample (n=20), not a clinical trial evaluating a treatment or intervention.

summary: This is a computational fluid dynamics study, not a clinical trial — it used fluid-structure interaction (FSI) simulation to model how COVID-19-associated blood hyperviscosity affects hemodynamics in a 3D carotid artery bifurcation model. The study compared simulated blood flow parameters (wall shear stress, arterial deformation, von Mises stress, velocity) between normal viscosity (0.0035 Pa·s) and COVID-19-associated hyperviscous blood (0.0098 Pa·s) using both Newtonian and Carreau-Yasuda non-Newtonian rheological models. Under hyperviscous conditions, maximum wall shear stress nearly doubled (from ~5.09 to ~9.44 Pa in the Newtonian model; from ~4.83 to ~9.32 Pa in Carreau-Yasuda), time-averaged WSS rose from 5.018 to 9.882 Pa, and arterial wall deformation decreased. This is a computational modelling study with no patients and no clinical outcomes; its relevance to Long COVID treatment is indirect at best.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a clinical trial and is NOT eligible for inclusion in a Long COVID clinical trial meta-analysis. It is a purely computational FSI simulation study examining hemodynamic effects of COVID-19-associated blood hyper-viscosity in a carotid artery model. There are no human participants, no randomization, no intervention arms, no clinical outcomes, and no patient-level data. All 'results' are simulation outputs (velocity magnitudes, wall shear stress values, von Mises stress, arterial deformation) from a mathematical model. Quantitative simulation outputs reported include: maximum velocity magnitudes (Newtonian normal: 0.058, 0.095, 0.068 m/s; hyper-viscous: 0.043, 0.093, 0.057 m/s at t=0.21, 0.3, 0.7 s); max WSS (Newtonian normal: 5.094 Pa, hyper-viscous: 9.438 Pa; Carreau-Yasuda normal: 4.827 Pa, hyper-viscous: 9.317 Pa); TAWSS (Newtonian normal: 5.018 Pa, hyper-viscous: 9.882 Pa; Carreau-Yasuda normal: 3.651 Pa, hyper-viscous: 8.021 Pa); max deformation values at multiple time points; and von Mises stress values. These are not extractable into the clinical trial schema.

trial_rating.result_basis: No clinical trial was conducted; all results are from computational simulation. Maximum WSS increased from 5.094 to 9.438 Pa under hyperviscous conditions in the Newtonian model — a simulation output, not a clinical outcome measure.

summary: This preclinical study examined long-term changes in the nasal tissue of Syrian hamsters infected with wild-type SARS-CoV-2, tracking animals for up to 120 days post-infection (equivalent to roughly 15 human years). Viral RNA and nucleocapsid protein remained detectable in nasal tissue in a subset of animals at 120 days (57% positive for subgenomic RNA, 18% positive for nucleocapsid protein), accompanied by sustained elevation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6, and others), persistent cell death in the nasal epithelium, and a 7.7-fold upregulation of CX3CR1—a receptor used by respiratory syncytial virus—compared to uninfected controls. These findings suggest that residual viral components may drive chronic nasal inflammation and tissue damage, and potentially increase susceptibility to secondary respiratory infections, though results are from an animal model and cannot be directly extrapolated to humans.

summary: This is not a Long COVID clinical trial. It is a Bayesian epidemiological modelling study of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron transmission dynamics in China following the December 2022 exit from the 'dynamic zero-COVID' policy. Using national surveillance data (reported case counts and weekly ILI/virological data), the authors estimated that approximately 87.8% of China's population was infected by mid-February 2023, with 84.1% infected within one month of the policy shift. The effective reproduction number peaked at 5.69 on 8 December 2022, and transmission rates were strongly correlated with population behavioural responses to perceived infection risk.

summary: This observational study used single-cell RNA sequencing to profile immune cells in the lungs and blood of 21 patients with persistent respiratory symptoms or CT abnormalities three years after COVID-19, with no therapeutic intervention tested. The key finding is that cytotoxic CD8+ tissue-resident memory T cells (GZMB+ and GZMK+ subtypes) remained elevated in airway fluid up to three years post-infection and were negatively correlated with lung function (FVC), while SPP1+ macrophages and LAMP3+ dendritic cells correlated positively with FVC. The study proposes that SPP1+ macrophages suppress these T cells via PD-L1/PD-1 signalling, potentially restraining lung damage while enabling repair, and identifies SPP1+ macrophages as a candidate therapeutic target — though no clinical intervention was evaluated.

summary: This cross-sectional study tested whether an electronic nose (e-Nose) device analyzing volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in exhaled breath could screen for Long COVID in 78 Mexican university students (median age 20 years) with prior COVID-19 infection. The e-Nose, analyzed using machine learning methods including PLS-DA and Random Forest, distinguished Long COVID cases (29.5% of participants) from healthy controls with high accuracy: PLS-DA achieved 97.4% accuracy, and the Random Forest model produced an ROC AUC of 0.966 with an out-of-bag error of 3.42%. All participants had normal spirometry, suggesting that standard lung function tests miss the metabolic or systemic changes detectable in breath. The study is proof-of-concept only — the sample is small, the design is cross-sectional, and the e-Nose device is a custom research instrument not yet validated in independent cohorts.

summary: This observational study used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to measure cerebral blood flow patterns in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during cognitive tasks in 12 Long COVID patients, compared to 12 age-matched coronary artery disease patients and 12 young healthy controls. The primary finding was that Long COVID patients showed reduced temporal variability (lower sample entropy, mean 0.026 vs 0.030 in CAD during N-back, p=0.030) but higher spatial variability (CV of sample entropy 0.263 vs 0.213 in CAD vs 0.172 in controls during N-back, p=0.002) in prefrontal blood flow regulation during cognitive tasks. Long COVID patients also performed worse cognitively, with reaction times averaging 776ms vs 546ms in healthy controls (p=0.003) and lower accuracy. This is a small cross-sectional observational study with no intervention; it characterises a biomarker of cerebrovascular dysregulation rather than testing any treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a cross-sectional observational study, NOT a clinical trial or RCT. It has no randomization, no intervention being tested, and no treatment arms — it compares PCS patients to two control groups (CAD patients and healthy young adults) on fNIRS-derived cerebral blood flow metrics during cognitive tasks. The study design fields have been filled as best as possible given the observational nature. RoB2 is not applicable; high risk assigned due to non-randomized design. Tukey HSD differences in Table 2 are reported as pairwise differences (PCS minus CAD, CAD minus CTRL), which have been used as effect values. ANOVA overall p-values are reported (not per-comparison p-values); Tukey's HSD p-values are listed as column values in Table 2 and appear to be shared across the overall ANOVA result row. Age IQR data for PCS were listed in Table 1 (median 57.6, IQR 10.1, range 40.0-63.7) but IQR low/high boundaries are not explicitly given. Regression analysis results (Table 3) for CV(SampEn) vs. reaction time and accuracy are not included as separate outcome objects but are noted here: intercept for RT=412.1±91.3, CV coefficient=1102.5±399.8, adjusted R²=0.17, F(1,31)=7.60, P=0.01; intercept for accuracy=0.996±0.016, CV coefficient=-0.172±0.069, adjusted R²=0.14, F(1,31)=6.17, P=0.02.

summary: This preclinical mouse study tested whether combining antiviral drugs (nirmatrelvir and molnupiravir) with the corticosteroid dexamethasone could prevent neurological long COVID features in mice infected with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2. Infected mice developed persistent loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the olfactory bulb and substantia nigra, sustained microglial inflammation, and measurable motor deficits lasting at least 120 days post-infection — changes mirrored in brain tissue from deceased COVID-19 patients. Antivirals alone failed to restore motor function or tyrosine hydroxylase expression, but combining antivirals with dexamethasone — even when started 3 days after infection — significantly improved rotarod performance and open-field movement compared to vehicle controls (p<0.05 to p<0.0001). Dexamethasone alone was uniformly lethal in infected mice, underscoring that the anti-inflammatory benefit requires concurrent antiviral coverage.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL LIMITATION: This is a preclinical animal study (mouse model), NOT a human clinical trial of Long COVID patients. It does not meet standard eligibility criteria for human meta-analyses. The paper describes (1) a mouse PASC model with antiviral/anti-inflammatory treatment arms and (2) a small human autopsy case series (n=26, Table 1) examining TH+ cell counts in SN — neither is a human RCT. RoB2 tool is not applicable. All quantitative outcome data (means, SDs, exact p-values) for behavioral and biomarker outcomes are presented exclusively in figures with no numerical values in text or tables, making verbatim extraction impossible — all result fields are set to null with result_source='not_reported'. Human autopsy data from Table 1 provides individual TH+ cell counts per patient: COVID-19 patients (n=12): 529, 610, 809, 739, 1189, 360, 645, 279, 367, 390, 117, 536 (mean ~548); Uninfected controls (n=14): 297, 1090, 1210, 774, 851, 624, 857, 639, 703, 1563, 841, 715, 1327, 1418 (mean ~921). Statistical comparison p<0.01 by Mann-Whitney U test. Dexamethasone-alone arm was not carried to behavioral endpoints because it caused 100% lethality. The human arm_id assignments in outcome 6 are repurposed: arm_id=1 = uninfected controls (n=14 with available TH data), arm_id=2 = COVID-19 patients (n=12 with available TH data), which differs from the mouse study arm assignments.

trial_rating.result_basis: Mice receiving nirmatrelvir + molnupiravir + dexamethasone showed significantly improved rotarod time and open-field distance vs vehicle controls at 100-110 dpi (p<0.05 to p<0.001); antiviral-only group showed no significant improvement on either measure (p not significant vs vehicle).

summary: A Pfizer-funded decision tree model estimated the public health and economic impact of increased uptake of an additional dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech KP.2-adapted COVID-19 vaccine (2024-2025 formula) among US adults aged 65 and older. At the observed uptake of 8.9%, the model estimated the additional dose would prevent approximately 271,000 COVID-19 cases, 8,400 hospitalizations, 285 deaths, and 65,000 Long COVID cases annually, saving $623 million in direct medical costs. Raising uptake to 41.1% (matching initial dose uptake) was projected to avert nearly 39,000 hospitalizations and $2.8 billion in costs. This is a modelling study, not a clinical trial, and all authors are Pfizer employees or Pfizer-funded contractors, which is a significant conflict of interest.

summary: This observational study examined immune cell mitochondrial function and cytokine responses in 27 long COVID patients (median symptom duration 3.1 years, 70% female) compared to 27 COVID-recovered healthy controls. Long COVID patients showed significantly reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in CD56bright natural killer cells and, upon stimulation, lower IFNγ production in response to bacterial (LPS) and viral (R848) immune triggers. Specific symptom-biomarker associations emerged: reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in CD4+ T cells correlated with breathlessness and walking difficulties, while blunted IFNβ and IL-10 responses to viral stimulation were linked to chronic cough and cognitive/social difficulties respectively. This is a small, single-centre observational study that cannot establish causality, and the identified immune signatures represent potential biomarkers rather than therapeutic targets at this stage.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is NOT a clinical trial or RCT — it is a cross-sectional observational case-control study with no intervention, randomization, or treatment arms. The JSON schema fields for RCT design (randomization, blinding, allocation concealment, intervention arms, follow-up duration, adverse events) are largely not applicable. All quantitative outcome data (mitochondrial MFI values, cytokine concentrations, exact C19-YRSm scores) appear only in figures without tabulated numeric values in the text; per-arm means, SDs, and exact p-values are therefore not extractable. Duration of LC was reported as median 1118 days (IQR 964.5–1331) in the text and as 1130 days (SD 367) in Table 1 — both are included. Omitted outcomes (all numeric values only in figures): mitochondrial mass of all cell types, MMP of CD8+ T cells, B cells, monocytes, all 11 cytokine levels under unstimulated/polyI:C/IFNalpha2 conditions, classical monocyte cell counts and percentages association with breathlessness at rest.

summary: This observational study from the University of Tokyo analyzed plasma lipid profiles in 215 COVID-19 patients (with and without Long COVID/PASC) and 115 healthy controls to identify potential biomarkers of PASC. Using targeted lipidomic mass spectrometry, researchers found that ceramides and sphingomyelins were significantly lower in PASC patients compared to both COVID-19 patients without PASC and healthy controls, while phosphatidylglycerol showed a relative rebound toward normal levels in PASC. Distinct lipidomic clustering between groups was confirmed by multivariate analysis, with ceramide and phosphatidylglycerol identified as key discriminators of PASC status. This is a biomarker discovery study with no intervention tested; it identifies candidate metabolic signatures but does not establish causation or clinical utility.

summary: This observational study compared 39 Military Health System beneficiaries with persistent dyspnea at least 3 months after COVID-19 against 76 whose dyspnea had resolved, using comprehensive cardiopulmonary testing including pulmonary function tests, chest CT, echocardiography, ECG, and a six-minute walk test (6MWT). Participants with ongoing dyspnea walked significantly less far (396 m vs 447 m, p=0.01) and reported higher breathlessness scores at rest and after exertion, but showed no significant differences in lung function (FEV1, FVC, DLCO), chest imaging, or cardiac tests. Standard clinical investigations failed to explain persistent post-COVID dyspnea, suggesting the mechanism is not captured by routine cardiopulmonary workup and that 6MWT distance and Borg scores may be useful endpoints for future Long COVID trials.

The p-value reported in the abstract for 6MWT distance is stated as p=.01 while Table 2 shows p=.012 — the table value was used as it is more precise. The percent previously hospitalized (38.5%) refers to cases only (first recorded infection). summary: This observational study assessed fatigue severity in 35 Long COVID patients attending a clinic in Detroit, Michigan, using the Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS), alongside depression screening (PHQ-2/PHQ-9) and cognitive testing (MoCA). Over half of patients (51%, n=18) had severe fatigue, and these patients reported significantly higher rates of depression symptoms (PHQ-2/PHQ-9 scores, p=0.01-0.04) as well as physical symptoms including shortness of breath, dry cough, headache, and muscle pain. Cognitive impairment measured by MoCA did not correlate with fatigue severity (p=0.2), suggesting depression rather than cognitive dysfunction is the key neurological co-factor in severe Long COVID fatigue.

The total n=35 but the paper states 18 (51.5%) had severe fatigue, implying 17 had mild-to-moderate fatigue. summary: This observational study used the NIH All of Us Research Program to examine whether daily step counts (measured via wearable devices and EHR data) are associated with Long COVID risk in adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. Researchers built a phenotype risk score (PheRS) for Long COVID and found that higher step counts at all time periods — before and after infection — were independently associated with lower odds of Long COVID, with odds ratios of 0.90–0.92 per unit increase in step count (all p<0.05). Notably, it was sustained activity across all periods rather than changes in activity level that predicted lower risk, suggesting baseline fitness matters more than reactive increases in exercise after infection.

AUC values (0.85 vs 0.75) are comparisons between two PheRS algorithms, not between patient groups. Sample sizes, baseline demographics, and most quantitative data are not reported in the abstract text and appear only in referenced figures (Figure 1, 2, 3). summary: This study tested whether smartwatch-derived heart rate data combined with daily symptom surveys during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection could predict which patients would develop Long COVID. summary: This is a preclinical mouse and human tissue study (not a clinical trial) investigating TCF4 (Tcf7l2), a transcription factor that governs alveolar macrophage (AM) stemness, as a potential therapeutic target for post-COVID lung fibrosis. summary: This is a preclinical mouse study, not a human clinical trial, investigating sex differences in acute and post-acute SARS-CoV-2 sequelae. Adult C57BL/6 mice infected intranasally with the mu variant (B.1.621) showed that males suffered worse acute disease, while infected females developed persistent neurocognitive deficits — including spatial working memory impairment in the T-maze and failed novel object recognition at 42 days post-infection — accompanied by prolonged hippocampal neuroinflammation and activated microglia. Using XY* transgenic mice, the study identified that having two X chromosomes (rather than sex hormones) drives both protection against acute disease severity and susceptibility to post-acute neurocognitive sequelae, mediated through infection-induced upregulation of X-linked genes Xist and Tlr7 in pulmonary macrophages. This is animal research only and cannot be directly applied to human Long COVID treatment or outcomes.

summary: This pilot study tested whether the Aethlon Hemopurifier — a blood filtration device using Galanthus nivalis agglutinin (GNA) lectin resin — could capture mannose-glycosylated extracellular vesicles (EVs) from plasma of 30 Long COVID patients (with and without neuropsychiatric symptoms) compared to 15 recovered controls. The primary finding was that Long COVID patients had significantly higher levels of mannose-positive large EVs than recovered individuals (approximately two-fold higher, p<0.05), and GNA resin removed 31-42% more small EVs from Long COVID plasma than controls, though this difference was not statistically significant. Seven specific miRNAs were significantly depleted by GNA resin treatment, with pathway analysis inferring this could down-regulate JAK-STAT signaling and up-regulate endothelial repair pathways — but these are computational inferences, not clinical outcomes. Critically, the study is funded by Aethlon Medical (manufacturer of the Hemopurifier) and three authors are company employees, making this a mechanistic biomarker study rather than a clinical trial; no patient symptoms or clinical outcomes were measured.

summary: This observational study measured plasma levels of complement system proteins in 159 Long COVID patients and 76 healthy COVID-recovered controls to identify biomarkers of disease. The key finding is that MASP-2/C1Inh, a marker of lectin pathway complement activation, was significantly elevated in Long COVID patients compared to controls (p=0.0003), indicating sustained activation of the lectin complement pathway in Long COVID. A four-marker panel combining MASP-2/C1Inh, TCC, iC3b, and properdin achieved an AUC of 0.796 (95% CI 0.664–0.905) for distinguishing Long COVID from recovery, suggesting the lectin pathway as a potential therapeutic target. This is a biomarker discovery study with no intervention tested; it has notable conflicts of interest as several authors consult for Omeros Corporation, which develops lectin pathway inhibitors.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is NOT a clinical trial or RCT. It is an observational cross-sectional case-control biomarker study. It should not be included in a meta-analysis of clinical trials. No intervention was administered, no randomization occurred, and the study design does not map onto the RCT extraction schema. All per-arm quantitative biomarker data (means, SDs) appear only in figures (Figure 1 density/dot plots; Figure 4 density plots) with no numeric values reported in text or tables — result_source set to not_reported throughout. The Z-statistics in Tables 1 and 2 represent the GLM model Z-scores, not effect sizes between arms. The SE values in Tables 1 and 2 are model SEs from GLMs used for AUC calculation. The C1s/C1Inh 13% increase mentioned in text is a relative change without absolute values. RoB2 tool is not applicable to this study design.

trial_rating.result_basis: MASP-2/C1Inh was elevated in Long COVID vs controls (p=0.0003); four-marker panel AUC=0.796 (95% CI 0.664–0.905), indicating moderate discriminative ability but no clinical intervention was tested.

summary: This is a preclinical and observational study, not a clinical trial. Researchers used a viral vector to transiently express the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (Ancestral and Delta variants) in transgenic K18-hACE2 mice, then tested whether aspirin (10 mg/kg daily for 17 days) could prevent the resulting pathology. In vehicle-treated mice, spike protein expression caused 45% mortality with weight loss between days 7-10, while aspirin-treated mice achieved 100% survival with significantly less weight loss and reduced lung inflammation. In a separate observational component, serum from 80 long COVID patients showed significantly elevated IGFBP-1 compared to 15 non-COVID controls, and higher CXCL13 levels were associated with more severe long COVID symptoms. This is mouse mechanistic research with a small human biomarker cohort; no clinical intervention in Long COVID patients was tested.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper is NOT an eligible long COVID clinical trial. It is a preclinical animal study with a cross-sectional observational biomarker component in long COVID patients. No randomized clinical intervention was tested in humans. The human component (N=80 long COVID patients, N=15 controls) is a biomarker association study only, with no randomization, intervention arms, or treatment. The aspirin intervention was conducted only in mice (K18-hACE2 transgenic mice), not in human long COVID patients. Consequently, most RCT-specific fields are null. Arm IDs in the outcomes section are used descriptively to represent comparison groups (arm 1=long COVID patients overall, arm 2=non-COVID controls, arm 3=mild long COVID, arm 4=moderate-to-critical long COVID, arm 5=no comorbidity, arm 6=comorbidity present, arm 7=age <50, arm 8=age ≥50), not intervention arms. Quantitative IGFBP-1 and CXCL13 per-arm median values with IQRs are available only from Table 1 subgroup breakdowns; overall group medians for long COVID vs control were not reported numerically in text or tables (data only in Figure 6E-F). Risk of bias assessment is inapplicable; the RoB2 judgment of 'high' reflects non-applicability rather than genuine bias domain ratings.

trial_rating.result_basis: Aspirin-treated mice: 100% survival vs 55% survival in vehicle controls (45% mortality); weight loss significantly reduced (p<0.05 by log-rank and multiple t-tests). Human cohort: IGFBP-1 significantly elevated in long COVID patients vs controls (Mann-Whitney U, p<0.05, n=80 vs n=15).

summary: This study profiled chemical modifications on RNA molecules (m5C, m6A, and pseudouridine) in blood samples from six hospitalised COVID-19 patients compared to nine healthy controls, using Oxford Nanopore direct RNA sequencing. The researchers identified hundreds of modification sites that were more abundant in infected individuals, concentrated in immune-related genes such as CSF3R, PIK3CD, and CAPZB, with pathway analysis pointing to endocytosis, phagocytosis, and phagosome maturation as key affected processes. This is a small, descriptive molecular profiling study with no intervention and no clinical outcomes; the modification sites are computationally predicted and require experimental validation. It has no direct relevance to Long COVID treatment or patient outcomes.

summary: This is not a Long COVID trial. The paper is an observational microbiome sub-study nested within the APPROACH phase I/IIa clinical trial, which tested an adenovirus serotype 26 (Ad26)-vectored mosaic HIV-1 vaccine in healthy, HIV-uninfected adults from Uganda, Rwanda, and the United States. The study analyzed gut bacterial and viral communities from 154 fecal samples to identify correlations with immune responses to the HIV vaccine. The key finding was that geography, not vaccination, drove microbiome differences: East African participants had higher gut bacterial diversity than US participants but generated weaker antibody and T-cell responses to the vaccine. This paper is not eligible for a Long COVID trial summary.

summary: This paper reports a 6-year integrated safety analysis of upadacitinib (a once-daily oral JAK1 inhibitor) in 2,683 adults and adolescents with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis across three phase 3 randomised controlled trials, representing over 9,000 patient-years of exposure. This is a safety-focused analysis rather than an efficacy trial; the primary finding is that rates of adverse events of special interest — including serious infections, herpes zoster, major cardiovascular events (MACE), venous thromboembolism (VTE), and malignancies — remained stable over 6 years with no evidence of cumulative increased risk. MACE and VTE incidence rates were low (≤0.2 per 100 patient-years for both doses) and broadly comparable to background rates in the atopic dermatitis population; dose-dependent side effects including herpes zoster (3.2 vs 5.2 per 100 patient-years for 15 mg vs 30 mg), hepatic disorders, neutropenia, and CPK elevation were more frequent with the higher dose but rarely led to discontinuation. This paper is not a Long COVID trial and does not address Long COVID; it concerns atopic dermatitis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a long-term safety analysis of atopic dermatitis clinical trials (upadacitinib), NOT a Long COVID clinical trial. It should be excluded from a Long COVID meta-analysis. All outcomes are adverse event/safety rates (E/100 PY or n/100 PY), not efficacy outcomes for Long COVID symptoms. No efficacy outcomes (e.g., EASI, IGA) are reported in this paper — only safety data are presented. There is no placebo arm for the long-term period (placebo patients were re-randomized to active treatment at week 16), so this is effectively a comparison of two active doses only. Several rate values in Table 3 are reported as '<0.1' without an exact number; these are captured as rate_text in the notable_aes section. Age-stratified data from Table 5 were summarized in subgroup_analyses rather than fully extracted due to complexity. COVID-19 as an adverse event is listed in Table 4 and represents SARS-CoV-2 infection occurring during the trial, not Long COVID.

summary: This is not a Long COVID clinical trial. It is a secondary analysis of Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 data examining global trends in sense organ diseases (hearing loss, blindness/vision loss, and other sensory impairments) across 204 countries from 1990 to 2021. The study found that the global age-standardised DALY rate for sense organ diseases rose from 884 to 913 per 100,000 population over this period, driven primarily by population growth and ageing, with the COVID-19 pandemic appearing to worsen the burden (observed DALYs in 2021 were 77.3 million versus a projected 65.7 million). This paper has no intervention, no trial population, and no clinical outcome relevant to a Long COVID trial registry.

summary: This study tested a four-test non-invasive electrodiagnostic protocol (sympathetic skin responses, cutaneous silent period, quantitative thermal thresholds, and electrochemical skin conductance) to detect small fibre neuropathy (SFN) in nine Long COVID patients with neuropathic and autonomic symptoms attending a multidisciplinary clinic in South Australia. The primary aim was proof-of-concept feasibility, not a therapeutic intervention; 3 of 9 patients (33%) met the threshold for SFN on at least two of the four tests, with different patients showing abnormalities on different test combinations. No significant difference in symptom or disability scores was found between those with and without SFN, highlighting that questionnaires alone cannot identify which patients have objective nerve damage. The study is limited by very small sample size (n=9) and lack of a control group, and the authors explicitly frame it as proof-of-concept only.

summary: This study used Mendelian randomization (MR) and single-cell RNA sequencing to investigate the biological mechanism by which COVID-19 infection causes pulmonary fibrosis — it is not a clinical trial testing an intervention in patients. Using genetic data from over 1.3 million people, the researchers found that COVID-19 infection causally increases the risk of developing idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (OR 1.15, 95% CI 1.05–1.25). Follow-up analyses identified lactate metabolism — specifically a gene called SLC16A4 that transports lactate out of lung cells — as a key intermediate pathway, and lab experiments showed that blocking SLC16A4 reduced fibrosis-associated gene activation in fibroblasts. The findings are mechanistic and exploratory; no patients were treated, and the authors note the work lacks in vivo animal model or clinical validation.

summary: This German RCT (RELOAD, NCT05172206) tested a 3-week inpatient, multimodal, symptom-based rehabilitation programme versus usual care in 132 adults with Long COVID, 90% of whom had mild non-hospitalised acute COVID-19. The programme was tailored to each participant's dominant symptom cluster (fatigue, cognitive problems, or somatic symptoms) and delivered by a multidisciplinary team. Physical quality of life (SF-12 PCS) improved significantly more in the rehabilitation group at 3 weeks (mean difference +2.9 points, 95% CI 0.2–5.7, p=0.038), with the benefit persisting and widening at 3 months (+4.2 points, p=0.003); mental quality of life, depression, and anxiety also improved significantly at 3 weeks. No adverse events occurred, though unblinded participants and the modest effect size on the primary outcome limit confidence in the magnitude of benefit.

summary: This observational study examined immune cell gene expression in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) from 19 COVID-19 survivors with post-COVID interstitial lung disease (ILD), comparing 6 patients who developed persistent fibrotic lung abnormalities at 18 months against 13 who fully resolved. Patients with persistent post-COVID ILD showed significantly elevated innate immune activation — including upregulation of pro-fibrotic SPP1 and monocyte chemoattractants (CCL2, CXCL8) — and a higher proportion of monocyte-like cells in lung fluid (4.6% vs 3.0%, p=0.03), while patients who recovered showed stronger T-cell and adaptive immune gene signatures. Lung monocyte accumulation at 6 months strongly predicted worse lung capacity one year later (Spearman r=−0.85, p=0.002). This is a mechanistic study with no treatment intervention; its primary value is in identifying immune biomarkers that may predict who will develop fibrosis after COVID-19.

summary: This is a computational chemistry study, not a clinical trial. Researchers used density functional theory (DFT) to calculate electronic properties of the 13-amino-acid N-terminal domain of the SARS-CoV-2 envelope (E) protein, with the goal of identifying it as a potential drug target relevant to Long COVID. The key finding is that this domain has high electrophilicity (electrophilicity index ω = 14.17 eV) and moderate reactivity (HOMO-LUMO gap of 2.95 eV), leading the authors to propose that nucleophilic compounds could bind to it and potentially block ion channel activity or viral assembly. No patients were enrolled, no intervention was tested, and no clinical outcomes were measured; the paper is purely theoretical and provides no direct evidence of therapeutic benefit in Long COVID.

summary: This cross-sectional multimodal MRI study examined brain structure, white-matter microstructure, functional connectivity, and cerebral blood flow in 76 COVID-19 survivors compared with 51 healthy controls, scanned 3-6 months after recovery in India. COVID-19 survivors showed focal subcortical atrophy in right-hemisphere basal ganglia (putamen, caudate, pallidum) and limbic regions (thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala), reduced gray-matter volume in the right superior temporal gyrus and insula, and microstructural disruption in the uncinate fasciculus and cingulum bundle; no global brain atrophy or cerebral blood flow differences were detected. Severity-stratified analyses found that hospitalized patients had additional cortical thinning in the left medial prefrontal cortex and reduced default mode network connectivity with the insular cortex and caudate, while resting-state functional connectivity differences were absent when comparing all survivors against controls as a single group. Key limitations include small subgroup sizes (21 hospitalized vs. 46 non-hospitalized), a cross-sectional design preventing conclusions about recovery trajectories, a large age gap between severity subgroups, absence of pre-infection baselines, and reliance on self-reported rather than standardized cognitive outcomes.

summary: This is not a Long COVID clinical trial. It is an observational social science study examining whether the COVID-19 pandemic altered global trends in religiosity, using interrupted time series analysis of Gallup World Poll survey data from 2.6 million respondents across 165 countries (2005–2024). The study found that global religiosity, which had been slightly declining before 2020, rebounded after the pandemic onset, with the post-2020 slope increasing by approximately 0.39 percentage points per year relative to the pre-pandemic trend. The religious rebound was more pronounced in the Americas and Europe and among more affluent individuals, while religiosity remained unchanged in Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, and actually declined in former Soviet countries.

summary: This is a preclinical mechanistic study, not a human clinical trial, using hamster and guinea pig animal models plus human stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes to investigate how SARS-CoV-2 causes cardiac arrhythmias. The study found that COVID-19 induces a triphasic pattern of cardiac conduction system dysfunction — including bradycardia and atrioventricular block — without direct viral infection of heart tissue, instead driven by innate immune activation and mitochondrial oxidative stress. Two interventions tested in infected hamsters, the JAK/STAT inhibitor ruxolitinib (2 mg/kg/day) and the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant mitoTEMPO (1.1 mg/kg/day), both significantly reduced tachypnea and prevented persistent AV block at 14–28 days post-infection; mitoTEMPO additionally blunted early bradycardia and late sinus pauses. This is animal and in vitro research only — no human patients were enrolled — so findings cannot be directly applied to Long COVID treatment without further clinical trials.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This is a preclinical animal study (hamster and guinea pig models with in vitro hiPSC-CM components), NOT a human clinical trial of Long COVID. It does not meet the eligibility criteria for a Long COVID clinical trial meta-analysis. The paper examines mechanisms of COVID-19-induced cardiac arrhythmias and tests ruxolitinib and mitoTEMPO in hamsters, not in human Long COVID patients. Arm assignments in this extraction are approximate mappings: guinea pig PIC experiment arms are mapped to arm_id 1 (PIC-treated) and arm_id 4 (vehicle control) for outcome_ids 8-10, which is distinct from the hamster arms. Sample sizes per group are mentioned only vaguely ('3-11 hamsters per group per parameter; n=3 for 4 dpi groups, n=4 for 28 dpi groups') and are not reported for most individual outcomes. Nearly all quantitative data that could be extracted appears in figures with only select values given in the text (breathing rate, RR interval percent changes, RMSSD, AV block counts). RoB2 tool is not applicable to animal studies. The between-group effect p-values for breathing rate are threshold values (P<0.005, P<0.0001) extracted from figure legends. Outcomes omitted from extraction due to data only in figures: Cx43 ICD percentage, conduction velocity, field potential duration in hiPSC-CM, Ca2+ transient amplitude in hiPSC-CM and guinea pig cardiomyocytes, PR interval in guinea pig PIC model, sinus pauses in guinea pig PIC model, IFN-stimulated gene fold-changes.

trial_rating.result_basis: MitoTEMPO reduced peak breathing rate by 36–48% vs untreated infected animals at 5–7 dpi; both mitoTEMPO and ruxolitinib eliminated persistent AV block at 14–28 dpi (p<0.05 vs SARS-CoV-2 alone); RR100 sinus pauses at 21–28 dpi were not significantly different from baseline in treated groups.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested 8 weeks of inspiratory muscle training (IMT) at 50% of maximal inspiratory pressure in 19 adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome, measuring lung aerosol deposition and pulmonary perfusion using gamma scintigraphy. The IMT group showed significant increases in total lung aerosol deposition (p=0.028, effect size r=0.50) and total lung perfusion (p=0.013, r=0.57), while the sham control group showed no improvement and actually declined in perfusion. Peripheral oxygen saturation also rose significantly in the IMT group (95.5% to 98%, p=0.028) but not controls. The trial is small (10 vs 9 participants) and lacked CT imaging to confirm lung boundaries, limiting precision of regional measurements.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. IQR values for baseline medians in Table 1 are given as single IQR width rather than low/high bounds (e.g., Age IMT: 46.50 (22) means median 46.50, IQR=22 — bounds not derivable). IQR bounds for the 'Difference Post-Pre' column in Tables 2 and 3 are explicitly stated as ranges and were extracted as iqr_low/iqr_high. Adverse event percentages reported as proportions (8%, 12%, 4%) without explicit n counts; IMT group n=10 so 8%≈1 person for dizziness and 12%≈1 person for muscle pain; sham group n=9 so 4%≈0.36 (likely 0 with rounding issue or 1 of 9 reported). Post-COVID time in Table 1 reported as median (IQR): IMT 35.65 (2.07) months, Control 35.70 (0.50) months. Baseline FEV1 (% predicted) IMT: 70 (25.25), Control: 86 (26); FVC IMT: 89.50 (25), Control: 85 (25); FEV1/FVC IMT: 90 (42.75), Control: 93 (25.50) — these spirometry values were not extracted as separate outcome objects as they are baseline-only characteristics. The between-group p-value for inhalation total lung and right/left lungs was reported as <0.001 and 0.001 respectively in Table 2 — recorded as p<0.001 (not exact). summary: Surovatamig (AZD0486), a CD19xCD3 bispecific T-cell engager, was tested in 61 heavily pretreated patients with relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma (median 3 prior lines of therapy) in an ongoing Phase 1 dose-escalation study. Among 52 evaluable patients receiving doses ≥2.4 mg, the overall response rate was 96% and the complete response rate was 92%, with 93% of CR-evaluable patients achieving undetectable minimal residual disease; all 11 patients who completed 24 months of treatment remained in complete response off therapy. The safety profile was manageable: cytokine release syndrome occurred in 51% of patients on the double step-up dosing schedule but was predominantly grade 1, and no patients discontinued due to treatment-related adverse events.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial — it is a phase 1 oncology study of surovatamig in relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma (a B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma). It has no relevance to Long COVID. The study is single-arm with no control group; RoB2 is not applicable. No per-arm SD, means, or between-group comparisons exist (single-arm design). n_completed (11) refers to pts completing 24 months of treatment. The 43 pts who received double SUD schedule are a subset of the 61 total FL pts; CRS rates (51%, 49%, 2%) applied to n=43: calculated n_CRS_any=22, n_CRS_grade1=21, n_CRS_grade2=1. Percentages for grade ≥3 AEs applied to n=61: neutropenia 20%=12, hypertension 8%=5, lymphopenia 7%=4, pneumonia 7%=4. Infections not COVID-19 in 38% of 61 pts=23; hypogammaglobulinemia in 23% of 61 pts=14. Median follow-up of 16 months (range 1–47) reported for pts receiving ≥2.4 mg. Treatment duration up to 24 months (96 weeks calculated). No baseline demographics (age, sex, BMI) reported in abstract.

summary: This Phase II study (MorningSun) tested subcutaneous mosunetuzumab, a CD20xCD3 bispecific antibody, as first-line treatment in 101 patients with previously untreated, low-tumor burden follicular lymphoma. summary: This multicenter open-label RCT (CAME-COVID study) tested clarithromycin (CAM) at 800 mg/day or 400 mg/day for 7 days versus standard care in 55 hospitalized Japanese adults with mild COVID-19 pneumonia not requiring oxygen. The primary endpoint — time to 50% reduction in a composite 7-symptom severity score — was not significantly improved in either CAM group versus control (trend only in the 800 mg arm, p=0.08). As a prespecified secondary endpoint, CAM 800 mg/day did significantly accelerate recovery from fatigue specifically (p=0.005), and also reduced several inflammatory and fibrotic cytokines; no serious safety concerns were attributed to CAM, though gastrointestinal and liver-related adverse events occurred exclusively in the 800 mg group.

summary: This trial (EPCORE NHL-2) tested epcoritamab — a CD3×CD20 bispecific antibody — added to standard R-CHOP chemotherapy in 47 patients with newly diagnosed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and high-risk disease (IPI scores 3–5). After a median follow-up of 38.8 months, the overall response rate was 98% and the complete response rate was 85%, with an estimated 80% of patients remaining progression-free and 87% alive at 33 months. Safety was manageable, with serious infections concentrated in the first 6 months of treatment and no new grade 5 adverse events reported in extended follow-up. However, this is a single-arm phase 1b/2 study with no control arm, so the favorable outcomes cannot be directly attributed to epcoritamab without the ongoing phase 3 comparison against R-CHOP alone.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is NOT a Long COVID trial. It is a hematologic oncology study of epcoritamab + R-CHOP for newly diagnosed DLBCL (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma). It has no relevance to Long COVID. The study is also a single-arm trial (no randomization, no control arm), so RoB2 is technically inapplicable — rated 'high' to reflect absence of randomization. Withdrawal reason Ns are calculated as approximate percentages of 47 patients: AEs 11%≈5, PD 9%≈4, patient withdrawal 6%≈3, COVID measures 2%≈1, other 4%≈2. Median follow-up of 38.8 months converted to ~166 weeks. Treatment duration of 1 year converted to ~52 weeks. Post-treatment follow-up (median 25.3 months post-EOT) converted to ~110 weeks. PFS/OS figures appear to be Kaplan-Meier estimates, not exact event counts. Several efficacy figures (PFS curve, OS curve) reference images not available in extracted text. n_withdrawn calculated from percentage approximations.

trial_rating.result_basis: CR rate 85%, estimated 80% progression-free at 33 months, and 87% alive at 33 months in a high-risk IPI 3-5 population; no randomized control arm for comparison.

summary: This paper is not a Long COVID clinical trial. It reports 6-year follow-up data from the ALPINE phase 3 study of zanubrutinib (a BTK inhibitor) versus ibrutinib in patients with relapsed/refractory chronic lymphocytic leukemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma — a blood cancer, not Long COVID. The primary finding is that zanubrutinib showed durable progression-free survival with a median PFS of 52.5 months and a 60-month PFS rate of 47.3% in R/R CLL/SLL patients. This paper should not be included in a Long COVID dashboard.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial. It is an oncology study (CLL/SLL) reporting long-term follow-up of zanubrutinib vs ibrutinib in the ALPINE phase 3 trial. It does not involve Long COVID patients, COVID-19 infection outcomes, or any Long COVID intervention. The paper was likely misidentified for inclusion.
