summary: This single-arm trial (the STOP Trial) tested a sequential treatment strategy in 59 treatment-naïve CLL/SLL patients aged ≤65: 12 cycles of zanubrutinib monotherapy followed by 4 cycles of zanubrutinib plus fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and obinutuzumab (ZFCG). Among 30 patients who completed all 16 cycles, 76.7% achieved complete remission and 73.3% achieved undetectable minimal residual disease (uMRD) in both peripheral blood and bone marrow, enabling all 30 to stop treatment. At a maximum follow-up of 20 months post-cessation, 29 of 30 patients remained in CR with uMRD without further therapy. Grade ≥3 adverse events were common during the ZFCG phase, including thrombocytopenia (32.5%), neutropenia (27.5%), and serious lung infection (15%).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a Long COVID trial — it is a CLL/SLL hematology trial (Stop Trial, NCT05287984) testing zanubrutinib-based therapy. It was misclassified as eligible. There is no randomization, no control arm, and no Long COVID population; all extraction fields relating to Long COVID definition, infection timing, and between-group comparisons are null. AE rates for ZFCG phase were reported as percentages (thrombocytopenia 32.5%, neutropenia 27.5%, leukopenia 25%, lung infection 15%, febrile neutropenia 5%) but denominator was 40 patients (those in ZFCG phase), not 30 completers — exact n counts not directly stated so left as null with percentages noted here. Post-treatment follow-up maximum was 20 months (~87 weeks); median follow-up approximately 1 year (~52 weeks). RoB2 is not applicable to single-arm studies; judgment set to 'high' for absence of randomization/control. This abstract should be excluded from a Long COVID meta-analysis.

trial_rating.result_basis: 76.7% (23/30) achieved CR and 73.3% (22/30) achieved CR with PB+BM uMRD after 4 cycles of ZFCG, with 100% PB uMRD rate; 29/30 maintained treatment-free CR at maximum 20 months follow-up.

summary: This paper is not a Long COVID trial. It reports 96-week results from ASC4OPT (NCT04948333), a Phase 3b study of asciminib (a BCR-ABL1 inhibitor) in patients with chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic phase who had failed or were intolerant to two or more prior tyrosine kinase inhibitors. At 96 weeks, major molecular response rates were 43.6% overall (vs 39.4% at 48 weeks), with deep molecular responses maintained. The drug was generally well-tolerated; grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 37.5% of patients, and only 7.1% discontinued due to adverse events.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL MISMATCH: This paper is a CML (chronic myeloid leukemia) clinical trial of asciminib — it is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial. The paper is completely ineligible for a Long COVID meta-analysis. COVID-19 appears only as an adverse event (13.1% incidence) in the AE table, not as the indication being treated. All extracted data reflects CML outcomes (molecular response rates). No quantitative data (means, SDs) are available for MDASI-CML scores — described in narrative only as 'decreased slightly and quickly.' Per-arm sample sizes were not reported explicitly; the main cohort had 169 pts total and the exploratory cohort had 30 pts (n=199 total), but the 1:1 randomization implies ~84-85 per arm in the main cohort. The overall AE percentages are combined totals not broken out per arm in all instances. Arm-level n values for MMR response events not reported — only percentages given.

trial_rating.result_basis: MMR rate increased from 39.4% at Week 48 to 43.6% at Week 96 overall; no placebo comparator was included as this was a non-comparative study.

summary: This phase III RCT (FLAIR trial) tested ibrutinib plus rituximab (IR) versus the standard chemoimmunotherapy regimen FCR in 771 previously untreated CLL patients across 113 UK centres, excluding those over 75 or with >20% 17p deletion. IR produced superior progression-free survival (median 112 vs 80 months; HR 0.53, p<0.001) and superior overall survival (HR 0.66, p=0.014), with 7-year OS of 87.5% vs 81.1%. The benefit was driven largely by patients with unmutated IGHV, while those with mutated IGHV showed no significant PFS or OS advantage. A notable safety caveat is that cardiac serious adverse events were substantially higher on IR (10.7% vs 1.1%), with 11 cardiac/sudden deaths in the IR arm versus 5 on FCR, though IR showed far fewer secondary MDS/AML cases (2 vs 22).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a Long COVID trial — it is a CLL (chronic lymphocytic leukemia) trial comparing ibrutinib+rituximab vs FCR chemoimmunotherapy. It does not meet eligibility criteria for a Long COVID meta-analysis. SAE percentages reported for each arm (FCR 54%, IR 60.7%; infections FCR 33.6% vs IR 33.1%; blood/lymphatic FCR 20.4% vs IR 12%; cardiac FCR 1.1% vs IR 10.7%) but absolute Ns not given. Median PFS reported in months (not weeks). Per-arm age and sex breakdowns not provided — only overall (median age 63, 73.3% male). The 7-year OS percent for IR (87.5%) is reported as an estimate, with total deaths in IR arm being 60; the 81.1% FCR figure similarly. No per-arm means/SDs exist as outcomes are time-to-event. MRD, response rates, and QoL outcomes mentioned as secondary endpoints but no quantitative data provided in this abstract.

trial_rating.result_basis: PFS HR 0.53 (p<0.001), median PFS 112 vs 80 months; OS HR 0.66 (p=0.014), 7-year OS 87.5% vs 81.1%.

summary: The SEQUOIA phase 3 trial tested zanubrutinib (a BTK inhibitor) versus bendamustine plus rituximab (BR) in 479 treatment-naive CLL/SLL patients, with a separate non-randomized arm of 111 patients with del(17p). At 6-year follow-up, zanubrutinib showed sustained superiority over BR: 72-month progression-free survival was 74% vs 32% (HR 0.28, p<0.0001), and 89% vs 55% of patients had not yet needed subsequent treatment. In the high-risk del(17p) cohort, 72-month PFS was 64% and overall survival 83%, outcomes comparable to patients without this historically poor-prognosis feature. Notably, this paper is an ASH conference abstract for a CLL trial, not a Long COVID study.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: THIS PAPER IS NOT A LONG COVID TRIAL. It is an ASH 2025 conference abstract reporting 6-year follow-up data from the SEQUOIA phase 3 trial of zanubrutinib vs bendamustine+rituximab in treatment-naive CLL/SLL (chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma). This paper has no relevance to Long COVID and should be excluded from the meta-analysis. No per-arm means/SDs are available as all outcomes are time-to-event (survival endpoints). Exact event counts not reported, only Kaplan-Meier rates at 72 months. Median follow-up was 72.8 months (range 0.0-90.0) for arms A/B and 76.7 months (range 5.0-86.9) for arm C.

summary: The MorningSun Phase II study tested subcutaneous mosunetuzumab (a CD20xCD3 bispecific antibody) with optional maintenance therapy in 103 previously untreated patients with high-tumor burden follicular lymphoma. The primary endpoint — 12-month progression-free survival rate — was 85.5% (95% CI: 76.2–91.3%), with an overall response rate of 87.4% and complete metabolic response in 64.1% of patients. The safety profile was notable for high infection rates (77.7% of patients), including COVID-19 as the most common infection (24.3%), and five grade 5 adverse events including two COVID-19 pneumonia deaths.

Serious AE count (n=37) calculated as 35.9% of 103. Follow-up duration: treatment was 17 cycles of 21 days (~52 weeks/12 months) plus up to 12 months maintenance; median follow-up was 22.3 months (~96 weeks).

summary: This phase II trial tested pirtobrutinib (a non-covalent BTK inhibitor) plus venetoclax (a BCL2 antagonist) as a fixed-duration regimen in 27 previously treated Waldenström macroglobulinemia patients with the MYD88 mutation. The primary endpoint — achieving a very good partial response or complete response (VGPR/CR) — was met, with 56% of patients (15/27) achieving VGPR/CR and an overall response rate of 100% at 6 months; 12-month progression-free survival was 94%. The regimen was generally well tolerated, though grade ≥3 neutropenia occurred in 37% of patients; notably, patients with CXCR4 or TP53 mutations had significantly lower VGPR/CR rates.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial — it is a phase II oncology study of pirtobrutinib plus venetoclax in Waldenström macroglobulinemia (a B-cell lymphoma). It does not study Long COVID, post-COVID syndrome, or any COVID-19 sequelae as outcomes. The paper was likely included in the queue in error. No randomization occurred (single-arm study). N_analyzed for AEs calculated as ~38 enrolled (all treated); n per percentages back-calculated from 27 MYD88-mutated evaluable patients. The 4% rate AEs were calculated as approximately 1-2 patients of 27. Death was unrelated to study therapy (COVID-19 after progression and subsequent treatment in an MYD88-WT patient). Per-arm SD data not available for any continuous outcomes (medians only reported). Between-group comparisons for biomarkers are within-patient pre/post comparisons, not between randomized arms.

trial_rating.result_basis: VGPR/CR rate of 56% (15/27 patients) exceeded the pre-specified null hypothesis threshold of 12/42 patients; IgM dropped from 2510 to 239 mg/dL and hemoglobin rose from 9.4 to 12.1 g/dL (both p<0.001), with 12-month PFS of 94%.

summary: This paper reports final results of CLIMB SCD-121, a phase 3 trial of exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel), a one-time CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing therapy, in 46 patients aged 12–35 with severe sickle cell disease and at least 2 vaso-occlusive crises (VOCs) per year. All patients showed durable increases in fetal hemoglobin above 40% with near-normal total hemoglobin levels maintained for up to 5.6 years. This is not a Long COVID trial and does not belong in a Long COVID dashboard.

It is a phase 3 trial of exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) gene therapy for sickle cell disease (SCD). It should be excluded from a Long COVID meta-analysis. The paper is a single-arm trial with no randomization or control group, so most RCT fields (randomization method, allocation concealment, per-arm comparisons) are not applicable. summary: This phase 1 single-arm study tested equecabtagene autoleucel (Eque-cel), a fully human BCMA CAR T-cell therapy, in 16 transplant-ineligible patients with high-risk newly diagnosed multiple myeloma after induction chemotherapy. summary: This laboratory study examined whether IgG antibodies from COVID-19 patients (n=56) activate and damage vascular endothelial cells, a proposed mechanism for thrombotic complications in Long COVID. COVID-19 patient IgG caused significantly higher VCAM-1 expression (a marker of endothelial activation) compared to healthy donor IgG, and 11 of these samples produced faster, larger clots on endothelial cells with a 4-fold increase in tissue factor mRNA and 30-fold increase in PAI-1 mRNA. COVID-19 IgG also disrupted the endothelial barrier by triggering internalization of VE-cadherin and stress fiber formation. This is a mechanistic in vitro study, not a clinical trial, so findings cannot be directly translated to patient outcomes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a preclinical in vitro laboratory study presented as an ASH 2025 conference abstract — it is NOT a clinical trial and does not involve randomization of human participants to interventions. The 'arms' here are COVID-19 patient IgG (n=56 donors) vs healthy donor IgG (n=12 donors) applied to HUVEC cells in vitro. No clinical Long COVID outcomes are measured. The study design fields, participant eligibility criteria, and most clinical metadata fields are not applicable. Arms were coded as arm_id=1 (COVID-19 IgG) and arm_id=2 (healthy donor IgG) for data structuring purposes only. The VE-cadherin internalization and stress fiber formation findings are described qualitatively only (no numeric data extractable). The clot lysis delay finding is also qualitative only.

summary: This mechanistic study (not a clinical trial) investigated whether extracellular vesicles (EVs) and tissue factor (TF) in the blood of Long COVID patients promote abnormal clotting. Comparing 71 non-hospitalized Long COVID patients to 72 healthy controls, researchers found that Long COVID plasma contained elevated TF activity and significantly more EVs, both of which accelerated thrombin generation in lab assays. In a mouse model, infusion of Long COVID-derived EVs caused venous clots in 100% of animals versus 50% with control EVs, and those clots were significantly larger and heavier. This is mechanistic preclinical evidence, not a therapeutic trial, and no patient interventions were tested.

summary: This phase II study tested dasatinib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor) plus inotuzumab ozogamicin (an anti-CD22 antibody-drug conjugate) without intensive chemotherapy in 21 newly diagnosed Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL) patients, median age 60. The primary endpoint — achieving deep molecular remission (MR3 or better) after 2 treatment courses — was met in 81% of patients, with 62% reaching the even deeper MR4 level; by the end of course 3, 100% of patients achieved MR4 and/or undetectable disease by next-generation sequencing. summary: Tisagenlecleucel (an anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy) was tested in 97 adults with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma who had failed at least two prior treatment lines, including an anti-CD20 antibody and an alkylating agent. After a median follow-up of 61 months, 86% of patients responded and 68% achieved complete remission, with an estimated 5-year progression-free survival of 46% overall and 60% among complete responders; median overall survival was not reached, with 74% of patients alive at 5 years. Long-term safety was acceptable, though infections (40% of patients beyond one year, including 18% COVID-19) and second primary malignancies (7% of patients) were notable late complications.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial — it is a hematology oncology trial (CAR-T cell therapy for relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma, ELARA trial). It was incorrectly submitted for Long COVID data extraction. All participant eligibility fields, long_covid_definition, and related fields are null/not applicable. The paper is a conference abstract (ASH 2025) with limited detail; full demographic breakdowns (age, sex, BMI) are not reported in this abstract. The 'n_randomized' fields are null because this is a non-randomized single-arm study; 97 patients were infused and 94 were evaluable for efficacy. Median follow-up of 61 months = approximately 265 weeks (used for total_duration_weeks). AE percentages converted to approximate Ns based on N=84 denominator for infections (40.5% × 84 ≈ 34 verbatim) and N=84 for other post-1-year AEs. Second primary malignancy event types listed include: basal cell carcinoma (n=2), myelodysplastic syndrome (n=2), squamous cell carcinoma of skin (n=2), acute myeloid leukemia (n=1), bladder transitional cell carcinoma (n=1), Bowen's disease (n=1), malignant melanoma (n=1), metastatic squamous cell carcinoma (n=1) — total 11 events in 7 patients.

trial_rating.result_basis: 5-year PFS 46% (95% CI 35.0–56.3) in the overall population and 5-year OS 74.1% (95% CI 63.0–82.3); CR rate 68.1% with median DOR not reached in a heavily pre-treated population with 60–68% high-risk disease characteristics.

summary: This phase 1/2 study tested subcutaneous (SC) blinatumomab — a bispecific T-cell engager antibody — as a single agent in 79 adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) who had received a median of 2 prior therapies. The primary endpoint of complete remission (CR or CRh) within two cycles was achieved in 77% of patients (61/79), with 88% of responders testing negative for measurable residual disease. At a median follow-up of 13.7 months, the estimated 12-month overall survival rate was 69.1%, and responses appeared durable regardless of whether patients subsequently received a stem cell transplant. No new safety signals were identified compared to prior reports.

summary: This paper is not a Long COVID trial. It reports long-term follow-up data from a phase II trial (NCT02339922) of oral ixazomib (a proteasome inhibitor) plus short-course rituximab in 33 patients with previously untreated indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (iNHL), primarily follicular lymphoma. Long-term toxicity was modest, with only 2 patients stopping due to ixazomib-related adverse events after 12 months.

summary: This phase II trial tested lenalidomide plus rituximab (R2) as first-line treatment in 79 previously untreated follicular lymphoma patients, reporting 15-year follow-up data. The overall response rate was 99% with a best complete response rate of 87%; median progression-free survival reached 16.5 years and 10-year overall survival was 95%. Patients achieving complete response at 30 months had dramatically better PFS (hazard ratio 0.04 vs. those who progressed earlier), though no OS difference was seen. This is a conference abstract for a lymphoma trial, not a Long COVID study.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a Long COVID trial — it is a phase II trial of lenalidomide plus rituximab (R2) for follicular lymphoma. Median PFS of 16.5 years was reported for the overall cohort (95% CI 9.9 years to not reached). 10-year PFS 95% CI was 49-71%. Overall, 36 patients (46%) were lost to follow-up at data cutoff. Nine total deaths reported: 1 AML, 1 COVID, 1 endocarditis, 1 pancreatic cancer, 1 pneumonia, 3 unknown, 1 lymphoma. Five patients developed transformation (range 9 months to 15 years). Total follow-up weeks calculated as 14.2 years × 52 = 738 weeks (median). Schedule B treatment duration: 12 cycles × 28 days = 336 days ≈ 48 weeks.

summary: Epcoritamab, a subcutaneous CD3×CD20 bispecific antibody, was tested as monotherapy in 157 heavily pretreated adults with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma (median 3 prior lines of therapy, 39% prior CAR-T). After more than 4 years of median follow-up, 59% of patients responded and 41% achieved complete remission, with 42% of complete responders still in remission at data cutoff and a median duration of complete remission of 37.7 months. At the 4-year landmark, 57% of complete responders remained alive. The safety profile was manageable with few new serious adverse events beyond 3 years, though one patient died from COVID-19.

summary: This paper is not a Long COVID trial. It reports interim results from XTEND-ed (NCT04644575), a Phase 3 long-term extension study of efanesoctocog alfa (a factor VIII replacement therapy) in adults, adolescents, and children with severe hemophilia A. Over up to 4 years of once-weekly prophylaxis, annualized bleed rates remained very low (mean ABR ~0.60 in adults, ~0.64 in children) and no factor VIII inhibitors developed in any participant. The therapy was well tolerated with no treatment-related serious adverse events.

summary: This paper is not a Long COVID trial. It reports updated results from the ELM-2 study (NCT03888105), a Phase 2 trial of odronextamab — a CD20×CD3 bispecific antibody — in 61 patients with rare subtypes of relapsed/refractory aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (including transformed DLBCL, HGBL NOS, PMBL, and follicular lymphoma Grade 3b). summary: This Phase 2 trial (VERITA PALG-CLL5) tested MRD-guided venetoclax plus rituximab in 103 previously untreated CLL patients across 10 Polish centers, adjusting treatment duration (12, 18, or 24 cycles) based on whether patients achieved undetectable minimal residual disease (uMRD) in bone marrow. The trial met its primary endpoint: 61.4% of evaluable patients achieved complete remission with bone marrow uMRD at therapy completion, well above the prespecified 35% target, with 30-month progression-free survival of 92.7%. Treatment was generally well tolerated with no clinical tumor lysis syndrome; the main toxicity was neutropenia (70% any grade), and grade 3+ infections occurred in only 8.7% of patients.

summary: This phase II trial tested time-limited acalabrutinib plus obinutuzumab in 55 previously untreated patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), with treatment duration guided by minimal residual disease (MRD) testing rather than given continuously. The primary endpoint was 36-month progression-free survival (PFS), which was 69% (95% CI: 57–84%), with a median PFS of 42 months across the cohort. Of 46 patients who entered a treatment-free observation period, the median time before disease progression was 25 months, demonstrating that a time-limited BTK inhibitor strategy without adding a BCL2 inhibitor is feasible. Note: this paper is not a Long COVID trial — it is a CLL oncology study and should not be included in a Long COVID dashboard.

summary: This is not a Long COVID trial. The paper is a 96-week exploratory tolerability analysis of the ASC4FIRST phase 3 trial, which tested asciminib versus investigator-selected tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib or second-generation TKIs) in patients with newly diagnosed chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic phase. The primary focus was adverse event burden: patients on asciminib had more adverse-event-free days (22.6% vs 4.3% in the second-generation TKI stratum) and lower rates of dose reduction, interruption, and discontinuation due to side effects. At week 96, 67% of asciminib patients reported being not at all bothered by treatment side effects versus 46.1% on comparator TKIs.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a CML (chronic myeloid leukemia) trial — NOT a Long COVID trial. It should not be included in a Long COVID meta-analysis. The FACIT GP5 result of 67% vs 46.1% is reported for ASC pooled vs IS-TKI pooled (all strata combined), not broken down by arm. Withdrawal counts due to AE were calculated by summing grade 1/2 and grade >=3 discontinuation percentages converted to events. Median follow-up reported in months: ASC IMA 25.1 mo, IS-TKI IMA 24.3 mo, ASC 2G 28.2 mo, IS-TKI 2G 27.7 mo. Individual 2G TKI AE-free day data also reported: nilotinib 13.5% (any AE), 30.3% (symptomatic); dasatinib 4.2% (any), 8.5% (symptomatic); bosutinib 0.1% (any and symptomatic) — not extracted as separate arms due to schema constraints.

summary: This conference abstract reports long-term safety and treatment duration data for axatilimab (a CSF-1R-targeting monoclonal antibody) in 239 patients with refractory chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD) who had failed at least two prior lines of therapy, enrolled in the phase 2 AGAVE-201 trial. The primary finding is that the FDA-approved dose (0.3 mg/kg every 2 weeks) achieved a 74% overall response rate in the first 6 cycles, and at median follow-up of 31.7 months, the 46-month overall survival rate was 77.6% with 15 patients (19% of the approved-dose cohort) remaining on treatment at a median duration of 33 months. No new safety signals emerged during long-term follow-up; the most common adverse events at the approved dose were fatigue (30%) and upper respiratory infections (53% among those still on treatment), with grade ≥3 treatment-related events in 19% of the approved-dose cohort.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial — it is an ASH 2025 abstract reporting long-term safety data from AGAVE-201, a phase 2 RCT of axatilimab for chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD). There is no COVID-19 infection or Long COVID indication; the mention of 'COVID-19' in the results refers only to an adverse event (upper respiratory infection) in patients on treatment. This paper should be excluded from any Long COVID meta-analysis. Quantitative data extracted are limited by conference abstract format: no per-arm baseline demographics, no SD/SE for survival outcomes, and the 46-month OS for arms 2 and 3 is reported as a pooled all-dose figure (74.1%) rather than per-arm. Treatment discontinuation reasons are reported only for the overall population (n=239). The all-dose grade >=3 TEAE count for still-on-treatment patients (n=12, 36.4%) covers all 33 patients across arms 1-3 combined, not per-arm.

summary: This phase 2 single-arm study tested whether adding oral montelukast (10 mg) to standard premedication reduces infusion reactions in 40 patients receiving monoclonal antibodies (rituximab, daratumumab, obinutuzumab, and others) for hematologic or oncologic conditions. Compared to historical registration trial data for the same antibodies, adding montelukast was associated with a 43% reduction in infusion reactions (p < 0.001). Patients with a history of medication allergy or atopic conditions remained at significantly higher risk despite montelukast, and the study was terminated early due to COVID-19, limiting its power.

summary: This is not a clinical trial. It is a retrospective epidemiological study using CDC WONDER mortality data to analyze U.S. death trends involving co-occurring respiratory failure and anemia from 1999 to 2023. The study found that age-adjusted mortality rates for this combined condition more than doubled over the study period, rising from 1.23 to 3.56 per 100,000, with a sharp spike during the COVID-19 pandemic (2018–2021 APC: 16.97%). Disparities were identified by race (Non-Hispanic Black individuals had the highest mean rate at 3.20), sex, age, and geography, with no intervention tested and no Long COVID treatment evaluated.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: THIS PAPER IS NOT A CLINICAL TRIAL AND IS NOT ELIGIBLE FOR A LONG COVID CLINICAL TRIAL META-ANALYSIS. It is a retrospective U.S. national mortality surveillance study using CDC WONDER administrative data with Joinpoint regression. There are no study arms, no randomization, no intervention, no Long COVID patient population, and no clinical outcomes relevant to a Long COVID treatment meta-analysis. The paper focuses on mortality trends in co-occurring respiratory failure and anemia from 1999-2023. All RCT-specific JSON fields (arms, per-arm demographics, sample sizes, risk of bias domains) are null or empty. Quantitative data extracted represents population-level AAMR statistics and Joinpoint regression parameters, not per-arm clinical trial data. Age group exact definitions (older adults, middle-aged, younger adults) and exact racial/ethnic AAPC CIs beyond NH White are not provided in the abstract.

trial_rating.result_basis: No intervention or treatment was tested; this is a descriptive trend analysis. National AAMR rose from 1.23 (1999) to 3.56 (2023), with a pandemic-era APC of 16.97 (95% CI: 11.2–23.1, p=0.000006), but no comparative effect size is applicable.

summary: This phase 1 trial tested venetoclax (400mg) plus dexamethasone (20mg weekly) in 12 patients with relapsed/refractory AL amyloidosis carrying the t(11;14) translocation, all of whom had previously received anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies. summary: The PROLONG trial tested whether adding dexamethasone (DXM) to rituximab improved initial platelet response in 127 adults with immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) of less than one year duration who had failed corticosteroids. Adding dexamethasone to rituximab significantly improved the response rate at week 24 compared to rituximab alone (60.3% vs 37.5%, p=0.01), and also delayed time to first bleeding episode (p=0.03). Notably, this paper is an ITP trial, not a Long COVID trial; the maintenance phase results comparing rituximab to placebo were not yet available at time of abstract submission.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a Long COVID trial — it is a trial of rituximab ± dexamethasone for immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), an autoimmune platelet disorder unrelated to Long COVID. summary: This paper is not a Long COVID trial — it reports a Phase 2 study of lisaftoclax, a BCL-2 inhibitor, in 77 Chinese patients with relapsed/refractory chronic lymphocytic leukemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma who had previously failed BTK inhibitor therapy. Among 72 evaluable patients, the objective response rate was 62.5% (per independent review), with a median progression-free survival of 23.89 months and median duration of response of 18.53 months. Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 74% of patients, most commonly neutropenia (28.6%) and thrombocytopenia (23.4%), though no tumor lysis syndrome or lisaftoclax-related deaths were reported.

It is a registrational Phase 2 study of lisaftoclax (a BCL-2 inhibitor) for relapsed/refractory CLL/SLL (chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma) in patients who failed BTK inhibitors. It has no relevance to Long COVID and should be excluded from the meta-analysis. The paper was published as an ASH 2025 abstract (Blood 146:88-89). No randomization was performed (single-arm design). Time-to-response median was 3.68 months (not extracted as separate outcome as no arm-level distributional data provided). Female percentage calculated as 100% - 59.7% male = 40.3%.

summary: The ECHO phase 3 trial tested acalabrutinib plus bendamustine-rituximab (ABR) versus placebo plus bendamustine-rituximab (PBR) as first-line therapy in 598 patients aged 65 or older with previously untreated mantle cell lymphoma. This updated 50-month follow-up analysis found that ABR reduced the risk of needing third-line therapy or death by 24% compared to PBR (HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.59–0.98), with median progression-free survival of 72.5 months versus 47.8 months (HR 0.68; p=0.002). Only 3.3% of ABR patients required third-line treatment compared to 12.4% in the PBR arm. Extended follow-up showed no cumulative safety concerns with prolonged acalabrutinib use, though adverse event-related discontinuation was higher in the ABR arm (44.5% vs 32.4%).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is an ASH 2025 conference abstract for a mantle cell lymphoma RCT — it is NOT a Long COVID trial and does not meet the inclusion criteria for a Long COVID meta-analysis. No Long COVID-relevant outcomes (fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, dyspnea, etc.) are reported. Per-arm means and SDs are not applicable given the time-to-event design. Median time to 2L therapy reported (26.3 mo ABR vs 19.6 mo PBR) but no HR or CI provided for this endpoint. The n_withdrawn_due_to_ae figures (133 ABR, 97 PBR) are calculated from reported percentages (44.5% of 299 = ~133; 32.4% of 299 = ~97). Figures referenced in the abstract contain additional data not extractable from text. Overall survival median not reached in either arm.

summary: The COBRA phase III randomized trial compared carfilzomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (KRd) versus bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (VRd) in 250 newly diagnosed multiple myeloma patients. KRd met both co-primary endpoints: more patients achieved MRD-negative complete response at 12 months (31% vs 18%, OR=2.08, p=0.016) and progression-free survival was significantly longer (median not reached vs 49 months, HR=0.57, p=0.0095). KRd carried more grade ≥3 adverse events (72% vs 62%), more neutropenia (21% vs 11%), and more cardiac events (18% vs 10%), though it caused far less peripheral neuropathy (17% vs 56%).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a multiple myeloma trial (ASH 2025 abstract), NOT a Long COVID trial — it is not eligible for a Long COVID meta-analysis. Adverse event percentages are reported but absolute counts per arm are not stated (only percentages). KRd arm median PFS is stated as 'not reached'; VRd arm median is 49 months. MRD measurement details: 163 patients had MRD measured, 147 had available results; patients without results were counted as MRD-positive in ITT analysis. Total treatment duration calculated as 24 months = ~96 weeks; median follow-up 35 months (~152 weeks). Notable AE percentages: KRd vs VRd — Grade ≥3 any AE: 72% vs 62%; Grade ≥3 neutropenia: 21% vs 11%; Grade ≥3 lower respiratory infection: 10% vs 10%; peripheral neuropathy any grade: 17% vs 56%; cardiac events any grade: 18% vs 10%.

summary: This phase II trial (NCT04304820) tested rapid initiation of low-dose cyclosporine and eltrombopag in 45 treatment-naive severe aplastic anemia patients while awaiting definitive therapy, with the primary endpoint being safety and feasibility. The composite primary endpoint was met with a 4% rate of serious adverse events or protocol failures, and ANC significantly improved from treatment initiation to the start of definitive therapy (median 0.3 vs 0.42 K/µL, p=0.03). Secondary outcomes including 6-month overall response rate (79% vs 87% historical control, p=0.52) and 2-year survival (90% vs 93%, p=0.8) were comparable to historical controls, though a notably low 2-year high-risk clonal evolution rate of 3% was observed versus 13% in controls (p=0.07). This paper does not concern Long COVID and should not be included in a Long COVID trial dashboard.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is NOT a Long COVID trial. It is an abstract from the 67th ASH Annual Meeting reporting a phase II trial of early cyclosporine + eltrombopag for severe aplastic anemia (SAA), a bone marrow failure condition. It has no relevance to Long COVID. This paper appears to have been submitted to the extractor in error. All extracted data reflects the SAA trial context. Per-arm numeric values for cytokine and T-cell flow cytometry outcomes were only reported as p-values (no means or SDs given); actual measurement values are data only in figures or not reported in this abstract. Median follow-up was 755 days (arm 1) and 2415 days (historical cohort); total_duration_weeks calculated from 755 days (~107 weeks) for the prospective arm. ANC comparison: paper states 'median 0.3 vs 0.42' — direction appears to be historical cohort (0.3) vs prospective arm (0.42) at pre-hATG, confirming improvement in intervention arm.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary composite feasibility endpoint met at 4% rate; ANC improvement was significant (p=0.03) but secondary outcomes including ORR (79% vs 87%, p=0.52) and survival (90% vs 93%, p=0.8) were non-significant versus historical controls.

summary: This open-label phase 4 safety study tested daily (once-daily) dosing of rimegepant 75 mg — an oral CGRP receptor antagonist — for up to 24 weeks in 250 adults with episodic migraine (4–14 attacks per month) at 19 US sites. The study had no efficacy endpoints; its sole purpose was to establish the safety profile of once-daily dosing before a planned placebo-controlled efficacy trial. Over 24 weeks, no serious adverse events occurred, only 2.8% of participants discontinued due to adverse events, and the most common adverse events were nasopharyngitis (9.2%), COVID-19 (6.4%), and nausea (6.0%). Hepatic enzyme elevations above 3× the upper limit of normal were rare (1.3%), with no cases meeting Hy's Law criteria, and no cardiovascular events, medication overuse headache, or Raynaud's phenomenon were observed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial — it is a migraine prevention safety study of rimegepant. COVID-19 appears only as an incidental adverse event (16/250 participants developed COVID-19 during the study, not as the condition being treated). The paper has no Long COVID definition, no infection-related inclusion criteria, no Long COVID outcomes, and no control arm. This paper should be excluded from a Long COVID meta-analysis. Study design classified as quasi-experimental (single-arm open-label) since it is not randomized. n_randomized set to null as participants were enrolled/treated without randomization. The 250 participants are the safety analysis set (≥1 dose). Total follow-up of 32 weeks calculated as 24 weeks treatment + 8 weeks post-treatment follow-up (the longer of two follow-up visits). Participant disposition figure referenced but full breakdown of discontinuation reasons not extractable from text alone.

trial_rating.result_basis: No efficacy outcome was assessed; this was a safety-only open-label study with no control arm. The primary endpoints were adverse event rates: serious AEs 0%, AEs leading to discontinuation 2.8% (7/250), severe AEs 1.6% (4/250).

summary: This preclinical mouse and cell culture study tested whether the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N) protein causes cognitive impairment and investigated the underlying mechanism. Mice intranasally administered the N protein via lentiviral vector showed significantly impaired spatial working memory in Y-maze tests (reduced spontaneous alternation rate and novel arm entries) alongside hippocampal neuronal damage, elevated amyloid precursor protein, and increased phosphorylated Tau. Mechanistically, the N protein induced microglial senescence by promoting excessive mitochondrial fission and glycolytic reprogramming; blocking glycolysis with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG) reversed both microglial senescence markers and cognitive deficits in mice. This is entirely a mouse/cell study with no human participants, so findings cannot be directly applied to Long COVID patients without further clinical validation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This is a preclinical animal/in vitro mechanistic study, NOT a human Long COVID clinical trial. It does not enroll human patients and should not be included in a clinical meta-analysis. All quantitative outcome data (means, SDs) are presented exclusively in figures (bar graphs) with no accompanying tables or in-text values; therefore all result_source fields are 'not_reported' and mean/sd/se fields are null throughout. Statistical significance is reported only as threshold categories (*P<0.05, **P<0.01, ***P<0.001) with no exact p-values. The in vivo arm sample sizes for behavioral outcomes are n=8; for Western blot/PCR in the first experiment (Figs 1-2) n=6; for the three-arm experiment (Figs 5-6) n=8 for behavioral and n=8 for Western blot. In vitro BV2 cell experiments used n=3 independent replicates. Omitted outcomes (data only in figures, no numeric values): Y-maze training total distance and resting time, p21/p53/p16 protein expression by Western blot, SA-beta-gal positive cell percentage, Ki67 fluorescence intensity, glycolysis genes (Glut-1, Pfkfb3, Ldha, Hif-1alpha mRNA), HK2/LDHA protein expression, mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1), p-DRP1/DRP1 protein expression, ZO-1 immunofluorescence, IBA1+p21 co-localization.

trial_rating.result_basis: N protein mice showed significantly reduced spontaneous alternation rate and novel arm entries vs controls (p<0.05 to p<0.001 across behavioural measures, n=8/group); 2-DG treatment significantly reversed these deficits (ANOVA, p<0.05 to p<0.001).

summary: This Canadian RCT tested an 8-week individualized tele-rehabilitation program (three supervised video sessions per week with kinesiologists, including aerobic, strengthening, and flexibility exercises) against usual care in 132 adults with long COVID — 78% of whom had never been hospitalized, and 93% of whom had post-exertional malaise at enrollment. The primary outcome, functional mobility measured by the AM-PAC Basic Mobility scale, showed no statistically significant between-group difference (mean difference 0.61 points, 95% CI -0.91 to 2.13). However, the intervention group showed statistically significant improvements over controls in fatigue, dyspnea, pain/discomfort, and overall health status. No severe adverse events occurred, though 52% of intervention participants reported mild-to-moderate adverse events, most commonly post-exertional malaise flares, particularly in those with higher baseline PEM scores or comorbid cardiac disease.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: TDI data in Table 2 is reported as post-intervention scores (not change from baseline) in the lower section of the table; control and intervention SDs were extracted from the table columns. Baseline per-arm data for most continuous secondary outcomes (means and SDs at baseline) were not reported in the paper beyond AM-PAC and BDI median/IQR and DSQ-PEM; change-from-baseline CIs are reported rather than SDs for most outcomes. N for DSQ-PEM analysis was 34 control and 36 intervention (subsets). Health care utilization outcomes (doctor visits, other HCP visits, ER visits) at 30 days post-intervention were extracted from Table 2 but omitted from the outcomes array to stay within size limits — no significant between-group differences were found for any HCU measure. summary: This cross-sectional observational study examined immune cell death (apoptosis) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from 30 elderly individuals (mean age 72 years) who had recovered from COVID-19 at least six months prior, compared to 30 age-matched controls with no COVID-19 history. Elderly post-COVID individuals showed roughly double the rate of early apoptosis (22.6% vs 11.3%) and late apoptosis (18.9% vs 9.4%) in immune cells compared to controls, with pro-apoptotic protein Bax elevated and anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 reduced, indicating a persistent shift toward immune cell self-destruction months after recovery. Notably, participants with long COVID symptoms were excluded, meaning these immune changes occurred in people who appeared clinically recovered, and higher apoptosis correlated with greater initial infection severity (r=0.61).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is a cross-sectional observational study, NOT a clinical trial or RCT. It does not test an intervention. There is no randomization, no treatment arm, no follow-up measurement — only a single cross-sectional comparison of biomarkers between post-COVID elderly and age-matched controls. It is likely ineligible for inclusion in a clinical trial meta-analysis. Per-arm means and SDs are extracted as reported. All p-values are reported as thresholds only (p<0.05) except for the time-since-recovery correlation (p=0.03 exact). Active Caspase-3 numeric values (mean/SD) were not reported in text — only stated as significantly increased (p<0.05) — data likely only in figures. Bax/Bcl-2 ratio itself was not reported numerically, only described qualitatively. CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subset-specific apoptosis percentages were not separately quantified in text (only stated as significantly increased, p<0.05). Table 2 is truncated and does not provide per-participant outcome data. Per-arm demographic breakdowns are not reported — only overall mean age 72.4±4.8 years and overall male:female ratio 1:1.1. Vaccination status breakdown per arm not explicitly quantified as percentages.

summary: This phase 3 open-label extension study tested rimegepant 75 mg (an oral CGRP receptor antagonist taken every other day) as preventive migraine treatment in 458 adults in Japan who had 4-18 migraine days per month. Over 40 weeks of open-label treatment (up to 52 weeks total), participants experienced a sustained reduction in monthly migraine days from a baseline of 9.2 to 4.4 days by the final month, a mean reduction of 4.7 days; 60% of participants achieved at least a 50% reduction in migraine days by week 52. Safety was favorable with mostly mild-to-moderate adverse events and no cases of drug-induced liver injury, though the open-label design without a placebo comparator limits interpretation of the effectiveness findings.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports an open-label extension (OLE) of an RCT — the DBT phase had a placebo comparator (arm_id=2) but the OLE phase did not; all OLE outcomes are single-arm (arm_id=1) with no between-group comparisons possible. Baseline observation phase MMD values (9.2 any intensity, 6.3 moderate/severe) are reported as overall population figures, not broken down by DBT arm for OLE effectiveness analyses. Many effectiveness results by monthly timepoints (M4-M12) appear only in supplemental tables (Table S2-S5) and figures — only M13 and overall OLE text values are extracted here. The primary DBT phase efficacy result (statistically significant reduction in MMD for rimegepant vs placebo at 12 weeks) is referenced but numerical details are from the previously published paper [23] and not fully reproduced in this text. Per-arm AE data in Table 3 covers both OLE-only and combined DBT+OLE periods with different denominators; I have used the DBT+OLE combined figures (n=247 rimegepant, n=231 placebo) for adverse events as these are the most complete. The ≥75% and 100% responder rates for moderate/severe MMD at M13 and overall OLE phase are: ≥75% at M13=45.6% (95% CI 40.7-50.4), 100% at M13=28.3% (95% CI 23.9-32.7); ≥75% overall OLE=34.2% (95% CI 29.8-38.6), 100% overall OLE=3.8% (95% CI 2.0-5.6) — these are not extracted as separate outcome objects to limit response size but are noted here. NOTE: This paper is about migraine, not Long COVID — it appears to have been submitted to the extractor in error.

trial_rating.result_basis: Mean monthly migraine days reduced by 4.7 days (95% CI -5.1, -4.3) from a baseline of 9.2 days at week 48-52 (n=417); 60.0% achieved ≥50% reduction in MMD.

summary: This observational cohort study followed 75 adults with PCR-confirmed COVID-19 in Northern Colorado from July 2020 to April 2021, comparing blood biomarker profiles between those who developed Long COVID (PASC, n=34) and those who did not (n=41). In the first 35 days after infection, plasma levels of Factor IX, Tissue Factor, and tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA) were significantly elevated in patients who went on to develop PASC, and D-dimer levels between days 36–76 also differed significantly between groups. Patients with active PASC showed persistently elevated inflammatory and tissue-remodeling proteins (including HMGB1, complement C3, and annexins) and a higher proportion of activated platelets (CD41+CD62P+PAC-1+ cells) compared to non-PASC participants. This is a biomarker discovery study, not a treatment trial; the sample size was too small to establish diagnostic cutoffs, and results require validation in a larger independent cohort.

summary: This is a preclinical mouse study testing recombinant protein-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccine formulations combining spike RBD domains (from Wuhan, Beta, and Omicron BA.4/5 variants, each fused to a mouse IgG Fc fragment) with nucleocapsid (N) protein, delivered via intranasal, subcutaneous, or intramuscular routes. The primary finding is that an intramuscular prime followed by two intranasal booster doses produced substantially higher serum IgG titres, neutralizing antibody activity (mean inhibition rate 60-64% against BA.4/5), and T-cell responses (IL-2, IFN-γ, TNF) compared to intranasal-only vaccination, with antibody levels remaining stable over a 20-week follow-up. Adding a low dose (0.5-1 µg) of N protein to RBD-based formulations modestly enhanced RBD- and spike-specific humoral and cellular responses (1.4-1.8-fold higher IgG titres) and improved mucosal IgA in bronchoalveolar lavage samples. This is a mouse study only with no human data; the N protein adjuvant effect was consistent but not statistically significant in most comparisons, and no approved mucosal adjuvant was used.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL NOTE: This paper is a preclinical mouse vaccine immunogenicity study and is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial. It does not study Long COVID patients, post-COVID symptoms, or therapeutic interventions for Long COVID. This paper should be excluded from any Long COVID clinical trial meta-analysis. The outcomes extracted (IgG GMTs, neutralizing antibody inhibition rates, FluoroSpot T cell responses) are immunological endpoints in mice, not clinical outcomes in humans. GMTs reported as 'percent' fields in arm_results are actually the GMT titre values (unitless endpoint titres), not percentages — this was a workaround to fit the schema. The paper describes three separate experiments; arms 1-5 described here are from the third (final) experiment. IgG subtype data for arms 2-5 at week 12 is only partially reported in the visible text (Table 8 appears truncated). Neutralization inhibition rate range in group 4: 22-96% (mean 64%); group 5: 8-97% (mean 60%). Most cellular immune (FluoroSpot) data from the second study groups, not the third study arms modeled here. Additional outcome data from first and second studies (N-specific, S-specific, saRBD-specific IgG GMTs from Tables 4 and 5) not fully extracted as these are from different experimental cohorts with different arms than the primary five-arm structure described. Full IgG1/IgG2a subtype data table (Table 8) appears cut off in the provided text.

trial_rating.result_basis: N protein addition produced 1.4-1.8-fold higher RBD/S-specific IgG GMTs vs no-N group at termination (e.g. wuRBD GMT 459,760 vs 325,100), but differences were not statistically significant; intramuscular prime groups achieved mean BA.4/5 neutralisation inhibition rates of 64% (group 4) and 60% (group 5) vs negligible in intranasal-only groups.

summary: This Norwegian randomized controlled trial tested a brief outpatient rehabilitation program using a cognitive-behavioral approach (2–8 sessions with a doctor and physiotherapists) versus care as usual in 314 non-hospitalized adults with Long COVID. The primary outcome—SF-36 Physical Function Subscale at approximately 6 months—was significantly higher in the intervention group (mean difference 9.2 points, 95% CI 4.3–14.2), with the effect sustained at 12 months. The cost-effectiveness analysis found the intervention dominated care as usual: it produced 0.056 more QALYs (95% CI 0.024–0.077) while costing NOK 20,682 less per patient (~$1,958 USD), largely because the intervention group used far less inpatient rehabilitation and other healthcare services.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) companion to the primary trial (Nerli et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(12):e2450744). Detailed clinical outcome data (per-arm means, SDs for SF-36-PFS and secondary clinical outcomes) are NOT reported here — only the primary between-group effect size is cited from the original paper. EQ-5D-5L utility values are reported as group means without SDs at each timepoint. QALY data are reported as group totals without SDs. Cost data are reported as per-patient means without SDs per arm. Adverse event data are referenced as lower in the intervention group but not quantified in this paper — refer to original trial paper. Arm randomization numbers (157 per arm) are inferred from the 1:1 ratio and total of 314; the paper provides analyzed n as 125 (intervention) and 106 (CAU) at T0-T1, and 125 (intervention) and 102 (CAU) at T1-T2. T1 mean was 200 days (SD=75) and T2 mean was 396 days (SD=37) from inclusion. Weeks from randomization for T1 estimated as 200/7 ~29 weeks; T2 as 396/7 ~57 weeks. The cost mean difference of -20,682 NOK is stated verbatim (intervention minus CAU is negative, meaning intervention is cheaper). Sensitivity analysis: with extreme CAU patient excluded, CAU costs drop to 33,178 NOK (CI -20,443 to -781). Complete case analysis (n=204): QALY gain 0.035, cost difference 31,537 NOK savings.

trial_rating.result_basis: SF-36 Physical Function Subscale mean difference 9.2 points (95% CI 4.3–14.2) in favor of intervention at T1; QALY gain 0.056 (95% CI 0.024–0.077) with cost saving of NOK 20,682 per patient (95% CI −47,230 to −1,614).

summary: This triple-blind randomized controlled trial tested 8 weeks of inspiratory muscle strength training (IMST) at 50% of maximal inspiratory pressure in 40 adults with Long COVID who had CT-confirmed pulmonary involvement, comparing it against thoracic expansion exercises. The primary outcomes were quadriceps femoris muscle oxygenation and functional exercise capacity: the IMST group walked an average of 96.4 metres further on the six-minute walk test than the control group (p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.65), and maintained muscle oxygen saturation during exercise while the control group's levels declined (p<0.001). Secondary benefits included large gains in inspiratory muscle strength (MIP improved by ~52 cmH2O more than controls, Cohen's d=1.24), significant increases in upper and lower limb muscle strength, and meaningful reductions in fatigue (FSS score fell by ~14 points in IMST vs ~1 point in controls, p<0.001) and dyspnea during daily activities; physical activity levels did not improve.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper describes the study as 'triple blind' (participants, researchers, data analysts), though the control group used a clearly different exercise (thoracic expansion), making participant blinding questionable. The between-group effect size CI for 6-MWT% was reported as [7.94-22.40] in the text (note: lower bound reported as 7.94 in one place and 7.94 in another — used verbatim). Some outcome CIs (e.g., for deltoid effect size) were given in the text as Cohen's d ranges, not mean difference CIs — for deltoid the mean difference CI [39.62-79.15] N was extracted as stated. LCADL self-care subscale (p=0.240 between groups, not significant) and LCADL leisure subscale (p=0.445, not significant) were not included as separate outcomes to save space but data is available in Table 4. Non-dominant deltoid muscle strength also showed significant treatment effect (p<0.001) — data available in Table 4 but not included as a separate outcome item. Physical activity sub-outcomes (total energy expenditure, active energy expenditure, steps, sleep duration, lying down) not included as separate outcomes; summary data available in Table 4. Additional SmO2 sub-measures (SmO2 min, SmO2 max, recovery values, THb measures) available in Table 3 but not all extracted as separate outcomes given volume; ΔTHb showed within-group but not between-group significant effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome 6-MWT distance improved by 96.44 m more in IMST vs control (95% CI 51.39–141.49 m, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.65); ΔSmO2 during 6-MWT was significantly better in IMST vs control (p<0.001).

summary: This observational multi-omics study analysed plasma proteomics and metabolomics from 307 hospitalised COVID-19 patients in Beijing to identify molecular markers linked to poor outcomes, with a specific focus on skeletal muscle mass loss. The key finding is that low plasma citrulline levels at admission were strongly associated with muscle mass loss and 28-day mortality: patients with muscle mass loss had significantly lower survival probability (p<0.0001), and a survival random forest model using citrulline, GLUL, and GOT1 achieved an AUROC of 0.94 at 5 days and 0.79 at 15 days on the test set. In vitro experiments supported a mechanistic link, showing that citrulline depletion worsened LPS-driven M1 macrophage polarisation while citrulline supplementation attenuated it, and Mendelian randomisation confirmed a causal relationship between low citrulline and sarcopenia. This is an exploratory observational study with no therapeutic intervention tested; the prognostic model was validated on only 20 test-set patients, limiting conclusions about clinical utility.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a clinical trial and is NOT a Long COVID intervention study. It is a retrospective observational multi-omics cohort study of hospitalized COVID-19 patients. There are no randomized arms, no intervention administered, and no control group receiving a comparator treatment. The JSON schema fields for RCT design (arms, randomization, blinding, allocation concealment, per-arm demographics, per-arm sample sizes) are all inapplicable and set to null/empty. The paper references long COVID only in its introduction as background motivation; the study population consists of acutely/severely ill hospitalized COVID-19 patients, not post-COVID/long COVID patients. Per-arm means and SDs for outcomes are not reported numerically in text — most quantitative results appear as Kaplan-Meier curves, box plots, and rose plots in figures without tabulated values. The in vitro experiment (Fig. 5D) reports bars as mean±SD with n=9 but does not provide numeric values in text. The survival model metrics (AUROC, C-index with 95% CIs) are extracted verbatim as they appear in text. Omitted biomarker outcomes (due to data only in figures): differential protein/metabolite counts by tissue, MOFA factor correlations, immune infiltration proportions, MR analysis effect estimates for sarcopenia/citrulline/COVID-19 death (forest plot values not reported in text).

summary: This in vitro laboratory study examined extracellular vesicles (EVs) isolated from blood serum of 16 Long COVID patients and 16 matched recovered controls to characterise their molecular cargo and functional effects on multiple human cell types (lung epithelial, lung fibroblast, endothelial, aortic smooth muscle, and mesenchymal stem cells). EVs from Long COVID patients carried elevated platelet-activation markers (CD29, CD41b, CD42a, CD69), increased RUNX2 mRNA, and reduced hsa-miR-204-5p compared to controls; when applied to recipient cells, they consistently upregulated RUNX2 protein and activated the p53/p21/sestrin stress pathway across all cell types tested. Long COVID EVs also impaired mitochondrial metabolic flexibility under resource-limited conditions—maximal respiration, ATP production, and basal respiration all declined significantly at higher cell densities (p<0.005)—whereas control-EV-treated cells maintained stable respiration. A key caveat is that this is a pooled-sample in vitro study with no clinical intervention; it identifies a potential disease mechanism rather than testing any treatment, and findings require validation in larger cohorts with individual-level EV analysis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is NOT a clinical trial or RCT — it is an in vitro mechanistic study using EVs isolated from Long COVID patients vs. healthy controls exposed to cell lines. The schema fields for randomization, blinding, ITT analysis, adverse events, and follow-up duration are not applicable. Per-arm quantitative results (means/SDs) for most biomarker outcomes are only available in figures, not tables or text; result_source set to 'not_reported' for those. Clinical data (6MWT, spirometry) are only from the Long COVID arm (no control comparator performed the 6MWT per study design). Individual patient spirometry values are available in Table 2 but group means/SDs are not explicitly summarized in text. EV analyses were performed on pooled samples, limiting individual-level inference. summary: This case-control study examined circulating metabolic profiles in 42 survivors of critical COVID-19 (21 with Long COVID, 21 fully recovered controls) one year after hospital discharge, using proton NMR spectroscopy and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry to identify biomarkers of persistent symptoms. Two metabolites differed significantly between groups: alpha-ketoglutarate (aKG) was elevated in Long COVID patients (p=0.014) and creatine was reduced (p=0.017), each with modest discriminative ability (AUC 0.70–0.75). A machine-learning multilayer integration of 72 metabolites identified a nine-metabolite signature—including aKG, creatine, oxidative stress markers (CMC, CML), fumarate, lactate, and LDL particle size—achieving higher classification accuracy (AUC 0.80–0.91), pointing to mitochondrial and energy metabolism dysfunction as contributors to Long COVID. The study is observational and hypothesis-generating with a small sample, no intervention tested, and no causal relationships established.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a randomized controlled trial — it is an observational matched case-control metabolomics study. There is no intervention, no randomization, and no treatment arms; the two 'arms' are Long COVID cases vs recovered controls. RoB2 is not applicable. Per-arm means and SDs for metabolite concentrations are not reported numerically in the text or tables — only 'average differences' between groups are given (aKG difference=0.306, creatine difference=-9.965, ratio difference=0.049), and metabolite data appears in violin plots (Fig. 1) without tabulated values. AUC values for individual biomarkers and ML models are verbatim from text. The table provides detailed clinical outcome data (mMRC, FACIT, SF-12, BC-CCI, HADS, spirometry, 6MWT) with medians and IQRs per group. The n_analyzed for FACIT and SF-12 differs (N=41 total, one missing); DLCO n=39 total; TLC n=35 total. The study does not test any treatment intervention — it is purely a biomarker/diagnostic accuracy study and should not be included in a meta-analysis of clinical trials.

trial_rating.result_basis: aKG elevated in Long COVID vs controls (p=0.014, AUC 0.73); creatine reduced (p=0.017, AUC 0.70); nine-metabolite ML signature AUC 0.80–0.91; N=21 per group.

summary: This observational case-control study examined 161 male Long COVID patients in Iraq, divided by severity of their initial SARS-CoV-2 infection (mild vs. severe, based on peak body temperature and oxygen saturation). Patients who had more severe acute illness showed significantly higher levels of NLRP3 inflammasome-associated biomarkers (NLRP3, caspase-1, GSDMD, IL-1β, IL-18, fibronectin) during Long COVID, and these biomarkers correlated with worse neuropsychiatric and fatigue symptoms. Regression analysis found that IL-1β, IL-10, CRP, IL-18, and fibronectin together explained 45.7% of the variance in overall Long COVID symptom severity. This is not an intervention trial — no treatment was tested; the study identifies inflammatory biomarkers as correlates of Long COVID severity and proposes the NLRP3 pathway as a future therapeutic target.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is NOT a clinical trial or RCT. It is an observational case-control study comparing two naturally-occurring severity subgroups of Long COVID patients; there is no intervention, no randomization, and no treatment arm. The schema has been completed as best as possible by mapping 'arm 1' to severe acute COVID-19 group and 'arm 2' to mild acute COVID-19 group, but these are not intervention arms. RoB2 is inapplicable. Table 2 biomarker data are expressed as estimated marginal means (SE) from GLM analysis adjusted for age, sex, education, and smoking — not raw means/SDs; the SE values are placed in the 'se' field accordingly. CRP data appear in Table 3 (correlation only) but not as per-arm means — no arm-level CRP data available. The F-statistics and p-values reported in Table 1 for group comparisons are from one-way ANOVA. Between-group p-values for Table 1 outcomes are reported as <0.001 (not exact); p_value_exact set to false for those. The IPS index cutoff used for subgroup definition was the median (0.41). No follow-up duration in weeks is defined as this is a cross-sectional assessment. Outcomes zPBT - zSpO2 and IPS composite are reported as group-defining variables, not separate outcomes — not extracted as outcomes. The multiple regression results (Table 4, Table 5) provide standardized betas but not per-arm means for regression-specific analyses; these are noted in the summary but not separately extracted as outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: NLRP3 composite biomarker score explained 24% of variance (R²=0.240) predicted by SpO2 (β=-0.490, p<0.001); overall Long COVID severity predicted by IL-1β, IL-10, CRP, IL-18, fibronectin (R²=0.457, F=26.09, p<0.001); severe vs. mild group NLRP3 difference p=0.026.

summary: This is a laboratory study, not a clinical trial, investigating how the SARS-CoV-2 spike S1 protein drives brain cell aging (cellular senescence) in human astrocytes — a mechanism proposed to underlie neurological Long COVID. Researchers found that S1 protein enters astrocyte endolysosomes and, via its multibasic motif (RRAR), binds to the immune sensor TLR7, triggering lysosomal dysfunction and a senescence-like state marked by elevated IL-6, increased senescence markers (SA-β-gal, p16, p21), and release of inflammatory factors galectin-3 and cathepsin B. Blocking TLR7 or its downstream p38 MAPK signalling prevented these effects, identifying TLR7 and p38 as potential therapeutic targets for neuro-PASC. No patients were studied; all findings are from cell cultures, so clinical relevance remains to be established.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial. It is a basic science/in vitro mechanistic study investigating SARS-CoV-2 S1 protein-induced endolysosome dysfunction and cellular senescence in primary human astrocyte cell cultures. There are no human participants, no randomization, no clinical arms, no patient-level outcomes, and no clinical endpoints. All quantitative data pertain to cell culture experiments (n values refer to independent cell culture replicates, not patients). The paper does not meet eligibility criteria for a meta-analysis of Long COVID clinical trials. All clinical trial extraction fields are null/empty as not applicable.

trial_rating.result_basis: TLR7 siRNA knockdown blocked S1-induced IL-6 release, SA-β-gal activity, and p16 upregulation (n=2-5 independent cultures per assay); p38 inhibitor SB203580 abolished S1-induced p21, p16, and IL-6 increases; all comparisons significant by two-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc, p<0.05, but exact p-values and effect sizes are not reported numerically in the paper.

summary: This observational study used single-cell RNA sequencing to profile immune cells in blood samples from nine hospitalized female COVID-19 patients — three who developed Long COVID with cardiovascular complications, three with pulmonary complications, and three who fully recovered — at acute infection, 3 months, and 1.5–2 years post-infection. Long COVID patients showed a distinct immune signature including elevated classical monocyte proportions, increased immature CD4+ T cells, and reduced plasma B cells and dendritic cells compared to recovered patients. At the cellular level, Long COVID patients had persistently elevated cytotoxicity markers (GNLY, GZMH, KLRK1) and exhaustion-associated markers (LAG3, TOX, VSIR) in proliferating lymphocytes and CD8+ T cells up to two years post-infection, alongside a blunted type I interferon response during acute infection and sustained inflammatory signalling at follow-up. The key caveat is that this is a mechanistic observational study with only three patients per group, not a clinical trial, so no intervention was tested and no effect size or p-value for a primary clinical outcome is reported.

summary: This observational neuroimaging study used 7 Tesla task fMRI to compare brain functional connectivity (FC) patterns in 17 Long COVID patients, 27 ME/CFS patients, and 24 healthy controls while they performed a cognitively fatiguing Stroop colour-word task. Both Long COVID and ME/CFS patients showed reduced FC across subcortical regions — including the amygdala, hippocampus, nucleus accumbens, anterior cingulate cortex, and cerebellar vermis — compared to healthy controls, who instead showed increased connectivity between these regions as the task progressed. Long COVID patients showed more prominent subcortical (deep grey matter) connectivity disruptions, while ME/CFS patients showed greater involvement of default mode and salience network nodes; no intervention was tested, as this is a cross-sectional mechanistic study identifying potential neuroimaging biomarkers rather than a clinical trial.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a clinical trial — it is a cross-sectional observational neuroimaging study comparing three groups (Long COVID, ME/CFS, Healthy Controls) using 7T task fMRI. There is no randomization, no intervention, and no treatment arm. The JSON schema fields for study_design arms, risk_of_bias, adverse_events, and follow-up are therefore largely null or marked as not applicable. All outcome data are neuroimaging FC beta coefficients with associated t-values and FDR-corrected p-values, not clinical symptom scores with per-arm means and SDs. The 'between_group_effects' fields for FC outcomes use 'effect_value' to store the beta coefficient from the weighted GLM (not a true mean difference between arms), and 'comparison' strings describe the actual contrast tested. Duration of illness reported as years: pwLC mean=0.8±0.6 years (converted to ~9.6±7.2 months for time_since_infection field). The pwME/CFS duration mean stated as 12.7±11.0 years in Table 1, but discussion states 'mean=12.4 yrs±11.2' — verbatim table values used. Table 1 originally enrolled n=19 pwLC/n=32 pwME/CFS/n=27 HC (78 total); 10 excluded as MRI outliers leaving n=17/27/24 (68 total) for analysis. summary: This is a mathematical modelling study, not a clinical trial. Researchers at Shanghai University developed a six-variable differential equation model of SARS-CoV-2 dynamics in the vasculature and lung tissue, fitting it to published viral load data from eight hospitalised patients in Munich (2020). The model found that most patients' pulmonary viral loads exhibit persistent periodic oscillations rather than clearance, and that under simulated potent antiviral treatment some patients show coexisting chaotic and periodic attractors, suggesting single-drug regimens are unlikely to fully eliminate the virus. Four chaos-control methods (adaptive, active, linear feedback, and periodic perturbation) were mathematically demonstrated to drive the system toward either a disease-free or protective-immunity state, with adaptive control proposed as the most clinically translatable approach.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. CRITICAL: This paper is not a clinical trial and is not eligible for inclusion in a meta-analysis of Long COVID interventions. It is a mathematical modeling study that proposes a system of ordinary differential equations to model SARS-CoV-2 dynamics in tissue and vasculature compartments. The only 'data' used are previously published viral load measurements (lung sputum samples) from 8 patients hospitalized in Munich in 2020 (cited as reference [25]), used solely for parameter fitting. There are no randomized arms, no intervention groups, no control group, no clinical outcomes, no patient-reported outcomes, and no effect sizes. All JSON fields have been set to null or empty arrays accordingly. The paper does discuss long COVID mechanisms theoretically and proposes chaos control methods as analogues for therapeutic strategies, but this is purely computational/theoretical with no empirical trial data.

summary: This study is not a Long COVID clinical trial. It is a retrospective hospital infection control study that applied whole-genome sequencing (nanopore sequencing with BadTrIP Bayesian analysis) to reconstruct transmission pathways during a 9-case SARS-CoV-2 ward outbreak in April 2022 and a 22-case multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter (MDRA) outbreak from 2012-2014. The primary finding was methodological: BadTrIP produced transmission trees consistent with conventional epidemiology for the short SARS-CoV-2 outbreak, but was less reliable for the prolonged MDRA outbreak using stored isolates. No patient intervention was tested and no Long COVID outcomes were measured.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is NOT a Long COVID clinical trial and is NOT eligible for inclusion in a Long COVID meta-analysis. It is a retrospective observational study of hospital-acquired infection outbreaks (SARS-CoV-2 nosocomial outbreak and MDRA outbreak) using whole-genome sequencing for transmission pathway reconstruction. There are no trial arms, no randomization, no Long COVID patients, and no Long COVID outcomes. The 'arms' in Table 2 (spreader vs non-spreader) are post-hoc epidemiological categories, not trial arms. CI values for OR in Table 2 appear to be on the log-odds scale and are unusual (e.g., OR 0.50 with CI -2.4 to 1.0), suggesting possible reporting irregularities in the original table. All outcome data extracted here comes from Table 2 comparing MDRA spreaders (n=12) vs non-spreaders (n=10).

trial_rating.result_basis: No clinical intervention or outcome measure applicable; this is a genomic epidemiology methods study, not a clinical trial. summary: This is a computational genetics study, not a clinical trial testing an intervention in patients. Researchers developed a multi-omics bioinformatics framework combining Transcriptome-Wide Mendelian Randomization and Control Theory to identify genes that may causally contribute to Long COVID. Applying this to publicly available GWAS, eQTL, RNA-seq, and protein-protein interaction data, the framework prioritized 32 putative causal genes (19 previously linked to COVID-19/Long COVID, 13 novel), and used their expression profiles to cluster 158 Long COVID patients into three symptom subtypes: respiratory-sleep (n=65), neuropsychological-dental (n=53), and gastrointestinal-metabolic (n=36). No intervention was tested and no clinical outcomes were measured; all findings are computational predictions requiring experimental and clinical validation.

summary: This retrospective genetic association study examined whether variants in the SERPINE1 (rs6092) and IFNAR2 (rs1051393, rs2229207) genes were linked to post-COVID-19 respiratory syndrome in 85 Indonesian patients (43 cases, 42 controls) hospitalised between 2020 and 2021. The primary finding was that none of the three SNPs were significantly associated with the presence or absence of post-COVID-19 respiratory syndrome across any inheritance model. Secondary analyses found that the IFNAR2 variant rs2229207 was associated with higher blood potassium levels (B=0.317, p=0.003), the only association to survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction after multivariable adjustment; rs1051393 showed nominal association with fever (p=0.037) and rs6092 with basophil levels (p=0.027) and eGFR (p=0.036), but neither survived multiple-comparison correction. The study is substantially limited by its small sample size, retrospective design, and the fact that its main genetic hypothesis was not supported.

summary: This Stanford study tested whether continuous heart rate data from consumer smartwatches, combined with symptom reports, could predict Long COVID in 126 adults who had confirmed acute SARS-CoV-2 infections (31 with Long COVID, 95 without). summary: This study is not a clinical trial but a bioinformatics analysis of existing single-cell RNA sequencing data from 12 Long COVID patients collected 8 months after infection. Researchers used a computational method called Window-based HERV Alignment (WHA) to detect activity of human endogenous retroviral (HERV) sequences — ancient viral DNA embedded in the human genome — across different immune cell types. They found that a specific HERV locus on chromosome 3, located within a gene called xCR1 (normally a marker of dendritic cells), was abnormally active in CD14+ monocytes (a type of innate immune cell) in 11 of 12 Long COVID patients but not in healthy controls, pointing to an unusual hybrid immune cell population that may contribute to persistent immune dysfunction. The study is limited to a single small dataset and no intervention was tested; findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating only.

summary: This is a preclinical mechanistic study, not a human clinical trial. Researchers administered the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein S1 subunit intranasally to rats to model the neurological effects of long COVID, then tested whether metformin could mitigate the resulting damage. Rats receiving S1 showed significant spatial memory impairment in the Morris water maze (3.5-fold longer escape latency on day 5 vs. controls, p=0.0007) and 56% less time in the target quadrant during the probe trial, alongside hippocampal neuronal loss, accumulation of phosphorylated tau, and aggregated alpha-synuclein by 6 weeks. In cell culture experiments, metformin co-treatment restored expression of synaptic genes (GRIN2A, JPH3, SHANK1, GRIA2) and reduced tau and alpha-synuclein aggregation, apparently by suppressing HIF-1α stabilization. These findings are entirely from rat and cell-line models; no human patients were studied, and the results cannot be directly applied to Long COVID treatment without clinical trials.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. CRITICAL: This paper is a preclinical animal/in vitro study, NOT a human clinical trial of Long COVID. It should be excluded from a meta-analysis of Long COVID clinical trials. The study uses male Sprague-Dawley rats administered SARS-CoV-2 S1 spike protein intranasally, and N2A/H4 neuronal cell lines for metformin experiments — there are no human participants. Most quantitative outcome data (means ± SEMs) appear only in figures and are not reproduced as numeric values in the text or tables, except for: MWM escape latency (S1: 24.0±4.1s, control: 6.9±0.9s on day 5; p=0.0007), platform crossings (S1: 2.7±0.3 vs control: 5.0±0.4; p=0.005), probe trial time in target quadrant (S1 reduced by 56% vs control; p=0.0322), open field center time (p=0.002), open field center distance (p=0.0003), episodic-like memory what-when discrimination in control group (p=0.0038, p=0.047, p=0.0052). Western blot data for NMDAR2A, JPH3, HIF-1α, p-tau, and α-synuclein are shown only in figures. The metformin intervention is only tested in cell culture (in vitro), not in the in vivo rat model. Reference [52] (Bramante et al., COVID-OUT trial) is cited as supporting clinical evidence for metformin.

trial_rating.result_basis: No human clinical outcome was measured; this is an animal/in vitro study. The metformin intervention was tested only in cell lines (N2A, H4), not in the S1-injected rats, so no in vivo effect size for metformin is available. Rat memory impairment was significant (escape latency 24.0±4.1 s vs. 6.9±0.9 s, p=0.0007) but this is a model endpoint, not a clinical outcome.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Participants with submaximal effort had significantly lower 30s-STS z-scores (mean -2.11 vs -1.23) and fewer repetitions (mean 12.2 vs 16.8) compared to those with maximal effort; no differences in clinical or demographic characteristics between groups were identified.

Participants with very severe PEM completed fewer 30s-STS repetitions, while those with mild, moderate, and severe PEM showed comparable values; the association was weak (Spearman r not explicitly reported for PEM grade but overall symptom correlations were r=0.22 to 0.32).

summary: This study evaluated the measurement properties of the 30-second sit-to-stand test (30s-STS) as a functional capacity measure in 150 adults with Long COVID, using data from the PYCNOVID randomised controlled trial. The 30s-STS showed good test-retest reliability (ICC 0.82) and was safe and feasible to administer, with no adverse events; however, 46% of participants scored below the 5th percentile for functional capacity, indicating widespread impairment in this population. The study's primary aim was psychometric validation rather than treatment efficacy — no intervention effect on functional capacity was tested — and a provisional minimal important difference of 2 repetitions was proposed based on distribution-based methods alone, as anchor-based approaches failed due to weak correlations (all below 0.3) between changes in test performance and symptom measures.

summary: This is a preclinical study, not a Long COVID clinical trial.
