summary: This was a preclinical animal study (not a human clinical trial) evaluating a COVID-19 fusion protein vaccine in female Syrian hamsters. Hamsters (n=5 per group) were vaccinated with COVID19-SF2+SF5 fusion protein, COVID19-SF2 alone, COVID19-SF5 alone, COVID19-SF6 alone, or PBS control over 42 days, then challenged with SARS-CoV-2 Omicron strain. summary: This small Ukrainian trial tested whether adding L-arginine (1000 mg twice daily) and phenibut (500 mg twice daily) for three months to standard cardiac therapy improved neuropsychiatric and autonomic outcomes in 31 patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) who had experienced moderate-to-severe COVID-19 and had Long COVID symptoms. summary: This preclinical mouse study investigated how SARS-CoV-2 infection affects the brain's orexin (hypocretin) system and cortical neurons, with relevance to Long COVID neurological symptoms. In K18-hACE2 transgenic and wild-type BALB/c mice, SARS-CoV-2 infection caused rapid suppression of hypothalamic orexin expression (dropping to below 2% of normal levels at 6 days post-infection) and produced patchy loss of the cortical neuronal marker NeuN that persisted for up to 90 days, whereas influenza A virus did not cause these effects despite comparable brain viral RNA levels. Treating infected mice with exogenous orexin-A/B peptides increased whole-brain NeuN protein levels approximately 1.8-fold without altering viral load, suggesting orexin signalling may protect neuronal integrity. This is an animal study only, with no human participants; whether orexin dysfunction drives Long COVID neurological symptoms in people remains unestablished.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a preclinical mechanistic study using animal models of SARS-CoV-2 infection, not a clinical trial of Long COVID patients. No randomized controlled trial structure, no human participants, and no clinical outcomes. Multiple quantitative endpoints (viral RNA, mRNA levels, protein levels, immunohistochemistry semi-quantification) extracted where reported. Numerical data for many outcomes (e.g., mean viral loads, exact fold-changes in gene expression) appear only in figure panels rather than tables or text values; these are noted as 'not_reported' per instructions. Western blot densitometry values reported as fold-changes relative to β-actin normalized controls without absolute values or SDs. The study explicitly states that in vivo biochemical analysis was performed on whole-brain lysates, which may not fully capture focal cortical NeuN-low regions identified histologically, and the authors acknowledge this as a limitation. No formal safety monitoring or adverse event grading system applied; animal morbidity/mortality tracking was standard for in vivo infection studies. Approximately 10-12 distinct mechanistic outcomes assessed across different experimental arms; only outcomes with quantifiable data have been extracted. The paper reports this as an 'accepted manuscript in press' and notes this is an unedited version.

trial_rating.result_basis: Hcrt mRNA fell to <2% of mock levels at 6 dpi (Pearson r = -0.8336 between brain viral load and Hcrt expression, p reported as significant); exogenous orexin-A/B increased NeuN protein ~1.8-fold versus vehicle in infected mice; cortical NeuN-depleted regions persisted to 90 dpi in both mouse models.

summary: This observational study examined peripheral muscle oxygen delivery during submaximal cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) in 45 adults with Long COVID (without moderate-to-severe post-exertional malaise) compared with 10 healthy controls. Using near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) on the gastrocnemius muscle, the study found that Long COVID participants showed a diminished ability to sustain oxygen delivery during exercise: tissue oxygen saturation (TSI%) returned to resting levels after just 1-2 minutes of loaded cycling, whereas controls maintained elevated TSI% for up to 5 minutes. Long COVID participants also showed significantly higher ventilatory inefficiency (VE/VO2 17% higher, p<0.001) and lower peak work rate (73±15 W vs 85±0 W, p=0.001) compared to controls, with no adverse events reported. A key caveat is that between-group TSI% comparisons were not made due to probe placement variability and adipose tissue differences, and the control group was significantly younger (33 vs 52 years), which may confound ventilatory findings.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study is observational and cross-sectional, not a clinical trial; randomization field set to N/A. Age matching was not performed; LC cohort significantly older than controls (p<0.001), which authors acknowledge may impact ventilatory responses. NIRS data unavailable for 9 LC participants (n=6 due to symptom exacerbation during test, n=3 due to device signal error), preventing valid between-group TSI% comparisons as stated by authors. VT1 not identifiable in control participants; limited VT1 reporting (n=24 for LC). Multiple intermediate timepoints extracted for TSI% during exercise, though formal statistical comparisons between time points not all reported in text. Two LC participants could complete test on both days due to symptom exacerbation (totaling 6 non-completers stated in results). Time since COVID-19 infection not reported. Study focused on mechanistic assessment rather than treatment efficacy.

trial_rating.result_basis: Long COVID showed earlier return of TSI% to rest (after minute 2 on day 1) vs controls (after minute 5), and iso-time peak work rate was lower (73±15 W vs 85±0 W, p=0.001); no formal between-group TSI% statistical comparison was made due to methodological limitations.

summary: This observational genetic study from St. Petersburg examined whether two cytokine gene variants — IL-6 (rs1800795, -174G>C) and IL-10 (rs1800871, -819C>T) — are associated with neurological and psychiatric symptoms of Long COVID in 130 patients aged 18–60 who had confirmed prior COVID-19 infection, compared to 116 healthy controls. The primary finding was a striking reduction in the IL-6 'wild-type' GG genotype among Long COVID patients (6.9% vs 28% in controls; OR=0.195, p<0.001), with a corresponding excess of the heterozygous GC genotype (69.2% vs 50%; OR=2.25, p=0.003), suggesting these variants modulate susceptibility to neurological post-COVID complications. A secondary IL-10 finding showed the TT genotype was rarer in Long COVID patients (5.4% vs 15%; p=0.018). No causal intervention was tested; this is a cross-sectional genetic association study, not a clinical trial, and the small sample size — particularly for rare genotypes — limits the reliability of the findings.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a genetic association case-control study, not a clinical trial; therefore, it does not fit the typical RCT outcome extraction model. Extracted genotype frequencies and between-group comparisons (odds ratios) as the primary quantitative outcomes. No treatment interventions tested. Study compared genotype distributions between long COVID patients and healthy controls. TREC analysis reported only as descriptive finding without quantitative per-genotype data. Gender-specific observation noted: GG and TT genotypes were found exclusively or predominantly in female participants, attributed by authors to limited sample size. Neurological findings (Figure 1) referenced but not extracted as specific outcome percentages were not provided for all symptom categories in tabular form.

trial_rating.result_basis: IL-6 GG genotype frequency 6.92% in Long COVID patients vs 28% in controls (OR=0.195, 95% CI 0.089–0.430, p<0.001); GC genotype 69.23% vs 50% (OR=2.25, p=0.0032); IL-10 TT genotype 5.38% vs 15% (OR=0.33, p=0.0176).

summary: This study tested Immunovac-VP-4 (ACOPB), an immunostimulating drug containing antigens from four opportunistic bacteria, first in a Syrian hamster model of SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia and then as an add-on therapy in 78 hospitalized patients with moderate COVID-19. In hamsters, spray and inhalation administration of ACOPB before infection reduced lung viral load by more than 2.5 log units compared to untreated controls, and treated animals gained weight (4.2% spray, 8.8% inhalation) while controls lost 5.6%. In the human trial, patients who received ACOPB alongside standard treatment had significantly shorter hospital stays (16 vs 19 days, p=0.05), shorter fever duration (1 vs 3 days, p=0.03), and higher secretory IgA levels in nasal and pharyngeal samples at day 30. The human trial was small, unblinded, and conducted during the original COVID-19 wave rather than in a Long COVID population, limiting generalisability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports findings from animal models (hamster experiments 1 and 2) alongside a clinical observational study. The clinical study was not a true RCT—patients were 'randomly divided' into two groups but there is no description of allocation concealment, and the design is open-label. Animal model data (viral titers, weight change) cannot be directly compared to clinical outcomes as the study populations differ. The paper emphasizes viral load reduction and mucosal immunity (sIgA) markers, not Long COVID severity outcomes. This study was reviewed as submitted, though it does not meet Long COVID trial inclusion criteria (acute COVID-19, not post-acute phase). Baseline sIgA values at day 1 appear to be identical across arms, suggesting possible data entry or reporting issue. No data on hospitalization comorbidities or disease severity beyond CT lung involvement percentage reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Hospital stay reduced from 19 to 16 days (p=0.05) and fever duration from 3 to 1 day (p=0.03) in 78 patients; hamster viral load reduced by >2.5 log TCID50/mL.

summary: This observational study examined 431 patients with stable coronary artery disease who had previously recovered from SARS-CoV-2 infection (>12 weeks prior), comparing those with mild COVID-19 (n=203) to those with moderate COVID-19 (n=228) to identify predictors of hemodynamically significant coronary artery stenosis (≥70% blockage). Patients who had moderate COVID-19 had significantly higher rates of hemodynamically significant stenosis than those with mild COVID-19 (86.4% vs 68.0%, p<0.001), as well as more multivessel disease and coronary restenosis. Multivariate logistic regression identified eight independent predictors of significant stenosis, including moderate COVID-19 history (OR 1.84), aortic diameter >3.28 cm (OR 2.52), segmental myocardial contractility disorders (OR 3.72), extracranial artery atherosclerosis (OR 2.56), hyperuricemia (OR 2.22), low HDL (OR 1.99), and high residual LDL risk (OR 2.48); these were used to build an online risk calculator. This was a single-centre observational study without randomisation, so the findings reflect associations rather than causal effects, and the groups differed at baseline on multiple clinical characteristics.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational comparative study, not a randomized trial, stratified by COVID-19 severity. Participants were not randomly assigned; groups were prospectively enrolled and stratified post-hoc based on documented COVID-19 severity. No intervention was tested; rather, this is a cross-sectional analysis of the association between prior COVID-19 severity and coronary angiography findings in patients with stable CCS in the post-COVID period (>12 weeks after infection). Adverse events were not systematically reported. Some baseline clinical and demographic characteristics differ significantly between groups (e.g., hospitalization, hypertension duration, diabetes prevalence), which may confound the main findings despite multivariate adjustment. The study included multiple secondary outcomes; prioritized extraction was given to primary angiographic outcomes (GZSCA prevalence, multivessel disease, restenosis) and the key biomarkers and echocardiographic parameters. TNF-α, IL-1β, MCP-1 cytokine data, and blood pressure control data were extracted from Table 3 but not formatted as separate outcome objects due to space constraints.

trial_rating.result_basis: Hemodynamically significant coronary stenosis was present in 86.4% of moderate COVID-19 patients vs 68.0% of mild COVID-19 patients (OR 3.0 [1.8–5.0], p<0.001); moderate COVID-19 remained an independent predictor in multivariate analysis (OR 1.84 [1.02–3.39], p=0.047).

summary: This study translated, culturally adapted, and validated the Modified Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale (C19-YRSm) — a 17-item questionnaire measuring symptom severity, functional disability, and overall health — in Spanish for use with Mexican adults who had experienced COVID-19. Among 889 participants recruited via social media, the scale showed good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha 0.87 for symptom severity, 0.82 for functional disability) and a two-factor structure confirmed by factor analysis. Hospitalized participants scored markedly higher on symptom severity (mean 15.33 vs 10.60) and functional disability (mean 4.96 vs 2.26) than non-hospitalized participants. This is a psychometric validation study, not a clinical trial testing an intervention; no treatment effect was measured.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a psychometric validation study, not a clinical trial, so design is quasi-experimental/cross-sectional rather than RCT. No randomization or control arm. N=889 represents the full sample completing the scale once. Table 1 sociodemographic data required calculation of some percentages (e.g., hospitalization 4.8% from 43/889). Item-mean range reported as 0.28-0.67 for SS and 0.45-0.75 for FD; presented as midpoint values in outcomes. CFA results: RMSEA=0.72 (90% CI: 0.69-0.74), SRMR=0.099, CFI=0.919, TLI=0.914. All validity comparisons (hospitalization, symptom burden tertiles) used non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis) with Dunn post-hoc. No between-group effect data available for correlations; presented as endpoint values only. Female respondents were predominant (80%), and 74% had university/postgraduate education, limiting generalizability.

trial_rating.result_basis: No intervention or treatment effect was tested; the primary outcome was scale validation. Cronbach's alpha was 0.87 (SS) and 0.82 (FD); CFA RMSEA was 0.72, indicating suboptimal model fit.

summary: Ten sessions of individualized respiratory and motor physical therapy were tested in 26 adults with Long COVID (symptoms persisting beyond 12 weeks) attending a multidisciplinary post-COVID rehabilitation service in Bahia, Brazil. Across functional tests, patients showed significant improvements: Timed-Up-and-Go improved from a median of 10 to 8 seconds (p=0.002), the 2-minute step-in-place test improved from 55 to 80 steps (p=0.006), and global muscle strength increased from MRC grade 4 to 5 (p<0.001). Self-reported fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and dry cough also decreased significantly. This was a small quasi-experimental study with no control group, meaning spontaneous recovery cannot be ruled out as a contributor to the observed gains.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Single-arm quasi-experimental design with no control group. Sample is small and includes selection bias (63 patients screened, only 26 completed 10 sessions). Median values with IQR reported for baseline characteristics and all outcome measures; exact individual timepoint values for endpoints extracted from text and figures. No between-group comparisons possible; pre-post changes reported with Wilcoxon test p-values (continuous) and McNemar test p-values (binary symptoms). Time to re-evaluation reported as median 47 days for 10 sessions. Baseline symptom prevalence calculated from reported percentages. Study lacks formal risk of bias assessment structure due to quasi-experimental design; ROBINS-I tool applied as most appropriate for non-randomized studies. No adverse events reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: 2-minute step-in-place test improved from median 55 to 80 steps (p=0.006); Timed-Up-and-Go improved from 10 to 8 seconds (p=0.002); global muscle strength MRC 4 to 5 (p<0.001).

summary: This observational study examined how Long COVID affects quality of life in 546 non-hospitalized adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 who received placebo in the ACTIV-2/A5401 clinical trial, assessed approximately 9 months after acute infection. At that point, 13% of participants met the definition for Long COVID (self-reported ongoing symptoms). Compared to those without Long COVID, participants with Long COVID were 3.5 to 6 times more likely to report problems with mobility, usual activities, pain, and anxiety/depression on the EQ-5D-5L scale, and scored substantially worse on both the physical and mental components of the SF-36 (median physical score 46.8 vs 58.7, mental score 49.0 vs 57.6). These quality-of-life deficits were present regardless of whether participants had pre-existing medical conditions, suggesting Long COVID itself — not underlying health status — drives the impairment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational analysis, not a randomized trial testing an intervention. The 'arms' represent participants with vs. without long COVID (a grouping variable, not a treatment assignment). Individual SF-36v2 domain scores (outcomes 9–16) were reported as significantly different (all p<0.001) in text but numeric values (means/medians) were not provided in tables or results section—data appear to be in figures only (Supplementary Figure 5 and 7), so those outcome results are marked as 'not_reported'. The study lacked pre-COVID HrQOL data and baseline values for comparison, limiting ability to assess change from baseline. No adverse events were reported as this was an observational analysis of self-reported HrQOL outcomes, not a treatment trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: Long COVID associated with SF-36 physical component score median 46.8 vs 58.7 (p<0.001) and mental component 49.0 vs 57.6 (p<0.001); EQ-5D usual activities risk ratio 6.0 (95% CI 4.1-8.9, p<0.001).

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Strong association between elevated BMI and cognitive impairment; 73.8% of cognitive impairment group had BMI >30 vs 24.8% in non-impairment group (p<0.001). BMI >28.36 kg/m² is a predictor of cognitive impairment (RR 3.0, 95% CI 1.15-4.04).

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: More severe COVID-19 (hospitalization with pneumonia) strongly predicted cognitive impairment: 37.5% of cognitive impairment group vs 14.4% in non-impairment group had severe disease (p<0.001); RR 2.8 (95% CI 1.63-4.92).
Strong association: 77.5% of cognitive impairment group vs 9.6% without impairment reported concentration difficulties (p<0.001); RR 8.1 (95% CI 4.84-13.99).
Brain fog present in 63.8% of cognitive impairment group vs 25.6% without impairment (p<0.001); RR 2.5 (95% CI 1.75-3.50).

summary: This cross-sectional observational study examined predictors of cognitive impairment in 205 hypertensive patients with long COVID (NICE criteria), recruited from an outpatient clinic over 3 years in Russia. Among them, 39% developed cognitive impairment detected by the SEMOGRAPH speech-analysis system. Key predictors identified via ROC analysis included BMI above 28.4 kg/m² (OR 8.5), hospitalisation with pneumonia during acute COVID-19 (relative risk 2.8, 95% CI 1.63–4.92), brain fog (RR 2.5), poor attention concentration (RR 8.1), abnormal blood pressure circadian patterns (non-dipper/night-peaker RR 1.9; over-dipper RR 18.8), and elevated blood markers of inflammation (CRP >3.9 mg/L, ESR >26 mm/h, TNF-alpha >0.016 pg/mL), iron dysregulation (ferritin >171.1 µg/L, haemoglobin <126 g/L), myocardial stress (NT-proBNP >101.9 pg/mL), and apoptosis (caspase-6 >28.8 pg/mL). This is an observational, non-interventional study with no control arm, so no causal treatment effect can be established; pre-COVID cognitive baseline data were also limited.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a cross-sectional observational study, not a randomized controlled trial. It compares two groups (with and without cognitive impairment) rather than testing an intervention. No adverse events reported. No treatment or follow-up duration. Study identifies predictive biomarkers and symptoms via ROC curve analysis. Some baseline characteristics show p>0.05 between groups, indicating no significant differences at baseline for several variables (age, smoking, many comorbidities, BP measurements), as appropriate for a cross-sectional design. Blood pressure circadian pattern outcomes (Dippers, Non-dippers with night-peaker, Over-dipper, Masked nocturnal HTN) derived from 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring. Additional secondary biomarkers measured but not reported with per-arm values (platelet count, WBC count, lymphocytes, fasting glucose, HbA1c, fibrinogen, serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation, transferrin, IL-6, TIMP1). Cognitive impairment prevalence in total population: 39.0% by SEMOGRAPH, 36.1% by MMSE.

trial_rating.result_basis: Hospitalisation with pneumonia increased cognitive impairment risk RR 2.8 (95% CI 1.63–4.92); ferritin >171.1 µg/L AUC 0.667 p<0.001; caspase-6 >28.8 pg/mL AUC 0.702 p=0.002 — moderate associations in a cross-sectional design with no intervention.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Cognitive flexibility (perseverative reaches on reversal trials)
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Female macaques exhibited greater impairment in cognitive flexibility with more perseverative reaches on reversal trials compared to males at 85 days post-infection.
Only females showed significantly longer latencies to retrieve the reward after SARS-CoV-2 infection at 85 days.
Sex-specific differences in nighttime activity after infection: males showed greater nighttime activity at 1 week post-infection, while females showed greater activity at 11 weeks post-infection.
Females exhibited decreased SDNN after infection compared to males, indicating reduced heart rate variability and poorer autonomic function.
Sex differences in intradaily stability: females had lower IS during acute infection (1 wpi) but higher IS than males at 11 and 15 wpi.
Males had significantly higher relative amplitude (more robust circadian rhythm) compared to females from 11-19 weeks post-infection.

summary: This is a preclinical study, not a human clinical trial, examining the neurological consequences of mild SARS-CoV-2 infection in 10 adult rhesus macaques (5 female, 5 male) inoculated with the original WA1/2020 strain. Animals showed persistent alterations in taste and smell (significantly reduced preference for highly preferred foods at 77 and 119 days post-infection, p<0.001), decreased cognitive flexibility at 85 days post-infection (increased perseverative errors, p=0.003), and sex-differentiated sleep disturbances and autonomic dysfunction lasting up to 4.5 months. These behavioral changes correlated with acute cytokine elevations (notably IL-6) and increased microglial activation (IBA1+ cells) in brain tissue at up to 135 days post-infection, suggesting a causal link between the acute inflammatory response to mild COVID-19 and persistent neurological symptoms. This is a non-human primate mechanistic study with no intervention tested and no human patients enrolled; findings do not directly translate to treatment efficacy.

summary: This observational study (not an intervention trial) followed 20 Long COVID patients and 10 fully recovered controls from the NIH RECOVER cohort, collecting blood samples at roughly 0, 3, and 6 months post-infection to characterize immune differences. Long COVID participants showed persistently elevated IgG antibodies against the SARS-CoV-2 envelope protein (1.98-fold higher mean OD450, p=0.0022) and nucleocapsid protein (p=0.0419) compared to recovered controls, alongside a 1.73-fold increase in mucosal-associated invariant T cells (p=0.0461) and elevated circulating T follicular helper cells (p=0.0352). Additional findings included a pro-inflammatory cytokine signature (elevated IL-11, LIF, Eotaxin-3, HMGB-1) and higher rates of autoantibodies in Long COVID participants, consistent with persistent immune dysregulation possibly driven by viral antigen persistence. The study is exploratory and observational with a small sample size (n=30 total), and no intervention was tested.

Between-group p-values from 2-way ANOVA are reported; fold-changes and correlation coefficients are reported verbatim. Secondary outcomes include the full 96-plex cytokine panel (not all 96 individually extracted due to space constraints—only module 2 cytokines mentioned as most associated with LC are noted), and additional immunoglobulin subclass data from mass spectrometry. CyTOF analysis describes multiple myeloid and innate cell populations (dendritic cells, monocytes, basophils, NK cells, ILC-2, gamma-delta T cells) with no significant between-group differences; only CD4+ TCM, cTFH, and MAIT cells showed significant group differences and are extracted. Virus neutralization titers varied markedly with no significant difference between groups (not formally extracted as quantitative outcome). Time post-infection stratification is included as a subgroup analysis per paper's supplementary Figure 7. Autoantibody analysis identified 16 significantly elevated targets in LC but provided no per-target quantitative values. Study spans enrolled participants from December 2021 to October 2022.

trial_rating.result_basis: No intervention was tested; this is a biomarker/immunology observational study. Primary immunological finding: anti-envelope IgG 1.98-fold higher in LC vs CONV (p=0.0022), but no clinical intervention or primary efficacy outcome was assessed.

summary: This study tested a tailored topical and systemic treatment regimen for chronic non-infectious conjunctivitis in 66 post-COVID patients (aged 50–70), with treatment assigned based on laser Doppler flowmetry (LDF) classification of conjunctival microcirculation as either hyperemic or stagnant. Patients with hyperemic microcirculation received topical antioxidant eye drops (emoxipine), sodium hyaluronate, heparin eye drops, and systemic metabolic agents; those with stagnant microcirculation received sodium hyaluronate, heparin, and systemic venotonics. Treated patients in both groups showed meaningful improvement in perfusion parameters over 3–6 months (e.g., mean perfusion normalised to 24.8 ± 5.5 perfusion units in the hyperemic group at 3 months; stagnant group showed 35% increase in mean perfusion and 52.2% reduction in coefficient of variation by 6 months), while control subgroups receiving only hyaluronate drops showed no statistically significant change. No safety concerns were reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Stagnant-type treated group (2a): mean perfusion increased 35% at 3 months and coefficient of variation decreased 52.2% by 6 months (Kv = 15.2 ± 7.4%); control subgroups showed no statistically significant changes (p > 0.05).

summary: This 30-day randomized trial tested Livodinol MAX (adenosylmethionine 500mg, N-acetylcysteine 250mg, reduced glutathione 300mg) added to standard antibacterial therapy in 62 patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), grade I obesity, and moderate COVID-19-associated community-acquired pneumonia (mean age 52.5 years). Compared to controls receiving standard therapy plus alpha-lipoic acid, the Livodinol MAX group showed significantly greater reductions in insulin resistance (HOMA-IR fell 2.2-fold vs 1.2-fold, p<0.05), fasting glucose (12.2% reduction, p<0.05), and fasting insulin (1.9-fold reduction, p<0.05), alongside larger improvements in liver-related clinical syndromes. The study is limited by small sample size (n=31 per arm), single-centre design, 30-day follow-up only, and the fact that the active comparator (alpha-lipoic acid) itself has hepatoprotective effects, making it difficult to isolate the specific contribution of Livodinol MAX.

Adverse event data are not reported in the paper; only statement that treatment was well tolerated is given. summary: This is a preclinical animal study, not a human clinical trial. Researchers infected Golden Syrian hamsters (young males, young females, and aged males) with the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant to model Long COVID, then assessed viral persistence, lung pathology, brain transcriptomics, behavior, neuroimaging, alpha-synuclein changes, and gut microbiome at 4 and 30 days post-infection. The key findings were that viral RNA persisted in the lungs of male hamsters at 30 days post-infection, young females developed significantly greater lung fibrosis (p=0.0043), aged and young males showed sustained behavioral deficits in the marble burying test (p=0.0281), and all animals showed reduced fractional anisotropy in the cortex and hippocampus at 30 days, indicating lasting brain microstructural changes. As an animal model study with no human intervention tested, these findings are mechanistic and hypothesis-generating rather than directly applicable to Long COVID treatment.

summary: This observational study examined immune marker expression on CD8+ T cells in 64 Long COVID patients (stratified by prior mild, moderate, or severe COVID-19) compared to 20 healthy controls. Patients who had severe COVID-19 showed significantly fewer CD8+ T cells, lower PD-1 expression (6.35% vs 9.10% in controls, p=0.041), lower TIM-3 expression (6.38% vs 9.30% in controls, p=0.046), higher PD-L1 expression (4.34% vs 2.49% in controls, p=0.003), and higher CD38 expression (6.71% vs 4.83% in controls, p=0.042). The authors interpret this pattern of immune checkpoint dysregulation as evidence of CD8+ T cell exhaustion and argue it may predispose severe-COVID survivors to autoimmunity, though the study is observational with no intervention and cannot establish causation.

summary: This observational study compared immune cell markers in 50 Long COVID patients, 30 elderly controls (no Long COVID), and 40 healthy middle-aged controls. The researchers measured expression of CD38 (activation/metabolic dysfunction marker) and CD366/TIM-3 (exhaustion marker) on cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and NK cells. Long COVID patients showed significantly elevated CD366 on CD8+ T cells compared to healthy controls (6.55% vs 4.05%, p=0.0001), and elevated CD366 on NK cells vs healthy controls (6.97% vs 2.84%, p<0.0001). Crucially, Long COVID patients were statistically indistinguishable from elderly patients on nearly all markers, suggesting Long COVID produces an immune exhaustion profile resembling accelerated ageing rather than a distinct pathology.

summary: This open-label extension study (OLYMPIA LTE) assessed long-term safety and efficacy of nemolizumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting the IL-31 receptor, in 508 adults with moderate-to-severe prurigo nodularis (a chronic skin condition causing intense itch and nodular lesions) over up to 148 weeks. At week 148, over 70% of evaluable patients achieved clear or almost clear pruriginous nodules, over 85% achieved clinically meaningful itch improvement, and approximately 90% achieved clinically meaningful quality-of-life improvement. The safety profile was consistent with prior findings, with most adverse events occurring in the first year and decreasing in frequency over time; there was one death from myocardial infarction deemed unrelated to treatment. Key limitations include the open-label, single-arm design with no control group, making it impossible to attribute outcomes to treatment versus natural disease course.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper describes prurigo nodolaris treatment, NOT Long COVID. Paper does not match inclusion criteria for Long COVID systematic review. Study is open-label, single-arm LTE with no randomization or control group. Multiple baseline demographic and disease severity values extracted for the overall cohort and two subgroups (continuous nemolizumab n=307, nemolizumab-naïve n=174) as reported in Table 1. Efficacy outcomes at week 148 are reported as percentages without corresponding Ns or confidence intervals in the main text; figures referenced but not provided in extractable format. Safety data presented by time-of-occurrence windows (<12 months, 12-24 months, ≥24 months, ≥36 months) rather than by study visit. Mean treatment duration reported as 927.5 days (approximately 132.5 weeks); median treatment duration reported as 1147.5 days (approximately 164 weeks). Study duration is 184 weeks but data cut-off was at interim analysis on 21 July 2025, with evaluable data up to week 148. One patient death (myocardial infarction) deemed unrelated to study treatment. Phase 2 study patients did not contribute change-from-baseline data due to ≥6 months gap between phase 2 completion and LTE entry.

trial_rating.result_basis: At week 148, >70% of evaluable patients achieved IGA 0/1 (clear/almost clear nodules), >85% achieved clinically meaningful itch improvement, and mean DLQI was 2.9 (SD 4.4) in the overall nemolizumab group; no placebo comparator or p-values reported due to open-label single-arm design.

summary: This observational study examined psychoemotional status and hormone levels in 126 adolescent girls aged 11–16 years, comparing 44 with Long COVID symptoms, 40 who had recovered from COVID-19 without persistent symptoms, and 42 healthy controls. Girls with Long COVID showed significantly higher rates of depression (41% with moderate-to-severe symptoms vs. 0% in healthy controls), elevated anxiety, and reduced wellbeing and activity, with peak severity at 6–12 months post-infection. Cortisol levels were markedly elevated in the Long COVID group (mean 592 nM/L vs. 447 nM/L in controls, p<0.001), and 21% showed subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH above reference range with normal free T4). Strong correlations were found between depressive symptom severity and TSH (r=0.897, p=0.002) and between anxiety and cortisol (r=0.991, p=0.001), persisting up to 24 months after infection.

summary: This Swedish RCT tested whether adding inspiratory muscle training (IMT) twice daily to a standard individualized exercise program improved breathing muscle strength in 44 adults with Long COVID who had confirmed inspiratory muscle weakness. The intervention group showed significantly greater gains in maximal inspiratory pressure than the exercise-only control group, with a mean between-group difference of 18 percentage points (95% CI: 5–30), and were 7 times more likely to achieve a clinically meaningful improvement (OR 7.08, 95% CI: 1.31–38.32). The IMT group also reduced cough frequency more than controls. The trial enrolled only 44 of the 90 planned participants, and those with the most severe fatigue were largely unable to participate, limiting how broadly these results apply.

No post-treatment follow-up period; outcomes assessed at 8-week post-intervention only. ITT analysis used with imputation for missing data; sensitivity analysis via complete case yielded similar results.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary outcome MIP improved by 18 percentage points more in the IMT group than controls (95% CI: 5–30, p<0.05); OR for clinically meaningful improvement 7.08 (95% CI: 1.31–38.32).

summary: This observational study examined 62 patients with post-COVID joint syndrome to assess the role of circulating immune complexes (CICs) in the pathogenesis of four clinical variants: isolated arthralgia, arthritis, new-onset osteoarthropathy, and progression of pre-existing arthropathy. High CIC levels (median 8.05–11.45 µg/mL, threshold >5.0 µg/mL) were found in arthralgia, arthritis, and new-onset osteoarthropathy, accompanied by elevated IgM and IgG, implicating immune-complex-mediated tissue damage in these variants. In contrast, patients with progressing osteoarthropathy had borderline CIC levels (median 4.29 µg/mL, p=0.005 vs new-onset group), low IgM/IgG, but markedly elevated IgE—suggesting a distinct mast-cell activation mechanism drives disease progression. The study is observational with no control intervention, a small sample, and no pre-registration, limiting causal conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational phenotype-classification study, not a randomized trial. summary: This observational genetic association study examined whether two TMPRSS2 gene variants (rs12329760 and rs2070788) are linked to Long COVID symptoms in 363 Brazilian healthcare workers recruited at a single hospital in Sergipe. The primary finding is that the rs2070788 variant, in a recessive genetic model, was associated with brain fog (memory and concentration problems) in Long COVID — with carriers of the GG or AG genotype showing higher rates of brain fog than AA carriers (p=0.014 in the full sample; p=0.007 among those with persistent post-COVID symptoms), and an odds ratio of 1.73 to 2.08 for brain fog. The study is limited by non-probabilistic convenience sampling, self-reported outcomes with no medical record verification, and lack of a COVID-negative control group, meaning causation cannot be established.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper is an observational GWAS study, not a clinical trial, therefore many RCT-specific fields are not applicable (no randomization, no treatment arms, no allocation concealment, no interventions). The study enrolled a convenience sample of 363 healthcare workers and assessed post-COVID symptoms via self-report questionnaire, with genetic analysis via qPCR. Sample sizes reported in subgroup analyses (e.g., n=230 for symptomatic post-COVID) were calculated from the categorical breakdowns in Tables 2-5. Tables 4 and 5 provide chi-square p-values for the genetic association models but do not report odds ratios per cell; OR estimates (1.73 and 2.08) are from binary logistic regression reported in the text. Loss of smell/taste showed association with rs2070788 recessive model (p=0.028) but logistic regression did not support it (p=0.112), so that association was not extracted as a primary finding. rs12329760 showed no significant associations and was excluded from between-group_effects. The study has no active intervention, treatment arms, or control group comparisons typical of clinical trials.

trial_rating.result_basis: rs2070788 recessive model associated with brain fog: p=0.014 (full sample, OR=1.73) and p=0.007 (symptomatic subgroup, OR=2.08); overall Long COVID was not significantly associated with either SNP.

summary: This open-label controlled trial tested 10 days of inhaled nitric oxide (iNO, 60 ppm) combined with inhaled molecular hydrogen (iH2, <4%) versus iNO alone versus standard rehabilitation care in 60 Long COVID patients (average symptom duration ~2 years) with persistent respiratory symptoms. Both inhaled gas groups showed significant improvements in dyspnea, fatigue, anxiety, depression, and quality of life scores compared to controls, with microcirculation improvements in venular blood flow velocity. The iNO/iH2 combination outperformed iNO alone on exercise capacity (6-minute walk distance improved by 44.7±41.5 m, p<0.05) and was the only group to significantly reduce oxidative stress markers (FORT dropped from 595 to 409 units, p<0.05). Adverse events were mild and non-specific across both treatment groups.

summary: This feasibility study tested whether machine learning models trained on wearable sensor data could predict next-day fatigue levels in 68 adults with post-COVID fatigue. Participants wore a wrist accelerometer and a chest ECG patch for up to 21 days, generating heart rate variability (HRV), activity, and sleep features that were used to train XGBoost and Random Forest models. The XGBoost model achieved strong predictive accuracy (R² = 0.79, mean absolute error = 3.18 on a 0–100 fatigue scale), with HRV non-linear measures (sample entropy, approximate entropy) and low-frequency power emerging as the top predictors, followed by activity timing and demographics. A key caveat is that the cross-validation did not separate participants between training and test sets, so performance likely overestimates true generalisability to new individuals.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a machine learning feasibility study, not a traditional clinical trial comparing interventions; the three randomized arms (active taVNS, sham, placebo) are from the parent RCT, but the analysis reported here uses all 68 participants with complete data pooled across a machine learning prediction task (no between-arm comparisons reported). Baseline demographics only reported for the overall sample, not per-arm. No adverse events reported. Only 68 of 114 enrolled participants had complete datasets; reasons for exclusion (Bluetooth connectivity, device malfunction, questionnaire non-completion) detailed but per-arm dropout not specified. Feature importance rankings (top 5 features) reported narratively for both XGBoost and Random Forest but full feature importance values not provided in tabular form. Five-fold cross-validation results presented with individual fold values for R², MAE, and correlation. Study is a predictive modeling feasibility analysis rather than an efficacy trial.

trial_rating.result_basis: XGBoost mean R² = 0.789 ± 0.041, MAE = 3.18 ± 0.63 on 0–100 VAS; however, standard 5-fold CV (not leave-one-subject-out) was used, inflating estimates.

summary: This observational study characterized immune activation markers (CD169 and HLA-DR) on blood cells and plasma extracellular vesicles (EVs) in 48 acute COVID-19 patients, 25 Long COVID individuals, and 22 healthy donors. The study found that HLA-DR+CD169+ double-positive EVs were significantly elevated in both acute COVID-19 and Long COVID patients compared to healthy donors, with SARS-CoV-2 Spike antigen-carrying EVs also persisting in Long COVID (Spike RBD median 6.41% vs 1.33% in healthy donors, p<0.01). Long COVID patients with neurological symptoms showed significantly reduced concentrations of CD169+/HLA-DR+ EVs compared to those without neurological symptoms, suggesting a distinct immune profile. This is a biomarker discovery study with no intervention; it cannot establish causality between EV profiles and Long COVID symptoms.

summary: This pilot proteomic study examined blood plasma microclots (insoluble fibrin-amyloid deposits) from 14 people with persistent symptoms lasting 12+ weeks after COVID-19 vaccination (termed PV/PIS — Post-Vaccination/Post-Infection Syndrome) compared to 16 healthy controls. Using mass spectrometry, researchers found 52 significantly altered proteins in PV/PIS patients, including elevated inflammatory markers (serum amyloid A1 at 1.72-fold, serum amyloid A2 at 1.66-fold, attractin at 2.57-fold) and elevated coagulation factors X (2.06-fold) and XI (1.63-fold), alongside reduced immune-regulatory proteins such as S100-A9 and immunoglobulin components. The proteomic signature only partially overlapped with a previously published Long COVID cohort, suggesting shared symptoms may arise from distinct molecular pathways. Key limitations include a very small sample size, a 16-year age gap between groups (mean 59.9 vs 43.9 years) that could confound inflammation and coagulation markers, and inability to rule out prior asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection in participants.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an observational case-control proteomic study, not a randomized controlled trial. It analyzes protein fold-changes detected by LC-MS/MS in microclot deposits but does not report absolute per-arm mean values or SDs for any outcome — only fold-change values from the comparison between arms (Table 2). Per-arm baseline proteomic data are not provided; between-group effects are reported only as fold-change ratios with p-values. 26 proteins were significantly downregulated and 26 significantly upregulated; only the most notable are listed here (serum amyloid A1/A2, coagulation factors X/XI, attractin, albumin, S100-A9, platelet factor 4). The paper also mentions 26 additional significantly altered proteins but provides fold-change and p-values for all in Table 2. All outcomes reported are biomarkers measured at a single cross-sectional timepoint with no longitudinal follow-up. Study has a major age confound (PV/PIS mean 59.9±15.8 vs controls 43.9±15.2) and small sample size (14 vs 16).

trial_rating.result_basis: Significant protein alterations identified at adjusted p<0.05 with log2 fold-change >1; top upregulated proteins include coagulation factor X (2.06-fold, p<0.001) and attractin (2.57-fold, p<0.001), but the study is observational with n=14 cases vs n=16 controls and no clinical outcome measures.

summary: This is a genome-wide association study (GWAS) investigating genetic variants linked to Long COVID (PASC) in Indian populations, not a clinical trial testing an intervention. Researchers genotyped 60 Indian individuals with prior COVID-19 infection and combined this with existing datasets totalling 698 South Asians, comparing 37 PASC cases against 661 controls. The study identified 8,247 SNVs across 4,769 candidate genes associated with PASC, with key candidates including CNTNAP2, WWOX, and ADAMTS17, pointing to neurological and cardiovascular pathways. Polygenic risk score analysis suggested higher genetic predisposition to PASC among tribal groups from Central India, Andamanese tribes, Tamilians from Sri Lanka, and Bengalis compared to North and Northwest Indian populations. The PASC GWAS is explicitly exploratory and severely underpowered (N=37 cases), and the authors caution that findings require replication in larger cohorts.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a genomic/genetic association study (GWAS + transcriptomics), not a clinical trial. It is NOT a treatment trial for Long COVID. The study compares genetic variants between case and control groups without intervention or randomization. The paper does not report traditional clinical trial endpoints (e.g., symptom improvement, functional outcomes). Instead, it reports genetic associations (SNVs, OR/RR for comorbidities predicting COVID-19 severity/mortality, candidate gene identification from GWAS). The sample sizes refer to number of genotyped individuals, not randomized participants. Outcomes extracted focus on: (1) demographic risk factors for COVID-19 severity and mortality with OR/CI, (2) number of SNVs reaching significance in GWAS models, (3) candidate genes shared between severity and PASC cohorts. Transcriptomic data (fold-change values in Tables 5-6) are hypothesis-generating only and are not organized as comparative clinical outcomes. This does not meet criteria for a Long COVID clinical trial extraction per the meta-analysis scope, but genetic association findings are reported as extracted from available tables and results sections.

trial_rating.result_basis: Exploratory GWAS with only 37 PASC cases; 8,247 SNVs reached p<0.0001 suggestive threshold but the study used a relaxed discovery threshold and authors explicitly state the sample size limits statistical power and the findings are hypothesis-generating only.

summary: This observational study measured 17 autoantibodies in 237 Long COVID patients and 54 fully recovered COVID-19 patients in Salvador, Brazil, comparing them to 220 pre-pandemic healthy controls; the population was predominantly Black and Mixed-race. Autoantibody prevalence was actually higher in recovered individuals (37%) than in Long COVID patients (24%) or pre-pandemic controls (19%), and no autoantibody consistently distinguished Long COVID from the other groups. Anti-cardiolipin IgM was the most common autoantibody detected but was three times more frequent in recovered individuals (24%) than in Long COVID patients (8%), and was not associated with symptom persistence or thrombotic events.

The primary finding was a significant T-helper cell imbalance in post-COVID sarcoidosis patients: they had higher Th1 cells (11.30% vs 5.48% in COVID-naive sarcoidosis, p<0.001) and Th2 cells (4.15% vs 2.84%, p=0.004), more effector memory T cells, and elevated regulatory T cells, alongside reduced naive CD4+ T cells — a pattern the authors interpret as potentially driving progression of chronic lung sarcoidosis. This is a cross-sectional immunophenotyping study with no treatment intervention and no clinical outcome data, so it cannot establish whether these immune changes cause disease worsening or are transient post-infection effects.

summary: This is not a clinical trial but a bioinformatics study that analyzed 73,110 peripheral blood immune cells from 8 individuals across four COVID-19 severity groups (healthy, exposed, infected, hospitalized) using single-cell RNA sequencing. summary: This is a preclinical laboratory study, not a clinical trial in Long COVID patients. Researchers at the Mario Negri Institute tested whether aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid, ASA) could interfere with the binding of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein S1 subunit to the ACE2 receptor, which is relevant to Long COVID because circulating spike protein persists in some patients and drives ongoing tissue damage. In cell-based and cell-free experiments, pre-incubating S1 with ASA at clinically achievable concentrations (20 mg/L) reduced S1-ACE2 binding by approximately 50%, and in transgenic mice expressing human ACE2, pre-treating S1 with ASA markedly reduced lung injury, fibrosis, and immune cell infiltration compared to untreated S1. The mechanism involves ASA altering spike protein glycosylation at two key sites (N61 and S325), confirmed by site-directed mutagenesis showing that a double mutant lacking glycosylation at both sites similarly failed to cause lung pathology in mice. No human clinical data are presented; these findings provide mechanistic rationale for aspirin repurposing but require clinical validation.

summary: This observational study used single-cell RNA sequencing to compare immune cell gene expression in 44 Long COVID patients and 44 matched convalescent controls. The key finding was a broad downregulation of pro-inflammatory genes in classical monocytes of Long COVID patients, including IL1B and multiple chemokines (CCL3, CCL4, CXCL2, CXCL8), with reduced activity of inflammation-related pathways including TNF-alpha signaling via NF-kB. Additional analysis suggested the affected monocytes have an immature, possibly exhausted phenotype with impaired differentiation capacity, and plasma CXCL2 protein levels confirmed the RNA sequencing findings. This is a mechanistic observational study with no intervention; it does not test a treatment but identifies a potential immune dysfunction signature that may help explain Long COVID pathology.

summary: This observational immunology study examined 60 Chilean adults four months after acute COVID-19 — 34 who had developed ARDS and 26 who had not — to investigate why severe patients show higher anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibody levels. Patients who had ARDS had significantly higher circulating IgG antibodies than those without ARDS, and serum levels of the inflammatory chemokines CXCL9 and CXCL10 positively correlated with IgG levels. In laboratory experiments using healthy donor B cells, both chemokines directly promoted plasma cell differentiation (increased CD27+CD38+ and CD138+ cells) and boosted total IgG secretion, while CXCL9 also upregulated CD40L and CXCR3 on CD4+ T cells, suggesting a mechanism by which chronic inflammation amplifies antibody production. Patients with combined CT abnormalities and reduced lung diffusion capacity (DLCO) had the highest levels of IgG, CXCL9, and CXCL10, implying the CXCL9/CXCL10–CXCR3 axis as a potential therapeutic target for post-COVID pulmonary complications.

summary: This observational single-cell RNA sequencing study examined peripheral blood immune cells from 10 female participants with Long COVID-associated ME/CFS and 10 recovered controls, all sampled approximately 12 months after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection. The study found widespread immune remodeling in Long COVID-ME/CFS, including depletion of naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, MAIT cells, and gamma-delta T cells, alongside expansion of effector T cells, activated platelets, and low-density neutrophils; monocytes shifted toward a pro-inflammatory profile with reduced phagocytic gene expression. A key mechanistic finding was that elevated plasma Galectin-9 drives MAIT and gamma-delta T cell depletion through TIM-3-mediated apoptosis, with in vitro experiments showing recombinant Galectin-9 significantly increased MAIT cell apoptosis (p<0.0001) and this effect was partially reversed by lactose. This is a descriptive mechanistic study with no therapeutic intervention tested; the small sample size (5 per group for sequencing) and all-female design limit generalizability.

summary: This observational study used principal component analysis (PCA) to characterize the cytokine profiles of 44 Long COVID patients, 289 acute COVID-19 patients, and 51 healthy donors. Three functionally distinct cytokine clusters were identified in Long COVID: Cluster A (IL-13, CCL7/MCP-3, IL-4) linked to dysregulated Th2 immunity, Cluster B (IL-18, CCL2/MCP-1, CCL4/MIP-1b, CXCL8/IL-8, M-CSF) linked to neuroinflammatory processes, and Cluster C (sCD40L, CXCL1/GROa, PDGF-AA, EGF, FGF-2, FLT-3L, IL-7, IL-17F) linked to platelet activation and vascular injury. Notably, many cytokines elevated in acute COVID-19 were reduced in Long COVID, suggesting immune exhaustion rather than simple hyperactivation. Results are associative and limited by a small Long COVID cohort (n=44), female predominance (73%), no adjustment for confounders, and absence of treatment or clinical intervention.

summary: This observational mechanistic study examined immune profiles in 215 participants — 66 healthy controls, 35 fully recovered convalescents, and 114 long COVID patients (median ~5 months post-infection) — using antibody assays, multiplex cytokine profiling, flow cytometry, and single-cell RNA sequencing of blood immune cells. Long COVID patients showed significantly elevated SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies compared to healthy controls, but paradoxically had lower levels of both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines (including IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-10) relative to both control groups, pointing to immune exhaustion rather than ongoing inflammation. Flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing consistently identified a marked depletion of classical NK cells (CD56+CD16+) and broad transcriptional suppression in the remaining NK cells, including downregulation of genes involved in olfactory perception, neurotransmitter signalling, and GABA-channel activity — pathways that may underlie hallmark symptoms such as loss of smell, brain fog, and fatigue. This is a cross-sectional observational study with no intervention and no control for confounders such as age differences between groups, so causal conclusions cannot be drawn.

summary: This preclinical mouse study used a mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strain (MA30) and influenza A (PR8) to model Long COVID-like lung and brain pathology in C57BL/6 mice observed up to 28 days post-infection. Both viruses caused persistent lung inflammation and fibrosis through 28 days, but only SARS-CoV-2 (MA30) infection produced sustained brain pathology — including microhemorrhages (elevated at 5–7 days post-infection vs. controls, p=0.0197), persistent microglial activation across all timepoints, and transcriptomic signatures of neuroinflammation, neurotransmitter dysregulation, and hypothalamic-pituitary axis disruption — despite no detectable virus in the brain. Influenza-infected mice showed lung repair via KRT5+ progenitor cell migration that was absent in SARS-CoV-2-infected mice, suggesting divergent recovery mechanisms. This is an animal study with no human participants, so findings cannot be directly extrapolated to Long COVID patients.

summary: This observational proteomic study examined blood plasma from 92 non-hospitalized Long COVID patients and 73 recovered controls (matched by age and sex) at a mean of 34 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Using a 358-protein proximity extension assay panel, researchers identified 26 proteins significantly elevated in Long COVID patients, with Oncostatin M (OSM) and IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL1RN) most upregulated, alongside IL-6, IL-12B, IL-2, and proteins linked to tissue remodeling and angiogenesis. Enrichment analysis showed activation of inflammatory pathways (TNF-α/NF-κB, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, IL-2/STAT5) indicating persistent low-grade immune activation years after infection, with no distinct inflammatory subgroups identified. Notably, plasma SARS-CoV-2 spike protein levels did not differ between patients and controls, and none of the 26 differentially expressed proteins correlated with symptom severity scores, suggesting systemic inflammation and subjective symptom burden are decoupled in this population.

summary: This is an observational multi-omics study, not a clinical trial testing an intervention. Researchers reanalyzed published transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets from Syrian hamster models and human cohorts to characterize molecular changes in Long COVID (post-COVID syndrome, PCS). Across tissues and time points extending to 12 months post-infection, they consistently found suppressed mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), elevated oxidative stress markers, and persistent immune activation in PCS patients compared to recovered controls, with skeletal muscle showing the most pronounced and durable OXPHOS repression. The study is purely observational and re-analytical with no intervention tested; it proposes mitochondrial dysfunction as a potential mechanistic framework for PCS but cannot establish causality.

summary: This laboratory study (not a clinical trial) tested whether the SARS-CoV-2 spike S1 protein activates harmful signalling pathways in human retinal endothelial cells, and whether blocking the protein HIF-2α with belzutifan could reverse those effects. In 41 Long COVID patients, plasma levels of VEGF and MCP-1 were elevated compared to 24 healthy controls. When retinal endothelial cells were exposed to recombinant S1 protein in the lab, they showed increased oxidative stress, activation of HIF-1α (peaking at 8 hours) followed by sustained HIF-2α activation (persisting to 72 hours), and a significant drop in barrier integrity (TEER AUC 89.2 vs 120.5 for controls); adding belzutifan restored barrier integrity (TEER AUC 143.4). This is a mechanistic in vitro study — no patients were treated with belzutifan — so clinical applicability is unproven, and the authors note that chronic HIF-2α inhibition carries risks including anaemia.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper is a mechanistic in vitro study, not a clinical trial. It reports observational clinical data (n=41 PCS patients vs n=24 HC) paired with extensive in vitro cell culture experiments using HRECs exposed to S1 protein and patient plasma, with assessment of HIF-2α inhibition by belzutifan. Quantitative data for many outcomes (VEGF, IL-6, etc. in plasma) are shown in Figure 2 only with p-values reported; actual per-arm means and SDs were not provided in text or tables and appear only in the figures. For cell culture outcomes, p-values are reported in text but per-arm numeric values are shown only in figures. Effect sizes and confidence intervals are not reported. Study design is observational case-control for clinical measures; experimental arms in in vitro work represent different treatment conditions (mock, S1, S1+belzutifan, CoCl2, PCS-plasma, HC-plasma, etc.). No randomization, blinding, or allocation concealment apply. Analysis used Mann–Whitney U tests, Kruskal–Wallis tests, t-tests, ANOVA, and Spearman/Pearson correlations depending on data distribution. TEER effect sizes and pairwise comparisons are provided in Tables 1 and 2. The 'arms' field in study_design is left empty because this is not a comparative trial; instead, comparison groups are listed separately (PCS patients vs HC; S1-treated cells vs control cells, etc.).

trial_rating.result_basis: S1-treated cells had TEER AUC 89.2 (95% CI 74.56–103.9) vs control 120.5 (106.3–134.7); belzutifan rescued this to 143.4 (132.2–154.6), S1 vs S1+belzutifan p<0.001 at 48h and 72h — but all findings are in cell culture, not in patients.

summary: This Pakistani observational study measured inflammatory markers (IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α, Substance P) in 90 participants divided into symptomatic long COVID (n=30), asymptomatic post-COVID (n=30), and healthy controls (n=30), then used computational drug screening to identify potential NK1R antagonists. Blood biomarker analysis found significant upregulation of IL-6, IL-10, and Substance P in both symptomatic and asymptomatic COVID-19 survivors compared to controls (p<0.001), with symptomatic patients showing the highest elevations. No clinical intervention was tested; instead, in silico molecular docking identified aprepitant (binding affinity -9.3 kcal/mol) and N-acetyl-L-tryptophan (-8.7 kcal/mol) as computationally promising NK1R antagonists based on docking scores, molecular dynamics stability, and favorable pharmacokinetic profiles — but no in vivo or in vitro validation was performed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is primarily a biomarker/computational study, not a randomized clinical trial. It uses an observational design with three comparison groups (symptomatic long COVID, asymptomatic long COVID, controls) and includes substantial in silico drug screening work with no clinical intervention. Clinical outcomes (fatigue, headache, anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment) are reported as prevalence percentages in the symptomatic group only (n=30). Biomarker data are from ELISA (protein levels) and RT-qPCR (mRNA fold-changes). The paper reports binding affinities for 9 compounds tested computationally, but extraction focuses on the top 2 candidates (aprepitant and NAT). Molecular dynamics parameters (RMSD, RMSF, Rg) are reported as averages ± SD over 50 ns simulations. The paper includes subgroup analyses by age, gender, and symptom duration, but these are limited to biomarker data presentation without formal interaction testing. No formal adverse events monitoring is reported (as expected for an observational/computational study). Duration of long COVID-19 symptoms is reported as mean ± SD ranges for < 30 weeks (19 ± 6) and >= 30 weeks (44 ± 6) groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: No clinical intervention was tested; the primary finding is a biomarker association (IL-6, IL-10, SP elevated at p<0.001 in long COVID vs controls) and in silico docking scores only (aprepitant -9.3 kcal/mol, NAT -8.7 kcal/mol) — no patient outcome data.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: In 23 patients with normal IENFD, both PMNFD and SGNFD remained significantly reduced compared to healthy controls (p=0.0003 and p=0.0017, respectively), indicating autonomic small fiber damage can occur independently of somatic fiber loss.

No significant correlations found between autonomic morphological parameters (PMNFD, SGNFD) and disease duration (r=-0.06, p=0.723; r=-0.06, p=0.723), disease onset (r=-0.3, p=0.114), or COVID-19 severity (r=-0.23, p=0.21).

summary: This retrospective observational study examined autonomic nerve fiber damage in 31 adults with painful long COVID by analyzing skin biopsies from the distal leg. Researchers measured nerve fiber density in piloerector muscles (PMNFD) and sweat glands (SGNFD) as markers of autonomic innervation, comparing them to 42 healthy age- and sex-matched controls. Both measures were significantly reduced in long COVID patients (PMNFD: 78.4 vs 93.2 fibers/mm, p=0.012; SGNFD: 3.27 vs 3.91 on a 0-4 scale, p<0.0001), and these reductions persisted even in the 23 patients who had normal somatic nerve fiber density, indicating autonomic damage can occur independently of the more commonly tested small fiber neuropathy. Neither measure correlated with self-reported autonomic symptom severity (COMPASS-31 scores), suggesting structural nerve loss and functional symptoms are driven by partly separate mechanisms.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective observational case-control study, not a randomized controlled trial. No intervention is being tested. The study is cross-sectional with single timepoint assessment via skin biopsy. Baseline demographics table includes information about disease onset (time from COVID-19 to symptom onset) and disease duration (time from symptom onset to biopsy visit). One subject had acute onset during infection, remainder within 3 months. COVID-19 severity distribution: mild (n=23), moderate (n=5), severe (n=2), critical (n=1). Of 31 patients, 23 had normal IENFD and 8 had reduced IENFD; all 8 with reduced IENFD met Besta criteria for small fiber neuropathy. Subgroup analysis comparing normal IENFD subgroup (n=23) to controls uses same control group (n=42) for both comparisons. No adverse events reported (not applicable to observational study). Paper reports correlations between histological findings and COMPASS-31, disease duration, disease onset, and COVID-19 severity using Spearman correlation test. All correlation analyses yielded non-significant results. Figure 1 and Figure 2 show representative immunofluorescence images but no quantitative data extracted from figures.

trial_rating.result_basis: SGNFD reduced from 3.91 (controls) to 3.27 (patients) p<0.0001; PMNFD reduced from 93.15 to 78.44 fibers/mm p=0.0118; both remained significant in normal-IENFD subgroup (p=0.0003 and p=0.0017).

summary: This study tested donepezil (an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) in Long COVID patients who were seropositive for anti-SITH-1 antibodies — a marker of HHV-6B reactivation in olfactory bulb astrocytes — as a post-hoc subgroup analysis of a prior randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted in Japan. Among the 52 anti-SITH-1-positive PASC patients (71.7% of the 73-patient subgroup), donepezil significantly reduced depression scores on the HADS at week 3 and fatigue scores on the Chalder Fatigue Scale at week 8 compared to placebo; no significant improvement was seen in seronegative patients, and donepezil tended to worsen symptoms in that group, likely due to gastrointestinal side effects. This subgroup analysis was unplanned and exploratory — the original 110-patient RCT showed no significant overall effect (CFS mean difference 0.34, 95% CI -2.23 to 2.91, p=0.79) — so these findings should be treated as hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in a prospective biomarker-stratified trial.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The primary RCT data extraction is based on the subgroup analysis of 73 PASC patients (38 donepezil, 35 placebo) with anti-SITH-1 antibody testing, not the full original cohort of 110. Figure 4 shows change-from-baseline data but exact numerical values are not provided in tables; data appears to be displayed graphically only. BH-FDR adjusted q-values are referenced in Supplementary Table S1 but not provided in the main text. The original RCT (Nakabara et al., 2025) did not show statistically significant efficacy overall (mean difference in CFS at 3 weeks: 0.34; 95% CI, -2.23 to 2.91; P=0.79), but the post hoc subgroup analysis by anti-SITH-1 status showed efficacy in the positive subgroup.

trial_rating.result_basis: The primary RCT was a null result (CFS mean difference 0.34, 95% CI -2.23 to 2.91, p=0.79); the positive signals (HADS depression at week 3 and CFS at week 8 in anti-SITH-1-positive subgroup, n=52) come from an unplanned post-hoc analysis with no pre-specified primary endpoint.

summary: This Brazilian pilot RCT tested creatine monohydrate supplementation (6 g/day or 18 g/day for 4 weeks) combined with supervised physical rehabilitation in 67 adults with Long COVID who had significant fatigue. The primary outcome was fatigue as measured by the Revised Piper Fatigue Scale (PFS-R): the 6 g/day group showed a statistically significant reduction in fatigue score of 2.05 points compared to placebo (95% CI: -3.47 to -0.63; p=0.005), along with a 4.40 kgf improvement in handgrip strength (p=0.037); the higher 18 g/day dose showed no significant benefit on fatigue. Gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, bloating, diarrhea) were more common at higher doses but resolved within days without medical intervention, and both creatine groups showed small but statistically significant increases in serum creatinine that were not considered clinically meaningful.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Data extracted per intention-to-treat analysis as stated in methods. Baseline tables indicate n=24, 22, 21 randomized to 6g, 18g, placebo groups respectively, with 21, 19, 18 completing the protocol. Between-group effects presented as DiD (difference-in-differences) estimates per prespecified statistical approach. The 18g/day group showed one isolated ultrasonographic finding (biceps brachii short head left): DiD 0.52 cm (95% CI 0.01 to 1.03; p=0.045), but this was noted as clinically not meaningful and should be interpreted cautiously given multiple comparisons. Supplementary Table 1 referenced for additional laboratory parameters (eosinophil count, serum sodium) but full detail not provided in main text — effect estimates extracted as reported in main text Results section.

trial_rating.result_basis: PFS-R score decreased by 2.05 points in the 6 g/day group vs. placebo (95% CI: -3.47 to -0.63; p=0.005) on a scale where scores range roughly 0-10, representing a moderate absolute change but from a small pilot with 21 completers in the effective arm.

summary: This study evaluated the psychometric properties and factor structure of the PHQ-9 depression screening questionnaire in 177 Colombian survivors of severe COVID-19, assessed more than 20 months after hospital discharge. The primary finding was that the PHQ-9 functions as a unidimensional (single-factor) instrument in this population: both one- and two-factor models fit the data acceptably, but the two-factor model offered no significant improvement (Δχ²=0.27, p=0.602), and the single-factor solution showed better internal consistency (α=0.81, ω=0.86). A notable caveat is that the fatigue item performed poorly, showing the weakest factor loading (0.39) and lowest item-total correlation (0.40), suggesting Long COVID fatigue may overlap with but not cleanly reflect depressive symptoms as measured by this scale. This is a psychometric validation study, not a clinical intervention trial, and no treatment was tested.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a psychometric validation study, not a clinical trial. It has no intervention arm, treatment duration, or between-group comparisons. No per-arm individual item scores are reported in Table 2; only frequencies of responses are given. Study evaluated two competing factor structures (one-factor vs two-factor) but these are latent constructs, not separate intervention arms. The paper reports reliability estimates (Cronbach's alpha, McDonald's omega) for the unifactorial solution but does not provide detailed mean/SD values for individual items in the sample. Sex-stratified analyses show clinically meaningful differences but the paper does not conduct multi-group CFA due to sample size constraints. No adverse events reported (not applicable to observational study).

trial_rating.result_basis: Chi-square difference test between one- and two-factor models: Δχ²=0.27, p=0.602, indicating no significant improvement for the more complex model; this is a null psychometric result.

summary: This is not a Long COVID clinical trial. It is a retrospective epidemiological time series study analyzing SARS-CoV-2 case trends and seasonality in Ecuador from 2020 to 2024 using ARIMA modelling, with no patient intervention, no Long COVID population, and no treatment outcome. The study found that COVID-19 cases peaked in 2022 (up to 52,300 weekly cases) and declined steadily through 2024 (averaging 350 weekly cases), with a consistent dual-peak seasonal pattern each year. The ARIMA (0,2,1)(0,0,1)[52] model projected continued decline into early 2025, though out-of-sample forecast accuracy was limited (MAPE 23.5%).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is not an eligible Long COVID clinical trial. The paper is an epidemiological surveillance and time series forecasting study of SARS-CoV-2 incidence in Ecuador (2020–2024), not a randomized controlled trial or clinical intervention study. No patient cohort with Long COVID was enrolled, no treatment was evaluated, and no baseline demographics, outcome measurements on patients, or adverse events are reported. Tables 1–7 contain epidemiological summaries (case counts by year, ARIMA model diagnostics, forecast accuracy metrics), not patient-level clinical trial data. Study design, participant characteristics, and outcome data fields are therefore null or empty as there is no trial design or clinical intervention to extract.

trial_rating.result_basis: No clinical intervention or primary outcome; out-of-sample ARIMA model error was MAPE=23.53%, RMSE=1.73, reflecting limited predictive accuracy outside the training period.

summary: This observational study compared lung diffusion capacity in 37 Long COVID patients versus 37 recovered COVID-19 patients with no lingering symptoms, using simultaneous DLCO and DLNO testing at Mayo Clinic. Long COVID patients showed significantly reduced gas transfer (DLCO 21.4 vs 26.1 mL/min/mmHg, p=0.015; DLNO 125.6 vs 144.0 mL/min/mmHg, p=0.009), lower pulmonary capillary blood volume (43.4 vs 56.4 mL, p=0.003), and smaller alveolar volume (5.06 vs 5.95 L, p=0.004), with no difference in membrane conductance or lung fluid content. The findings point to reduced lung volume — rather than membrane damage or fluid accumulation — as the primary driver of impaired gas exchange in Long COVID, though the group differences disappeared after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI, with sex (female) identified as a key confounding variable.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is not a randomized controlled trial but an observational cross-sectional comparison study. The abstract mentions 'LC vs. NS, DLCO: 25.94 ± 7.65 vs. 21.71 ± 6.35 mL/min/mmHg, p = 0.009' but the results section and Table 2 report different values (21.4 ± 6.5 vs. 26.1 ± 8.3). The table values are used as they are the official results reported in Table 2. The paper reports that when adjusted for covariates (age, sex, BMI), the primary findings (DLCO, DLNO, Vc) were no longer significant (p=0.273, p=0.135, p=0.192 respectively), which is a critical limitation. Six subjects withdrew prior to completion. No adverse events were reported. The study was observational/quasi-experimental in design with no intervention tested.

trial_rating.result_basis: DLCO was lower in Long COVID vs non-symptomatic (21.4 vs 26.1 mL/min/mmHg, p=0.015), but differences were no longer significant after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI (p=0.273).

summary: This paper is not a Long COVID clinical trial. It is a computational modelling study that developed a hybrid deep learning algorithm (GA-BiLSTM-ARIMA) to forecast COVID-19 case counts using population-level surveillance data from Japan and Germany. The model achieved an R² of 0.9764 and MAPE of 6.81% on Japanese data, outperforming standalone ARIMA and BiLSTM models. No patients were enrolled, no intervention was tested, and Long COVID is not mentioned.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is ineligible for Long COVID systematic review. It is a methodological/computational study focused on developing machine learning algorithms for epidemic forecasting, not a clinical trial of interventions for Long COVID patients. The study uses only epidemiological surveillance data (daily confirmed COVID-19 cases) from Johns Hopkins University. There are no participant groups, no randomization, no treatment arms, and no clinical outcomes. The only quantitative results presented are model performance metrics (RMSE, MAE, MAPE, R²) for different forecasting algorithms applied to historical COVID-19 case data from Japan (April 20, 2022 – March 5, 2023) and Germany (same period). Tables 1-6 report algorithm hyperparameters and model evaluation metrics, not clinical trial results.

trial_rating.result_basis: No clinical outcome was measured; the primary metric is predictive model accuracy (RMSE 2,262.42, R² 0.9764 on COVID-19 case count forecasting), which is not a treatment effect.

summary: This paper is not a Long COVID clinical trial. It is a machine learning study that developed and compared three deep learning models (LSTM, BiLSTM, and GRU) to forecast COVID-19 case counts and detect outbreak anomalies in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, using Google Trends search data. The best-performing model, BiLSTM, achieved an F1-score of 0.83 for anomaly detection using the search term 'COVID' at a one-week lag on the test dataset. This paper has no patient population, no intervention, and no clinical outcomes; it is not relevant to Long COVID treatment or management.

trial_rating.result_basis: No clinical trial conducted; BiLSTM anomaly detection F1-score of 0.83 on test data is a model performance metric, not a clinical outcome.
