summary: This observational study examined 41 Long COVID patients presenting to a neurology clinic with cognitive complaints at least 4 months after infection, assessing whether their subjective cognitive symptoms were better explained by objective neuropsychological test performance, psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, depression), fatigue, or blood inflammatory markers. Patients' self-reported cognitive decline was elevated (mean MyCog score 16.6, well above the clinical threshold of 7), and regression models explained about 36% of the variance in self-rated symptoms through a combination of neuropsychological test scores and anxiety, while observer-rated symptoms were explained almost entirely by neuropsychological tests alone (33% of variance). Notably, inflammatory cytokine levels and fatigue did not predict cognitive symptom severity in either model, supporting the view that Long COVID brain fog reflects genuine changes in brain function detectable by standard testing rather than being driven by mood or systemic inflammation. The study is limited by its small sample, single-centre design, lack of a healthy control group, and industry funding from Sage Therapeutics.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an observational cohort study, not an RCT, with no intervention arms or control group. The study design is cross-sectional with measurements collected at a single baseline visit approximately 10.2 months post-infection. All outcomes are baseline characteristics and correlational analyses only; there are no follow-up measurements, treatment arms, or between-group comparisons. Risk of bias assessed using ROBINS-I (observational) rather than RoB2 (randomized). No adverse events reported. The paper focuses on parsing relationships between subjective cognitive complaints and objective test performance via regression modeling in a single neurology clinic population (Spain). Cytokine data from supplementary materials not fully detailed in main text but identified as within normal clinical ranges.

trial_rating.result_basis: This is a non-interventional observational study with no treatment comparison; regression models explained 36% of MyCog variance (Adj. R²=0.36, p<0.001) and 33% of TheirCog variance (Adj. R²=0.33, p<0.001), but no effect size for an intervention can be reported.

authors: Luke S. Watson; Youssef Toubouti; Sarah M. Gray; Núria Guillén; Agnès Pérez-Millan; Lorena Rami; Raquel Sanchez-Valle; Jason K. Johannesen

summary: This is not a clinical trial. It is a bioinformatics study that used genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from the COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative to identify candidate genetic variants that may be relevant to Long COVID risk. The study analyzed data from over 159,000 COVID-19 cases and nearly 3 million controls, prioritizing 62 candidate single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) — grouped by whether they were linked to severe COVID-19, both severe and mild COVID-19, or mild COVID-19 only — and then evaluated these variants against published Long COVID GWAS datasets. Of the 62 candidate SNPs, only one (rs12660421 near FOXP4) reached genome-wide significance for Long COVID (p = 1×10⁻⁹), while most others showed only weak, nominally significant associations; gene expression analyses similarly found much weaker links to Long COVID than to acute COVID-19 outcomes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is not a clinical trial and does not meet inclusion criteria for this extraction schema. It is a bioinformatics/GWAS analysis paper that: (1) contains no study arms, randomization, or intervention; (2) analyzes existing GWAS summary statistics rather than enrolling participants; (3) reports no clinical trial outcomes, baseline demographics of trial participants, or adverse events from any intervention; (4) has no sample of long COVID patients being treated. Tables 1 and 2 present GWAS association statistics (effect sizes, standard errors, p-values) for candidate SNPs across three COVID-19 GWAS datasets and Table 3 presents transcriptome-wide association results, none of which represent trial outcomes. The study does not fit the randomized controlled trial or any clinical intervention study design.

trial_rating.result_basis: Only 1 of 62 candidate SNPs reached genome-wide significance for Long COVID (rs12660421/FOXP4, p = 1×10⁻⁹); all other 61 SNPs showed weak or non-significant associations, and no long COVID TWAS gene passed the genome-wide threshold (P < 3.5×10⁻⁷).

summary: This is not a clinical trial of a Long COVID intervention; it is a laboratory study examining whether antibodies raised against the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N) protein cross-react with human proteins. Researchers immunised mice, rabbits, and hamsters with recombinant N protein, then tested whether the resulting antisera bound to lysates of eight human cell lines using Western blot and mass spectrometry. Anti-N antibodies consistently recognised human proteins including heat shock proteins (HSP90, HSP70), histones (H2B, H3), and metabolic enzymes (pyruvate kinase PKM, GAPDH), while antibodies raised against influenza nucleoprotein showed no such cross-reactivity. The authors speculate this autoreactivity could contribute to post-COVID autoimmune sequelae, but explicitly note the findings are in vitro only and require in vivo validation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a clinical trial and does not meet inclusion criteria for systematic review of Long COVID interventions. It is a mechanistic in vitro study using animal-derived sera and monoclonal antibodies tested against human cell lysates. No human participants, no randomization, no intervention arms, no clinical outcomes. The only numerical data extracted are animal counts and experimental design parameters (cell lines, immunization doses, etc.), not clinical data. Tables 1, 2, and 3 contain protein identifications and bioinformatic alignment scores, not clinical outcome measures. This extraction confirms the paper's ineligibility for a Long COVID trial meta-analysis.

trial_rating.result_basis: No clinical outcome measured; study is a qualitative in vitro Western blot experiment with no statistical testing of a primary outcome and no patient population.

summary: This diagnostic accuracy study tested whether a virtual-reality eye-tracking device (VR-OTS) could distinguish 330 Long COVID patients from 99 healthy controls by measuring pupil diameter, gaze behaviour, and 3D stereoscopic task performance. Using support vector machine classifiers trained on 95 extracted features, pupil diameter was the best-performing feature group with an AUROC of 0.73, followed by gaze direction (0.68) and stereoscopic reaction time (0.66); combining all features achieved 0.71. The index of pupillary activity (IPA) — a measure of cognitive load derived from pupil oscillations — was the single most predictive feature, consistent with cognitive impairment as a core mechanism of Long COVID. The study is observational and diagnostic rather than therapeutic, the patient and control groups were unequal in size and sex ratio, and findings may not generalise beyond European populations.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a cross-sectional case-control diagnostic study, not a clinical trial testing an intervention. The study compares ocular biomarkers between PCS patients and healthy controls using machine learning to distinguish group membership. No per-arm outcome data (means, SDs) were reported for the participant groups; only AUROC values (model performance metrics) were provided in results. The paper is primarily a diagnostic accuracy/classifier performance study rather than a therapeutic intervention trial. Follow-up duration is zero as this was a single-session assessment. Adverse events are not applicable to this type of non-intervention study. Additional secondary outcomes from Appendix A (Tables A1–A3) with individual feature AUROCs were extracted selectively to capture the most important findings per feature group.

trial_rating.result_basis: Best classifier AUROC = 0.73 (pupil diameter group); combined all-feature model AUROC = 0.71; these represent modest discriminative ability above chance but below strong diagnostic thresholds.

summary: This cross-sectional observational study examined plasma biomarkers and genetic risk factors in 51 non-hospitalized adults with neurological Long COVID symptoms (brain fog, memory difficulty, anxiety/depression) compared to 35 fully recovered COVID-19 patients and 51 pre-pandemic healthy controls, all assessed 4–53 months post-infection. The key finding was that soluble CD14, a monocyte activation marker, was the only biomarker that significantly distinguished neurological Long COVID patients from recovered patients, and was elevated alongside IL-1β, IL-8, GFAP, and hemopexin compared to healthy controls. Additionally, 35% of neurological Long COVID patients carried the APOE ε4 allele (a genetic risk factor for neurodegeneration) versus 11% of recovered patients. A combined panel of four plasma proteins (IL-1β, IL-8, CD14, GFAP) plus age, APOE4 status, and BMI identified neurological Long COVID with approximately 76–82% overall accuracy (AUC 0.81), though this is a small observational study without intervention, longitudinal follow-up, or objective cognitive assessment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cross-sectional study, not a clinical trial. No intervention was tested. Data presented are from group comparisons (HC vs Cov vs nLongC) with biomarker measurements and correlational analyses. Many outcome values appear only in figures or as p-values/statistical results without exact per-arm means/SDs; per-arm numeric data (median, mean, SD) were extracted where explicitly stated in text and tables. Between-group p-values extracted from figure captions and text. APOE4 and prediction accuracy results were extractable from tables. Correlation slopes for time-trajectory analyses (IL-1β over time) were reported as Spearman r coefficients and p-values only, without raw means per timepoint. Risk of bias assessment is not applicable (observational design); key limitation noted is heterogeneity in HC plasma sourcing (purchased from vendor vs. in-house COVID+ cohorts).

trial_rating.result_basis: CD14 was the only biomarker significantly differentiating recovered COVID from neurological Long COVID (p≤0.05); the multivariate classifier achieved AUC 0.8137 (95% CI 0.72–0.91, p<0.0001) with 76.5% overall correct classification in a sample of 35 Cov and 50 nLongC participants.

summary: This observational cohort study from Ukraine followed 265 children (ages 1 month to 18 years) for up to 12 months after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection to identify risk factors for developing long COVID, which occurred in 52% of participants. Using multivariate regression, the researchers developed two predictive scoring models: the first (for all patients) identified obesity, allergic disease, vitamin D deficiency, and vitamin D level as significant predictors; the second (for hospitalized patients only) identified fever, three or more acute symptoms, allergic disease, thrombocytosis, neutrophilia, and altered prothrombin time as predictors. By 12 months, 32.5% of children still had at least one persistent symptom, most commonly fatigue (19.8%), reduced physical activity (13.9%), and headache (12.3%). The models showed very high R² values (0.971 and 0.964), though the study was single-centre, lacked external validation, and had no control intervention — it is a risk-prediction model, not a treatment trial.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper describes an observational cross-sectional study with predictive modeling rather than a randomized controlled trial. No intervention arms are present; the 'arms' represent outcome categories (long COVID developers vs. fully recovered). The study includes extensive multivariate regression analysis with 36 predictors in Model 1 and 58 in Model 2. Primary outcome data (long COVID development) reported as percentages (52.0% vs. 48.0%) across the entire follow-up period. Secondary outcomes include detailed symptom prevalence at multiple timepoints (1-3, 3-6, 6-9, and 9-12 months). Follow-up assessments: 127 participants at 1-3 months, 125 at 3-6 months, 122 at 6-9 months, 101 at 9-12 months. Mean follow-up duration reported as 10.9 ± 2.0 months. Recovery milestones: 14.0% at 6 months, 43.9% at 9 months, 67.5% at 12 months. No adverse events reporting. Regression coefficients and p-values extracted from Tables 1, 2, 3, and 4. No per-arm demographic comparisons provided in paper.

trial_rating.result_basis: Model 1 Nagelkerke R²=0.971 (p<0.00001); obesity coefficient B=0.4266 (p<0.0001), vitamin D deficiency B=0.3972 (p<0.0001); Model 2 R²=0.964 (p<0.00001), neutrophilia B=0.4646 (p<0.0001).

summary: This observational study compared immune markers and psychological symptoms in 65 people with ME/CFS, 54 with Long COVID, and 70 healthy controls. Both patient groups showed significantly reduced total lymphocytes, CD8+ T cells, and NK cells compared to controls (e.g., NK cells: 0.205 and 0.180 × 10⁹/L in ME/CFS and Long COVID vs. 0.336 × 10⁹/L in controls, p<0.001), along with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-6, IL-2, IL-4, IL-10) and higher anxiety, depression, and fatigue scores. Critically, no statistically significant differences were found between the ME/CFS and Long COVID groups on any immune or psychological measure, suggesting the two conditions share a very similar immunological profile. The main limitation is that the healthy control group was substantially younger (mean age ~32) than the patient groups (~45–51), which may have influenced immune parameters despite statistical age-adjustment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a cross-sectional observational study, not a randomized controlled trial, comparing three groups (ME/CFS, LC, healthy controls). No intervention was tested. Age imbalance between groups is acknowledged as a limitation but was adjusted for in ANCOVA. Exact values for some cytokines (TNF, IL-10, IL-6, IL-4, IL-2, IFN-γ, IL-17A) in LC and HC groups were not explicitly provided in Table 4 or text for all comparisons; only CFS group values are clearly stated in Results section 3.2. Complete cytokine data across all three groups appears to be in figures only (Figures 2 and 3) without corresponding table values for LC and HC. Correlation analyses were extensive but only summarized; detailed correlation coefficients are shown in Tables 6-9.

trial_rating.result_basis: NK cells significantly lower in both patient groups vs. controls (p<0.001); no significant differences between ME/CFS and Long COVID on any biomarker (ANCOVA p-values all non-significant between patient groups); healthy controls were ~13–19 years younger, limiting comparability despite age adjustment.

summary: This observational study used macromolecular proton fraction (MPF) MRI mapping to compare brain white matter myelination across 76 long COVID patients grouped by symptom profile (insomnia only, depression only, comorbid insomnia-depression, or post-COVID without these symptoms) and 22 healthy controls. Long COVID patients with insomnia showed the greatest brain demyelination, with significant MPF reductions in 50% of studied brain structures (58/115), averaging a 3.03% decrease in juxtacortical white matter versus 0.95% in post-COVID patients without these symptoms. Unexpectedly, patients with comorbid insomnia and depression showed less demyelination (14% of structures affected) than those with insomnia alone, despite reporting more severe symptoms; elevated anti-PLP autoantibodies correlated with both greater demyelination and insomnia severity, suggesting an autoimmune mechanism. The study is small and cross-sectional with no intervention, limiting causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study is observational/cross-sectional, not a clinical trial, so no randomization, allocation concealment, or blinding occurred. Five participants were excluded post-enrollment due to incidental neuroimaging findings (cavernoma and vascular anomalies), reducing PostCovid analysis group from 37 to 32. Table 2 contains formatting issues with merged cells and unclear data presentation for some HADS/anxiety scores. MPF raw values per arm not provided in tables; only percentage changes relative to controls reported. Between-group MPF comparisons were presented as percentage differences with SEs in figures rather than tables, extracted from text descriptions. Cognitive test results in Table 3 show multiple superscript annotations indicating significant differences but exact p-values not always provided. Anti-spike IgG antibody data in Table 4 shows non-zero values even in control group without COVID history, suggesting background antibody presence. No adverse events reported because this is an observational study with no intervention. Study design is quasi-experimental observational with no randomization or interventions.

trial_rating.result_basis: Insomnia group showed mean MPF decrease of 3.03% in juxtacortical WM vs 0.95% in PostCovid group; significant reductions vs controls in 58/115 brain structures (p<0.05 to p<0.001); ISI correlated with mean MPF PC in WM pathways r=-0.59, p<0.05.

summary: This cross-sectional observational study assessed 60 adults with Long COVID (post-COVID syndrome lasting >3 months) attending a Brazilian outpatient clinic, examining how resting lung function measured by impulse oscillometry and lung ultrasound relates to exercise capacity measured by cardiopulmonary exercise testing. Nearly all participants (97%) had severely reduced peak oxygen consumption (mean VO2peak 18.4 mL/kg/min), and significant negative correlations were found between VO2peak and lung ultrasound aeration score (rs = -0.261, p = 0.044) and oscillometry resonance frequency (rs = -0.312, p = 0.019), indicating that worse lung structural changes and small airway dysfunction track with poorer exercise capacity. This is not a clinical trial testing an intervention but rather a diagnostic/observational study; the correlations, while statistically significant, are weak-to-moderate and causality cannot be established from the cross-sectional design.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cross-sectional study, not a randomized controlled trial. Subgroup analyses presented in the Results section compare defined subgroups (mechanically ventilated vs. not, hospitalized vs. not) using Student's t-test. Spearman correlations are reported for associations between VO2peak and various clinical/physiological variables. Some outcomes (total exercise time, FEF25-75%, Fres, R5, R20, R5-R20) are reported as median and IQR rather than mean and SD. No formal risk-of-bias assessment is applicable for cross-sectional observational studies using RoB2 or similar tools. Adverse events are not reported for this observational physiology study. No clinical trial registration number or pre-specification of outcomes is mentioned.

summary: This observational study measured mitochondrial respiration in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) taken from 20 COVID-19 patients admitted to an intensive care unit in Strasbourg, France, then followed survivors by phone three years after discharge to assess Long COVID symptoms. Patients with the most severe Long COVID symptoms had significantly lower PBMC mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation capacity than healthy controls across multiple respiratory chain complexes (e.g., OXPHOS complex I: 3.04 vs 8.24 pmol/s/10⁶ cells, p=0.037; OXPHOS complex II: 4.91 vs 14.13, p=0.008), and this impairment was also seen in patients who died. The inflammatory marker ISG15 was significantly elevated in deceased patients and negatively correlated with mitochondrial respiration, suggesting a link between immune dysregulation and mitochondrial dysfunction. Key caveats are the very small sample size (only 12 survivors assessed for Long COVID) and the purely observational, non-interventional design, which cannot establish causation.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Spike protein S1 induced region-specific and time-dependent changes in ferroptosis markers. Hippocampus showed significant FPN1 increase at 2 weeks. Prefrontal cortex showed significant DMT1 increase at 2 weeks. Cerebellum showed significant FPN1 increase at 2 weeks and MDA-conjugated proteins increase at 12 weeks, with GPx4 increase at 2 weeks. Olfactory bulb showed significant FPN1 increase at 12 weeks. These regional differences suggest distinct temporal vulnerability patterns across brain regions.

summary: This preclinical study administered the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein S1 subunit intranasally to K18-hACE2 transgenic mice (n=38 male mice) to model Long COVID neurological effects, then measured ferroptosis-related protein markers across four brain regions at 2, 6, and 12 weeks. The study found region-specific and time-dependent changes in iron-handling proteins (TFR1, FPN1, DMT1), antioxidant markers (GPx4, NrF2), and lipid peroxidation markers (MDA-conjugated proteins), with the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus also showing ultrastructural features consistent with ferroptotic cell death under electron microscopy. This is an animal study with small group sizes (n=4-5 per time point), no human subjects, and no therapeutic intervention tested — it provides mechanistic evidence that spike protein exposure may trigger ferroptosis pathways in brain tissue, but cannot demonstrate clinical relevance to Long COVID in people.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a preclinical animal model study (not a human clinical trial), which does not meet the stated criteria for Long COVID clinical trial extraction. The paper tests ferroptosis mechanisms using SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in transgenic mice, not a human patient population. Specific numerical outcome data (means, SDs) for protein expression measurements were not provided in the text or tables — only F-statistics, p-values, and qualitative descriptions of statistically significant findings from two-way ANOVA post hoc comparisons. Supplementary Tables S1-S4 referenced in the paper would contain the detailed quantitative data, but these were not provided in the full text. Sample sizes per arm and per timepoint (n=4-5) are mentioned generally but not explicitly broken down by treatment group assignment in the methods. The study was explicitly conducted unblinded (stated in Results section: 'Statistical analyses were performed unblinded') which introduces substantial bias risk for an animal biomarker study.

trial_rating.result_basis: Significant post hoc increases were scattered across regions and time points (e.g. cerebellar MDA at 12 weeks adjusted p=0.043; cerebellar GPx4 at 2 weeks adjusted p=0.0033; hippocampal FPN1 at 2 weeks adjusted p=0.013), but many ANOVAs with significant main effects yielded no significant post hoc pairwise differences after correction, and no single primary outcome was pre-specified.

summary: This preclinical study infected female transgenic mice expressing the human ACE2 receptor with the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant (BA.1.17) to investigate whether infection produces lasting pain sensitivity and inflammatory changes resembling post-COVID-19 pain. At 28 days post-infection (roughly equivalent to three human years), infected mice showed no statistically significant change in thermal pain thresholds on the hot-plate test compared to uninfected controls, and no detectable expression of IL-6, IL-1β, or IL-18 in the saphenous nerve. Plasma cytokine profiling identified non-significant trends toward higher CXCL5 and CXCL12 and lower IL-10, CCL11, and CCL22, suggesting a mild residual inflammatory imbalance that may predispose to later nociceptive changes. A notable caveat is the 42% mortality rate in the infected group during the first week, leaving only seven surviving animals, which substantially limits statistical power.

summary: This study used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to investigate the molecular basis of persistent bitter taste dysfunction in 6 Long COVID patients compared to 6 healthy pre-COVID controls, by profiling salivary epithelial cells (SECs). The key finding was a significant reduction in Type II and Type III taste receptor cell (TRC) gene expression in Long COVID patients with taste dysfunction: genes including TAS1R1 (1.55% vs 2.53% of cells), TAS1R2 (1.06% vs 1.69%), CD36 (6.38% vs 9.34%), SNAP25 (3.55% vs 5.49%), and GAD1 (1.15% vs 1.89%) were all lower in the affected group, alongside downregulation of 171 genes involved in epithelial homeostasis, synaptic signaling, and GPCR pathways. This is a mechanistic observational study, not a clinical trial testing an intervention, and the very small sample size (n=6 per group) and cross-sectional design limit generalizability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cross-sectional study, not a randomized controlled trial. The 42 LC participants with taste loss were recruited from a registry, and 6 with impaired bitter taste (LC-D) were selected for scRNA-seq, compared to 6 pre-COVID healthy controls from a saliva bank. No intervention was tested; this is a mechanistic biomarker study. No p-values were reported for the validated RT-qPCR and flow cytometry results, only for scRNA-seq cluster comparisons. Baseline demographics (age, BMI, sex) were reported only for the overall LC cohort (n=42), not separately for the 12 sequenced samples. SNAP25 MFI values from flow cytometry were reported only as comparisons between three groups (LC-D, LC without dysgeusia, healthy), not individual mean/SD values.

summary: This observational immunophenotyping study compared immune cell profiles in 103 ME/CFS patients, 63 long COVID patients, and 41 healthy controls using 12-parameter flow cytometry of peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Long COVID showed progressive M2-like monocyte polarization, elevated CD80 costimulatory expression on both monocyte subtypes, expanded dendritic cell numbers, and reduced CD69+CD38 activation markers — suggesting persistent but 'exhausted' immune activation. ME/CFS showed a contrasting pattern of immune suppression, with reduced M1-like CD80 expression and more severely impaired CCR7-mediated immune cell trafficking. A partial least squares discriminant analysis model separated the conditions from healthy controls with moderate accuracy (AUC 0.758, cross-validated accuracy ~69%), but the study is cross-sectional and observational with no intervention tested.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a cross-sectional observational study comparing immune phenotypes, not an intervention trial. No arms received intervention or were randomized. Study design does not fit RCT framework. Risk of bias tool (RoB2) is not appropriate for this design but was assessed per instructions. Healthy controls served as comparison group rather than randomized control arm. All outcome data are from cross-sectional biomarker measurements by flow cytometry. PCA and PLS-DA statistical results extracted from regression analyses. Some biomarker data (e.g., dendritic cell CD69+CD38 in HC) not explicitly stated in text but inferred from figure description patterns. Multiple regression model R-squared and beta values extracted for associations with clinical symptoms. Study demographics show significant age difference between groups (HC median 27 years vs CFS/LC median 48 years), which was controlled for in analyses via age-adjusted ANCOVA.

trial_rating.result_basis: PLS-DA model distinguishing LC/CFS from healthy controls achieved AUC 0.758 (95% CI: 0.633–0.88) with cross-validated predictive accuracy of approximately 69% and limited generalizability (Q2 = 0.113); no randomized intervention was tested.

summary: A 12-week non-aerobic core stabilization exercise program (the MORETA program, 24 sessions of plank-based trunk exercises) was tested in 17 women with Long COVID symptoms lasting over one year. The primary outcomes were body fat percentage and perceived fatigue; total body fat decreased significantly from 37.1% to 35.4% (p=0.003, ES=1.08), and overall fatigue scores on the Modified Fatigue Impact Scale dropped from 66.6 to 52.6 (p=0.012, ES=0.94), with the largest gains in physical fatigue (29.7 to 21.1, ES=1.20). The study had no control group, enrolled only 17 participants, and cognitive fatigue did not improve significantly, limiting causal conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study is non-randomized, pre-post quasi-experimental with single arm; no control or comparison group. IPAQ-3 (walking days per week without minimum duration) also reported (pre: 2.00±0.88, post: 2.21±1.19, p=0.796) and IPAQ-5 (sitting time weekends) (pre: 4.88±2.21, post: 5.38±1.62, p=0.455) and IPAQ-7 (total physical activity time) (pre: 7.08±3.98, post: 7.92±2.81, p=0.517) presented in Table 5 but excluded from outcomes list due to space constraints. Muscle mass percentages reported for right arm, left arm, right leg, left leg, and trunk regions—all non-significant changes (all p > 0.05). Body water data for regional distributions (right arm, left arm, right leg, left leg, trunk) reported but omitted. Correlations between fat mass reduction and outcome changes (MFIS r=-0.84 p=0.765; EQ-5D-5L r=-0.121 p=0.694; IPAQ r=-0.241 p=0.532; TSK-11 r=0.014 p=0.961) reported but effect sizes not sufficient for extraction. trial_rating.result_basis: Overall MFIS fatigue score decreased from 66.59 to 52.59 (p=0.012, ES=0.936); total body fat from 37.09% to 35.41% (p=0.003, ES=1.079) in n=17 with no control group.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Failure to complete active 10-minute standing test (orthostatic intolerance)
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Among 9 patients with disequilibrium (positive Romberg and/or tandem gait tests), 6 (67%) failed to complete the 10-minute standing test. Among 23 patients without disequilibrium, only 1 failed to complete the test. Multiple regression analysis showed disequilibrium was significantly positively associated with OI (partial regression coefficient: 0.64, p<0.001, 95% CI 0.32-0.96), whereas POTS was significantly negatively associated (partial regression coefficient: -0.38, p=0.049, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.62).

Six patients with disequilibrium received 6 weeks of oral minocycline therapy (5 patients) or minocycline followed by 2 weeks of rTMS (1 patient). After treatment, 5 of 6 treated and retested patients showed resolution of OI associated with improvement in disequilibrium, although 1 patient experienced symptom recovery without a repeat standing test.

summary: This single-centre observational study of 32 long COVID patients (all meeting ME/CFS criteria) assessed whether balance dysfunction (disequilibrium) or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) better explained orthostatic intolerance (OI) — the inability to sustain standing. In a multiple regression analysis, disequilibrium was the only factor significantly associated with OI (partial regression coefficient 0.64, p<0.001), while POTS was actually negatively associated (coefficient -0.38, p=0.049); 6 of 7 patients who failed the 10-minute standing test had disequilibrium, versus none with POTS alone. A subset of 7 patients with OI was then treated with oral minocycline and/or repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and 5 of 6 re-tested showed resolution of OI alongside improvement in balance. The study is very small and uncontrolled, making it impossible to attribute treatment outcomes to the interventions rather than natural recovery.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study design: not a randomized controlled trial; single-arm quasi-experimental design with prospective enrollment and pre-post treatment assessments in a subset. No control group or randomization. Table 1 provides individual patient data for 7 patients with OI who received treatment; 6 were retested post-treatment. Table 2 compares patients with and without OI at baseline (25 with OI, 7 without). Multiple regression CI for POTS association reported as (-0.31 to -0.62) which is unusual formatting; extracted as written. Death noted was of co-researcher Yukichi Inoue, not a study participant, during the conduct of the research. Risk of bias tool (RoB2) is not appropriate for this quasi-experimental design; overall judgment reflects that this is not an RCT and lacks key design features necessary for RCT bias assessment.

trial_rating.result_basis: 5 of 6 re-tested patients resolved OI after minocycline/rTMS, but no control group; disequilibrium-OI association: partial regression coefficient 0.64, p<0.001 in n=32.

interventions: Oral minocycline and/or repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS)

summary: This observational neuroimaging study (ACDC) examined 30 adults with Long COVID cognitive symptoms who had been hospitalised with PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, assessed on average two years after infection. Using multimodal brain MRI including magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), volumetric analysis, diffusion tractography, and resting-state connectivity, the study found consistent neurometabolic abnormalities in frontal white matter: elevated choline, myo-inositol, and glutamate-glutamine ratios alongside reduced N-acetylaspartate, all surviving correction for multiple comparisons, indicating neuroinflammation and reduced neuronal integrity. Neuropsychological testing confirmed selective deficits in attention and working memory (e.g. Digit Span Forward z = -1.12, 33% impaired), and a focal reduction in left posterior hypothalamic volume was detected, but no widespread cortical atrophy or white matter lesion burden differences were found, and none of the neuroimaging findings correlated significantly with cognitive performance after correction.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an exploratory single-group pilot study, not an RCT. No intervention arm or control arm; participants underwent cross-sectional assessment at single timepoint (mean ~2 years post-infection). Imaging findings (volumetry, connectivity, MRS) were compared against historical controls or normative datasets. Neuropsychological tests compared against published normative reference standards, not a concurrent control group. Study included 30 participants recruited; 1 withdrew mid-MRI (incomplete scan); analyses conducted on n=29 for imaging, n=30 for cognitive/screening measures. No between-arm comparisons possible. MRS findings are the primary quantitative biomarker output with robust statistical support (FDR-corrected p<0.05 for all metabolite ratios). No treatment duration or follow-up interval as this was a single-visit descriptive study. Vaccination status not systematically recorded (noted as limitation). Risk of bias assessed using exploratory study quality criteria rather than RoB2 (tool not applicable to observational design).

trial_rating.result_basis: No brain-behaviour correlations survived BY-FDR correction; the MRS findings were significant vs. normative values (e.g. NAA/Cr T(28)=-3.96, FDR p=0.002) but this is a descriptive observational study with no intervention and no primary outcome effect size to rate.

summary: This study tested whether eye-tracking (ET) metrics combined with machine learning could screen for cognitive impairment in 172 adults with Long COVID (post-COVID condition), comparing ET alone, the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) alone, and a combined ET+MoCA Random Forest model. ET features alone could not predict individual neuropsychological test scores (all regression R² values near or below zero), but when used as a binary classifier alongside the MoCA, the combined model achieved an AUC of 0.80 for detecting overall cognitive impairment, outperforming MoCA alone (AUC 0.73) and ET alone (AUC 0.68). The improvement of the combined model over MoCA alone was statistically significant (McNemar's χ²=10.11, p=0.001), though the overall discriminative performance remains moderate rather than clinically definitive, and the study is cross-sectional with a relatively small, single-centre sample.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is an observational cross-sectional study, not a randomized trial, with no active intervention or control group. The study has a single cohort of PCC patients assessed once with concurrent eye-tracking and neuropsychological testing. Individual eye-tracking metric means and SDs are not provided in tables or text; per-arm baseline neuropsychological test descriptive statistics are extracted from Table 1. Regression results (Table 2) show R² and RMSPE but no per-arm means, so between-group effects cannot be calculated. Classification results (Table 3) report ROC-AUC values for various machine learning models predicting binary outcomes (altered vs. not altered). A secondary normative reference sample (n=133) was used only to derive z-score cutoffs and is not presented as a separate arm. No adverse events were reported. This was identified as an ineligible study design for the meta-analysis (observational, not RCT), but numeric data extracted as requested.

trial_rating.result_basis: Combined RF-ET+MoCA achieved AUC=0.80 vs MoCA alone AUC=0.73 for global cognitive composite; improvement over MoCA alone was significant (McNemar's χ²=10.11, p=0.001), but ET-only regression R² values were universally near or below 0 across all neuropsychological outcomes.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: This is a machine learning diagnostic validation study on secondary metabolomics data from published sources, not a clinical trial. Standard RCT bias assessment tools do not apply. Key limitations include: age confounder between training and testing datasets (training cohort older than testing cohort, both older than healthy controls), reliance on datasets that may vary by demographics, use of only LC-MS/MS and FIA-MS/MS assays limiting generalizability, and inability to distinguish PASC from fibromyalgia.

summary: This study tested whether a machine learning model trained on molecular descriptors of plasma metabolites could distinguish Long COVID (PASC) patients from healthy individuals and from five conditions with overlapping symptoms: fibromyalgia, ME/CFS, Lyme disease, POTS, and irritable bowel syndrome. The best-performing model (a multi-layer perceptron) achieved an AUC-ROC of 98.37% in cross-validation and 87.7% on an independent test set, and successfully separated PASC from Lyme disease, ME/CFS, and IBS with high confidence, and from POTS with weak confidence. A notable finding was that the model could not distinguish PASC from fibromyalgia at all — fibromyalgia metabolites were classified as PASC at rates equal to or higher than the PASC test set itself, suggesting strong molecular overlap between the two conditions. This is a computational diagnostics study using secondary analysis of existing metabolomics datasets, not a clinical trial, so findings require prospective validation before clinical use.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a methodological study applying machine learning to metabolomics data from secondary sources, not a clinical trial. No arms received interventions; the study trained and tested ML classifiers on metabolomic datasets from published sources. Per-arm demographic data (Table 1) represents sample characteristics from four different datasets (PASC training n=117, healthy training n=28, PASC testing n=48, healthy testing n=37), not randomized trial arms. No adverse events, treatment duration, or follow-up periods are applicable. Specific proportions and confidence intervals for disease classification are not numerically reported in Figure 4 text; values reported in Results section are limited. The study demonstrates the feasibility of automated metabolomics-based PASC diagnosis but requires validation with more diverse datasets before clinical application.

trial_rating.result_basis: MLP model achieved AUC-ROC of 87.7% on the independent PASC test set; a classification threshold of 0.912 at confidence level 0.868 separated PASC from POTS; FM could not be separated (classification proportion overlapping or exceeding PASC test set).

summary: This open-label randomized controlled trial tested 4 g/day of L-citrulline supplementation for three months in 43 adults who had been hospitalized for moderate-to-severe COVID-19 and were attending a post-COVID clinic in Mexico City. The primary outcome was endothelial function measured by ICAM-1; the L-citrulline group showed a significant reduction in ICAM-1 of 32.59 ng/mg protein (95% CI: -52.85 to -12.33, p=0.001) compared to no change in controls (p=0.034 for group × time interaction). A notable secondary finding was greater improvement in six-minute walk test distance in the L-citrulline group (+141 m vs +68 m in controls, p=0.011 between groups), though both groups improved, likely reflecting natural recovery. The study is limited by its small sample size (21 per arm), open-label design, single centre, and the primary endothelial biomarker ICAM-1 may not directly reflect physiological endothelial function.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 baseline characteristics included median and IQR for hospital stay (reported in days as 18 [11-26] vs 30 [11-47]); these were not extracted as outcome data. The study was open-label (not blinded). Adherence to L-citrulline was reported as 85%. All 43 randomized participants completed the study with no reported withdrawals or loss to follow-up. Nutrient intake data were reported but showed no significant changes between groups; these were included in Table 2 but not extracted as separate outcomes since they are secondary measures of intervention exposure. The p-value of 0.034 for the ICAM-1 between-group effect was from a repeated-measures ANOVA adjusted for E-Selectin and hospital stay; the paper did not report the unadjusted comparison, so the calculated mean difference (305.61 - 32.59 = 273.02 for intervention vs 305.67 - 2.31 = 303.36 for control, difference = -30.34) is approximate.

trial_rating.result_basis: ICAM-1 decreased by 32.59 ng/mg protein in the intervention group vs -2.31 in controls; group × time interaction p=0.034.

summary: This Brazilian randomized controlled trial tested two 6-week supervised rehabilitation programs in 29 adults who survived severe COVID-19 requiring hospitalization: multicomponent exercise alone (aerobic, resistance, and balance training) versus the same program combined with inspiratory muscle training (IMT) using a threshold loading device. Both groups showed large improvements across all primary functional outcomes, including a 123-meter increase in 6-minute walk distance (378m to 501m, +32%), a 27% reduction in Timed Up and Go time (9.6s to 7.0s), a 38% increase in sit-to-stand repetitions, and significant gains in handgrip strength and respiratory muscle pressures. No statistically significant differences were found between the two groups on any outcome, and no adverse events occurred; the study lacked a no-treatment control arm and was underpowered for between-group comparisons, so natural recovery cannot be ruled out.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CPET was performed only at baseline per study design (high cost/logistical constraints), so no post-intervention VO2peak data available. No between-group interactions reported in tables; p-values shown reflect between-group comparisons at each timepoint (p(GEm vs. GEmTMI/1o) and p(GEm vs. GEmTMI/2o)).

summary: A 12-week multi-strain probiotic (Saccharomyces boulardii DBVPG-6763, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG, and two Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains) was given to 34 adults with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection (13 with Long COVID, 21 fully recovered) in a non-randomised double-blind trial in Serbia, with 25 healthy non-supplemented adults as reference controls. The primary outcomes were gut microbiota composition and biochemical markers: overall microbial diversity did not change significantly, but in Long COVID participants the probiotic significantly increased Bifidobacterium (delta +0.026 vs -0.007 in controls, p=0.037) and reduced Prevotella_9 abundance (p=0.013), with non-significant trends toward lower CRP, ALT, and AST. The study was small (only 23 Long COVID participants total, 13 in the probiotic arm), non-randomised, and lacked a placebo control group, severely limiting causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study is quasi-experimental (non-randomized allocation) rather than RCT. Initial enrollment n=90, but final analyzed sample was n=74 (34 probiotic recipients: 13 long COVID + 21 convalescent; 40 non-supplemented controls: 10 long COVID + 5 convalescent + 25 healthy). Exclusions due to unclear labeling (n=9) and incomplete paired sampling (n=7). Alpha and beta diversity results reported as p-values only with no per-arm numeric data; set as not_reported. Multiple secondary outcomes related to microbiota composition changes reported as log-fold changes or relative abundance changes with p-values; prioritized major findings. Several MetaCyc pathway results omitted from Table 5 (6 of 7 reported) as detailed in extraction; all 7 are now included. Biochemical parameters reported as median changes with Wilcoxon test p-values; no raw means/SDs reported for baseline or endpoint values. Correlation analysis results (30 associations in all participants, 217 in long COVID) noted but not separately extracted as distinct outcomes due to scope; summarized in text. Probiotic compliance monitored by self-report only; no objective compliance measure reported. Study used flow-pack technology packaging but no viability testing beyond manufacturer validation. No serious adverse events, withdrawals, or mortality reported.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary microbiota and biochemical outcomes were largely non-significant; the strongest finding was a significant increase in Bifidobacterium relative abundance (delta +0.026 probiotic vs -0.007 control, p=0.037), but overall diversity metrics showed no change (PERMANOVA p=0.422) and biochemical trends did not reach p<0.05.

interventions: Multi-strain probiotic (Saccharomyces boulardii DBVPG-6763, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum LP6595, L. plantarum HEAL9), No probiotic supplementation, No intervention (reference control)

summary: This observational transcriptomic study examined peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from 21 COVID-19 survivors (11 without pneumonia, 10 with severe pneumonia) and 13 healthy controls approximately one year after infection. RNA sequencing revealed that severe COVID-19 was associated with persistent upregulation of cancer-related gene pathways, with 30 genes from the severe pneumonia group overlapping with known oncogenes or tumor suppressors, and the hub gene SQSTM1/P62 showing elevated expression linked to worse prognosis in thymoma (HR=2.27, p=0.044) and adrenocortical carcinoma (HR=0.53 for decreased expression, p=0.003). Five hub genes (H3-5, H3C13, EGR1, JUN, NOTCH1) identified in all COVID-19 survivors were associated with poor prognosis in brain lower-grade glioma (HR=2.1, p=0.00012), adrenocortical carcinoma (HR=2.9, p=0.01), and bladder cancer (HR=1.4, p=0.022). The study is hypothesis-generating bioinformatics work with very small groups and no clinical cancer incidence data as a primary endpoint; three cancer diagnoses were observed among participants over four years of follow-up, but no causal inference is possible.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a transcriptomic/bioinformatics study of a prospective cohort, not a clinical intervention trial. No intervention was tested. The study documents RNA-seq analysis of PBMC samples from COVID-19 patients and controls at 1-year follow-up. Long-term symptoms were observed in 4/11 (36%) NP group and 5/10 (50%) SP group. No clinical outcome data (quality of life, symptom scores, etc.) beyond presence/absence of long-term symptoms were reported. The primary findings are at the molecular/gene expression level, with survival risk associations derived from TCGA cancer databases rather than clinical follow-up of cancer incidence in the study cohort. Two cases (one thymoma and metastatic colorectal cancer, one neuroendocrine tumor) developed malignancy within 4 years of follow-up but long-term outcomes still being monitored. Adverse events section not applicable as no intervention was administered.

trial_rating.result_basis: Hub gene expression associated with poor prognosis in LGG (HR=2.1, p=0.00012) and ACC (HR=2.9, p=0.01), but these are survival correlations in TCGA cancer databases, not clinical outcomes in the study cohort of n=21.

summary: This observational study examined liver and biliary tissue samples from 34 patients with a prior history of mild-to-moderate COVID-19 (averaging 12 months post-infection) compared to 28 controls without COVID-19 history, all undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstone disease. The primary finding was that post-COVID-19 patients showed significantly more hepatocyte regenerative changes than controls, including binucleated hepatocytes (58.8% vs 25.0%, p=0.001), anisokaryosis (44.1% vs 14.3%, p=0.01), and ductular reaction (32.4% vs 10.7%, p=0.04), suggesting active liver repair following infection. No significant differences were found in overall inflammation severity, steatosis, fibrosis, or vascular pathology between groups, and no SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins were detected in liver tissue at follow-up.
summary_of: observational comparative pathology study (not a clinical trial)

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a clinical trial — it is an observational comparative histopathology study of tissue samples from two groups of surgical patients. The study design lacks randomization, intervention, and the hallmarks of an RCT. Outcomes are morphological and immunohistochemical measurements on fixed tissue samples, not patient clinical outcomes. The paper provides no adverse event reporting, as it involves only tissue analysis during clinically indicated surgery. Risk of bias assessment using RoB2 is not applicable; this is an observational study. All quantitative data extracted represent tissue pathology findings with frequencies/percentages and cell counts with means and standard deviations.

trial_rating.result_basis: Regenerative changes present in 76.5% of post-COVID-19 patients vs 28.6% of controls (p=0.0007); binucleated hepatocytes 58.8% vs 25.0% (p=0.001); no significant differences in the primary inflammation measures (portal inflammation p=0.06, periportal necrosis p=0.08, fibrosis p=0.13).

summary: This is a preclinical mouse study, not a human clinical trial. Researchers infected female transgenic mice (K18-hACE2) with the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant and examined cardiac tissue 28 days post-infection to model post-COVID cardiac inflammation. The key finding was selective upregulation of two inflammatory markers in cardiac tissue: IL-6 (p=0.028) and the integrin CD11d (p=0.016), while classical inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-18) and the TLR4/MyD88/NFκB signaling pathway showed no significant changes. No markers of serious cardiac tissue damage (iNOS, PAI-1, connexin-43) were significantly elevated, suggesting subclinical inflammation without overt structural injury at this timepoint; the small sample size (7 animals per group) and animal-only design severely limit clinical translation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an animal model study, not a human clinical trial. All numeric outcome data (Western blot densitometry values, means, SDs) are reported only in figures without accompanying numeric tables, so per-arm means and SDs cannot be extracted. Between-group p-values are reported in the text. Sample sizes vary by biomarker due to technical failures in some Western blot assays. The paper does not report absolute numeric values for protein expression, only p-values and visual representation in bar graphs. The IL-6 and CD11d correlation analysis reports Pearson r=0.274, R²=0.075, p=0.655 for n=11 pooled infected and control animals. Survival was reported as 5/12 deaths in infected group (p=0.017 by Log-rank Mantel-Cox test) vs 0/11 in control group.

trial_rating.result_basis: IL-6 elevated in infected vs non-infected cardiac tissue (p=0.028); CD11d elevated (p=0.016); all other markers non-significant. N=5-9 animals per comparison.

summary: This observational study examined 211 Japanese adults from the Iwaki Health Promotion Project who received three doses of mRNA COVID-19 vaccines (Pfizer Comirnaty or Moderna Spikevax combinations), measuring spike protein IgG antibody titers and self-reported adverse reactions after the third dose. In adults under 60, those who received Spikevax as their third dose (after two Comirnaty doses) had significantly higher antibody titers than those who received a third Comirnaty dose (median 26,150 vs 15,450 AU/mL, p=0.001), along with more frequent fever symptoms (74% vs 49%, p=0.025); no such differences were seen in those over 60. Using Bayesian network machine learning analysis of over 3,700 health variables, the study identified daily green tea consumption, serum IgM, and albumin as positively associated with antibody production, while lower NK cell counts, reduced grip strength, higher folate intake, and elevated luteinizing hormone were linked to adverse reaction risk. This is a single-region observational study with no randomisation, so causal conclusions cannot be drawn.

Table 3 reports medians and IQRs (not means/SDs) for sIgG; longitudinal design with 6-month sample post-second dose and 3-5 weeks post-third dose, but only third-dose endpoint extracted as primary outcome. Many biomarker findings from Bayesian network analysis reported but not all have complete per-arm quantitative data. Risk of bias assessment not applicable—observational cohort design with no randomization.

summary: This preclinical mouse study tested whether intranasal administration of the SARS-CoV-2 ORF8 accessory protein — isolated from the virus — causes oxidative stress and cardiovascular changes in healthy male BALB/c mice, as a model of long COVID organ damage. After 8 weeks, ORF8-treated mice showed significantly elevated systolic, diastolic, and mean blood pressure compared to controls (all p<0.05). At 2 weeks post-inoculation, ORF8-treated mice had significantly higher malondialdehyde (a lipid peroxidation marker) in both the prefrontal cortex (p=0.003) and kidneys (p=0.03), indicating early oxidative stress, though this was not sustained at 8 weeks. This is an animal study with n=6 per group and does not directly test any treatment intervention in Long COVID patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an animal model study (preclinical research), not a human clinical trial for Long COVID. Numeric outcome data appear exclusively in figures without tabular presentation in the text; exact per-arm means and SDs could not be extracted from the paper as written. ANOVA test statistics and p-values are reported verbatim (e.g., F-values and p-thresholds), but between-group mean differences and confidence intervals are not provided. Statistical significance thresholds (p<0.05, p<0.01, p=0.03, p=0.001) were extracted where reported. The study is ineligible for inclusion in a human Long COVID meta-analysis but was extracted per the provided instructions as the full paper was submitted.

summary: This preclinical mouse study tested two recombinant BCG vaccine candidates — rBCG-RBD and rBCG-LTB-RBD (BCG engineered to express the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor-binding domain, with or without the E. coli heat-labile toxin B subunit as an adjuvant) — followed by a protein booster dose, in BALB/c mice rather than human patients. The rBCG-RBD/rRBD prime-boost produced anti-RBD IgG antibodies lasting up to 9 months and achieved approximately 80% neutralization of the Wuhan pseudovirus. Notably, the rBCG-LTB-RBD/rRBD regimen was the only group to achieve over 80% neutralization of the Omicron BA.1 variant, whereas rRBD protein alone and mRNA-vaccinated positive controls did not neutralize Omicron. This is an animal study only with no human data, limiting direct clinical relevance.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a preclinical mouse immunogenicity study, not a human clinical trial. The timepoint structure differs between experiments (Figure 2: 8 weeks; Figure 4: 36 weeks with re-boost; Figure 5: 10 weeks). summary: This observational study from Bulgaria measured insulin resistance using two blood-lipid-based indices (TyG index and TG/HDL-C ratio) in 168 patients across three groups: active COVID-19 (n=100), post-COVID patients with newly diagnosed carbohydrate disorders such as T1DM, T2DM, or prediabetes (n=35), and COVID-negative patients with metabolic syndrome (n=33). Patients with active COVID-19 had the highest insulin resistance scores on both indices, significantly higher than the post-COVID and COVID-negative groups (TyG index mean 4.89 vs 4.68 vs 4.46; TG/HDL-C ratio mean 3.80 vs 1.93 vs 2.42). In post-COVID patients with new-onset carbohydrate disorders, both indices correlated significantly with inflammatory markers including IL-10, IL-17A, TNF-α, and the hypoxia marker HIF-1α, suggesting immune dysregulation and oxidative stress contribute to persistent insulin resistance. This is a small cross-sectional observational study with no intervention or control arm, so it can only identify associations rather than establish causation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cross-sectional study, not a randomized clinical trial. Study groups (Group 1, 2, 3) are observational cohorts rather than randomized arms, but are treated here as comparison arms for extraction purposes. Only baseline data are presented; there is no follow-up or longitudinal outcome data. Sample sizes differ between Tables 2 and 3: Table 2 reports n=68 for Group 1 and n=29 for Group 2, while Table 1 reports total enrollment of n=100 and n=35 respectively (the discrepancy appears to be due to incomplete biochemical data). Per-arm results use the analyzed sample sizes from Table 2. Correlation analyses were performed within the post-COVID group only. ROC curve analysis results for TyG index cutoff ≥4.296 and TG/HDL-C ratio cutoff ≥3.619 are reported but not included as separate outcomes. Additional biochemical markers (fasting glucose, HbA1c, triglycerides, HDL-C) showed significant correlations with indices in post-COVID group but detailed outcome results are not fully extracted as they were primarily supportive findings.

trial_rating.result_basis: TyG index significantly higher in active COVID-19 vs post-COVID (Mann Whitney U=677.0, p=0.015) and vs COVID-negative (p<0.001); TG/HDL-C ratio mean 3.80 in active COVID-19 vs 1.93 post-COVID (p=0.002); these are group differences in biomarkers, not clinical outcomes.

summary: This cross-sectional study compared physical fitness in 105 young adults (average age ~20 years) divided equally into three groups: those with Long COVID (persistent symptoms >12 weeks), those who recovered from COVID-19 without persistent symptoms, and healthy controls never infected. The primary finding was that Long COVID participants had significantly lower handgrip strength than controls (30.50 kg vs. 33.35 kg, p<0.05), while quadricep strength did not differ significantly between groups. Both post-COVID groups—with and without persistent symptoms—walked shorter distances on the 6-minute walk test (~589 m vs. 601 m for controls, p<0.05) and showed greater physiological strain after exercise, including higher heart rate, blood pressure, perceived exertion, and leg fatigue, suggesting that even apparently recovered individuals retain some functional impairment.

summary: This observational neuroimaging study compared brain structure in 316 adults over 60 who had recovered from COVID-19 against 316 matched controls using MRI data from the UK Biobank. The researchers applied two novel geometric metrics — discrete tortuosity (Td) and discrete compactness (Cd) — to quantify cortical shape changes, finding statistically significant increases in Td and decreases in Cd in the left cerebral cortex, left temporal lobe, left lateral orbitofrontal cortex, left superior temporal gyrus, and left transverse temporal gyrus of COVID-19 patients compared to controls. Traditional metrics (brain volume and mean cortical thickness) showed trends in the same direction but did not reach statistical significance in most regions, suggesting the new geometric measures are more sensitive to subtle atrophy. The study is observational with no data on COVID-19 severity, no cognitive assessments, and no pre-infection baseline scans, limiting causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper describes a neuroimaging biomarker study, not a clinical trial. No intervention was tested; this is purely an observational comparison of brain structure between COVID-19 recovered and control participants. Per-arm numeric values for Td, Cd, V, and Mct are presented only in box plot figures (Figures 5, 6, 7) without accompanying numeric tables; therefore, exact means and SDs are not extracted. Only p-values from statistical comparisons are available in text. The study has no outcomes related to Long COVID symptoms; it is a structural neuroimaging study investigating COVID-19-related brain atrophy using novel morphological metrics. This study is ineligible for inclusion in a Long COVID clinical trial meta-analysis.

summary: This observational cohort study from Belarus measured blood plasma nitrate/nitrite ion concentrations (NOx) and a panel of inflammatory cytokines and antioxidant markers in 137 adults who had recovered from mild-to-moderate COVID-19, comparing 98 patients with persistent Long COVID symptoms to 39 symptom-free controls. Inflammatory markers (IL-1, IL-4, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, TNF-α, CRP, procalcitonin) and antioxidant measures (SOD, T-AOC) remained within normal ranges across all groups and time points, providing no diagnostic signal. NOx concentrations were significantly higher in symptomatic Long COVID patients than in asymptomatic recovered individuals more than 6 months post-infection (p=0.0013), with ROC analysis yielding an AUC of 0.656, sensitivity 83%, and specificity 48% at the optimal threshold, suggesting NOx may serve as a marker of endothelial dysfunction but with limited discriminatory accuracy.

Between-group p-values reported for within-period comparisons (Kruskal–Wallis p=0.0000 for NOx across periods, and Mann–Whitney pMW for arm1 vs arm2 in period 3). ROC curve data extracted from Figure 2 showing AUC=0.656 for NOx; optimal threshold 41.075 μmol/L, sensitivity 82.8%, specificity 48%.

trial_rating.result_basis: NOx higher in symptomatic vs asymptomatic group at >6 months post-infection, p=0.0013; ROC AUC=0.656 (95% CI 0.556–0.755), sensitivity 82.8%, specificity 48%.

summary: This observational study examined immune markers in 58 patients with histologically confirmed gastric adenocarcinoma who also had post-COVID syndrome symptoms, divided into three age groups (mean ages 51.5, 64.1, and 73.7 years). The researchers measured cytokines, complement components, toll-like receptors, lymphocyte subpopulations, and autoantibodies to characterize how post-COVID immune dysregulation interacts with cancer progression across age groups. Key findings included markedly elevated IL-1β (7.5-fold in the youngest group, 14-fold in the oldest), severely elevated IL-2 in younger patients (608 vs 16.5 pg/mL reference), and age-dependent patterns of complement C3 elevation, NK cell exhaustion, and autoantibody profiles. This is not a clinical trial testing an intervention — it is a cross-sectional descriptive study with no control group, no intervention, and no pre-specified primary outcome, making it unsuitable for rating as a Long COVID therapeutic trial.

summary: This observational study examined growth hormone (GH) axis disruption in 88 Long COVID patients by comparing serum proteomic and metabolomic profiles across four groups stratified by peak GH response during insulin tolerance testing. There was no intervention tested; the study identified molecular correlates of varying GH levels, finding that lower GH was associated with dysregulation of complement and coagulation cascade proteins (including C2, C3, C5, C8A/B/G), lipid metabolism proteins (apolipoproteins B, H, F), and the protein SPARCL1. Two metabolites, L-glutamic acid (AUC 0.657) and traumatic acid (AUC 0.739), showed modest ability to distinguish patients with GH 5–10 ng/mL from those with GH 1–5 ng/mL, and are proposed as potential biomarkers for GH deficiency stratification in Long COVID.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational, non-randomized, non-interventional cross-sectional study examining proteomic and metabolomic profiles across GH-stratified groups; not a clinical trial with treatment arms. No adverse events, no follow-up beyond single timepoint ITT. Study classified as quasi-experimental observational design rather than RCT. Proteomic and metabolomic outcomes extracted from figures and results text; specific per-protein data from DAP comparisons and figures not fully enumerated here due to size limits. Focused on main GH/cortisol temporal responses and key clinical biochemistry data from Table 2. Omitted detailed listing of all 31 individual metabolites and 79+ differentially abundant proteins; see paper Figures 4, 5, 8, 9 for full proteomic/metabolomic results.

trial_rating.result_basis: Best discriminative biomarker (traumatic acid) achieved AUC 0.739 for distinguishing GH subgroups; no clinical intervention outcome was tested and no placebo-controlled effect size is reported.

summary: This retrospective cohort study compared peripheral blood immune cell profiles in 58 adults with post-viral vasculitis (26 post-COVID-19, 32 herpesvirus-associated) against 20 healthy controls, with no intervention tested. Both vasculitis groups showed significantly reduced regulatory T cells compared to controls (post-COVID-19: 5.1% vs 8.2% in controls, p<0.001), expanded memory CD4+ T cells, elevated cytotoxic NK cells, and markers of chronic immune activation. Immune dysregulation was more pronounced in older patients, with cytotoxic NK cells rising from 70.6% in younger to 84.9% in older post-COVID-19 patients (p<0.001). This is an observational immunophenotyping study with no treatment arm, so findings describe immune abnormalities associated with post-viral vasculitis rather than any therapeutic effect.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is an observational immunological study comparing immune cell populations by flow cytometry across three cohorts, not a clinical trial of an intervention. summary: This is not a clinical trial. Researchers at the University of Colima trained decision tree machine learning models on a combined dataset of 488 records drawn from publicly available datasets (primarily from AIIMS, India) to predict the severity of Long COVID symptoms and sequelae based on pre-existing conditions such as smoking, diabetes, and hypertension. The models achieved 93.87% accuracy on the symptoms dataset and over 95% on the sequelae dataset across three severity classes (moderate, severe, critical). The study demonstrates the feasibility of interpretable AI tools for Long COVID prognosis but is not an intervention trial and provides no evidence about treatment efficacy.

summary: This is a mathematical modeling study, not a clinical trial: it applies probabilistic modeling to longitudinal immune response data from 110 COVID-19 recovery patients at the University of Virginia to characterize how spike IgG antibody and cytokine levels evolve after infection and vaccination across demographic subgroups. The study found that biological males had a higher antibody peak after infection (θ₁: 79.3 vs 29.6) but the models were more similar than different across most other demographic comparisons; males and females showed the greatest divergence with only 32.4% overlap in their two-event antibody response models. For the Long COVID-relevant finding, patients with abnormal pulmonary function tests post-COVID had persistently elevated cytokine signatures compared to those with normal lung function (naïve overlap: 81.8% vs 92.9%), with IL-6, IL-10, IP-10, and IL-1RA identified as the key cytokines driving this difference, though the study is observational and limited by small subgroup sample sizes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is an observational cohort study using mathematical modeling (probabilistic models with gamma distributions) to characterize antibody and cytokine kinetics post-SARS-CoV-2 infection, not a clinical trial with intervention and control arms. No randomization, allocation, or outcome data presented as simple numeric values for per-arm comparisons. All quantitative results are embedded in probabilistic model parameters (θ₁, θ₂, κ₁, etc.) and probability density function (PDF) visualizations rather than as traditional outcome means and SDs. Sample sizes listed in Table 1 represent measurement counts for three classes (naïve, infection only, infection-then-vaccinated) used to fit the models, not trial arm assignments. Overlap metrics (Table 6, Figures 8 and 10) are computed using extended Weitzman overlap method on 2D time-dependent distributions. No between-group effect sizes (mean differences, odds ratios, hazard ratios) reported; only model parameter comparisons provided. Subgroup analyses (sex, age, smoking, diabetes, PFT status) compare fitted model parameters, not raw outcome data. This structure precludes standard clinical trial data extraction; the study design, sample size allocation, and outcome reporting do not match RCT/controlled trial protocols.

trial_rating.result_basis: Abnormal PFT group overlapped with naïve cytokine distribution at 81.8% vs 92.9% for normal PFT group; no p-values or CIs reported, and no intervention was tested.

summary: Researchers at the University of Science and Technology of China tested HR1-VV-HR2-VS, a recombinant fusion protein vaccine built around conserved coronavirus spike protein regions (the HR1-HR2 structural scaffold plus two conserved epitope peptides VV and VS), in mice — not in Long COVID patients or any human clinical trial. In mouse challenge experiments, the vaccine reduced lung viral loads by 58–65% against HCoV-229E and by 76–79% against ancestral SARS-CoV-2 and 36–64% against the KP.2 variant compared to controls, while also broadly inhibiting cell fusion across multiple coronavirus strains. This is a preclinical animal study with no human trial data; it has no relevance to Long COVID treatment or patient outcomes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a preclinical vaccine immunogenicity and efficacy study, not a clinical trial. Most quantitative outcome data (means, SDs) appear only in figures without numerical values provided in tables or text, making detailed extraction challenging. Immunization schedules: mice received three intraperitoneal (weeks 0/2/4) or intramuscular doses with CpG/Al(OH)3 or Montanide ISA 720VG. Challenge studies: BALB/c mice intranasally challenged with HCoV-229E (5×10^4 TCID50, two doses 24h apart) on day 14 post-final immunization; K18-hACE2 mice challenged with SARS-CoV-2 prototype (5×10^4.5 TCID50) or KP.2 (5×10^4.25 TCID50) on day 14 post-final immunization. Statistical analyses: T-test (two-group comparisons), One-way ANOVA (multi-group data), Two-way ANOVA (time-course experiments); significance thresholds: *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001, ****p<0.0001. Paper does not report adverse events from animal studies. Not applicable for clinical Long COVID extraction criteria.

trial_rating.result_basis: Lung viral load reductions of 58–65% vs adjuvant-only in HCoV-229E challenge and 76% vs PBS in SARS-CoV-2 prototype challenge (one-way ANOVA, p values not individually quoted but stated as significant); n=4–5 mice per group.

summary: This small Egyptian RCT tested a daily herbal sachet containing 2g galangal (Alpinia officinarum) and 2g cinnamon (Cinnamomum zeylanicum) added to the standard COVID-19 treatment protocol in 19 patients with mild-to-moderate RT-PCR-confirmed COVID-19, compared to 19 controls receiving standard treatment alone. subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Incident lung cancer (COVID-19 vs no COVID-19)
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Lung cancer risk increased post-COVID-19 across all smoking strata, with highest HR in current smokers (HR 1.50, 95% CI 1.42–1.58), followed by former smokers (HR 1.60, 95% CI 1.54–1.66), and lowest in never smokers (HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.35–1.49). All comparisons p<0.001.

Among COVID-19+ current smokers, unvaccinated vs vaccinated showed RR 1.08 (95% CI 1.03–1.13, p=0.42) and HR 1.02 (95% CI 0.97–1.07); among former smokers, RR 1.19 (95% CI 1.15–1.23) and HR 1.14 (95% CI 1.10–1.17, p<0.001).

summary: This study investigated whether SARS-CoV-2 infection increases lung cancer risk, using both a large retrospective human cohort (TriNetX Research Network) and mouse models exposed to SARS-CoV-2 Spike Protein (SP). In the human cohort, prior COVID-19 infection was associated with a significantly higher risk of lung cancer across all smoking groups: hazard ratios of 1.50 (current smokers), 1.60 (former smokers), and 1.42 (never-smokers), all p<0.001. In mice, intratracheal SP delivery followed by urethane treatment produced tumors in 50% of lung lobes versus 10% in controls (p=0.0485), and TYMP-deficient mice showed dramatically reduced tumor incidence (18%), identifying thymidine phosphorylase (TYMP) as a key molecular driver of SP-induced lung fibrosis and tumorigenesis. This is a mechanistic/observational study, not a clinical trial of a therapeutic intervention, and the human data are retrospective and cannot establish causation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT a Long COVID clinical treatment trial. It is a retrospective observational cohort study (TriNetX EHR data) examining cancer risk post-COVID-19, combined with preclinical mechanistic mouse studies. The cohort study used propensity-score matching on age, sex, race, ethnicity; sample sizes and detailed baseline demographics per arm not reported (only aggregate risk values and HRs). Mouse studies used small n (10–50 lobes per group) with histological outcome assessment. Most quantitative data on lung injury, RAGE staining, MPO+ cells, microthrombi, and fibrosis measurements appear in figures only, not tables or text; per-arm means/SDs not extractable for these outcomes. No detailed adverse event reporting. Study design does not fit standard RCT template (quasi-experimental retrospective + preclinical). Risk of bias assessed descriptively rather than via RoB2 (which applies to randomized trials only). Oral and bladder cancer secondary outcomes show no consistent increase post-COVID across smoking strata, supporting organ-specificity of lung cancer association.

trial_rating.result_basis: Human cohort: HR 1.50 (95% CI 1.42-1.58) for current smokers, HR 1.60 (1.54-1.66) for former smokers, HR 1.42 (1.35-1.49) for never-smokers, all log-rank p<0.001. Mouse model: tumor incidence 50% (SP) vs 10% (control), Fisher's exact p=0.0485.

summary: This Canadian observational study attempted to build a clinical prediction rule to identify adult emergency department patients at high risk of developing Long COVID three months after a confirmed COVID-19 infection. Among 6,070 patients across 33 hospitals in five provinces, 41.4% reported Long COVID symptoms at three months. The derived rule included nine risk factors (female sex, higher respiratory rate at arrival, rheumatologic disorder, mental health diagnosis, and acute symptoms including sputum production, dizziness, diarrhea, chest pain, and fatigue) plus one protective factor (self-reported South Asian race), but achieved only an AUC of 0.626 — only slightly better than chance — and was not accurate enough to guide clinical decision-making, so external validation was abandoned.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is NOT a randomized controlled trial of an intervention but rather an observational cohort study with a clinical prediction modeling component. No intervention arms are present—the 'arms' represent the random split (derivation vs validation) used for model development and validation. The study assessed associated factors for PCC but did not test any treatment. Validation cohort results were not analyzed because the derived rule's AUC was <80%, below the prespecified threshold for proceeding to validation. All quantitative outcome data for PCC prevalence is from Table 1. The clinical prediction rule coefficients and ORs are from Table 2 but represent associational findings, not intervention effects.

trial_rating.result_basis: The derived clinical prediction rule achieved an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.626 (95% CI 0.610–0.643), falling well below the pre-specified 0.80 threshold required to proceed to validation.

summary: This is a proteomic study, not a clinical trial testing an intervention. Researchers analysed blood samples from 16 healthy controls, 20 pre-COVID-19 POTS patients, 19 Long COVID patients (without POTS), and 18 Long COVID-POTS patients to characterise post-translational modifications (PTMs) within insoluble fibrinaloid microclot complexes (FMCs). The primary finding was that PTM patterns — not overall protein levels — distinguish the three disease groups: Long COVID showed advanced glycation end-products and oxidation modifications on fibrinogen (particularly fibrinogen alpha chain), pre-COVID POTS showed metabolic-oxidative changes in apolipoproteins (apoA1, apoB) and immune complement proteins, and Long COVID-POTS shared features of both. FMC counts were numerically higher in all disease groups compared to controls but did not reach statistical significance after Bonferroni correction (controls vs Long COVID p=0.011, controls vs PC-POTS p=0.049, both non-significant at adjusted α=0.0083).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational case-control study, not a clinical trial. No interventions were tested, making this paper ineligible for systematic reviews of Long COVID treatment trials. The paper focuses on biomarker discovery through proteomics of plasma samples collected at a single timepoint. Only baseline/cross-sectional data are available. Risk of bias assessment using RoB2 is not applicable; the study has inherent limitations of observational design including potential confounding, lack of blinding to group status during laboratory analysis, and uncontrolled differences in age and sex distribution between groups. Several outcomes had data only partially reported in supplementary tables; all available numeric values have been extracted. The paper includes extensive detailed proteomics findings on individual PTM peptides (29 base peptides, 64 uniquely modified peptides); primary focus was on between-group comparisons rather than per-arm descriptive statistics for individual peptides.

trial_rating.result_basis: Primary FMC count outcome was non-significant after multiple-testing correction (one-way ANOVA F=1.87, p=0.143; Mann-Whitney pairwise comparisons non-significant at Bonferroni-adjusted α=0.0083); PTM findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating with no pre-specified primary endpoint.
