summary: This observational neuroimaging study used normative brain modelling (CentileBrain) to map cortical structural deviations in 20 adults with persistent fatigue following mild COVID-19, compared to 20 matched recovered controls. At the group level, Long COVID patients showed subtly reduced cortical thickness in orbitofrontal regions and increased thickness in occipital/sensory cortices, but no individual brain region showed extreme deviations in more than 35% of patients, and no finding survived correction for multiple comparisons. Circuit-level analysis revealed that structural deviations clustered within anatomically connected networks, affecting up to 50% more Long COVID patients than controls within specific circuits; network diffusion modelling identified posterior-temporoparietal regions as likely propagation epicentres, and these regions also showed higher expression of TMPRSS2, the gene encoding the key SARS-CoV-2 entry protein. This is a small, cross-sectional, observational study with no intervention — it characterises brain structural patterns but cannot establish causation or treatment implications.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational neuroimaging study, not a clinical trial. No intervention is tested; the paper presents cross-sectional comparative neuroanatomical mapping between PCS cases and healthy controls. Quantitative outcome data (per-arm means, SDs) are not reported in tables or figures—only group-level statistical contrasts (p-values, Spearman correlations, CCA loadings) are provided. The network diffusion modelling result (r=0.703, p<0.001) is explicitly reported. Most individual-level data points are either summarized narratively or visualized only in figures (Figure 1 violin plots, Figures 2-4, Figure 6). Demographic details for baseline characteristics are stated as 'no significant differences' (p>0.5) but specific means/SDs are not provided. Blood routine parameters and cytokine data are referenced as in Supplementary Tables but not reproduced in the main text. Cognitive testing results mention specific p-values and Bayes factors for selective comparisons but not full per-arm metrics. This extraction reflects the limited quantitative detail available in a neuroimaging-focused observational study without an intervention component.

trial_rating.result_basis: No regional finding survived FDR correction; individual region deviations present in <35% of patients; circuit-level overlap difference up to 50% excess in PCS but based on uncorrected analyses in N=20 per group.

summary: This observational case-control neuroimaging study (not a clinical trial) examined resting-state brain dynamics in 20 adults with Post-COVID-19 Syndrome (PCS) compared to 20 recovered controls, using Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis (LEiDA) of fMRI data. PCS patients spent significantly less time in a brain state associated with visual and dorsal attention networks (State 1: probability 0.136 vs 0.185, p=0.004) and more time in a limbic/default mode network state (State 5: probability 0.277 vs 0.207, p=0.021), suggesting a shift away from externally focused attention toward internally directed processing. PCS patients also showed reduced transitions between attentional and frontoparietal states and increased transitions into the limbic-DMN state. summary: This preclinical mouse study investigated whether SARS-CoV-2 infection disrupts the brain's orexin (hypocretin) system and whether restoring orexin signalling can reverse associated neuronal damage relevant to Long COVID. In two mouse models (K18-hACE2 transgenic and wild-type BALB/c mice), SARS-CoV-2 infection suppressed hypothalamic orexin gene expression by up to 98% at peak infection (day 6) and caused persistent, patchy loss of the cortical neuronal marker NeuN lasting up to 90 days post-infection — effects not seen with influenza A virus despite comparable brain viral loads. Intranasal administration of recombinant orexin-A/B peptides to infected mice restored brain NeuN protein levels to approximately 1.8-fold above mock-infected controls without altering viral replication, identifying orexin system disruption as a potential mechanism underlying Long COVID neurological symptoms such as fatigue, cognitive impairment, and sleep disturbance. This is a preprint animal study with no human participants, so findings require significant further validation before any clinical conclusions can be drawn.

This paper describes a preclinical research study, NOT a human clinical trial, and therefore does not meet inclusion criteria for a systematic review of Long COVID clinical trials. The study uses animal models (mice) and in vitro cell systems to investigate mechanisms of SARS-CoV-2-induced neuronal pathology. No primary or secondary efficacy outcomes in human patients are reported. Quantitative data are presented in narrative form and supplementary figures rather than in traditional trial tables; specific numerical values for means, SDs, and effect sizes were extracted where explicitly stated in the text. The study does not have randomized control arms in the traditional RCT sense, randomization methods, or human participant demographics. Figure-based data were not quantified due to the extraction protocol limit. No adverse events data are provided for treated animals, only mortality rates. This paper should be excluded from a human Long COVID trial meta-analysis.

summary: This observational study measured IgG antibody subclasses (IgG1–4) and IgE against 14 SARS-CoV-2 spike protein variants in 15 Long COVID patients (symptoms >20 weeks) and 15 vaccinated non-Long COVID controls, using a biophotonic array platform. summary: This laboratory study screened 129 purified human monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) against the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor-binding domain (RBD), plus 10 hybridoma supernatants, to test whether any antibodies produced after COVID-19 infection mimic the enzymatic activity of ACE2 — the host enzyme that regulates blood pressure and which the virus uses as its entry receptor. Four of the ten hybridoma-derived anti-RBD mAbs showed measurable ACE2-like catalytic activity above the detection threshold, confirmed by co-depletion with immunoglobulin (>99.99% efficiency) and inhibition by competing RBD peptides; none of the 129 purified mAbs from three other sources showed activity, likely due to purification conditions disrupting fragile catalytic conformations. The catalytic efficiency of the active antibodies was approximately 10,000-fold lower than native ACE2 (Kcat/Km ~20–35 M⁻¹s⁻¹ vs ~868,000 M⁻¹s⁻¹), but the authors propose that long-lived circulating antibodies operating over months could cumulatively dysregulate blood pressure and inflammatory signalling in Long COVID. This is a mechanistic proof-of-concept study with no patient outcomes measured; it does not test any intervention.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a biochemical screening study of monoclonal antibodies, not a clinical trial. No patient enrollment, randomization, or clinical outcomes were assessed. The study analyzed 140 mAbs from 4 sources; only 4 mAbs (all from a single source, Precision Antibody) showed ACE2-like catalytic activity above the predetermined threshold. Additional 9 mAbs showed borderline activity but fell below the significance cutoff. All kinetic parameters (Km, Vmax, Kcat, Kcat/Km) are from Table 3 for the four positive-activity mAbs. IgG concentrations and depletion efficiency values are from Tables 3 and 4. No comparative arms, no randomization, no clinical outcomes — this is a discovery/characterization study. Risk of bias assessment is not applicable to this study design.

trial_rating.result_basis: 4 of 10 hybridoma supernatant mAbs exceeded the ACE2-activity threshold (slope >0.5 RFU/min); 0 of 129 purified mAbs showed activity; no patient clinical outcomes or statistical comparisons between groups were reported.

summary: This study evaluated the usability of eight public-facing knowledge mobilization resources (four online resource sheets and four interactive infographics) developed to communicate Canadian Long COVID clinical guidelines to adults in Canada, including people with and without lived Long COVID experience. summary: This observational EEG study examined resting-state brain oscillations in 31 Long COVID patients with new-onset chronic musculoskeletal pain compared to 31 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. The key finding is that lower peak alpha frequency (PAF) over the posterior scalp region was associated with greater pain severity in Long COVID patients, independent of age and depression (standardised β = -0.581, FDR-corrected p = 0.027). Subgroup analysis showed patients with severe pain had significantly lower posterior PAF than those with moderate pain, while patients with moderate pain unexpectedly showed higher PAF than healthy controls. No differences in alpha band power were found between groups, and the study was cross-sectional with a small sample (n=31 per group), limiting causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cross-sectional study, not a randomized controlled trial. It lacks treatment allocation, intervention arms, and randomization. Outcome data (per-arm means/SDs for PAF) not explicitly provided in tables or text for the overall patient and control groups—only regional/subgroup comparisons and regression model coefficients reported. Moderate and severe pain subgroups were post-hoc stratifications based on median split of pain severity, not pre-specified. Between-group comparisons at channel level available via cluster-permutation analysis but specific electrode-wise per-arm PAF values not tabulated. Study focused on biomarker associations rather than clinical trial outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: Posterior PAF negatively predicted pain severity (standardised β = -0.581, adj. R² = 0.352, FDR-corrected p = 0.027); no intervention effect tested — this is an observational biomarker association study.

summary: This exploratory immunological sub-study of the PAX LC trial tested a 15-day course of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) versus placebo/ritonavir in 82 adults with Long COVID, measuring immune and virological markers in blood before and after treatment. Neither arm showed changes in circulating SARS-CoV-2 spike protein levels, immune cell populations, or anti-spike antibody responses after treatment, providing a biological explanation for why nirmatrelvir failed to improve symptoms in the parent trial. Across both treatment arms regardless of drug assignment, participants who reported symptom improvement showed significantly lower levels of the inflammatory chemokine RANTES (CCL5), identifying it as a candidate biomarker of recovery rather than a treatment effect.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an exploratory immunological sub-study of the main PAX LC trial, not the primary efficacy trial itself. The study reports no between-group differences in major endpoints (spike protein, antibodies, immune cells) and focuses on within-group changes and post-hoc analyses of symptom improvers. Data on per-arm means and SDs for most biomarkers are not provided in the text/tables; values are only in figures (volcano plots, scatter plots). Per-arm baseline sample sizes for most biomarkers were not explicitly stated but inferred from the n=45 placebo and n=37 nirmatrelvir participants analyzed. The paper includes extended data tables referenced but not fully reproduced in the preprint; extracted p-values for within-arm comparisons are from text statements (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank test p-values for baseline vs day 28). Multiple outcomes measured 105 circulating cytokines; RANTES and IL-5 are highlighted as having the strongest associations with symptom improvement. A permutation test was used to validate the clustering of improvers vs non-improvers based on the top 10 immune modulators.

In females, Severe Neuro LC participants showed higher microbial diversity and evenness than No-Neuro participants, with shifts in community composition. Similar pattern observed in males at 6 and/or 12 months.

LC Neuro-derived GMEVs produced the largest reduction in colon length relative to vehicle. Serum LBP was increased in all GMEV-treated groups; serum BAFF was significantly elevated only in mice receiving Neuro-derived GMEVs compared with controls.

summary: This mechanistic study investigated whether gut microbiota-derived extracellular vesicles (GMEVs) from Long COVID patients link intestinal dysbiosis to neuroinflammation. Using a cohort of 103 participants (91 Long COVID, 12 pandemic controls), the researchers found that GMEVs isolated from Long COVID patients with neurological symptoms activated inflammasome pathways, disrupted intestinal barrier integrity, and triggered inflammatory responses in macrophages and iPSC-derived microglia in vitro. In germ-free mice colonized with Long COVID microbiota, and in wild-type mice given oral GMEV gavage for 6 weeks, researchers observed intestinal inflammation, behavioral changes consistent with impaired spatial memory, and glial activation in brain tissue. This is a preclinical mechanistic study, not a clinical trial, so findings demonstrate biological plausibility of a gut-brain inflammatory axis in Long COVID but do not establish clinical efficacy of any treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is primarily an observational cohort study combined with mechanistic animal and in vitro experiments, not a randomized controlled trial of a therapeutic intervention in humans. No primary or secondary outcome numerical data (means, SDs, p-values, effect sizes) are reported in tables or text for the human cohort analyses—all quantitative findings are presented as figures only. The experimental arms described (LC Neuro microbiota transplant, LC No-Neuro transplant, PC transplant, vehicle control, and GMEV treatments) are animal studies. No human RCT data comparing treatment efficacy are available. Outcome data extraction is limited to what can be inferred from the narrative description of results; specific per-arm means, SDs, and statistical comparisons for the animal experiments are not reported numerically in the paper text or tables.

trial_rating.result_basis: LC Neuro GMEVs produced the strongest reduction in TEER (barrier impairment) vs PC-derived GMEVs; 2,631 differentially expressed genes in microglia (adjusted P<0.05); mice receiving Neuro GMEVs showed increased locomotion and reduced successful Y-maze alternations vs controls, with significant GFAP and IBA1 upregulation in brain tissue. No specific p-values or effect sizes for primary outcomes were extractable from the provided text.

summary: This is not a clinical trial. It is a structural biology laboratory study examining how the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binds to contactin 1 (CNTN1), a neuronal cell adhesion protein thought to act as a co-receptor facilitating viral entry into the nervous system. Using surface plasmon resonance and cryo-electron microscopy, researchers found that spike binds CNTN1 with 67 nM affinity via the Ig1-4 horseshoe domain of CNTN1 interacting with the spike receptor-binding domain in its upward conformation. The binding site on the spike RBD is distinct from the ACE2 binding site but overlaps with class 4 neutralizing antibody epitopes, suggesting possible relevance to neurovirulence and Long COVID neurological symptoms. No patients were enrolled and no clinical outcomes were measured.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper does not meet the inclusion criteria for a Long COVID clinical trial extraction. It is a structural biology and virology research paper using recombinant proteins and cryo-EM. No clinical data, patient populations, randomization, intervention arms, or outcome measures are present. While long-COVID is mentioned in the abstract and introduction as motivation for understanding SARS-CoV-2 neurotropism, the study itself is bench-top molecular research with no therapeutic intervention tested in human subjects.

trial_rating.result_basis: No clinical trial was conducted; this is a preprint structural biology study with no patient population, no intervention, and no clinical outcome data. Binding affinity KD = 67 ± 12 nM is a biochemical measurement, not a clinical effect size.

summary: This laboratory study exposed olfactory neuroepithelial stem cells (ONEs) from a healthy donor to serum from either critically ill COVID-19 patients (n=6) or asymptomatic PCR-positive individuals (n=4), then used mass spectrometry to compare protein expression profiles. Exposure to critical-patient serum produced 199 significantly differentially expressed proteins (86 up-regulated, 113 down-regulated), with pathway analysis linking these changes to neurodegeneration, psychiatric disorders, coagulation dysfunction, and mitochondrial impairment. Key proteins affected included SOD2 and MOCOS (oxidative stress, up-regulated), and SMAD2, MECP2, and SRR (neuroplasticity and NMDA signalling, down-regulated), suggesting molecular mechanisms that could underlie Long COVID neurological symptoms. This is a very small ex vivo mechanistic study with no patient outcomes measured and no clinical intervention tested, so findings are hypothesis-generating only.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a basic science/translational cell biology study, not a clinical trial of Long COVID treatments. It uses ex vivo cell culture and proteomics, not clinical interventions or patient outcomes. No randomization, blinding, allocation concealment, or adverse events are applicable. Serum sample sizes are very small (n=4-6). The study demonstrates proof-of-concept that serum from critical COVID-19 patients triggers differential proteomic responses in neural progenitor cells that resemble patterns seen in neurodegenerative diseases, but it does not test any intervention or measure clinical efficacy. Multiple neurological and psychiatric disease pathways were identified via bioinformatic pathway analysis rather than clinical outcomes. The paper is not suitable for standard systematic review extraction of clinical trial data but may be relevant as mechanistic evidence for Long COVID neurological pathology.

trial_rating.result_basis: This is not a clinical trial; no patient outcome was measured. The study reports 199 DEPs (p<0.05, fold-change >1 or <-1) in an ex vivo cell model comparing n=6 vs n=4 serum samples, with no control arm or clinical endpoint.

summary: This study used spatial transcriptomics, RNAscope, and multiplex immunofluorescence to examine gut tissue biopsies (terminal ileum and left colon) from 8 Long COVID patients and 5 healthy controls, investigating whether SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA and protein persist in the gastrointestinal tract and what immune changes occur in those regions. SARS-CoV-2 spike RNA was detected at significantly higher levels in Long COVID colon tissue versus controls (H-score median 3.158 vs 1.160, p=0.006), and regions containing spike protein showed enrichment of macrophages, non-classical monocytes, plasma cells, and regulatory T cells, with upregulation of antigen-processing pathways. The study is observational and mechanistic rather than a clinical trial, with a very small, sex-imbalanced cohort (predominantly female Long COVID, predominantly male controls) and no matched pre-pandemic controls, severely limiting generalisability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cross-sectional study, not a clinical trial, without randomization or intervention assignment. Data extracted are tissue-based biomarker measurements only; no patient-reported outcomes or clinical endpoints are available. Most quantitative results are reported as medians without SDs; per-arm means calculated from median values reported in text. Between-group p-values extracted from Mann-Whitney U tests; many comparisons show non-significant differences despite directional effects. Figure 1E data states 'Long COVID = 4; Healthy = 2' for RNAscope analyses, suggesting smaller n than overall cohort (n=8 LC, n=5 controls) for some outcomes. Several key findings (differential gene expression, pathway enrichment, immune cell proportions) reported qualitatively without complete quantitative data tables. Supplementary tables referenced but not provided in the paper text. No adverse events, withdrawals, or loss-to-followup reported (consistent with cross-sectional design with single tissue collection visit).

summary: This study measured circulating platelet-monocyte aggregates (PMA) in 20 Long COVID patients compared with 20 healthy controls to assess whether PMA levels reflect ongoing thromboinflammatory activity. PMA were markedly elevated in Long COVID patients (median 29.2% of monocytes) versus controls (median 4.6%), a difference that held across both sexes and was independent of age. Long COVID patients also showed a shift toward multiple platelets attached per monocyte (57% vs 30% in controls), suggesting more severe platelet activation. Key caveats: this is a small, cross-sectional, observational biomarker study — not an intervention trial — with groups that were not age-matched (median age 45 vs 25 years), and no causal or therapeutic conclusions can be drawn.

summary: This observational immunology study profiled T-cell receptor (TCR) beta-chain repertoires from 120 people in the INCOV cohort — 71 with Long COVID (PASC+) and 49 without — sampled longitudinally across the acute and post-acute phases of ancestral SARS-CoV-2 infection in 2020. Overall TCR repertoire statistics (gene usage, CDR3 length, clonality) did not differ between groups, but computational analysis identified distinct sequence motifs and clonal dynamics associated with PASC status, including a significant enrichment of Influenza A-specific TCRs among contracting clones in PASC+ individuals (p=0.016), suggesting viral co-infection as a contributor to disease severity. PASC+ individuals also harbored a modestly but significantly higher proportion of rare public SARS-CoV-2-specific TCRs than PASC- individuals (18% vs 14.4% MIRA matches, p=4.18×10⁻¹²), and the study identified 1,091 candidate TCR sequences potentially discriminating PASC+ from PASC- immune responses. This is a non-interventional mechanistic study on a preprint — no treatment was tested and findings require validation in larger, more recent cohorts with paired TCR chain sequencing.

Several key numeric values were extracted from table text and figures. The paper reports TCR matching percentages and p-values for group comparisons. Sample sizes for subgroup analyses (e.g., individuals with Influenza A-specific TCR matches) were extracted from text. No adverse events reporting is applicable as this was observational sequencing research. Follow-up durations were not standardized across participants (2-3 time points spanning 2-169 days post-enrollment). Risk of bias assessment using RoB2 is not applicable to observational studies; key concerns relate to confounding by baseline disease severity and lack of randomization.

summary: This is a preclinical mouse study, not a human clinical trial. Researchers infected 4-6-month-old mice with a mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 strain (SARS2-N501Y MA30) to model neurological Long COVID (neuroPASC), then used single-cell RNA sequencing and flow cytometry to map brain immune cell changes over 100 days. The key finding is that microglia — the brain's resident immune cells — underwent persistent inflammatory activation lasting at least 100 days post-infection, including sustained upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-1β, IL-18) and mitochondrial dysfunction, even without direct viral invasion of the brain. Infiltrating monocytes and neutrophils showed strong antiviral responses only during acute infection (day 6) and then declined, while microglial inflammation persisted, suggesting microglia are the primary driver of chronic neuroinflammation in this model.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a preclinical, mechanistic animal model study, not a clinical trial of human participants. The paper contains no quantitative per-arm summary statistics (means, SDs) for behavioral or immunological outcomes—only figures and descriptive text indicating statistical significance by p-value ranges. Sample sizes vary by analysis (scRNA-seq: 4-5 mice per timepoint pooled; flow cytometry: 9 infected + 12 mock controls at 6 dpi, 9 infected + ? controls at 30 dpi; behavioral tests: n=7-18 per arm per timepoint). All numeric data from behavioral tests (Fig. 1e, 1f, 1h) and flow cytometry (Fig. 2d-g) appear only in figures; no mean/SD values provided in text tables. scRNA-seq data presented as proportions in UMAP plots (Fig. 3d) and heatmaps (Figs. 4, 5, 6) with no per-population mean expression values tabulated. Outcome results marked 'not_reported' reflect absence of extractable numeric data in figures at resolution readable in the paper submission. Study includes scRNA-seq whole-brain immune profiling (20,153 cells total) with subclustering analyses but these are descriptive rather than quantitative outcome measures for meta-analysis.

trial_rating.result_basis: Infected mice showed significantly reduced social preference index at 20 dpi vs mock controls (p<0.05 by one-way ANOVA with Dunnett's test); 14.8% of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes significantly downregulated (log2FC ≤ -1) in inflammatory microglial subclusters. summary: This is a preclinical mouse study (not a human clinical trial) testing intranasal anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody (foralumab) in a mouse model of Long COVID, where SARS-CoV-2 infection was restricted to the respiratory tract but caused persistent brain inflammation. Mice treated with nasal anti-CD3 showed significantly reduced microglial and astrocytic activation in the hippocampus and white matter, restored hippocampal neurogenesis (increased DCX+ neuroblasts), and recovered short-term memory performance on a novel object recognition test compared to untreated infected controls. Treatment worked both when started early (1 week post-infection) and late (4 weeks post-infection, mimicking established Long COVID). A complementary analysis of a human Long COVID cohort found that patients with neurological symptoms including brain fog had significantly lower circulating regulatory T cell (Treg) populations, supporting the proposed mechanism, though no human treatment data are reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a preclinical mouse model study (not a human clinical trial). The paper presents two experimental paradigms: early intranasal anti-CD3 treatment (starting 1 week post-infection) and delayed treatment (starting 4 weeks post-infection). Sample sizes ranged from 3-7 mice per arm depending on outcome and timepoint. No formal randomization or blinding procedures described. Quantitative data for most neuroimaging outcomes (IBA1+, GFAP+, DCX+ cell counts) not explicitly stated in numeric form in text/tables but inferred from Figure descriptions and statistical reporting. Flow cytometry data (Foxp3+ cell frequencies) and cytokine/chemokine levels (CXCL10, IL-10, CCL11) reported as significant but exact numeric values for per-arm means and SDs not provided in the main text — only p-values and directional statements given. Clinical correlate analysis from MY-LC cohort (Klein et al., 2023) used cross-sectional data showing association between reduced circulating Tregs and cognitive symptoms in Long COVID patients but no per-group quantitative values provided. This extraction prioritized outcomes with the most complete quantitative reporting; secondary biomarker and exploratory analyses had limited numeric detail in the source text.

trial_rating.result_basis: Isotype-treated post-COVID mice failed novel object recognition (no preference for novel object), while nasal anti-CD3-treated mice showed restored preference comparable to mock-infected controls (p<0.05); DCX+ neuroblast density was significantly increased by anti-CD3 in both early and late treatment paradigms (p<0.05 vs isotype), and brain Foxp3+ Tregs were significantly expanded by anti-CD3 treatment.

summary: This case-control study from Vanderbilt University compared 25 adults with Long COVID postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (LCPOTS) to 15 COVID-recovered controls without persistent autonomic symptoms. The primary finding was a roughly threefold increase in circulating CD3+CD14+ T cell-monocyte doublets in LCPOTS patients, which were confirmed to represent true immune synapses via FRET imaging; the frequency of inflammatory cytokine-producing doublets (IFN-γ+ and IL-17A+) correlated positively with the magnitude of orthostatic heart rate rise and total COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom score. Monocytes from LCPOTS patients showed approximately twofold higher mitochondrial superoxide production, elevated IsoLG protein adducts across all monocyte subsets, and reduced expression of antioxidant genes including NFE2L2, SOD2, and GPX4, pointing to oxidative stress as a driver of persistent immune activation. This is a mechanistic observational study, not an intervention trial, so causal direction cannot be established from these cross-sectional data.

summary: This phase IIb randomized controlled trial (Neuromod-COV) tested whether working-memory cognitive training (CT), with or without transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) over the left prefrontal cortex, could improve cognition in 60 adults with Long COVID cognitive complaints (mean 13 months post-infection, 77% female). CT alone did not improve untrained working memory compared to progressive muscle relaxation (the primary outcome). However, among CT participants, those receiving active tDCS outperformed those receiving sham tDCS on harder working memory tasks at both post-intervention and one-month follow-up, and on a visuospatial memory task immediately after treatment; no intervention improved functional status or quality of life. The trial was well-conducted but small and single-site, limiting generalizability.

summary: This observational study used single-cell RNA sequencing to compare immune cell gene expression in 20 Long COVID patients and 18 recovered COVID-19 controls, all African American adults aged 50 or older. Across 156,478 profiled blood immune cells, Long COVID patients showed multi-compartment immune dysregulation: naive B cells were chronically activated via IL-4/BCR signaling, monocytes displayed heightened migratory and interferon-response programs with impaired differentiation, CD4+ central memory T cells were quiescent and blocked from differentiating into effector cells, and NK cells were terminally differentiated with high cytotoxicity but poor regulatory function. Severe Long COVID was specifically linked to AP-1-driven inflammation in NK cells and CD14+ monocytes, while less severe cases retained metabolically active NK cells with lower exhaustion scores. This is a mechanistic profiling study, not a clinical trial testing an intervention, so no treatment effect size is reported.

Viral repertoire findings (Retroviridae and Poxviridae enrichment in Long COVID) are reported qualitatively in figures 6F-G with no quantitative values extracted.

summary: This preclinical rat study examined whether chronic cocaine exposure worsens Long-COVID-like outcomes caused by a single intravenous injection of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (500 ng/kg), testing 38 male Sprague-Dawley rats across four groups over two months. Rats exposed to both spike and cocaine showed persistent reductions in weight gain (significant from day 11 post-spike), increased mechanical pain sensitivity (lower paw withdrawal thresholds vs. controls and their own baseline, p=0.010–0.023), and a pro-inflammatory shift in the hippocampus (elevated IL-6/IL-10 ratio, p<0.05 for both spike and cocaine main effects). Spike protein alone reduced time spent sniffing an odor attractant two months post-injection, recapitulating Long-COVID anosmia, while cocaine produced an anxiolytic-like and impulsive-like phenotype on the elevated plus maze. This is a non-clinical animal study using spike protein injection rather than live virus infection, and results in male rats may not translate to humans or account for sex differences.

summary: This observational case-control study examined whether salivary shedding of herpesviruses (EBV, HHV-6, HSV, CMV) and salivary hormone levels differed between 45 Long COVID patients and 45 age-sex-matched recovered controls in New York City, approximately two years after initial infection. The primary finding was that neither EBV nor HHV-6 salivary shedding rates or DNA levels differed significantly between Long COVID and control groups; however, higher salivary HHV-6 DNA copy numbers were positively correlated with a composite Long COVID symptom severity score (Spearman R=0.248, adjusted p=0.030) and were nominally associated with greater anxiety (GAD-7, p=0.045) and depression (PHQ-2, p=0.013) scores across all participants. Salivary cortisol, testosterone, and estradiol also showed no significant differences between groups. The study is limited by its small sample size, cross-sectional design, and the fact that several nominal associations with individual symptoms did not survive multiple testing correction.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an observational case-control biomarker study, not an RCT. The paper is a preprint (medRxiv) reporting primarily correlational/associational findings. Viral DNA values (mean and SD) were not explicitly reported per arm — only between-group p-values and effect size (r) were provided. Hormone values (cortisol, testosterone, estradiol) were shown in figures but exact per-arm means/SDs not clearly stated in text. No formal adverse event reporting section. Excluded from outcomes: S-LANSS (neuropathic pain scale) since only LC group measured (27 participants), making between-group comparison impossible. Multiple outcome analyses with liberal p-values and post-hoc corrections suggest need for hypothesis validation in future studies.

trial_rating.result_basis: No significant difference in HHV-6 or EBV shedding between LC and control groups (HHV-6 trend r=0.246, p=0.096; EBV trend r=-0.241, p=0.099); the only surviving association was HHV-6 vs. composite severity score (R=0.248, adj.p=0.030), a secondary exploratory finding.

summary: This laboratory study investigated whether host microRNAs (miRNAs) that are suppressed in Long COVID patients with co-existing periodontal disease (PD) can directly target and inhibit SARS-CoV-2 spike and nucleocapsid viral transcripts. Saliva samples from 10 patients per group showed broad downregulation of miRNAs in those with both prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and PD, with miR-106b-3p, miR-652-3p, and miR-30e-3p among the most reduced. In cell experiments, transfecting miR-106b-3p mimics into ACE2-expressing lung cells reduced spike-protein-positive cells by 84% (Beta variant) and 78% (Omicron) at 24 hours post-infection, while miR-652-3p reduced nucleocapsid RNA approximately 10-fold at 48 hours; these miRNAs also suppressed NF-κB activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine release in oral keratinocytes. This is a mechanistic lab study, not a clinical trial — no intervention was tested in patients, so results cannot be directly applied to Long COVID treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is an observational mechanistic study, not a clinical trial. The three comparison groups (arms) are observational cohorts, not randomly assigned. Some effect data from viral infection experiments are reported only in figures (not in tables), hence quantified spike-positive cells and nucleocapsid fold-reduction values are stated in results text but detailed per-arm means/SDs not always available; reported p-values for relative luciferase assay indicate significance but fold-change/effect-size values inferred from figure descriptions. Baseline demographics (age, BMI, gender distribution) not reported. Study has no placebo or active treatment arms — it is a cross-sectional/observational design with functional laboratory validation. Some outcomes are measured from cell line experiments (transfected with miRNA mimics) which are intervention-like but conducted in vitro; these results do not reflect clinical outcomes.

trial_rating.result_basis: miR-106b-3p mimic reduced spike-positive cells by 84% (B.1.351) and 78% (B.1.1.529) at 24 hpi (p<0.001); miR-652-3p reduced nucleocapsid RNA ~10-fold at 48 hpi with B.1.351 (p<0.01) and B.1.1.529 (p<0.0001); patient cohort n=10/group.

summary: This study tested whether culturally tailored animated educational videos (four ~60-second animations incorporating Latino cultural symbols and co-designed with Latino artists) increased Long COVID knowledge among 271 Hispanic/Latino adults in Arizona. Knowledge scores improved significantly after watching the videos, rising from a mean of 4.39 to 4.74 out of 7 (paired t-test t=3.788, p=0.000186), with gains observed across all education levels. Notably, the study has no control group, so the improvement cannot be definitively attributed to the videos rather than test familiarity; female participants scored lower than males after the intervention despite typically being more proactive health information seekers.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper is not a randomized controlled trial and does not test an intervention against a control comparator or alternative intervention in a traditional sense; it is a descriptive pre-post study of a single intervention. No arms with different treatments were compared. Demographic details (age, gender breakdown, BMI, comorbidities) were collected but not reported in summary form in the paper; only regression coefficients for gender and education interactions were provided. No adverse events were reported. The study uses a quasi-experimental design with significant limitations for causal inference. Internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.661) was reported for the 7-item knowledge scale. The regression model (R²=0.06) accounted for a modest proportion of variance. Several interaction effects involving age and design perception features were reported at the 0.05 and 0.10 significance levels. Time from pre- to post-survey was immediate (same day or within survey session), hence treatment and total follow-up duration are both 0 weeks.

trial_rating.result_basis: Mean knowledge score increased from 4.39 to 4.74/7 (paired t=3.788, p=0.000186), a raw gain of 0.35 points on a 7-point scale with no control group.

summary: This cross-sectional validation study tested whether remote (telehealth) versions of the 1-minute sit-to-stand test (STS) — delivered synchronously via video call or asynchronously via recorded video — produce valid and reliable results compared to in-person testing in 38 adults with Long COVID who did not require ventilatory support during their acute illness. The primary outcome was repetition count across modalities: both remote formats correlated significantly with in-person scores (synchronous ICC=0.86, asynchronous ICC=0.69), though remote testing produced about 10% more repetitions than in-person testing, likely due to a learning effect. Self-reported repetition counts showed excellent agreement with evaluator-scored asynchronous video (ICC=0.98, mean overestimation of only 3.3%), and inter-rater reliability between two independent video scorers was excellent (ICC=0.99). The study confirms remote STS testing is feasible and valid for Long COVID monitoring, but the systematic ~2-repetition increase with later test order and wider limits of agreement for asynchronous testing (MDC ~11 repetitions) mean individual longitudinal tracking requires caution.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a validation/reliability study, not a randomized controlled trial testing an intervention. It uses a within-subject crossover design comparing three assessment modalities. No adverse events reported. Sample size calculated a priori for correlation analysis with power 85%. Study had no dropouts. The paper reports SEM and MDC values, which are normally derived from test-retest data under stable conditions but here are applied to agreement between modalities per the authors' own acknowledgment in limitations. Bland-Altman limits of agreement are reported but not extracted as quantitative outcomes. The study was registered with ethics committee but not in a clinical trial registry (not applicable for a validation study). Learning/fatigue effect of 1.8 repetitions associated with test order identified in linear mixed-effects model analysis.

trial_rating.result_basis: Synchronous remote vs. in-person ICC=0.86 but with ~10% more repetitions remotely (mean difference -2.1 reps, limits of agreement -7.3 to 3.0); asynchronous ICC=0.69, just below the COSMIN threshold of 0.70 for adequate validity; n=38 total.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Mortality rates varied by site: Guangzhou 5.2% (44/845), Shenzhen 6.4% (34/531), Dongguan 6.9% (22/317). Age distribution differed significantly (p<0.001), with Dongguan having older patients (mean 66.9 vs 57.1-57.7 years). Severe pneumonia prevalence was higher at Dongguan (20.5%) vs Guangzhou (6.5%).

summary: This retrospective observational study analysed mortality risk factors among 1,693 adults hospitalised with COVID-19 pneumonia (Omicron B.1.1.529 variant) across three hospitals in Guangdong, China, between October 2022 and February 2023. The overall in-hospital mortality rate was 5.9% (100 deaths). Using multivariate logistic regression and three machine learning algorithms, the study identified 37 factors significantly associated with death, with severe pneumonia (adjusted OR 20.04), respiratory failure (adjusted OR 11.60), and elevated D-dimer (adjusted OR 7.72) among the strongest predictors. A random forest model achieved the best predictive performance (AUC 0.907, sensitivity 0.875, specificity 0.870), and a web-based risk calculator was developed for clinical use. This is not an interventional trial and does not test a treatment; it is a prognostic modelling study with no comparison group or control arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a clinical trial and should not be included in Long COVID systematic reviews. It is a retrospective observational cohort study focused on mortality risk prediction in COVID-19 pneumonia patients during acute hospitalization (October 2022–February 2023), not a study of Long COVID interventions. No treatment arms, no randomization to interventions, no efficacy outcome evaluation. The study uses machine learning to build predictive models but does not test any therapeutic intervention. Additionally, the paper does not explicitly define Long COVID; it focuses on acute COVID-19 pneumonia outcomes. Study population is hospitalized acute COVID-19 patients, not Long COVID patients. Participants were followed for one year to assess survival, not to evaluate treatment efficacy for persistent post-COVID symptoms.

trial_rating.result_basis: No intervention was tested; this is a prognostic observational study. The best-performing model (random forest) achieved AUC 0.907 (95% CI 0.849–0.957) for predicting in-hospital mortality. Effect_strength set to 0 as there is no treatment effect to rate.

summary: This paper is not a Long COVID clinical trial. It is a retrospective observational study of Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia in Japanese children, comparing macrolide-resistant (MRMP, n=399) versus macrolide-sensitive (MSMP, n=63) cases, and inpatients versus outpatients. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective case series of COVID-associated mucormycosis (CAM), not a long COVID treatment trial in the standard sense. There is no comparison group and no pre-post quantitative outcome data with statistical testing. The study describes clinical characteristics, comorbidities, and treatment approach for 59 CAM patients. Key quantitative data extracted: n=59, 7 deaths (11.86% mortality), 47 rhino-orbital (79.66%), 8 nasal/paranasal (13.56%), 3 rhino-orbital-cerebral (5.08%), 1 pulmonary (1.69%) mucormycosis types; 55/59 (93.2%) underwent surgery; 29/48 known diabetics had HbA1c>10 (60.41%). The paper does not report per-arm outcomes (single arm), nor pre-post comparisons with statistical testing. Some percentage figures in Table 2 appear to use denominator of 97 rather than 59 (e.g., diabetes 48/59=81.3% but reported as 49.48%), suggesting Table 2 percentages may reference a different denominator or contain errors — extracted verbatim. This paper is more appropriately classified as a case series describing CAM incidence and management rather than a long COVID treatment efficacy study.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is primarily a biomarker study with olfactory training as the intervention arm; controls are cross-sectional comparators, not concurrent randomized groups. The paper reports medians with ranges (not means/SDs) for calprotectin; SDs are provided in Table 3. The 'mean' column in Table 2 for TDI appears to report means (not medians) given context. The p-value for nasal calprotectin HT0 vs controls is stated as p<0.05 (not exact); serum HT0 vs HT1 p<0.005, HT0 vs CG1 p<0.05. No between-group statistical comparisons were reported for TDI, QOD, or NCS outcomes. Age reported as mean for groups (HT0/HT1: 52 years; CG1: 46; CG2: 45); sex distribution not reported. Lund Kennedy endoscopic score was 0 for all groups (no nasal pathology). The study was published as a preprint in 2023 and in Cytokine in 2024; DOI used is for published version.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cohort study examining whether acute in-hospital COVID-19 treatments (steroids, anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory agents, antivirals, or none) are associated with long-term outcomes 2 years post-discharge. The study found no significant associations for any outcome in either univariable or multivariable GEE analysis. Per-arm n_analyzed for each outcome not explicitly stated in Table 2 — only total n across all arms given (e.g., n=435 for recovery, n=460 for dyspnea, n=427 for FAS, n=432 for CFQ, n=432 for EQ-5D-5L, n=365 for 6MWT). For recovery outcome: total not completely recovered = 317/435 (72.9%) across all groups combined. Exact GEE effect sizes (ORs for binary, mean differences for continuous) with CIs were not reported in Table 2, only p-values. The 'n' in Table 2 header appears to refer to total analyzed, not per-arm. Percent female calculated as 100 minus percent male reported. BMI reported as medians with IQR in Table 1 but not transcribed as mean/SD. Univariable p-values also available: recovery 0.16, dyspnea 0.37, fatigue 0.44, CFQ 0.82, EQ-5D-5L 0.85, 6MWT 0.29.

This is an observational retrospective cohort study examining NMV-r for PREVENTION of PASC during acute COVID-19, not treatment of existing PASC. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Study has two separate matched cohort analyses (A: SARS-CoV-2 vaccination n=1679/arm; B: influenza vaccination n=692/arm) treated here as four arms. The primary outcome metric is 'symptom burden' (days per week a symptom reported) but per-arm mean/SD values are NOT reported in tables — only event counts (n and %) for symptom prevalence and linear regression betas for burden change are provided. Between-group beta coefficients represent differential change in symptom burden days/week (vaccinated minus control). Table 3 reports beta coefficients for 29 symptoms for Analysis A; no equivalent table for Analysis B (null results). Survival analysis HR value not reported numerically — only log-rank p<0.005. Note: skin burning CI in Table 3 appears to have a transcription error (upper CI -0.40 instead of positive value); extracted verbatim. Additional symptoms with Table 2 prevalence data for Analysis A not separately structured as outcomes due to output size: headache, cough, dizziness, rhinorrhea, lack of appetite, brain fog, sneezing, sore throat, nausea, ophtalmodynia, rigors, hoarse voice, fever, abdominal pain, delirium, earache, lymphadenopathy, palpitations, rash, red welts. All Analysis B (influenza) symptom data in Table 5 shows no significant differences. BMI reported as median [IQR] not mean/SD.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an RCT sub-study focusing on 3-month pulmonary sequelae. The comparator structure is complex: remdesivir (n=16) vs its SoC (n=27); HCQ (n=40) vs its SoC (n=47). Some SoC participants served as control for both drugs simultaneously, so n=108 total does not equal sum of all subgroups. Arm 3 (SoC) represents the combined SoC pool; per-arm SoC group sizes differ by comparison (n=27 for remdesivir; n=47 for HCQ). The overall total population n=108 is used for biomarker and CT prevalence analyses. Biomarker outcomes (MMP-9, VEGF-A, SP-D, TIMP-2) are reported for the full cohort vs healthy controls (n=24) — healthy controls coded as arm_id=4 and full patient cohort as arm_id=5 for biomarker outcomes. IQR values for biomarkers not reported (medians only from figure caption). Reversible CT findings in Table 3 arm 1 vs arm 3 comparison shows 3 (18.8%) vs 4 (14.8%) but uses n values from remdesivir comparison. The coefficient estimate CIs for FEV1 comparisons appear to be t-statistics or standardised, not raw mean differences — reported verbatim as stated. KCO results also extracted in Table 2 but not given separate outcome object due to space — overall: median 97.4% (IQR 84.1–107.0); remdesivir 96.1 (78.1–99.8), HCQ 102.0 (92.0–108.0), SoC 92.8 (79.4–107.0). Mosaic pattern, reticular pattern, interlobular septal thickening, consolidations, and bronchiectasis CT findings are all in Table 2 but not given separate outcome objects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective cohort study assessing nirmatrelvir/ritonavir for prevention of long COVID (taken during acute COVID-19, not as treatment of established long COVID). The primary outcome is binary (any long COVID symptom at 4 months). Forest plot of individual ORs shown in Figure 2 but exact OR values for non-significant symptoms not stated in text or tables — only p-values provided for those. The unadjusted primary outcome p-value is stated as 0.21 in abstract (44% vs 49.6%) but Table 2 shows 44% vs 50% with p=0.21; the 49.6% figure comes from 124/250. The n_screened of 11920 was calculated as 1162 (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir prescriptions) + 10758 (PCR-positive controls). Treatment duration inferred as 5 days (standard nirmatrelvir/ritonavir course). Follow-up of 4 months (120-150 days) equates to approximately 17-21 weeks; 17 weeks used as minimum. The paper reports percent_previously_hospitalized as 1% overall (5/500); 2 in treated arm, 3 in untreated arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study reports IPTW-adjusted risk ratios for the composite and 16 individual Long COVID outcomes. Exact RR values with CIs for each individual significant outcome are presented only in Figure 2 (not extractable from text — figures only); text confirms significance for: neuropsychiatric features, cognitive dysfunction, chest pain, cerebrovascular disease, thromboembolic disease, ischemic heart disease, diarrhea, headache, dysautonomia in overall population (all p<0.001 after Holm-Bonferroni). Per-arm event counts and percentages are not broken down by remdesivir exposure status in tables — Table 2 provides total n and rates per 100 person-years for ALL patients with ≥90 days follow-up pooled, not stratified by arm. Total follow-up: outcome assessment window is Day 90 to Day 270 post-admission = 180 days = ~26 weeks post-Day-90, or ~38.6 weeks total from admission. The 16 outcomes with nonsignificant results in overall population (dyspnea, fatigue, joint pain, cough, muscle pain, taste disturbance, smell disturbance) are reported but RRs only in Figure 2. Outcomes omitted from detailed extraction due to figure-only data: dyspnea/breathlessness, fatigue, joint pain/arthralgia, cough, muscle pain/myalgia, taste disturbance/dysgeusia/ageusia, smell disturbance/anosmia. Industry-funded study (Gilead Sciences, manufacturer of remdesivir); several authors are Gilead employees.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective cohort study examining interaction between nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and COVID-19 vaccination on post-acute outcomes (mortality and rehospitalization). The study uses 4 exposure groups rather than a simple 2-arm design; arm_id=1 is the primary treatment group (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir + fully vaccinated), arm_id=2 is the reference group (no nirmatrelvir-ritonavir + not fully vaccinated), arm_id=3 is vaccination only, arm_id=4 is nirmatrelvir-ritonavir only. Between-group HRs are all vs. arm_id=2 (reference) unless otherwise noted. The paper also reports additive interaction statistics (RERI, AP, S) for the combined effect: for rehospitalization RERI=0.10 (95% CI 0.02-0.19, p=0.018), AP=0.07 (95% CI 0.01-0.12, p=0.017), S=1.26 (95% CI 1.02-1.55, p=0.032); for mortality RERI=0.28 (95% CI -0.001-0.55, p=0.051), AP=0.10 (95% CI 0.0007-0.20, p=0.048), S=1.19 (95% CI 0.99-1.43, p=0.070) — these additive interaction measures are not captured in the standard outcome structure. Subgroup results for age <65 years, males, and >6 months since vaccine dose are noted as in Supplement Tables without specific point estimates in main text. Follow-up ended 31 October 2023 or 1 year after discharge, whichever came first. Median days from nirmatrelvir-ritonavir prescription to positive PCR was 0 days (IQR 0-1).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a target trial emulation study with two separate trials (Trial 1: nirmatrelvir/ritonavir vs no treatment; Trial 2: molnupiravir vs no treatment), encoded here as 4 arms. Per-arm event counts for all outcomes are not reported in text or tables — only RRs and RDs with CIs are given; cumulative incidence curves shown in figures only. The paper reports outcomes for 13 post-acute sequelae (congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, deep vein thrombosis, chronic pulmonary disease, ARDS, interstitial lung disease, seizure, anxiety, PTSD, end-stage renal disease, acute kidney injury, pancreatitis) but specific RRs are given only for: atrial fibrillation (31-180d and 181-360d), congestive heart failure (181-360d), and acute kidney injury (181-360d) for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir; end-stage renal disease and seizure increased risk noted for molnupiravir but no specific values given in text. Molnupiravir outcomes for 31-180d and 181-360d mortality and hospitalization described qualitatively as non-significant or higher risk but specific RR values not reported in text (only in Figure 2B). Follow-up median 189 days for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir group and 172 days for molnupiravir group (IQR 95-289 and 64-287 days respectively). The p-values reported as <0.001 throughout — these are listed as p_value_exact: false.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cohort study of COVID-19 vaccination vs. persistent PCC (not a treatment trial for established long COVID). The intervention is pre-infection vaccination, not treatment of long COVID. Arm 1 (unvaccinated, n=136,840) calculated from total (331,042) minus sum of vaccinated arms (11,484 + 157,287 + 25,431 = 194,202); 331,042 - 194,202 = 136,840, which matches the per-arm PCC incidence denominator stated in the text. Subgroup RRs for all 8 subgroups are presented only in Figure 1 (not in text tables) and could not be extracted numerically. Baseline demographics are reported by PCC outcome group (no PCC, nonpersistent PCC, persistent PCC) rather than by vaccination arm, so per-arm demographic extraction is not possible from published data. The paper reports 0.4% incidence for unvaccinated (575/136,840 = 0.42%), 0.3% for 1 dose (32/11,484 = 0.28%), and 0.1% for both 2 and 3 doses — these were used to populate arm_results.

Per-arm denominators for condition-specific outcomes (hypertension, diabetes, etc.) vary because patients with pre-existing conditions are excluded from those specific analyses — exact per-arm denominators for sub-analyses are not reported (only total N for the outcome row is given in Table 2/3 as 'Total, No.' which appears to be the combined eligible population for that outcome). The 28-day and 90-day outcomes for the same condition are treated as separate outcomes (different timepoints, different outcome IDs) due to the study design measuring cumulative incidence separately. No vaccine type, dose, or brand information is reported. Attributable risk (risk difference) per 1000 is also reported in the paper tables but was not separately extracted as between-group effects since RR is the primary reported measure.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Protective effect of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir on PCC increased with age: ≥65y aHR 0.88 (0.87-0.90), 50-64y aHR 0.93 (0.92-0.95), 18-49y aHR 0.98 (0.97-0.99), 12-17y aHR 1.06 (0.66-1.13, NS).

Follow-up end date was 31 December 2022; index dates were 1 April–31 August 2022, giving a maximum follow-up of ~35 weeks but minimum 60 days (≈8.6 weeks) for PCC ascertainment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a retrospective service evaluation/descriptive case series comparison with no treatment outcomes, no pre-post measurement, and no control group in the intervention sense. The two 'arms' are two different NHS service sites, not an intervention vs. comparator. There are no quantitative treatment effect data to extract. All outcomes are descriptive proportions (diagnoses, intervention types, appointment counts). No validated patient-reported outcome measures were administered systematically; Care Aims framework was applied retrospectively. IQR values for appointment numbers: Bolton IQR=4 (range 2-12), East Suffolk IQR=4 (range 2-10) — note the paper states IQR=4 for Bolton but the note says IQR=2 in a later sentence, which appears to be a transcription inconsistency in the original paper. Hospitalization data: Bolton 76.8% non-hospitalized (63/82), 23.2% hospitalized (19/82), 2.4% intubated (2/82); East Suffolk 89.5% non-hospitalized (77/86), 10.5% hospitalized (9/86), 2.3% intubated (2/86). Figures 2 and 3 contain referral reason vs. diagnosis comparison data but numerical values are provided in text and tables. This paper has no treatment efficacy data and would not be suitable as an intervention study for meta-analysis of treatment outcomes.

Individual HR and 95% CI values for the 13 individual post-acute sequelae (outcomes 5-12 and ischemic heart disease, diabetes, dysautonomia, shortness of breath, cough) are reported only in Figure 3 — exact numerical values are not stated in the text or tables. Only the directional finding is stated verbatim (molnupiravir associated with reduced risk of 8/13 sequelae; not statistically significant for ischemic heart disease, diabetes, dysautonomia, shortness of breath, cough). Per-arm event counts for individual sequelae are not reported. The PASC score is not a traditional clinical outcome scale but a composite weighted burden metric. This is a prevention study (treatment given during acute COVID-19 to prevent long COVID), not a treatment study of established long COVID. The study population is veterans (>91% male, predominantly older, US-based), limiting generalizability. The paper is an observational cohort study using IPTW, not an RCT.

summary: This retrospective propensity-score-matched case-control study from Italy enrolled 737 adults with COVID-19 (January 2021–March 2022) to evaluate whether early treatment with monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) or antivirals reduced the risk of long COVID (defined as symptoms persisting ≥4 weeks). In multivariable analysis, mAbs/antivirals were independently associated with reduced long COVID risk (OR 0.44, p=0.002), as was prior vaccination (OR 0.59, p=0.005); in propensity-score-matched analysis, long COVID occurred in 11% of treated patients versus 34% of untreated controls (p=0.001). The study concluded that both vaccination and early antiviral/mAb treatment significantly reduce the risk of developing long COVID.

summary: This retrospective cohort study from Vietnam compared standard of care (SoC) alone versus SoC plus antivirals (predominantly molnupiravir) in 142 vaccinated adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 breakthrough infection. Antiviral use was associated with numerically lower rates of residual respiratory symptoms >7 days (20.3% vs 27.9%) and long COVID-19 (8.1% vs 11.8%), but neither difference was statistically significant (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.22-1.20, p=0.12 and OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.16-1.90, p=0.35, respectively). Subgroup and sensitivity analyses also showed no significant benefit of antivirals, suggesting these agents should not be routinely prescribed for breakthrough COVID-19 prevention of long COVID in vaccinated, lower-risk populations.

summary: This propensity score matched cohort study from a single Hungarian center assessed the effect of remdesivir (RDV) administered during acute COVID-19 hospitalization on post-COVID condition (PCC) outcomes in 188 matched patients (94 SOC+RDV vs. 94 SOC). RDV was associated with significantly earlier attainment of asymptomatic status (adjusted HR 2.28, 95% CI 1.33–3.92, p=0.003) and at least 50% symptom score reduction (adjusted HR 2.08, 95% CI 1.43–3.02, p<0.001), and with significantly better sleep quality (PSQI 5.9 vs. 7.7, p=0.025) and less sleep disturbance at PCC (14% vs. 27%, p=0.003). No significant differences were observed in pulmonary function tests, 6-minute walk test, or other quality-of-life questionnaires.

summary: This retrospective observational cohort study used N3C electronic health records from 302,626 US adults with depression and COVID-19 (September 2021–December 2022) to evaluate whether SSRI use during acute COVID-19 reduces subsequent 12-month Long COVID risk. After aggressive nonparametric confounder adjustment using targeted maximum likelihood estimation and Super Learner, SSRI users showed a significantly lower risk of Long COVID compared to nonusers (adjusted RR 0.922, 95% CI 0.863–0.986), with a similar result in new SSRI users (aRR 0.886, 95% CI 0.780–0.985). Individual SSRI drug subtypes all showed protective point estimates but none were individually statistically significant, and no dose-response relationship was detected for fluoxetine.

summary: This retrospective cohort study examined the short- and long-term effectiveness of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir versus molnupiravir in 1,745 Hong Kong asthma patients infected with COVID-19 (Omicron era), using SMR weighting to adjust for confounding. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with significantly reduced risks of acute mortality (HR 0.27), post-acute mortality (HR 0.49), all-cause post-acute hospitalization (HR 0.72), and myocardial infarction (HR 0.10) versus no antiviral; molnupiravir reduced only acute mortality versus no antiviral. Head-to-head comparison showed nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was superior to molnupiravir for post-acute all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.65, p<0.001) and asthma exacerbation in moderate-to-severe asthma patients, suggesting nirmatrelvir/ritonavir offers broader post-acute protection in the asthma population.

All outcomes are time-to-event (Cox HR); no continuous means/SDs are available. The denominator n values for cause-specific hospitalization outcomes differ from total enrolled because patients with prior history of the condition were excluded from those analyses. summary: This propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US EHR platform examined whether SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with reduced long COVID risk in 5,162 matched pairs of adults with type 2 diabetes who contracted COVID-19 between 2020-2024. SGLT2 inhibitor users had a significantly lower risk of developing long COVID over 12 months (HR=0.85, 95% CI 0.79-0.91), with particularly pronounced reductions in anxiety/depression (HR=0.73), headache (HR=0.56), cognitive symptoms (HR=0.69), pain (HR=0.84), and abdominal symptoms (HR=0.84); fatigue, chest pain, abnormal breathing, and myalgia were not significantly reduced. The protective association was consistent across age groups and sexes and was replicated in three sensitivity analyses comparing SGLT2i to DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational retrospective cohort study — not an interventional trial. Outcomes are ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes (incident long COVID diagnoses), not patient-reported symptom scales, so no per-arm means/SDs are available. All quantitative results are event counts and Cox hazard ratios. The post-COVID-19 condition category (unspecified) HR=0.81 (95% CI 0.42-1.56, n=16 vs 20 events) was not extracted as a separate outcome given the very small event count and wide CI. Kaplan-Meier curves were presented in figures; exact numerical incidence rates from those curves not reported in text. The discussion section mentions HR=0.94 (95% CI 0.87-1.00) and HR=0.92 (95% CI 0.84-1.00) for 'overall HRs' but these appear to contradict the forest plot values and may refer to a different time window or unadjusted analysis — not extracted to avoid confusion. No adverse events were reported.

summary: This hypothesis paper from Lamb et al. (2020) describes COVID-19 Associated Cystitis (CAC) — de novo urinary urgency, incontinence, and high-frequency voiding in acute COVID-19 patients — and presents pilot data from 4 COVID-19-positive patients with CAC compared to 4 age-matched healthy controls. Urinary IL-6 (19.69 vs. 2.13 pg/mL, p=0.046) and IL-8 (258.12 vs. 13.31 pg/mL, p=0.002) were significantly elevated in CAC patients, while IP-10 showed a trend (863.13 vs. 38.72 pg/mL, p=0.097). The authors hypothesize that cytokine-mediated bladder inflammation underlies CAC, and that chronic CAC may contribute to long COVID urological symptoms, but this is not a long COVID treatment study.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a long COVID treatment study — it is a hypothesis paper about acute COVID-19 Associated Cystitis (CAC) with a small embedded pilot biomarker study (n=8 total). There is no intervention, no treatment arm, and no long COVID population. The paper_id in the prompt header (10.12998/wjcc.v11.i33.7987) appears to be a placeholder — the correct DOI inferred from the text is 10.1016/j.mehy.2020.110375. Individual patient cytokine values are available in Table 1 and have been used to verify/confirm the reported group means and SEMs. The SE for the control IP-10 group (38.72) equals the mean, which is consistent with one outlier (N3=154.89) and three zeros. One-tailed two-sample t-test with unequal variances was used for p-values per the paper.

summary: This prospective cohort study followed 222 COVID-19 survivors discharged from a single hospital in Saudi Arabia at a median of 122 days post-discharge to assess post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (PACS). summary: This EHR-based target trial emulation used the N3C database (445,738 patients with COVID-19 eligible for Paxlovid from April 2022-February 2023) to estimate whether Paxlovid treatment during acute COVID-19 prevents long COVID (PASC) onset. Paxlovid had no significant effect on overall PASC incidence (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.02) or respiratory symptoms, but showed small statistically significant protective effects on incident cognitive (RR 0.91) and fatigue (RR 0.94) symptoms. Stratified analyses identified small protective effects in patients aged ≥65 years (RR 0.92, NNT 233) and with CCI 3-4 (RR 0.83, NNT 76), but the authors conclude Paxlovid is unlikely to be a definitive solution for PASC prevention given the negligible absolute effect sizes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a PASC prevention study (Paxlovid given during acute COVID-19), NOT a treatment study for established long COVID. Study period: April 1, 2022 to February 28, 2023 (mostly Omicron BA and later subvariants). The pooled sequential trial cohort of 460,803 records differs from the 445,738 unique patients due to sequential trial design allowing some patients to appear in both treatment and control groups across different trials. Age data reported only as distributional bins (not means/SDs). Cumulative incidence values in Table 3 are reported as proportions (e.g., 0.045 = 4.5%). Death counts: Paxlovid arm 157 deaths (29-180 days), 51 deaths (1-28 days); control arm 609 deaths (29-180 days), 366 deaths (1-28 days). Extensive sensitivity analyses (14 variations) all confirm null primary result — see Table 3. Also note: the paper reports adjusted cumulative incidence estimates (4.53% treated, 4.60% untreated) in text but the raw (unadjusted) event counts show 4.4% treated vs 4.1% untreated, reflecting the IPTW adjustment. Vaccination subanalysis: 115,823 patients, 8 sites, 79.15% fully vaccinated, 45.67% treated. Doubly robust adjustment gave HR 0.983 (95% CI 0.950-1.018, p=0.305).

summary: This propensity score-matched longitudinal cohort study from Indonesia examined whether favipiravir (an antiviral given during acute COVID-19) reduced the incidence of post-COVID depression in 712 participants followed biweekly for 60 days. Depression occurred in 16.0% of favipiravir recipients versus 21.1% of non-recipients; after adjustment for multiple confounders using Cox regression, favipiravir was associated with a significantly lower hazard of post-COVID depression (aHR 0.488, 95% CI 0.339–0.701, p<0.001). Favipiravir showed specific protective effects against depressive mood (aHR 0.378) and anhedonia (aHR 0.543), but not sleep disorders, concentration disturbance, or fatigue; living alone was independently associated with greater anhedonia risk.

summary: This ambidirectional cohort study of 332 long COVID patients presenting to specialty PASC clinics in Atlanta, GA examined whether antecedent COVID-19 severity was associated with symptom profiles at clinic visit. In adjusted multivariable models, mild (non-hospitalized) antecedent COVID-19 was significantly associated with higher odds of fatigue (OR 1.83), subjective cognitive impairment (OR 2.76), headaches (OR 2.15), and dizziness (OR 2.41) compared to severe (hospitalized) antecedent COVID-19. Notably, receipt of remdesivir during acute infection was associated with significantly lower odds of fatigue (OR 0.47) and severe fatigue (OR 0.47) and severe cognitive impairment on PROMIS scales (OR 0.43), though this association is heavily confounded by the fact that nearly all remdesivir recipients were hospitalized severe cases.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is an observational cohort study, NOT an intervention trial — the 'remdesivir' finding is an adjusted association from a multivariable regression, not a controlled treatment comparison. The remdesivir association is severely confounded: 110/114 (97%) remdesivir recipients had severe COVID-19 vs. 4/114 (3%) with mild COVID-19, making it impossible to isolate the remdesivir effect from severity effects. The paper explicitly cautions that this should be interpreted carefully. Temporal analyses (PASC duration groups) represent cross-sectional comparisons of distinct patient cohorts at different time points — NOT longitudinal within-patient data. Per-arm event counts for some PROMIS outcomes are based on a subset (n=253, 263, 259, 127) with missing denominators per arm; these were approximated from overall percentages and total arm Ns where possible. Vaccination data was not collected and could not be included as a covariate. Additional outcomes reported in Table 2 but not extracted as separate outcome objects: cough (arm1 49/171=29%, arm2 48/161=30%, OR 1.34 CI 0.71-2.54, p=0.37), muscle pain (arm1 36/171=21%, arm2 25/161=16%, OR 0.85 CI 0.38-1.89, p=0.69), anxiety (arm1 40/171=23%, arm2 19/161=12%, OR 1.55 CI 0.73-3.31, p=0.25), depression (arm1 24/171=14%, arm2 28/161=18%, OR 0.49 CI 0.22-1.10, p=0.09), joint pain (arm1 34/171=20%, arm2 19/161=12%, OR 1.12 CI 0.48-2.59, p=0.78), palpitations (arm1 36/171=21%, arm2 17/161=11%, OR 1.47 CI 0.60-3.61, p=0.40), weakness (arm1 16/171=9%, arm2 27/161=17%, OR 0.66 CI 0.29-1.51, p=0.32), sleep disturbances (arm1 21/171=12%, arm2 19/161=12%, OR 0.99 CI 0.44-2.22, p=0.97), anosmia (arm1 21/171=17%, arm2 17/161=11%, OR 0.61 CI 0.23-1.66, p=0.34), dysgeusia (arm1 27/171=16%, arm2 23/161=14%, OR 0.76 CI 0.32-1.88, p=0.53). summary: This retrospective follow-up study of 1,236 Iranian adults hospitalized for COVID-19 who had previously reported long-COVID symptoms compared the persistence of symptoms (>1 year, termed 'long long-COVID') between vaccinated (n=1,185) and unvaccinated (n=51) individuals. The study is observational with a very small unvaccinated comparator group and serious confounding risk, limiting causal inference; the authors nonetheless strongly recommend vaccination given its well-established protection against severe disease and death.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational retrospective cohort, not an intervention trial. The 'intervention' is COVID-19 vaccination (self-selected, not randomized). The unvaccinated comparator group is very small (n=51), limiting statistical power for individual symptom comparisons. Table 1 reports p-values for individual symptoms but no ORs per symptom — p-values extracted as chi-square results. Several symptoms had zero events in unvaccinated group (muscle pain, chest pain, palpitation, loss of taste, sore throat, dizziness, concentration difficulty, diarrhea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite) — no p-value calculable for these (listed as '-' in paper). Remaining secondary symptom outcomes with p-values reported: cough (p=0.497), excess sputum (p=0.942), headache (p=0.679), excess sweating (p=0.667) — omitted from outcomes array for brevity but all showed non-significance. summary: This open prospective comparative study examined 1-year post-COVID outcomes in 132 metabolic syndrome patients (68 treated with favipiravir/Areplivir during acute COVID-19, 64 receiving standard care without antivirals) in Russia. Favipiravir use during acute infection was associated with a 2.66-fold lower risk of stroke and acute coronary syndrome (3 vs 12 events, p=0.01), and significantly lower incidence of blood pressure control failure, LDL elevation, and new glucose dysregulation over 12 months. Favipiravir-treated patients also showed persistently lower serum levels of IL-6, sIL-6r, LIF, and sLIFr at 10, 30, and 180 days post-recovery (all p<0.001), consistent with attenuation of the pro-inflammatory post-COVID cytokine response; however, the study was non-randomized with important baseline differences between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a non-randomized prospective comparative study, NOT an RCT despite the structured comparison. Assignment was physician/patient-decided. 2. Notable baseline imbalance: type 2 diabetes prevalence was 100% in favipiravir arm vs 40% in control arm per Table 1 — this likely reflects an error or differential eligibility rather than true enrollment difference (exclusion criteria included T1DM but not T2DM). 3. Total enrolled was 190 but only 132 are described in the two main arms (68+64); 170 are described as being surveyed at follow-up — the discrepancy (190-170=20) is not explained. 4. The relative risk values in Table 2 are presented identically for both arms, which appears to be a table formatting issue — the RR represents the ratio of events in the control group vs favipiravir group. 5. Table 3 cytokine footnote markers (asterisks with superscript numbers) indicate Wilcoxon/Mann-Whitney significance vs specified comparison groups; exact p-values not provided for individual timepoint between-group comparisons other than p<0.001. 6. Cox regression results in Table 4 show sLIFr >5074 pg/mL as the strongest predictor of cardiovascular complications (Beta=2.29, Wald=13.3, p=0.009, Exp(Beta)=4.75). 7. The paper is in Russian; English abstract and tables translated. 8. BMI per-arm medians are available in Table 1: favipiravir arm 38.9 [36.3-42.7], control 37.4 [35.2-40.4] — not extracted into demographics fields due to schema limitations but noted here.

summary: This retrospective cohort study of 405 post-COVID-19 patients attending a pulmonary clinic in Israel (February 2020–March 2021) compared long-term pulmonary function test (PFT) trajectories between 155 patients who received corticosteroids (CS) during acute COVID-19 and 250 who did not. Despite lower baseline FEV1 (-9.4%) and FVC (-12.3%), CS-treated patients recovered pulmonary function significantly faster (+0.9%/month FEV1, +0.85%/month FVC; both p=0.001), as shown by multivariable linear mixed-effects models adjusting for multiple confounders. The faster PFT recovery with CS was observed across all subgroups including those with BMI ≥30 and chronic lung disease, though substantial confounding by disease severity (CS-treated patients had 93% hospitalization rate vs. 20% in untreated) limits causal inference.

summary: This retrospective single-arm case series evaluated bisphosphonate combination therapy (intravenous zoledronic acid 5mg plus oral alendronate 35mg twice weekly) in 48 post-COVID-19 patients (88 hips) with osteonecrosis of the femoral head at a tertiary center in India. summary: This open-label, four-arm quasi-experimental study enrolled 243 post-COVID-19 patients in the early rehabilitation period in Uzbekistan to evaluate three hepatoprotectors—ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA, 10 mg/kg/day), glycyrrhizic acid plus phospholipids (Phosphogliv, 6 tabs/day), and ademeteonine (2 tabs/day)—versus standard care without hepatoprotectors over one month. summary: This retrospective cohort study used N3C electronic health record data from 74 US institutions (October 2021–April 2023) to compare incident PASC risk among T2DM adults on prevalent monotherapy metformin (n=5,596) versus sulfonylurea or DPP-4 inhibitor (n=1,451), using entropy balancing for confounding control. In the weighted analysis with ICD-10-defined PASC, 3-month and 6-month risk ratios were 0.86 (95% CI 0.56–1.32) and 0.81 (95% CI 0.55–1.20), respectively — directionally consistent with benefit but not statistically significant. The authors conclude that the results are compatible with a reduced PASC risk with metformin but that wide confidence intervals and methodological limitations (prevalent-user design, non-specific outcome definition) preclude causal inference.

summary: This large observational cohort study using target trial emulation analyzed 497,499 SARS-CoV-2-infected adults from 29 US PCORnet EHR repositories to assess whether nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) prescribed within 5 days of infection reduces Long COVID risk. Among high-risk non-hospitalized adults (n=431,707 analyzed), Paxlovid was associated with significantly reduced incidence of Long COVID (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.87-0.89; absolute risk reduction 2.99 events/100 persons), all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.70), and death (HR 0.53) in the 30-180 day post-acute period. No significant Long COVID risk reduction was observed in low-risk patients (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.95-1.11), suggesting Paxlovid's preventive benefit for Long COVID is limited to high-risk individuals.
