summary: This 2-year prospective observational cohort study (n=157, mean age 71.4 years) followed COVID-19 patients stratified by comorbidity burden to evaluate long-term impacts of long COVID and shifts in antithrombotic therapy (VKA vs. DOAC) in a Romanian family medicine practice. No formal control or comparison group without COVID was included, and the study cannot disentangle long COVID effects from natural disease progression or the effect of specific antithrombotic treatments due to confounding by disease severity.

Percentages in tables represent proportion of the TOTAL cohort (n=157), not proportion within each group arm — this creates apparent numerical inconsistencies (e.g. 17.8%+34.4%+15.9% = 68.2% of 157 for varicose veins). 4. summary: This retrospective observational cohort study used two large US EHR networks (N3C and PCORnet) to examine whether pre-existing metformin use in adults with diabetes or prediabetes was associated with a lower risk of developing post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC/long COVID) following COVID-19 infection. After IPTW weighting for baseline confounders, cumulative incidence of PASC (by U09.9 code) at 180 days was consistently lower in metformin-exposed versus comparator groups across both databases (e.g., N3C: 1.6% vs 2.0%; PCORnet: 1.28% vs 1.46%), and mortality was also lower in metformin users. Formal between-group hazard ratios or confidence intervals were not reported in this supplementary document; adjusted effect estimates are available in the primary manuscript.

summary: This Russian case series (n=44) assessed erectile dysfunction and hormonal changes in men who developed sexual complaints 3 weeks to 2 months after recovery from PCR-confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia. summary: This single-arm before-after study examined 91 COVID-19 pneumonia convalescents (aged 21-67, 64% female) who underwent a rehabilitation program centered on haloaerosol therapy (dry rock salt aerosol inhalation, 18-20 sessions) in Ukraine. summary: This retrospective single-center cohort study from Saint-Petersburg, Russia analyzed 324 patients with immunoinflammatory rheumatic diseases (IRD) who contracted COVID-19 between March 2020 and February 2021. summary: This open-label, non-randomised observational study (PARTMO) evaluated continuous remote ECG monitoring using the S-Patch EX wearable biosensor in 40 COVID-19 survivors in Sydney, Australia, compared to 200 matched standard-care controls. subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Multivariate regression found olfactory training was an independent positive predictor of TDI improvement (estimate 5.86, SE 1.49, p=0.0034).
Younger age was an independent positive prognostic factor for TDI improvement in multivariate regression (estimate -0.251 per year, SE 0.043, p=0.000232).
Smoking was an independent positive predictor of TDI improvement (estimate 9.51, SE 1.74, p=0.000403), a surprising finding the authors attribute to possible small-sample bias.
No significant differences in TDI scores between sexes at T0, T1, or T2, and no significant sex differences in TDI improvement in univariate or multivariate analyses.

summary: This prospective single-center cohort study from Italy followed 83 COVID-19 patients with chemosensory dysfunction over 4 years using Sniffin' Sticks psychophysical testing and self-reported VAS measures. Olfactory function improved significantly at each timepoint, with 92.3% of patients achieving normosmia by year 4 (TDI 27.9 at baseline vs. 38.0 at 4 years, p<0.001). Multivariate analysis identified younger age (p=0.000232) and olfactory training (p=0.0034) as independent positive prognostic factors for recovery, supporting olfactory training as a beneficial intervention for persistent COVID-19-related olfactory dysfunction.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm prospective cohort study with no control group; no between-group effects are applicable. Different patient subsets attended each follow-up: T0 n=83 (all enrolled), T1 n=34 (only OD patients who attended), T2 n=26 (OD patients from T0 with or without T1 attendance). The sVAS and tVAS p-values for T2 vs. T0 were reported as p<0.001 for both (verbatim in text) but Table 2 shows p=0.004 and p=0.003 for T2 vs. T1 — both were extracted. The T1 sVAS T2 p-value in the table shows 'p=0.004' but text says 'p=0.001'; table value used for T2 vs T1 comparison. Some boxplot data (Figure 2, Figure 3) may contain additional distributional data not available in text/tables. The study primarily documents natural history of olfactory recovery; olfactory training was offered to OD patients but was not randomized, so effect estimates for OT come from multivariate regression subgroup analysis only.

summary: This propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX global EHR network evaluated molnupiravir (vs. no antiviral) in 9,421 matched pairs of non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients with pre-existing psychiatric disorders (psychotic, mood, or anxiety disorders) during the Omicron period (January 2022–May 2023). Molnupiravir was associated with a 24% reduction in the risk of all-cause hospitalization or death within 30 days (HR 0.760, 95% CI 0.665–0.869, p<0.001). At 1-year follow-up, molnupiravir-treated patients had significantly lower rates of 9 post-COVID-19 conditions including fatigue (HR 0.718), cognitive symptoms (HR 0.769), chest/throat pain (HR 0.615), myalgia (HR 0.647), and palpitation (HR 0.641), all statistically significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. No per-arm event counts or incidence rates were reported for any outcome — only hazard ratios with CIs from Kaplan-Meier survival analyses. Kaplan-Meier curves appear in figures but no numeric values extractable from text. The paper does not report exact p-values for individual long COVID outcome HRs (only states significance via CIs not crossing 1.0); the log-rank p<0.001 is stated only for the primary composite outcome. Sleep disturbance was listed as one of the 10 post-COVID conditions in the methods but HR results for sleep disturbance are not reported in the results section — this appears to be an omission in the paper. Molnupiravir dose and duration of treatment not specified. Figure 3 caption states '90-180 days after index date' but the text and abstract clearly state 1-year follow-up; this appears to be a figure labeling error in the paper.

summary: This cross-sectional observational study examined 188 long COVID patients recruited at a single Spanish hospital, comparing biochemical, inflammatory, and gut microbiota outcomes between those with high (n=134, MEDAS14 >7) versus low (n=54, MEDAS14 ≤7) Mediterranean diet (MD) adherence. High MD adherence was associated with significantly lower levels of LDH (168 vs 177 U/L, p=0.04), LDL-cholesterol (110 vs 121 mg/dL, p=0.04), glucose (99 vs 111 mg/dL, p=0.03), insulin (8.0 vs 11.7 µU/mL, p=0.03), GOT (19.9 vs 23.7 U/L, p<0.001), and D-dimer (333 vs 379 ng/mL, p=0.04), while CRP and IL-6 did not differ between groups. Gut microbiota analysis showed significant beta diversity differences (p=0.005) and lower Oscillibacter abundance in the high MD adherence group; a significant interaction was found between Oscillibacter, EVOO consumption, and LDH levels, suggesting MD antioxidant properties may modulate oxidative stress through gut microbiota-mediated mechanisms.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a cross-sectional observational study (not an intervention trial) comparing self-selected groups by dietary adherence — there was no randomization or treatment assignment. Groups differ at baseline in age (49 vs 52y, p=0.02), sex (87% vs 80% female, p=0.03), and obesity prevalence, constituting significant confounders. The SD values in Table 1 appear unusually small for age (±0.8-0.9 years), suggesting these may actually be SE values, but were extracted as reported. Oscillibacter abundance per-arm quantitative values are only in figures (box plots) with no table values; only the between-group p-value direction was narratively reported. Anthropometric variables including BMI, waist, fat mass were borderline non-significant (p=0.08-0.11). Several outcomes not extracted as separate outcome objects due to null results and data completeness: uric acid, glycated hemoglobin, GPT, GGT, vitamin D, ferritin, vitamin B12, leukocytes, neutrophils, lymphocytes, neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio, platelets, hemoglobin, RDW, ESR, prothrombin activity — all available in Table 2 with means/SDs but p>0.05.

summary: This single-center retrospective cohort study examined 54 adults with post-acute COVID-19 VTE (PE or DVT within 90 days of infection) at a Romanian tertiary hospital between 2020-2022, comparing 11 patients who received systemic thrombolysis to 43 managed conservatively. Thrombolysis recipients had markedly lower TAPSE (13.0 vs. 20.8 mm), lower SpO2 (90.1% vs. 97.0%), and smaller LVEDD (24.4 vs. 46.1 mm), all statistically significant; in multivariable regression, each 1 mm decrease in TAPSE (OR 1.58) and each 1% decrease in SpO2 (OR 1.34) independently predicted thrombolysis. Inflammatory biomarkers (CRP, fibrinogen) and RV diameter were not associated with treatment group, supporting a non-invasive hemodynamic triad (low TAPSE, low SpO2, reduced LVEDD) as bedside risk-stratification markers for post-COVID VTE.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective cohort study using thrombolysis vs. no thrombolysis as a de facto two-arm comparison, but it is not an intervention trial — groups reflect physician-decided treatment. LVEDD values in the thrombolysis group (mean 24.4 mm) are unusually low (normal adult range ~37-53 mm), likely reflecting severe RV-mediated LV compression but should be noted as potentially extreme. Fibrinogen reported as median only without IQR. No long-term follow-up data reported — study captures only in-hospital period. The sPESI data in Table 2 reports mean±SD alongside medians. The paper is primarily a predictive/observational study of biomarkers for thrombolysis, not a treatment efficacy trial; caution is warranted in interpreting as evidence of thrombolysis efficacy.

summary: This propensity-score matched cohort study from the multicenter HOPE-2 registry examined the effect of corticosteroid therapy during acute COVID-19 hospitalization on 18-month all-cause mortality and long-term symptoms in 796 patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Corticosteroid use was not associated with differences in 18-month all-cause mortality (44.0% vs. 39.7%, log-rank p=0.52) or in-hospital mortality (41.2% vs. 36.4%, p=0.167), and no significant differences were found in any long-term post-COVID-19 symptom except for a higher rate of clinically relevant bleeding events in the corticosteroid group (4.1% vs. 0%, p=0.029). However, corticosteroid-treated patients had significantly shorter hospital stays (median 8 vs. 11 days, p<0.001), suggesting a possible benefit in recovery time without clear long-term benefit or harm in this high-risk cardiac subpopulation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Long-term symptom data denominator is 245 patients (122 corticosteroid, 123 no corticosteroid) out of the 487 survivors, with Table 3 header showing n=487 matched population but individual rows denominated /245 (i.e., subset with symptom data available). Additional long-term outcomes reported in Table 3 but not extracted as separate outcome objects (due to length) include: acute coronary syndrome, resting heart rate increase, syncope, atrial fibrillation, perimyocarditis, edema, incident hypertension, left ventricular dysfunction, headache, migraine, ageusia, tinnitus/hearing loss, mood disorder, paranoia, polypnea, sleep apnea, tongue involvement, digestive disorders, nausea/vomiting, intermittent fever, chills, hair loss, joint pain, sweats, attention disorder — all showing p>0.05. Corticosteroid type, dose, and duration were not collected in the registry. The Kaplan-Meier HR with 95% CI for the primary outcome was not reported numerically; only log-rank p=0.52 is available.

summary: This single-center prospective observational study assessed cognitive function in 63 convalescent COVID-19 patients (mean age 59.8 years, 74.6% male, 63.4% severe pneumonia) admitted for multidisciplinary pulmonary rehabilitation in Italy. Approximately 44% were classified as having reduced cognitive efficiency (RCE), primarily affecting spatial and verbal long-term memory and executive functions. RCE patients were significantly more likely to be non-dippers on 24-hour BP monitoring (75% vs 45.7%, p=0.01), to have had more severe COVID-19 illness (p=0.02), to report PTSD symptoms (p=0.02), and to have cognitive complaints (p=0.002), and showed higher anxiety scores (mean HADS-A 10.39 vs 8.25, p=0.017), suggesting an association between autonomic dysregulation and post-COVID cognitive impairment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cross-sectional study at rehabilitation admission — there is no longitudinal follow-up and no intervention outcomes. The two 'arms' represent RCE vs NCE subgroups defined post-hoc, not pre-specified treatment groups. No adverse events reported (observational study). The paper reports Mann-Whitney U test p-values for continuous variables and chi-square p-values for categorical variables; no effect sizes (OR, RR) or confidence intervals are provided for between-group comparisons. All between-group effect_values for continuous outcomes were calculated as mean differences. Raw neuropsychological test scores (FAS, TMT, RAVLT, Corsi) per arm are reported in supplemental Table S2, which is not included in this paper text and therefore not extractable. FVC% data appears in Table 1 row format but only the overall value 75.59 (SD 20.25) is unambiguously provided — per-arm breakdown not explicitly stated in the table for FVC. Disease duration p-value in Table 3 is stated as 0.739 but abstract says 'longer disease duration (p=0.04)' — this discrepancy likely reflects different variables (disease duration days vs duration of bed stay); extracted as reported in Table 3.

summary: This observational before-after study in 190 women (age 47.6 ± 11.1) recovering from mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in Serbia assessed associations between self-reported physical activity (IPAQ) and mental health (DASS) at 2-4 weeks and 14-16 weeks post-infection. Over the 12-week follow-up, depression (9.66 to 8.63), anxiety (10.86 to 9.53), and stress (15.28 to 14.47) all decreased significantly (all p<0.001, Cohen's d 0.09-0.16), and overall physical activity increased from 3665 to 4119 MET-min/week. Regression analysis showed that by the final measurement, higher physical activity levels were significantly associated with reduced anxiety (R²=0.15, F=3.97, p<0.001) and depression (R²=0.13, F=3.34, p=0.001) but not stress, with walking, moderate PA, high-intensity PA, and PA at home as the strongest predictors; however, the absence of a control group and reliance on self-report limit causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational single-arm before-after study, NOT an intervention trial — there is no treatment assigned. The study measures associations between naturally occurring physical activity changes and mental health during post-COVID recovery. No between-group effects are applicable. The t-test p-values in Tables 2 and 3 are reported as '<0.001' (threshold, not exact). Cohen's d values for mental health outcomes are very small (0.09-0.16). Regression beta coefficients in Table 5 are standardized betas, not raw unstandardized coefficients — notably the column header says 'B' for depression but context indicates these are standardized betas (β) consistent with Table 4 format. The t-statistics reported (e.g., t=19.98 for depression) seem unusually large for a paired t-test with n=190 and Cohen's d=0.11, suggesting possible table formatting issue or reporting error; extracted as stated. Study data collected February-May 2022 (Omicron era). 40 participants lost to follow-up (17.4% attrition). All t-test p-values for PA and mental health outcomes set to p<0.001 (not exact). This study is better classified as a cross-sectional/longitudinal observational study of post-COVID recovery rather than an intervention trial.

summary: This single-center retrospective observational study (n=65) described the natural history of long COVID symptoms over 3 months in patients attending a dedicated aftercare clinic in Japan; there was no specific intervention being tested. The five most common symptoms (general fatigue, dysosmia, dysgeusia, insomnia, headache) all improved substantially by 3 months, with approximately 37–52% of affected patients still symptomatic at that point. Serum anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibody titers were higher in patients with severe acute illness, and higher titers (≥200 U/mL) were associated with more residual symptoms at 1 month but not at 2–3 months, suggesting no direct role of antibody level in long-term symptom persistence.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a descriptive observational study with no intervention arm; outcome data (symptom counts over time by subgroup) are presented in figures (Figures 2, 3, 4, 6) without accompanying tables. Per-group means and SEMs referenced in the text appear only in figures and could not be extracted as precise numeric values. The percent values at 3 months for individual symptoms are verbatim from text. N at 3-month timepoint for individual symptom outcomes not explicitly stated (only overall cohort loss-to-follow-up reported). Antibody titer subgroup medians and IQRs are verbatim from text for subgroup comparisons. No intervention tested; not a treatment study in the usual sense — this is a natural history/prognostic study. The 'proportion remaining symptomatic at 3 months' figures represent proportion of those originally affected who still have the symptom, not proportion of total cohort.

summary: This single-center retrospective case series from Japan evaluated hypothalamic-pituitary function in 15 long COVID patients (mean age 35.6 years, mean 343 days post-infection) using combined CRH, TRH, and GnRH anterior pituitary stimulation tests. While peak hormonal responses were preserved across all axes (ΔACTH 247%, ΔTSH 918%, ΔPRL 820%, ΔLH 1150%, ΔFSH 187%), markedly delayed peaks were observed in FSH (87% of patients), LH (33%), and ACTH (13%), and significant sustained elevations at 120 minutes were detected for TSH, PRL, LH, and FSH. These patterns, particularly the delayed and prolonged gonadotropin responses, suggest functional hypothalamic dysfunction—specifically impaired GnRH pulsatility—rather than primary pituitary pathology, and may contribute to hypogonadism and menstrual abnormalities reported in long COVID patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a diagnostic/observational case series, not a treatment trial — there is no intervention arm with pre/post treatment outcomes in the conventional sense. The 'intervention' is the stimulation test procedure itself, used to characterize endocrine physiology. Some key data (time-course hormone response curves) are in figures only with limited numeric values extracted from text (baseline and 120 min values are in text; peak percent changes are stated but per-timepoint means/SDs at 15/30/60/90 min are only in figures). GH basal values split by sex reported in Table 2 but only male values with SE noted (male mean 0.52±0.25, female 0.6±0.32 ng/mL). The 120 min values for TSH (1.4 vs 5.7 mIU/L), PRL-male (25.7 vs 34.8 ng/mL), LH-male (5.2 vs 31.8 mIU/mL), LH-female (4.9 vs 38.1 mIU/mL), FSH-female (4.3 vs 11.8 mIU/mL) are verbatim from the paper. Significance levels cited as p<0.05 or p<0.01 without exact values. The study provides no treatment outcome data and should be classified primarily as a mechanistic/diagnostic observational study.

summary: This single-center prospective observational study in Spain followed 1,966 patients (hospitalized and non-hospitalized) over 12 months after acute COVID-19 infection to identify risk factors for post-acute sequelae (PASC) and evaluate the impact of acute-phase treatments. Approximately one-third of patients developed PASC; female sex, obesity, asthma, and disease severity were independent risk factors. Among hospitalized patients, treatment with remdesivir was associated with significantly shorter median PASC symptom duration in both moderate disease (109 vs. 262 days) and severe disease (187 vs. 284 days), as was dexamethasone in moderate disease (133 vs. 271 days) and severe disease (266 vs. 309 days), while tocilizumab and methylprednisolone showed no significant benefit.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational prospective cohort study — not an RCT. Treatment assignment was by physician protocol based on disease severity (severe confounding by indication). The primary comparative analysis uses Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank tests for symptom duration, but exact log-rank p-values and hazard ratios are not reported in table form — only the median durations with IQRs are given in Table 6 and referenced in the text/figure caption. Arm IDs 1-8 represent the 4 treatment comparison pairs (remdesivir moderate, no-remdesivir moderate, remdesivir severe, no-remdesivir severe, dexamethasone moderate, no-dexamethasone moderate, dexamethasone severe, no-dexamethasone severe). Arm IDs 9-11 represent mild/moderate/severe disease severity groups for PASC prevalence. Arm IDs 12-13 represent non-PASC and PASC groups for biomarker outcomes. The tocilizumab/sarilumab and methylprednisolone/prednisone comparisons (Table 6) are not extracted as separate outcomes but described in subgroup analyses. Ns for tocilizumab arms: moderate No=466/Yes=49; severe No=193/Yes=139. Ns for methylprednisolone arms: moderate No=395/Yes=120; severe No=126/Yes=206. Kaplan-Meier curve data (Figure 2) provides additional tocilizumab and methylprednisolone median values but no formal HR or p-values are tabulated. Some lab values in Table 3 had unusual n discrepancy (1159+286=1445 but hospitalized total is 1733); this likely reflects that not all hospitalized patients had blood tests available.

summary: This matched cohort study compared 216 hospitalized COVID-19 survivors who received intravenous Remdesivir during acute infection to 216 matched controls who received no antiviral treatment, assessing post-COVID-19 pain at a mean of 18.4 months post-hospitalization. Remdesivir-treated patients had significantly lower prevalence of any chronic post-COVID-19 pain (22.7% vs. 39.8%; adjusted OR 0.444, 95% CI 0.292–0.674, p<0.001), with specific protection against thorax/chest (OR 0.277, p=0.01) and lumbar spine (OR 0.347, p=0.02) pain. Remdesivir was also associated with significantly lower rates of post-COVID-19 anxiety and depression, but had no effect on sleep quality.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The Remdesivir arm had 300 invited but only 216 participated; the paper does not detail selection of the control arm beyond matching criteria. Follow-up duration of 18.4 months used to calculate weeks (≈79.6 weeks). Adjusted ORs for pain locations other than thorax/chest and lumbar spine (cervical, shoulder, elbow-wrist, hip, knee) were not reported in multivariate form — only unadjusted p-values from Table 1 are available; these locations were omitted from outcomes to avoid redundancy but raw counts are: cervical (arm1: 3/216 1.4%, arm2: 4/216 1.8%, p=0.705), shoulder (arm1: 1/216 0.5%, arm2: 4/216 1.8%, p=0.178), elbow-wrist (arm1: 1/216 0.5%, arm2: 4/216 1.8%, p=0.178), hip (arm1: 2/216 0.9%, arm2: 4/216 1.8%, p=0.414), knee (arm1: 3/216 1.4%, arm2: 7/216 3.3%, p=0.206). The anxiety/depression OR values (0.039 and 0.057) are unusually large protective effects that appear driven by the very low event rates in the Remdesivir arm (4 and 7 cases respectively) — these are reported verbatim as stated. The paper mentions figure 1 shows pain location distribution but no additional numeric data beyond Table 1 was present in figures.

summary: The P4O2 COVID-19 study is a multicenter prospective observational cohort study with a nested optional personalized lifestyle counseling intervention in 95 long COVID patients (aged 40-65) recruited from five Dutch post-COVID outpatient clinics at 3-6 months post-infection. This paper reports the study design and baseline characteristics only; no intervention outcome data are yet presented. At baseline (3-6 months post-COVID), the most prevalent persistent symptoms were respiratory (78.9%), neurological (68.4%), and fatigue (67.4%), with the majority (84.8%) showing pulmonary function or radiological abnormalities. Female sex (OR=0.25, p=0.002) and Delta vs. Beta variant infection (OR=3.54, p=0.014) were significantly associated with experiencing more than two symptom categories.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper is primarily a study design and baseline characteristics report — no intervention outcome data (pre-post or between-group comparisons) are presented. The nested intervention (personalized lifestyle counseling) uses self-selection rather than randomization, making it quasi-experimental. Arm-level N for intervention vs. control not reported at this stage. Baseline outcomes extracted are all cross-sectional at 3-6 months post-COVID. The note '610 have already participated in the second study visit' appears to be a typo in the original (likely '61'). TABLE A1 was truncated in the provided text. Pulmonary function test/radiological abnormality denominator: 14 without + 78 with = 92 (not 95), suggesting 3 missing values. Percent with abnormalities calculated as 78/92 = 84.8%.

summary: This non-randomized prospective study compared olfactory outcomes in 45 long COVID patients (anosmia/hyposmia ≥180 days post-infection) treated with um-PEA-LUT plus olfactory training for 3 months versus 40 MS patients on standard DMTs, using Sniffin' Sticks TDI scoring. At baseline, COVID-19 patients had markedly lower TDI scores (mean 12.6±5.1, mostly anosmic) versus MS patients (mean 33.5±4.9, mostly normosmic); after 3 months, 71.2% of COVID-19 patients recovered normal/borderline-normal olfaction (TDI 34.3±4.6), while MS patients showed stable olfactory function with no significant T0-T1 change. MS patients treated with IFN-beta 1a or glatiramer acetate had no olfactory dysfunction at follow-up (p=0.02 vs. other DMTs), suggesting a hypothesis-generating rationale for investigating DMT in refractory post-COVID olfactory loss.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is primarily a hypothesis-generating comparative study, not an RCT; the two arms have different underlying diseases making between-group effect sizes difficult to interpret clinically. Overall T1 TDI means for the full long COVID arm are not reported as a single summary statistic — they are split into 'recovered' (n=32, TDI 34.3±4.6) and 'non-recovered' (n=13, TDI 18.5±8.1) subgroups. MS arm T1 data are only reported for the 10 patients with residual olfactory impairment. Several figures (Figures 1–4) show estimation plots with additional data that could not be extracted numerically from the text. The arm_id=2 (MS) uses multiple different DMTs — heterogeneous comparator. Table rendering in the source appeared garbled (merged cells in DMT treatment table); patient counts per DMT were: Fingolimod 8, Teriflunomide 7, Ocrelizumab 4, Cladribine 3, Dimethylfumarate 6, IFN-beta 1a Avonex 1, Natalizumab 4, IFN-beta 1a Plegridy 3, Glatiramer Acetate 2 (total=38, slight discrepancy with n=40 analyzed — likely 2 counted differently or table formatting issue). EDSS correlation with identification score: Pearson p=0.006 (inverse correlation) — not extracted as separate outcome as no effect size reported.

summary: This retrospective cross-sectional pilot study from Romania assessed 117 long COVID patients at least 2 years after acute COVID-19 infection, comparing those with (n=49) versus without (n=68) imaging-confirmed pulmonary fibrosis. Patients with pulmonary fibrosis had significantly higher levels of inflammatory and prothrombotic markers (CRP p=0.048, neutrophils p=0.032, MPV p=0.038, D-dimers p=0.018, LDH p=0.039) and higher heart rate and QTc interval, but no significant differences were found in spirometry, body plethysmography, 6MWT distance, or SpO2. D-dimer levels were strongly negatively correlated with DLCO in the fibrosis group (r=-0.621) and ROC analysis demonstrated that elevated D-dimers predict impaired DLCO (AUC=0.772, p<0.001), suggesting D-dimers as a potential prognostic biomarker for long-term diffusion impairment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a cross-sectional observational study (not a treatment trial) comparing two groups defined by presence/absence of post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis. There is no intervention arm — both groups received supervised respiratory rehabilitation as part of routine care, but this was not the study focus. The study has no baseline (pre-infection) data and no longitudinal follow-up component — all measurements were taken at a single cross-sectional timepoint at least 2 years post-infection. Arms are labeled 'without pulmonary fibrosis' (arm_id=1) and 'with pulmonary fibrosis' (arm_id=2). Ferritin units not specified in table (likely ng/mL). The abstract mentions 'Hemoglobin: 14.70 vs 13.01 p=0.395' but also states 'p<0.05' for hemoglobin and platelets in the Discussion — the Discussion text appears to contain an error. Table 1 shows p=0.395 for hemoglobin and p=0.047 for platelets, which were used. Several additional outcomes reported in Table 1 (lipid panel, renal function, liver enzymes, hemoglobin, hematocrit, MCV, lymphocytes, eosinophils, glucose, HbA1c) were omitted from outcomes array to manage output size; all showed non-significant between-group differences.

summary: This retrospective single-center case series described 227 patients with neurological post-COVID-19 syndrome seen at an outpatient clinic in Croatia between May 2021 and June 2022. The most common presenting symptoms were headache (30%) and cognitive impairment (29%), followed by smell disorders, paresthesia, chronic fatigue, and dizziness. Of 109 patients (48%) who attended follow-up at a mean of 9.63 months, 53% had no change in symptoms and 45% had improvement or resolution; therapy was mostly symptomatic (vitamin supplements most common), and no controlled efficacy analysis was performed.

Follow-up outcomes are only categorical (no change / improved / worsened). Time since infection reported as 6.11 ± 11.15 weeks mean (converted to months: ~1.53 ± 2.79 months). summary: This single-center retrospective cross-sectional study characterized dysautonomia in 38 children and young adults (mean symptom duration >11 weeks) with post-acute sequelae after COVID-19 only (n=19), breakthrough COVID-19 after vaccination (n=12), or post-vaccination without infection (n=7), compared to 47 pre-pandemic healthy controls using active standing HRV testing. All three patient groups showed significantly elevated heart rates while standing (106, 103, and 115 bpm vs. 90 bpm controls), elevated sympathetic stress indices, significantly reduced pNN20 values (indicating vagal withdrawal), and elevated diastolic blood pressure compared to controls. Among the 38 patients, 8 met POTS criteria and 9 met inappropriate sinus tachycardia criteria, and were treated with omega-3 supplementation and/or pharmacotherapy (propranolol, ivabradine, or midodrine).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a cross-sectional observational study with no treatment intervention arm — it characterizes dysautonomia in pediatric long COVID, with 8 POTS and 9 inappropriate sinus tachycardia patients receiving treatment mentioned briefly but without pre/post outcome data. The study compares 3 patient exposure groups to historical healthy controls. p-values are only reported as thresholds (<0.05, <0.01, <0.001) via asterisk notation in Table 1; no exact p-values given. Supine HRV frequency domain data (Power HF, LF, VLF, Total, LF/HF supine) and standing frequency domain data (Power HF, LF, VLF, Total) were largely non-significant and are omitted from outcomes for brevity but are fully tabulated in Table 1 with all means and SDs. Notable: healthy control data were collected pre-pandemic, and the paper acknowledges lockdown may have affected HRV in controls as a limitation.

summary: This prospective case series from Chiba University Hospital (Japan) describes 9 long COVID patients (May-September 2021) treated with individualized Kampo (traditional Japanese herbal medicine) formulas — primarily tonic formulas (補剤) and Bupleuri radix-containing formulas (柴胡剤) — combined with lifestyle guidance including restriction of cold foods and drinks. summary: This retrospective single-arm case series evaluated bamlanivimab 700mg IV monotherapy in 39 high-risk COVID-19 outpatients in Umbria, Italy (March–April 2021), predominantly infected with the alpha variant. Despite early treatment (mean 4.2 days from symptom onset), the 30-day hospitalization rate was 20% (8/39) — far exceeding the 4% rate in the BLAZE-1 phase 2 trial — and 41% of patients developed new-onset non-restorative sleep at 30 days, with worsening asthenia (51% → 77%) and dyspnea (23% → 38.5%). No statistical comparison was possible due to the absence of a control group, and timing of treatment (early vs. late within 72 hours) did not significantly affect either hospitalization or viral clearance.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT a long COVID treatment study — it treats acute COVID-19 and documents post-acute sequelae at 30 days as a secondary observation. Symptom prevalence data (Figure 1) extracted from text descriptions since figure values were confirmed verbatim in text. The mean swab negativization time (16.64 days, SD 4.37) was calculated as weighted mean of early (16.58±4.10, n=15) and late (16.70±4.63, n=24) subgroups. Exact event counts for baseline symptoms derived from percentages: asthenia 51.3% of 39 = ~20 patients; dyspnea 23% of 39 = ~9; tachypnea 33.3% of 39 = ~13. Insomnia baseline assumed 0 as it is described as 'new onset' at 30 days. No between-group effects possible as no control arm. Hospitalization for COVID-related pathologies (15%) = 6 patients (4 pneumonia + 2 worsening of underlying diseases attributable to COVID). Vital signs data in Table 2 (temperature, HR, RR, BP, SpO2) not extracted as outcomes since they represent pre-infusion triage values only.

summary: This single-arm before-after study enrolled 82 COVID-19 survivors with deranged pulmonary function at AIIMS Bhopal, India, and examined the effect of an 8-week supervised selective yoga regime (pranayama, asanas, and chanting, 30 min twice daily) on spirometric parameters. summary: This single-arm retrospective cohort study examined the effects of a 14-day inpatient physiotherapy rehabilitation program in 30 post-COVID-19 patients (mean age 62.4 years) at a rehabilitation hospital in India. risk_of_bias.key_concern: Severe confounding by indication is the dominant concern: sicker patients were more likely to receive each drug class (especially steroids and IL-6 inhibitors), and although the authors adjusted for severity, hospitalization, ICU, and respiratory support, residual confounding cannot be excluded; additionally, symptom data were retrospectively collected for the majority of patients.

summary: This Italian national multicenter observational cohort study (n=1,534; mean age 60.3 years, 67% hospitalized) examined whether four drug classes administered during acute COVID-19 — antivirals (20.7%, mostly remdesivir), systemic corticosteroids (52.8%), IL-6 inhibitors (9.4%), and neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (3.9%) — reduced the subsequent burden of long COVID symptoms assessed at a mean of 338 days post-infection. In unadjusted analyses, several drug classes showed protective associations for individual symptoms, but none of these protective effects were maintained after multivariable adjustment for demographics, comorbidities, disease severity, hospitalization, respiratory support, and vaccination status. Notably, corticosteroid use was independently associated with increased odds of persistent dyspnea (AOR 1.56), joint pain (AOR 1.76), and muscle pain (AOR 2.02), and IL-6 inhibitor use was associated with a 3.4-fold higher risk of persistent cough, suggesting that confounding by indication substantially inflated apparent protective effects and that these drugs may worsen certain long COVID symptoms.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational cohort study, not an intervention trial. No per-arm means/SDs exist as outcomes are all binary symptom presence/absence. The study uses physician-decided treatment groups (exposure groups) rather than randomized arms; arm_id=5 (unexposed/no treatment in each drug class) serves as the implicit comparator but sample sizes for the unexposed group per drug class are not reported separately — only total exposed counts per class are reported. The adjusted OR for cough with IL-6 inhibitors: text states 1.84-6.41 but table shows 1.84-6.31; used table value 6.31 as primary. Symptoms reported by <20 cases (menstrual disorders, chilblains, delirium/hallucinations, fever) were excluded by the authors and are not extractable. Sleep disturbances, taste reduction, disorders of equilibrium/gait, hearing disturbances reported only with non-significant unadjusted ORs and no adjusted model run; these outcomes with only non-significant unadjusted associations are omitted from extracted outcomes to manage output size. Per-arm n for unexposed comparators not reported; total n=1534 with overlap possible as patients could have received multiple drug classes.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Residual confounding is the primary concern: nirmatrelvir/ritonavir prescription is heavily influenced by COVID-19 severity, vaccination status, and immunodeficiency severity, and unmeasured confounders (obesity, diabetes, smoking, mental health) were not adjusted for despite known association with long COVID risk.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Among n=597 patients with IEI only (excluding secondary/other immunodeficiency), nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with reduced long COVID risk (OR=0.28; 95% CI [0.07, 0.85], P=0.041).
Among n=2,340 vaccinated patients, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir remained associated with reduced long COVID risk (OR=0.54; 95% CI [0.30, 0.93], P=0.030).

Among nirmatrelvir/ritonavir-treated patients, females had higher long COVID risk than males (OR=3.03; 95% CI [1.18, 10.3], P=0.040); gender was not associated with long COVID risk in the overall cohort (OR=1.27; 95% CI [0.94, 1.74], P=0.123).
Sensitivity analysis including n=3,784 patients with COVID-19 diagnosed both before and after nirmatrelvir/ritonavir EUA showed consistent association (OR=0.42; 95% CI [0.30, 0.57], P<0.001).

summary: This retrospective EHR cohort study examined whether acute nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment reduces long COVID risk in 2,740 immunodeficient patients (597 with primary IEI, 2,143 with secondary/other immunodeficiency) at a single US center. Using inverse probability weighting to adjust for demographics, vaccination status, COVID-19 severity, lung disease, and immunodeficiency severity, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir use was significantly associated with a 57% reduction in long COVID risk (IPW-adjusted OR=0.43; 95% CI [0.24, 0.72], P=0.002). The protective effect persisted in subgroup analyses restricted to IEI-only patients and vaccinated patients, and in a sensitivity analysis including pre-EUA cases.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm long COVID event counts (numerators) are not reported; only overall cohort prevalence (2.7%, n=73/2740) and adjusted ORs are given. The unweighted n values in Table 1 represent the full cohort (n=1,678 no-nirmatrelvir, n=1,062 nirmatrelvir); IPW weighted values are effective sample sizes after weighting (2,744.4 and 2,716.8). Percent female was calculated as 100 minus percent male (arm1: 100-30.0=70.0%; arm2: 100-35.4=64.6%). Median time to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir initiation was 0 days (IQR: 0-0) from COVID-19 diagnosis. Race data appears inverted in Table 1 (90%+ labeled 'non-white' with high SMD resolved post-IPW; likely reflects the actual cohort composition). Follow-up duration is not explicitly defined. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir dose and treatment duration not specified.

summary: This observational cross-sectional study examined dyssomnia (sleep disturbance) in 126 outpatients in Belarus, comparing two post-COVID subgroups — coronaphobia (n=48, assessed H1 2022) and post-COVID syndrome (n=28, assessed H1 2023) — against a pre-pandemic neuropsychiatric comparison group (n=50) already receiving psychopharmacotherapy. Dyssomnia was present in 54.1% of the coronaphobia subgroup and 78.6% of the post-COVID syndrome subgroup (p=0.048), compared with only 4% in the comparison group that was receiving systematic psychopharmacotherapy. The post-COVID syndrome group showed a significant shift toward organic anxiety disorder over time and increasing cognitive dysfunction, suggesting progressive psychopathological deterioration; the authors recommend treating post-COVID dyssomnia with non-benzodiazepine anxiolytics, pro-cognitive antidepressants (vortioxetine, agomelatine), and cognitive-behavioral therapy.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an observational descriptive study, NOT a treatment trial — no intervention was administered to the post-COVID participants. The study describes the natural history and clinical characteristics of dyssomnia in post-COVID syndrome and compares against a pre-existing psychiatric comparison group receiving psychopharmacotherapy (creating a critical confound). The table reports mean ± SE (not SD) for GAD-7 and Vein scale, stratified by dyssomnia presence/absence within each subgroup. The paper is written primarily in Russian with an English abstract; values were extracted from both language sections. Percent female for arm 1 calculated as 37/48=77.1%; arm 2 as 23/28=82.1%; arm 3 as 36/50=72.0%. N with dyssomnia in arm 1 stated as 26 (coronaphobia) and arm 2 as 22 (post-COVID syndrome) totalling 48 across both arms — consistent with stated 48 total with dyssomnia in main group. Some syndromic prevalence data (asthenia 41% vs 23%, cognitive dysfunction 27% vs 8%) appear only in the text with non-significant p-values (p=0.368, p=0.119) and are not extracted as separate outcomes due to no per-arm Ns for these subgroups. Social perception ranking data (figures 1 and 2) are image-only and not extractable numerically.

summary: This small prospective observational cohort study (n=33) from Georgia examined biomarker changes in previously healthy individuals before (2019) and after (2023) SARS-CoV-2 infection, stratified by whether participants developed SIBO (n=18) or remained SIBO-free (n=15). Both groups showed significant reductions in blood melatonin and urinary melatonin sulfate post-COVID (p<0.01), but SIBO-positive participants had more pronounced melatonin depletion, markedly elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α, IL-12, IL-17), severe gut dysbiosis, and elevated tumor markers (CEA in 2/18; CA19.9 in 11/18), while SIBO-negative participants had none of these tumor marker elevations. No treatment intervention was evaluated; the study is purely observational and reports no numeric means or SDs for its primary biomarkers, severely limiting quantitative synthesis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical data quality issues: (1) No numeric values (means, SDs, units) are provided for melatonin or cytokine outcomes — only qualitative descriptions ('significant reduction', 'elevated beyond normal range') and p-values are stated. (2) Dysbiosis severity is reported categorically only (severe vs mild-to-moderate) with no quantitative microbial diversity metrics. (3) The paper is purely observational with no treatment intervention — it describes SIBO as a post-COVID complication, not a treatment study; its inclusion in this pipeline may warrant reconsideration. (4) Figures 1 and 2 appear to contain graphical data but no numeric values are extractable from the text. (5) The correlation coefficient r=-0.68 (p<0.01) between melatonin and cytokines and r=0.72 (p<0.001) between cytokines and dysbiosis are reported, but without per-arm numeric data these cannot anchor effect estimates. (6) The paper is published in what appears to be a low-credibility journal (Journal of Cancer Research, ISSN 2578-3726, Volume 2 Issue 1) and lacks standard reporting of units, confidence intervals, or adjusted analyses. (7) Tumor marker data in figures only — bar chart differences visible but no exact values extractable from text. (8) Follow-up duration calculated as approximately 4 years (2019 to 2023) = ~208 weeks.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Both groups responded similarly in first 5 days; from day 5 onward healthy patients improved faster than MS patients. Cox HR=1.003 (p=0.988), not statistically significant.

summary: This uncontrolled single-arm prospective observational study enrolled 183 adults with acute PCR-confirmed COVID-19 (Feb 2020–Jun 2022) from multiple countries, and evaluated a multi-component protocol including probiotics, vitamins D/C/E, zinc, selenium, glutathione, N-acetylcysteine, quercetin, and a low-carbohydrate diet, with pain killers as the only permitted medication. COVID symptom scores decreased significantly from a mean of 7.66 (SD 1.26) at baseline to 6.39 (SD 1.12) at 72 hours (p<0.005), with a regression-modeled daily reduction of 0.97 score points (R²=0.97, p<0.0001); overall median recovery was 13 days, shorter than historical comparators of 12–21 days. The study had no control group and was primarily aimed at preventing long COVID rather than treating it; the authors reported no long-term post-COVID complications at 6-month follow-up, but this claim cannot be evaluated without a comparator group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. IMPORTANT CLASSIFICATION NOTE: This is NOT a long COVID treatment study — it is an acute COVID-19 management study aimed at PREVENTING long COVID. Participants had active, not post-acute, COVID-19 infection. The paper should potentially be excluded from a long COVID treatment meta-analysis. The study lacks a control group; all subgroup comparisons (healthy vs MS, GS vs LRS, severity groups) are internal subgroups of the single intervention cohort, not separate arms. Baseline COVID score for mild (mean=5.0, SD=0.0) and moderate (mean=6.63, SD=0.52) and severe (mean=8.48, SD=0.67) groups extracted from Table 1. Some data are only in figures (daily COVID score trajectories by subgroup, Kaplan-Meier curves) — only summary statistics from tables and text were extractable. The Cox regression HR for age is per-year (HR=0.963, p<0.001, 95% CI 0.944–0.983), not per age group. Ethics approval was explicitly not obtained for this study.

summary: This single-arm prospective observational cohort study described sequelae at one month after hospital discharge in 104 ICU survivors of severe bilateral SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia at a Spanish tertiary hospital, assessed through a structured multidisciplinary outpatient programme. The most prevalent sequelae were fatigue (75.96%), dyspnoea (64.4%), and oxygen dependency at discharge (37.5%), with the MoCA indicating mild cognitive impairment (mean 21.35, SD 9.93) and the EQ-5D VAS averaging 60.6 points (SD 20.2). With no control group and no pre-post statistical comparisons, the study is descriptive only, but notably oxygen dependency fell from 37.5% at discharge to 8.7% at six months, and the FACIT-F at six months showed 53.8% of patients reporting no fatigue.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm descriptive cohort — no control group, no between-group effects extractable. No primary outcome was pre-specified; all outcomes are descriptive cross-sectional measurements at first clinic visit (~1 month post-discharge). FACIT-F data were collected at 6-month phone follow-up but only categorical proportions reported (no mean/SD). MoCA was only conducted on 47 of 104 patients (reason: not stated). Spirometry and MIP/MEP were only conducted in the subset of 66–83 patients with respiratory concerns. Table 4 MIP/MEP n for women stated as 17 in spirometry row context; the table header says n=66 for spirometry but MIP/MEP in women row shows n=17 (inferred as female subgroup of the 66). BCM values in Table 2 report both BCM (kg) and BCMI (kg) for men and women separately — BCM men: 28.43 (6.71), BCM women: 21.30 (11.97); BCMI men: 9.59 (2.54), BCMI women: 9.54 (6.51). The text states active BCMI of 9.6 kg in men and 9.5 kg in women. Fatigue table rows in Table 2 appear to have a formatting irregularity: 'Without aid 85 (81.73) / Walking stick/frame 16 (15.38) / Wheelchair 79 (75.96)' and 'Fatigue Total 3 (2.88) / Mild effort 10 (9.62) / Moderate effort 50 (48.08) / Great effort 19 (18.27)' — the wheelchair figure 79 (75.96%) appears to refer to fatigue total, not wheelchair users (2 patients used wheelchair per text). Extracted per text narrative rather than table where ambiguous. EQ-5D dimension tables have incomplete rows for mobility (only 'No problems' reported; moderate/severe not shown in table). No adverse events of the rehabilitation programme were reported.

summary: This single-arm prospective observational study enrolled 48 COVID-19 patients discharged from a tertiary care hospital in India with persistent dyspnea on exertion and followed them for 60 days while they underwent pulmonary rehabilitation (respiratory exercises, incentive spirometry, postural drainage). All three primary outcomes improved significantly from discharge (D0) to day 60 (D60): mMRC score decreased from 2.38 to 0.94, modified Borg from 3.15 to 0.94, and SGRQ total from 45.36 to 19.22 (all p<0.001 by paired t-test). Higher BMI, older age, longer hospital stay, and oxygen requirement during hospitalization were associated with worse initial scores; BMI was the strongest predictor of SGRQ improvement in multivariate analysis. The study lacked a control group, so the relative contributions of rehabilitation versus natural recovery cannot be determined.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm before-after study; no control group. Change SD not reported for within-group changes (only mean change and paired t-test t-value/p-value provided). Figure 3 shows subgroup data for oxygen receivers vs. non-receivers but no numeric values extractable from text for those subgroups. Multivariate regression tables report beta coefficients and effect sizes for numerous interaction variables but no adjusted outcome means. Paper states 'p<0.001' for all primary outcomes — p_value_exact set to false. The 60-day follow-up is approximately 8.57 weeks (60/7).

summary: This retrospective observational study compared blood laboratory values during convalescence in 143 COVID-19 discharged patients who received traditional Chinese medicine (herbal decoctions including Shen ling bai zhu san and Xiao chai hu tang) versus 425 who did not, at a single fixed-point isolation hospital in Shenzhen, China. The TCM group showed statistically significantly lower WBC, monocyte, IL-6, procalcitonin, GGT, and LDH levels, alongside higher platelet count, RBC, hemoglobin, MCHC, hematocrit, albumin, prealbumin, ApoB, and LDL-C compared to the non-treatment group. However, the study is cross-sectional with self-selected treatment allocation, no baseline comparisons, and no adjustment for confounders, making causal inference impossible.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a cross-sectional retrospective study, not a longitudinal before-after design — all values are single time-point endpoint comparisons during convalescence, not change-from-baseline. Sample sizes are inconsistent in the paper: the methods describe 191 TCM recipients with 158 having blood tests, but tables show n=143 for TCM and n=425 for non-treatment; the non-treatment n=425 substantially exceeds the 291 clinically examined, suggesting some patients were counted multiple blood draw visits or the 291 figure refers to a different subset. summary: This retrospective population-based cohort study of 188,532 Singaporeans aged ≥60 years with SARS-CoV-2 infection examined whether early outpatient nirmatrelvir/ritonavir treatment (n=10,905) reduced risk of postacute sequelae compared to untreated controls (n=177,627), using overlap-weighted competing-risks regression on national registry and claims data. No statistically significant reduction in any prespecified postacute outcome was observed at 31–180 days post-infection, including composite sequelae (aHR 1.06; 95% CI 0.94–1.19), MACE (aHR 0.80; 0.61–1.06), cardiovascular, neurological, respiratory, or autoimmune complications, or any symptom-based sequelae (aHR 0.97; 0.80–1.18). The authors attribute the null finding largely to a highly vaccinated/boosted cohort (95% with ≥3 doses) and a very low hospitalization rate (<2%), which may have left little additional benefit for antivirals to confer.

summary: This nationwide retrospective propensity-score-matched cohort study in South Korea examined whether oral antiviral treatment (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or molnupiravir) during acute COVID-19 reduces the risk of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) in adults aged ≥60 years diagnosed during the 2022 Omicron wave. Among 957,036 matched pairs for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and 243,360 matched pairs for molnupiravir, both antivirals were significantly associated with reduced incidence of multiple PASC outcomes (cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, neurological, gastrointestinal, and metabolic) between 30 and 120 days post-diagnosis, with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir showing broader and larger risk reductions (e.g., aHR 0.57 for new dialysis) compared to molnupiravir.

summary: This is a systematic review by the Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) of Ireland that identified and appraised 24 clinical guidelines and 2 models of care for the diagnosis and management of long COVID published internationally up to September 2022. summary: This observational study from St. Petersburg tested 129 Long COVID patients for markers of HIV, hepatitis B (HBV), and hepatitis C (HCV) to assess whether these co-infections are overrepresented in people with post-COVID syndrome. HIV was detected in 6.97% of participants (9/129), all on antiretroviral therapy — a notably high proportion compared to the general population, consistent with prior evidence that HIV infection roughly doubles the odds of developing Long COVID (OR ~2.2). Active HCV infection (RNA-positive) was found in 1.55% of patients, higher than population background rates, raising questions about a possible role for HCV in Long COVID pathogenesis. HBV markers were not overrepresented and showed no clear association with Long COVID in this sample, though the small cohort limits firm conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a serological/virological prevalence screening study, not a treatment trial or intervention study. No comparison arm. Single cross-sectional assessment of blood markers in established long COVID patients. Key quantitative data: sample size (n=129), proportions with 95% CIs reported for all major markers. Severity distribution and HIV subgroup data extracted from results section. Study does not report adverse events as not applicable to screening protocol. No follow-up duration (cross-sectional design). Female predominance (102/129, 79.07%) and mean age 38.12 years with range 19–60. Russian-language publication with English abstract; full text translated/bilingual provided.

trial_rating.result_basis: HIV prevalence was 6.97% (9/129) in Long COVID patients vs general population background; HCV RNA detected in 1.55% (2/129); no formal statistical comparison to controls was conducted and no p-values or confidence intervals for group differences are reported.

summary: This randomized controlled trial tested a combined rehabilitation program — using the DEVIRTA virtual reality biofeedback system plus halotherapy (salt therapy) — against standard rehabilitation (physiotherapy, massage, psychological correction) in 65 Long COVID patients (average age 47.5 years) at an outpatient clinic in Kazan, Russia. The primary finding was a 63% reduction in depression/anxiety symptoms on the HADS scale in the biofeedback group versus a non-significant 11.7% increase in the control group (p=0.0019), alongside a 55.6% reduction in dyspnea on the mMRC scale (p<0.001) and a 23.1% improvement in EQ-5D quality of life scores (p=0.0019). Fatigue (MFI-20) also fell by 43.2% in the intervention group (p<0.001). The study has no blinding and compares an active multi-component intervention against a different active comparator, making it difficult to isolate which component drove the effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Study conducted in Russian with English translation provided. Paper reports results as percentage reductions/improvements and provides both pre- and post-intervention means with SDs, allowing calculation of effect sizes. Oxygen saturation reported as 98.7±0.2% in all participants at baseline (within normal range). Total rehabilitation course duration stated as 10 sessions daily for DEVIRTA (30 min each) and halotherapy (40-45 min each), estimated as 2-week duration. Statistical analysis used Wilcoxon rank-sum test for non-parametric comparisons. Authors note this is an exploratory/descriptive study with relatively small sample. No adverse events section found in the paper. Baseline balance between groups not reported (includes only overall mean age 47.5±4.9). Post-hoc percentage improvements calculated from means provided in results.

trial_rating.result_basis: HADS anxiety/depression score fell from 9.2 to 3.4 (63% reduction, p=0.0019) in the intervention group vs a non-significant increase in controls; mMRC dyspnea reduced by 55.6% (p<0.001).

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: neutralizing antibody titer and viral load protection
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: TTR showed higher neutralizing antibody levels (1:1280 high-dose, 1:320 low-dose) compared to NNR and NTR after booster immunization. All three vaccines provided comparable protection against BA.2 challenge with no significant differences in viral load reduction between vaccine types.

Low-dose (1 μg) groups showed higher numbers of IFNγ and IL-4 spots than high-dose (10 μg) groups, indicating that 1 μg of recombinant vaccine was sufficient to induce high levels of T cell responses.

subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: clinical symptoms and viral load after challenge
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: All animal models showed protection with vaccinated groups maintaining normal behavior and body weight. Lung viral loads were significantly reduced in all vaccinated groups compared to controls across species.

summary: This preclinical study tested three recombinant RBD-based subunit vaccines (NNR, TTR, and NTR) incorporating high-frequency SARS-CoV-2 mutation sites (K417N/T, L452R, T478K, E484K, N501Y) in BALB/c mice and golden hamsters, not in human Long COVID patients. All three vaccines significantly reduced lung viral load after SARS-CoV-2 BA.2 challenge compared to controls, with the TTR formulation showing the highest neutralizing antibody titers (up to 1:1280 after booster) and best overall immunogenicity. The paper is not a Long COVID clinical trial; it is an animal immunogenicity and challenge-protection study with no human participants and no Long COVID outcomes measured.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports a preclinical vaccine immunogenicity and efficacy study in animal models (BALB/c mice and golden hamsters), not a Long COVID treatment study. It does not involve Long COVID patients or treatments for Long COVID. The study design uses 6-8 animal groups (120 young mice, 60 aged mice, 40 hamsters) with intramuscular immunization followed by SARS-CoV-2 BA.2 challenge. Outcome data are largely presented in figures (Figures 2-8) rather than in numerical tables; exact per-arm means and SDs are not provided in the text for most outcomes. Antibody titers are reported as dilution ratios (e.g., 1:1024000, 1:1280). ELISpot and Luminex cytokine data are shown graphically. Viral load and histology results are described qualitatively or shown in figures. Flow cytometry data are presented in plots without numeric summaries. Statistical comparisons are noted (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001, p<0.0001 or ns) but individual p-values are not consistently reported per outcome. The paper emphasizes that this is a vaccine platform study with preclinical development implications, not a clinical trial or Long COVID-specific research. No adverse event data are formally reported; animal welfare monitoring showed no significant clinical adverse events in vaccinated groups.

trial_rating.result_basis: TTR high-dose group reached neutralizing antibody titers of 1:1280 post-booster vs. no significant response in controls; lung viral load significantly decreased in all vaccinated groups vs. controls (p<0.05 by ANOVA), but no human data or Long COVID endpoints reported.
